008afac0-e38b-550a-a0d2-9a4b088b3083.name: Bowl with inscription
008afac0-e38b-550a-a0d2-9a4b088b3083.short_description: A ceramic bowl covered with a white slip and transparent glaze. The sole decoration on a white background is an Arabic inscription in black and a stylized flower in the centre. The inscription is benedictory in the *kufic* script: “Blessings and joy to the owner”. The bowl belongs to a type of pottery typical of the Samanid workshops in eastern Iran. The characteristic inscriptions usually include proverbs or wishes, and the reader is invited to rotate the object to read them.
keywords: Bowl; Kufic; Samanid; Earthenware; calligraphy

019b1d84-e6f3-5e53-a049-f7191924c562.name: Ottoman wooden spoons
019b1d84-e6f3-5e53-a049-f7191924c562.short_description: The Kunstkammer at Ambras contains a number of wooden Ottoman spoons. One such spoon is recorded in the Kunstkammer at Munich as early as AD 1596, suggesting that the ones at Ambras also date from the 16th century, despite only being listed on a later inventory. The spoons feature floral motifs such as tulips, carnations and hyacinths in gold paint. Their backs and part of the handles are decorated with wave-band motifs.

01c7dad2-5f26-5c46-9416-87c4c613cb64.name: Table and two chairs (*Peškuns*)
01c7dad2-5f26-5c46-9416-87c4c613cb64.description:
Interested in woodcut and its application on both profane and sacral objects, artist Branko Šotra (1906–1960) created several ensembles of *peškuns* during the 1930s. In interwar Yugoslavia, *peškun* (Tr. *peşkun*), a richly decorated (with carving, mother-of-pearl, and other) circular or polygonal low table/chair of Oriental origin, was an indispensable element of the so-called *Bosnian room* that was popular in homes in Belgrade, as an emulation of the royal family’s furnishings. They were made and decorated by skilled craftsmen, the most appreciated being those from Konjic.  
However, Šotra combined the traditional form of the *peškun* with the motifs he was personally interested in and treated them using the contemporary language of Art Deco. On the top hexagonal table and chair tops of the *peškuns*, he carved relief scenes of rural life, while the lower, supporting, parts with ogee arches are decorated with geometric ornaments, motifs of grain ears, flowers, affronted doves and parrots. On the tabletop, there is a representation of a kitchen where a mother is nursing a child, a father is sitting and smoking next to the table with a *fildžan* – a Turkish coffee cup (Tr. *kahve fıncanı*) – and a *džezva* – coffee pot (Tr. *cezve*) – while a cat is drinking milk from a bowl. On the chair-tops are depictions of a shepherdess spinning wool in a meadow under a tree, surrounded by sheep and a stack of hay, and, on another chair, a woman reaping grain, a tree, a water gourd, and, in the background, a road leading to the village.  
The introduction of contemporary features into tradition was not Šotra’s exclusive approach. As a contributor to the journal *Primenjena umetnost* (*The Applied Art*), he published, in 1937, a pattern and instruction for the woodcuts for peškun, with geometric and floral ornaments inspired by folk art. After graduating from The Royal Art School in Belgrade in 1929, Branko Šotra taught drawing in Sarajevo, Loznica, and Vršac, and woodcut in Ohrid. At the same time, he dealt with painting, fresco painting, icon painting, and woodcarving. After World War II, he dedicated himself to the art of printing and pedagogical work. He served as the rector and professor at The Academy of Applied Arts from 1948 to 1956.

01c7dad2-5f26-5c46-9416-87c4c613cb64.author: Bojana Popović
keywords: peškun; stool; side table; carving; Ottoman Balkans; Yugoslavia
materials: Beechwood; carving, dark varnish, matte polish

021c9362-ae4c-5a9d-94f5-0755ebb9c1cc.name: Mevlevi Kitchen (*Matbah-ı Şerif*)
021c9362-ae4c-5a9d-94f5-0755ebb9c1cc.description: The term *somat* (feast table) was used to describe the table where Mevlevis ate. Spoons would be placed face down to indicate the dervishes’ gratitude and to prevent the contents from being seen. A pinch of salt was placed in front of everyone. When the food had been cooked, Kazancı Dede would bring the cauldron to the table and open its lid. After reciting a prayer, those present would invoke the name of Allah Hu.
021c9362-ae4c-5a9d-94f5-0755ebb9c1cc.bibliography: Bakırcı, Naci, *Konya Mevlana Müzesi*, Istanbul: BKG Yayinlari, 2010.

02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.name: Bowl (*Sakızlık*)
02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.short_description: From historical sources, we learn that vessels made of gold and silver were widely used in the Ottoman palace. Starting from the end of the 18th century, Baroque and Rococo forms of Western style replaced classical Ottoman designs. We find roses in relief, the Ottoman coat-of-arms, architectural compositions, casted flowers, birds and animals on a multitude of the vessels of the era. This cylindrical cup with pedestal foot and cupola-like hinged lid was made of vermeil silver. On the body of the cup we see a floral pattern and hanging lambs placed alternatingly. Flowers, buds and leaves are made from rubies and diamonds nailed into gold and silver contours. On the lid – instead of lamb motif on the body – a chalice was used. The foot of the chalice is in the form of a cherub from which a bundle of rays projects.
02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.holder: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum
keywords: minor arts, applied arts, silver objects

02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.name: The Coffee Shop of Cairo
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.short_description: This colourful print depicts a typical 19th century coffeeshop in Cairo. An exclusively male domain, its design was characterised by an open front and wide benches for seating, to allow for easy congregation and the gathering of friends and acquainances. Not only in Cairo, which had over a thousands coffeehouses in Roberts's time, but all over the Middle East, coffeehouses were important social hubs for the exchange of news, entertainment, smoking (customers brought their own pipes and waterpipes) and - not rarely - political dissent. Musicians and storytellers often enhanced the experience further. In this image, the proprietor or an employee of the cafe can be seen serving a beverage in the centre. Interestingly, both the ewer and the large copper cup he uses are of a type usually associated with water, not coffee. Perhaps Roberts introduced these items for artistic effect.

03a41b10-16ab-52d7-8fef-d551e00d69c7.name: Vase (three items)
03a41b10-16ab-52d7-8fef-d551e00d69c7.description:
These massive gold and silver damascened engraved steel vases from 19th century Qajar-era Iran showcase exquisite craftsmanship and elaborate design. They feature a distinct shape, characterised by a trumpet foot, bulbous body, and decorative handles resembling curling arabesques.  
The surface of these metalworks is adorned with intricately etched and damascened decorations depicting scenes probably inspired by the *Shahnameh* (*The Book of Kings*). These scenes primarily portray royal garden parties, known as *bazm* or feast, where music, dance and merrymaking prevail. This decorative tradition reflects Persian kingly protocol, emphasising the concepts of *bazm* (feast) and *razm* (fight). *Bazm* is illustrated with joyful gatherings in royal gardens, while *razm* is depicted through scenes of combat and hunting.  
With their intricate designs and symbolic motifs, these metalworks provide insight into the rich cultural legacy of Qajar Iran in the 19th century. They serve also as ceremonial items used in dining and festive gatherings, enhancing their significance in depicting the customs and practices of the time. The vases are crafted using damascening, an ancient metalworking technique that involves inlaying gold and silver onto hard metal surfaces. The intricate designs are engraved in the steel surface, and then gold and silver are carefully hammered into these grooves. This meticulous process resulted in the detailed decorations on the vases, highlighting the skill and artistry of Qajar-era Iranian craftsmen.

065ee648-ada2-516d-a7cd-4adf36e94026.name: *Habb* water jar
065ee648-ada2-516d-a7cd-4adf36e94026.description: This large water jar (*habb*) combines a utilitarian function with ostentatious decoration. It occupied a place of honour in the domestic space. Water was drawn from it with a jug or pitcher as needed for daily living. The surface is adorned with stylised female figures that reflect the persistence, through millennia and civilisations, of the mother goddess.

06945f29-b3f5-5c43-b860-5d861b0794e2.name: al-Ghuta ash-Sharqiyya
06945f29-b3f5-5c43-b860-5d861b0794e2.description: Apricot paste is made from an apricot very specific to the Damascus oasis, the so-called *klabi*, a small, very juicy apricot with a bitter pit that grows on large trees with abundant foliage. Klabi apricots notably were found in some of the villages of Eastern Ghouta, south of the Barada valley. Klabi is characterised by its rapid ripening, with the fruit falling off as soon as it is ripe. As a result, the fruit had to be picked up from the ground day after day. Workshops for making *Qamr ad-Din* are always set up in sunny open fields in an oasis.

0785d4ab-66cd-56c3-9f20-d7b522279ae6.name: Black Cauldron
0785d4ab-66cd-56c3-9f20-d7b522279ae6.description:
The Black Cauldron, which is considered sacred by Bektashi devotees and the Janissary Corps, is situated on the large hearth at the axis of the entrance door. The Black Cauldron was constructed by fusing six substantial pieces of forged copper. Four distinct handles, two large and two small, are positioned on the exterior of the vessel. To grieve the martyrdom of Hz. Hussein – son of Hz. Ali, grandson of Hz. Muhammad – and his relatives in Karbala on Friday, 10 Muharram of the 61st year of the Hijra, Alevi-Bektashis observed a period of mourning. This was followed by a fast of mourning on the days of 1–12 Muharram, during which time the pain of those who were martyred was shared and the descendants of Ehlibeyt were commemorated. This practice continues today.  
In observance of the 10 Muharram, the Alevi-Bektashis engage in a water fast, which concludes at noon on the 10th day. The 10th day of Muharram is commemorated as Ashura, a period of solemn reflection and mourning. Ashura is observed as an important value that ensures social solidarity and unity. It is served to guests, neighbours and the needy.  
During the period when the Külliye was operating as a lodge, the Ashura (dessert)in question was cooked and distributed in the Black Cauldron Currently, people oberve this ritual in their homes and concludes with a visit to the Külliye.

0801264d-8475-5c87-a800-17b6d0cc190e.name: The drawings of Janissary clothes from The Album of Mecmua-i Tesavir-i Osmaniye (The collection of Ottoman Pictures)
0801264d-8475-5c87-a800-17b6d0cc190e.short_description: Arif Mehmed Pasha is considered one of the leaders of the western style of painting in Turkey. He developed a talent for drawing and produced a series of pictures detailing the clothes Ottoman state officials wore. He prepared these pictures under the name *Mecmua-i Tesavir-i Osmaniyye*. Although his work was supposed to come out in 12 volumes, only one volume was actually published in French in Paris in 1863 and in Turkish the same year. The other 11 volumes have been lost. The published volume is considered to be the first illustrated book in Turkey. What is amazing is the praise heaped onto Arif Mehmed Pasha for his portraits, the harmony of their colours and tones, the maturity of attitude and delicate detail, the artist’s control over his pen and watercolours. The clothing reflects the time when the Janissaries were still on the scene (before 1826 when the corps was disbanded).
0801264d-8475-5c87-a800-17b6d0cc190e.holder: Military Museum and Cultural Centre Command
keywords: Ottoman Clothes; Janissary Clothes

08735bbc-752f-5c86-962d-667f390393f6.name: Nails
08735bbc-752f-5c86-962d-667f390393f6.short_description:
These tools represent *baraka* (blessings) or *barkati* nails made of iron and adorned with fine inscriptions. Originating in Oman, talismanic qualities were attributed to the nails to protect property or vehicles.  
  
When constructing a home, furniture or vehicles such as dhows (boats), these blessed nails are hammered into the wood for additional support and protection. Islamic prayers in *naskh* calligraphy instil hidden blessings for oneself or on behalf of someone else for good fortune.  
  
Small ordinary objects like nails are transformed into talismans to dispel demons (*jinn*), evil and accidents on long journeys. As iron is a precious material in Islam, the nails gain further protective properties.

08c11707-3223-5e4f-98b6-ce06bf917293.name: *Zafraan* (Saffron)
08c11707-3223-5e4f-98b6-ce06bf917293.description:
*Zafraan* (Saffron) used to flavour coffee.  
Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving *dallah* referred to as a *mezallah*, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the mezallah with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.

08c11707-3223-5e4f-98b6-ce06bf917293.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: saffron; coffee

0c64afe8-ef31-5013-ab4c-0e70f49a6799.name: Traditional blue ceramic plate from Fez
0c64afe8-ef31-5013-ab4c-0e70f49a6799.description: This ceramic dish is a remarkable example of craftsmanship in Fez, a Moroccan city renowned for its pottery production since the Middle Ages. The decoration is dominated by a circular rosette in the shape of a six-petaled flower, an emblematic motif of Islamic art combining geometry and symbolism. The centre is decorated with an interlaced six-pointed star (Star of David), symbol of infinity and universal harmony. The petals, finely filled with small blue dots on an off-white background, add texture and depth. Secondary floral motifs occupy the spaces between the petals, accentuating the decorative richness of the piece. The design is framed by a thick cobalt blue border, lending the work an elegance and striking visual contrast. This technique, which combines meticulous painting under a protective glaze, testifies to the mastery of its artisans. After being painted, the dish was baked at a high temperature to fix the colours and obtain the glossy finish characteristic of Fez ceramics.
0c64afe8-ef31-5013-ab4c-0e70f49a6799.dates: Hegira mid of 13th century / beginning of the 14th century – AD end of 19th century

0c8d4c10-e0c7-58fa-9a01-827cb349e0f8.name: Perfume flask
0c8d4c10-e0c7-58fa-9a01-827cb349e0f8.description:
This type of bottle with a long and narrow neck, also called *qumqum*, was used to disperse perfumed waters – orange blossom, rose water – on the hands and faces of guests: a gesture of hospitality also intended to expel evil forces from the house.  
On the surface of the pear-shaped body, cypress and bouquets of leaves alternate, and flowers emerge from a vase flanked by two seals of Solomon.

0dd50fe0-14f2-5280-8a34-a024885bc7dc.name: Bedouin women cooking for a festival at Rusafa
0dd50fe0-14f2-5280-8a34-a024885bc7dc.description:
The tradition of cooking mutton in huge copper pots (*gidr*) on an open fire is still alive, although aluminium pots are available and weigh less. Surprisingly, these cooking pots do not come with lids, but serving plates (*siniyyat sufra*) are used instead. Food can be served directly on these while they are still hot. A big spoon (*jabjir*) is used to stir and distribute the meat and broth onto huge plates. The fatty mutton meat is cooked in broth that has been enriched with spices such as coriander, cumin, pepper and hot paprika.  
A copper pot is passed down from one generation to another, as it represents the generosity of ancestors. From the size of the pot one can imagine the number of people who were fed from it.

0e671219-31d0-5818-8e46-222c869924d9.name: al-Ghuta ash-Sharqiyya
0e671219-31d0-5818-8e46-222c869924d9.description: After being weighed, sorted and washed, then treated with sulphur, apricots are placed on a large cement platform sheltered from the sun. Exposing the apricots to sulphur vapour before pressing is a major innovation in the process. After some trial and error, sulphurisation is now a well-established part of the process; although the main argument in favour of it is commercial, the operation has the essential advantage of purifying or sterilising the fruit, therefore allowing better preservation of the *Qamr ad-Din*. A suction pump on the platform is used to load the press. A worker in boots enters the platform and pushes the apricots towards the mouth of the suction pump with a wooden shovel.

0e898325-2ca7-55a3-9b21-31bfc911229e.description: Tin-plated copper casket for transporting food on journeys and campaigns. The whole surface is decorated with intricated designs, inscriptions and medallion with geometric motifs.

0ec7070c-4723-5d21-8d20-fb151e3e884f.name: Coffee pots (*dallah*)
0ec7070c-4723-5d21-8d20-fb151e3e884f.description: With its slender waist, graceful handle and elegant spout, this coffee pot (or *dallah*) is an exquisite example of Nazwa silversmithing. The silver souq in Nazwa is famed for its superb wares; smiths tend to work alongside jewellers and khanjar-makers to produce particularly fine goods. This *dallah* features a combination of arabesque and geometric designs, while the inscription at the bottom reads, in Arabic, "K. R. 21/6/1974" – a reference to its maker, Khalfan bin Rashid al-Sabahi, and its date of completion.

0f423815-f3be-51a7-ab13-23fc5d185723.name: Takiyya al-Sulaymaniyya
0f423815-f3be-51a7-ab13-23fc5d185723.description:
Together with a *madrasa*, the Takiyya al-Sulaymaniyya was erected on the meadow belonging to a former Zangid parade ground, the Maydan al-Akhdar, located about 800 m west of the Old City of Damascus on the southern shore of the Barada River. It is the spot where once the Qasr al-Ablaq, the palace belonging to Sultan Baybars (r. AH 658–75 / AD 1260–77) stood, and where Timur resided during his attack on Damascus. The *takiyya* functioned as an inn for the accommodation of pilgrims where food was served, gratis.  
The whole complex was surrounded by an enclosure wall; to the west of the enclosure there was a vast area that was used as a tent encampment for pilgrims. From the main entrance on the east side, the visitor steps into the large courtyard where a central rectangular pool served as a meeting place. The mosque, preceded by a double portico, is by its twin minarets announced as a royal foundation. A row of cells is placed along either side of the courtyard while opposite the mosque is the *imaret* flanked by two long refectories along the east and west walls, each covered with 14 domes. Between them a large kitchen is preceded by a portico, the purpose of which may have been to offer shade to the pilgrims queuing for food, but which also gives a sort of splendour to the kitchen area. On each side of the kitchen, there are two twin-domed smaller rooms, which may have served as stores or dining chambers for the leaders of the *Hajj*. The enclosure to the north of the *imaret* is provided with a small entrance used by servants and to take in deliveries.  
Immediately after the Ottoman conquest and up until the AH mid-10th / AD mid-16th century, the local – and likewise modest – building activity continued in a traditional way indicating a tolerant takeover of power. This is manifested not only by the fact that Mamluk governors were re-instated to office, but also by the employment of Damascene master architect, Shihab al-Din Ahmad ibn al-Attar who, for example, was employed by Sultan Selim I for the renewal of the funeral mosque of the renowned Sufi, Ibn Arabi in Salihiyya. Although the *takiyya* was planned by the Turkish master architect of the Sultan, Sinan (AH 895–996 / AD 1490–1588), he did not supervise the work personally but delegated much of it to a local subordinate. Native workmen were consulted, leaving their fingerprints on details of the décor such as the horizontal rows of alternating dark-and-light stone walls (*ablaq*). The tiles also show the characteristics of locally produced Damascene tiles, referring to the Turkish production of Iznik, but paler in colour.  
The complex's location at a prominent place amidst the long-distance trade and pilgrimage routes made it popular stop-off point for pilgrims from all over the Ottoman Empire and beyond, who were accommodated before continuing to the Holy places in the Arabian Peninsula. Its characteristically Ottoman style, with porticoes and dominant use of cupolas and pencil-shaped minarets make it a clear display of Ottoman supremacy.
0f423815-f3be-51a7-ab13-23fc5d185723.short_description: Several hundred metres before the city gates, one of the early Ottoman sultans, Sulayman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66), built a hospice for pilgrims who gathered in Damascus from all over the empire before turning south towards Mecca. The complex comprises a mosque, a kitchen, dormitories and a *madrasa*. For the first time, Ottoman features such as multiple cupolas and pencil-shaped minarets appear in Damascus, doubtless meant as architectural symbols of Ottoman supremacy. This is the only building in Bilad al-Sham (Greater Syria) designed by the celebrated Turkish architect Sinan.
0f423815-f3be-51a7-ab13-23fc5d185723.method_for_datation: Several Arabic sources discuss the building activities of Sultan Suleyman (see Rihawi, 1957, p.132) for a detailed list of these sources.

109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.name: Drum
109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.short_description: Small round drum, pointed on the bottom, covered on the top with leather, and fastened with a linen rope. It was played with a wooden stick to create special sounds of music, and it was used during the Muslim holy month of Ramadan to wake up people to eat (*suhur*) before sunrise. Some people used to volunteer to go around before dawn to wake people up during Holy Ramadan, reflecting community spirit.

115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.name: Stone blazon.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.description:
In the Mamluk period, heraldry played an important role and was widely used on architecture, metalwork, textiles, glass and pottery. Its use was strictly the reserve of sultans and particularly of the officers who were awarded individual blazons, each according to their rank. While the early Bahri Mamluks used blazons which represented a distinct office held by an individual, the later Burji Mamluks combined several heraldic emblems which were commonly shared by a corps of *amirs* who served a distinct master.  
The stone roundel with the tripartite blazon from the Aleppo Museum represents a widely used composition from the late Mamluk period: it contains the symbol of the *jamdar* (master-of-the-robes) with a so-called “napkin” in the upper field, the stemmed cup of the cup-bearer (*saqi*) charged with the pen box of the *dawadar* (secretary) in the central field, flanked by what has been identified as a pair of powder horns. A second, smaller, stemmed cup is placed in the lower field.  
According to Meinecke (1972), this particular emblem was the most popular blazon of the late Burji period and is known to have been used by at least 47 *amir*s. Its first employment can be traced back to Sultan Qaytbay (AH 872–901 / AD 1468-96) when he was still an officer himself and he then conferred it upon his own followers. It was in use up to AH 922 / AD 1517 and came to represent something like the Mamluk “State blazon”.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.short_description: The use of royal emblems reached a high point during the Mamluk period. This carved stone roundel reveals a composition of symbols including those of the cup-bearer, the secretary and the master of robes.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.holder: National Museum of Aleppo, Islamic Department
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.dates: Hegira late 9th–early 10th century / AD late 15th–early 16th century.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.dimensions: Height 51.4 cm, width 55 cm, depth 18.7 cm.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.method_for_datation: The piece was dated by comparison with other similar pieces.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.method_for_provenance: Although the provenance is unknown, this medallion probably belonged to either Amir Uzdamur (also known as Özdemir), who ruled Aleppo twice in 884 / 1479 and between 889–99 / 1484–93, or the last Mamluk *amir*, Kha'irbak b. Bilbay. Both were closely connected to Sultan Qaytbay, leaving examples of this emblem on various buildings in the city: Uzdamur on his *caravanserai* (Khan al-Sabun), the Qastal al-Ramadaniyya, the Qastal Jami' al-Sharaf and the Jami' al-Sharaf itself; Kha'irbak on his mausoleum south of Bab al-Maqam and his *khan* in the *suq* not far from the citadel.

12bc77cd-3251-54d2-a1a9-9f5a47163fc7.name: *Dallah* (Coffee pot), *Khamra*; preparing stage largest pot
12bc77cd-3251-54d2-a1a9-9f5a47163fc7.description: This copper *dallah* goes back to a type allegedly first used in 17th-century Baghdad, and by the 19th century, there were several production centres in the Arabian peninsula. Its design cleverly reflects its functional needs. The broad base ensures stability on the fire or in the sand, whilst the large spout prevents too much coffee sediment from reaching the cup. The lid is purposely weighted to avoid it opening during the pouring process. Throughout the Near and Middle East coffee lay at the heart of social rituals and hospitality, while providing sustenance during chats, debate and political discourse in the many coffee houses in the region. In this light, the quality of the coffee served was an important indicator of both the wealth of the host and status of the guest. In continental Europe, the fashion for coffee was at its height in the 17th and 18th centuries, with coffee houses the preferred meeting places for intellectuals and artists. In Britain, meanwhile, tea soon overtook coffee in popularity, even though certain religious organisations tried to promote coffee houses for the poor in order to steer them away from public houses that primarily sold alcohol.

1304f4ee-e28f-57f0-a08d-b92839b37afe.name: Incense burner
1304f4ee-e28f-57f0-a08d-b92839b37afe.description: Incense burners like this are usually made of clay mixed with water and kneaded until a mixture is formed that can then be shaped. The burner is then adorned with engravings, intricate drawings, and different colors. The incense burners are then fired in a kiln, after which they are ready for use. Note the handle; it makes the burner safe to carry from room to room. Incense occupies a central place in Omani life, as the passing of a fragrant burner at the end of a visit is customary in every region of the country.
1304f4ee-e28f-57f0-a08d-b92839b37afe.holder: The national Museum - Sultanate of Oman

13bd50fd-6740-5159-92f1-64ca153e073c.name: Measuring instrument (*mudd*).
13bd50fd-6740-5159-92f1-64ca153e073c.description:
This measuring instrument, shaped like a trunk, consists of three welded pieces. The decoration is featured along three bands. The upper band holds the beginning of an inscription written in Maghrebi characters, which indicates that the object was made under the orders of the sovereign, Abu al-Hasan, as well as indicating its function. The space left empty by the writing is decorated with double palms. The middle band is adorned with four arches; each holds an inscription in Maghrebi characters that completes the preceding one; and one of these completes the inscription on the upper band. These four inscriptions offer information on both the genealogy of the sovereign and the calibration's origin, which goes as far back as the Prophet Muhammad. The space between the arches is decorated with double palms and floral ornaments. The lower band is decorated with two curving interlacing lines. This measuring instrument features a slit-pin to which a chain is attached made of foliage hooks at either end of which are double-palm shapes that are linked to two rings.  
This measuring weight of the *zakat al-fitr* (alms of the breaking of the *Ramadan* fast), used to weigh out the various cereals, was also used in commercial transactions.
13bd50fd-6740-5159-92f1-64ca153e073c.short_description: Alms-measure divided into three decorative sections including an inscription in Maghrebi characters mentioning the sovereign and the purpose of the object: to measure the *zakat al-fitr* (religious alms) or commercial transactions.

13d87f91-5798-5982-ac33-c5d1d97a1228.name: Ewer
13d87f91-5798-5982-ac33-c5d1d97a1228.description:
This brass ewer stands out among a series of distinctive brass vessels in the FBQ museum that are known for their unique shapes, sizes, and intricate designs. Many examples feature cylindrical bodies with fluted or faceted patterns and lions in relief on their necks. These Persian Islamic ewers served various purposes, including holding beverages, serving at parties, holding water for hand washing, or ablutions for affluent owners and guests. Crafted by artisans for the ruling class and aristocrats, this handle-less ewer is meticulously embossed and engraved with mythical creatures, calligraphy, and arabesques. The neck of the ewer bears two seated lions and a deer in relief, while the flattened shoulder displays an unusual pseudo-Kufic script and a human head. The faceted body is adorned with richly detailed decoration divided into four horizontal sections, featuring winged hares (some with human heads) and pseudo-Kufic script (some letters are human-headed).  
The use of a ewer carries religious significance, as running water is necessary for Muslims to perform ritual ablutions before prayer. Thus a family member would pour fresh water from the ewer over the individual’s hands, symbolising purification and spiritual cleansing. Crafted from brass, this ewer showcases meticulous beating and engraving techniques characteristic of Persian Islamic metalwork from the 12th to 13th centuries. The relief craftsmanship depicting mythical creatures and calligraphy would have been achieved through embossing and engraving, while the pseudo-Kufic script and arabesque designs show the influence of Islamic artistic tradition. The richly detailed decoration reflects the skill and artistry of the artisans of Khorasan or Herat in Iran during this period.

14764713-cb27-5756-8029-2aade64971eb.name: Lidded bowl.
14764713-cb27-5756-8029-2aade64971eb.description:
A squat, elliptically shaped, lidded bowl of stone-paste (fritware) with a flattened domical lid topped by a gilded copper-alloy finial. A blue, red and green rosette enhances the base of the finial; the pattern on the lid itself then opens out from the base of the finial where, from leafy stems, four mythical, blue, serrated *saz* leaves with red centres sprout, moving in an anti-clockwise direction, their stems crossing. In between the *saz* leaves, there are four floral pairs, each consisting of a blue lily and a red-orange hyacinth. These also emerge from leafy stems, sinuously crossing over each other.  
The edge of the rim is decorated by a scalloped border of white on blue, a black dot in the centre of each scallop. The upper edge of the body receives a guilloche border rendered in red and green. Below, nine blue tulips with red dotted detailing flow around the bowl in a clockwise direction, giving the impression of a horizontally disposed garland, although they all rise in fact from the base. A second band below the tulips is composed of carnations, this time flowing in an anti-clockwise direction, their stems again springing from the baseline below. The well of the bowl receives a decorative roundel defined by three linear borders. It contains five flower sprays with red and blue petals. Six abstract motifs in blue fill the remaining spaces.  
The shape of this bowl recalls Iranian metal and ceramic bowls dating to the AH 7th / AD 13th century and also appears among the tableware of the Italian courts during the 15th century (as seen, for example, in an engraving by Mantegna where an attendant serves at table during a card game). In Ottoman court culture lidded bowls such as this were produced in gilt copper (*tombak*), and occurred as an integral part of the tableware used to serve food at mealtimes.
14764713-cb27-5756-8029-2aade64971eb.short_description: In Ottoman court culture lidded bowls like this one were produced in gilt copper (*tombak*) as well as pottery and occurred as an integral part of the crockery used to serve food at mealtimes. Its style of decoration places it among other floral Iznik wares dated to the AH 10th / AD late 16th century.
14764713-cb27-5756-8029-2aade64971eb.method_for_datation: The decorative style of this lidded bowl places it among a group of floral Iznik wares dated to the 10th / late 16th century.

15d519f5-c26e-5c05-ba07-ac169b9cafb2.name: ‘Attarin Suq
15d519f5-c26e-5c05-ba07-ac169b9cafb2.description:
As well as *funduq*s, Fez possessed markets, *suq*s, whose reputation extended far beyond the town walls. The *qaysariya*, a term signifying a commercial neighbourhood, which was situated at the heart of the Qarawiyin Quarter, with its numerous *suq*s and shops, is one of the oldest of its kind, offering goods imported from Europe and the East ever since the Middle Ages.  
Destroyed at first by a great fire in 724/1324, and then by floods in 725/1325, the *qaysariya*, with its thousands of terraced houses, was then rebuilt. The ‘Attarin Suq, one of the most reputable in the *qaysariya*, occupies the length of a long street which links up to the Merinid *madrasa* of the same name, at *Bab al-Faraj*. Complemented by trade on adjacent streets and places, this market extends over more than 600 m. and was equipped with a large gate at each end, whose “*guardians*”, wrote Leon the African, “*do their rounds at night, with dogs, with weapons, holding up lanterns in their hands. They were paid by the traders themselves*”.  
The *suq*, according to Leon the African, consisted of 150 stalls, which grew in number to 170 a few years later according to the Portuguese historian Mármol de Carvajal (16th century). Originally specialising in the sale of medicinal products and groceries, medicinal stalls stood shoulder to shoulder with hardware stalls which were distinct for the opulence of their ornamentation. Doctors themselves made up the medicinal preparations, and then sent them to specialised stalls where staff would dispense them under medical supervision.  
In the 10th/16th century, the *suq*, through the importance it had gained in terms of the geographical area it fulfilled, through the number of important shops it represented and through the abundance of specialised products it sold, was unrivalled. Even if the *suq* of today has lost a little of its identity through the growth of product variety, one can still find some traditional hardware sellers who are living examples of this market, typical of its kind.

17063181-2e66-5196-bb7a-7cc70632a717.name: Bani Isguen.
17063181-2e66-5196-bb7a-7cc70632a717.description:
When Abu al-Hattab, lord of the town of Kairouan under the orders of the Kharijites, was killed, the Ibadi appointed his companion, Ibn Rustam, as their leader, who went on to found a kingdom in AH 161 / AD 778 within the central Maghreb that extended from Kairouan to Fez, with Tahert as its capital. The word 'Kharijite' (from *kharaja*, to leave) is illustrative of recurring dissents that lead to a rupture with the dominant doctrine. In AH 37 / AD 658, four thousand followers left the town of Kufa, outraged by the decision to deny 'Ali, the Prophet's son-in-law, of his rights of succession in favour of Mu'awiya. The event is at the heart of the fracture that continues to run through and divide the Islamic world into Shi'ites and Sunnis.  
The Rustamids dominated the central Maghreb for a century and a half, but, under the assaults of the Fatimids, they were forced to take refuge first at Sédrata (near Ouargla), then in the M'zab region, where they founded five towns in succession that constitute the 'Pentapolis' (Ghardaïa, Mélika, Bani Isguen, Bou Noura and El Atteuf). Through ingenious means of capturing and distributing the little water that was available, they were able from as early as the AH 6th / AD 12th century to create plantations of palm trees and gardens that still testify to an efficient ecological control of natural resources.  
Built on the face of a rocky hillside, Bani Isguen, founded in AH 441 / AD 1050, is the holy town of the M'zab. It is surrounded by a vast rampart that is flanked by towers and pierced by three gates, which, until recently, were closed every night. Another tower, which dominates the town, is believed to have been built in a day in anticipation of an attack.  
The houses that sit in the valley of the M'zab were designed to allow for a certain amount of diurnal 'nomadism'. They are usually built on two levels, on which one can find the same items necessary for daily life: the hearth, the latrines, the washroom, the bedrooms, the living room and the loom. This configuration allows one to live in the cool shade of the ground floor in summer, and at night-time, to carry on with the activities upstairs where it is fresher at night. In winter, the reverse applies. The summerhouses within the palm plantations are designed along the same lines. Beyond their functionalism, 'they were additionally endowed with beauty. The heterodox puritans preferred to live according to their own beliefs in the desert, rather than consent to live in opulence but according to the truths of others; however they did not concern themselves with beautifying their own homes. This was not through lack of good taste, rather, it was because they did not have the opportunity or the spare time to do so. Survival was first and foremost.'(From Ravereau, see Bibliography.)
17063181-2e66-5196-bb7a-7cc70632a717.short_description: Built on the side of a rocky hill, Bani Isguen is the holy town of the M'zab region. It is defended by a vast rampart flanked by towers and crossed via three gateways, and a tower that dominates the town. The rooms, built on two storeys, included bathrooms, bedrooms and a living room, along with a loom. The summer houses in the palm grove are laid out in the same fashion. Gardens could be cultivated thanks to ingenious devices that allowed the little available water to be used.

Ravereau, A., *Le M'zab, une leçon d'architecture*, Paris, 1987.
17063181-2e66-5196-bb7a-7cc70632a717.author: Ali Lafer
keywords: Town; civic architecture; religious architecture; water; irrigation; M’zab.

17634e8b-75c4-531c-a525-4f57d46e78f9.name: Bowl
17634e8b-75c4-531c-a525-4f57d46e78f9.description: This bowl is a fine example of pottery from the Samanid (AD 819–1005) workshops of eastern Iran. Its design is stark and striking, featuring a single line of Arabic calligraphy that encircles the deep rim. The script, with its elegantly elongated horizontals and sharp-tipped verticals, is an early form of Arabic calligraphy known as New Style Kufic. The bowl's decoration is minimal yet visually compelling, with the inscription reading: “Knowledge is the most noble lineage and chivalry the most intricate.” The inscription’s meaning is elevated by the artistic manipulation of the letters. Through shortening, bending, and elongating, the script is transformed into abstract motifs of remarkable visual impact. The vertical flourishes interspersed among the horizontal flow create a rhythmic interplay that draws in the viewer. Likely used for serving on special occasions, the bowl’s message about the virtues of knowledge and chivalry is particularly apt.
17634e8b-75c4-531c-a525-4f57d46e78f9.bibliography: Christie's London, *Art of the Islamic and Indian World*, 2011.
17634e8b-75c4-531c-a525-4f57d46e78f9.author: Teslim Sanni
materials: Earthenware, opaque white glaze with black painting

17d6e18b-8628-5642-bf1b-3e753e6d63d6.name: Painted wooden ceiling of the Palatine Chapel.
17d6e18b-8628-5642-bf1b-3e753e6d63d6.description:
The painted wooden ceiling of the Palatine Chapel, erected by Ruggero II immediately after his coronation in 1131, is the only monumental-scale pictorial cycle from the Fatimid period in the Mediterranean basin to have survived in its entirety. The ceiling, made up of star-shaped polygons, is decorated with lively scenes, painted in a clean, clear style with an undeniable Middle Eastern influence, depicting dancing girls, musicians, gamblers, lions and other animals, horsemen and wrestlers, all combined with geometric and vegetal decorations. The polygons are surrounded by inscriptions of good omens in *kufic* script. The band between the ceiling and the walls is decorated with *muqarnas*.  
The identification of the craftsmen responsible for the decoration remains the subject of lively debate. G. D’Erme (1995) suggests the persistence of a late Sassanid, early Islamic pictorial tradition probably upheld in the Mediterranean basin over the centuries due to the circulation of collections of figurative models. The extremely cultured artists could have been either descendents of the island’s Iranian conquerors (whose presence in Palermo is confirmed by historical sources) or indeed Iranian Seljuq craftsmen brought to Palermo by the Norman king. D’Erme is inclined to exclude the possibility of craftsmen from North Africa or Cairo.  
J. Johns (1995) maintains that the paintings would have been done by a workshop imported at the behest of Ruggero II directly from Fatimid Egypt, challenging the traditional theories according to which the painters were Sicilian Arabs and the chapel ceiling the ultimate expression of the artistic legacy of the island’s Islamic past, now passed on to the new Norman kingdom and used by it for political and ideological ends. Among other things, Johns provides evidence of the close political and cultural links established between Ruggero II and the Cairo Caliphate, through the personal correspondence with Caliph al-Hafiz, the frequent exchange of gifts, the presence of Egyptian diplomatic experts at the Palermo court and the use of the same epigraphic formulas, as in the exquisite Fatimid inscription once in the Palatine Chapel (now in the Abatellis Palace regional gallery) likening the king’s palace to a sanctuary.  
With regard to the possible meaning of the pictorial cycle, many academics, drawn by the apparently irreconcilable nature of the secular character of the cycle and its ecclesiastical context, contrive to see a celebration of the pleasures of Qur’anic paradise, often overloading their interpretation of individual figures with religious symbolism when a more simple interpretation would be a joyful celebration of life in the royal court (celebrations that were also common in court culture in the Islamic world) and its earthly pleasures: gambling, drinking, music and hunting. Both Johns (1995) and Aurigemma (2004) interpret the cycle on the basis of this assumption, stripped of symbolic and religious implications, with the latter drawing plausible comparisons between these paintings and their contemporaries on the wooden ceiling of Cefalù Cathedral, also commissioned by Ruggero II.
17d6e18b-8628-5642-bf1b-3e753e6d63d6.short_description: This painted wooden ceiling, produced during the reign of Ruggero (Roger) II, depicts lively scenes of dancing girls, musicians, gamblers, lions and other animals, all set against a background of plant and geometric decoration. The transition from ceiling to wall is softened by *muqarnas* (honeycomb decoration). Recent studies have revealed that the craftsmen employed included painters from Egypt, or at least painters influenced by contemporary Fatimid art.
17d6e18b-8628-5642-bf1b-3e753e6d63d6.method_for_datation: Historical sources report the date the chapel was founded (1131) and consecrated (1140).

1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.name: Norias (*nawa’ir*) of Hama.
1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.description:
The waterwheel, or *noria* (properly pronounced *na'ura* (singular) and *nawa'ir* (plural)), is an ancient hydraulic structure designed for collecting and distributing water by utilising the power of a running stream. It is also the visual and aural hallmark of the city of Hama, 226 km north of Damascus, straddling the meandering River Orontes. The use of waterwheels in Syria dates to the Classical and Hellenistic periods, possibly even the Nabataean period (2nd century BC–AD 2nd century), and the first visual depiction of a *na'ura* is found on a mosaic from the ancient city of Apamea, 55 km north of Hama, dated AD 469. During the medieval period, however, there was a marked increase of references to *nawa'ir* in Islamic geographical writing, indicating their improved and multiplied development.  
Under the Seljuq sultanate and their various Atabeg, Zangid and Ayyubid vassals, when Syria's cities witnessed robust urban development, the *nawa'ir* of Hama received special attention. Nur al-Din Mahmud bin Zangi went on a rebuilding campaign after the earthquake of AH 551 / AD 1157, which included the restoration of Hama's water system and *nawa'ir*.  
The earliest of the surviving *nawa'ir* are attributed to the Ayyubid period (late AH 6th – 7th / AD 11th - 12th centuries) while the earliest inscribed *na'ura* tower, named al-Muhammadiyya, dates to the Mamluk period in AH 763 / AD 1361. This is also one of the two largest *nawa'ir* of the city: 21 m in wheel diameter and 17.5 m in aqueduct height. The aqueduct of al-Muhammadiyya is particularly long as it supplies water for the Great Mosque quarter, nearly a kilometre away from the banks of the River Orontes. The second largest *na'ura*, also 21 m in diameter and known as al-Mamuriyya, is early Ottoman, dated AH 867 (1453).  
*Nawa'ir* are constructed basically in two parts: the mobile wheel, usually made of poplar wood, and the static aqueduct, usually made of stone. The wheel consists of a group of broad beams fixed perpendicularly around the axle, creating a quadrangular formation in the centre, and radiating out towards the wheel's periphery. These beams are held together by circular frames and further supported by more beams that are nailed in at successive angles. At the periphery of the wheel are paddles that facilitate the wheel's circular movement and compartments (*sanadiq*) that collect the water. Given that the wheel is largely a wooden construction, its beams need regular maintenance and changing every 15 years or so.  
Stone constructions, like the aqueduct for transporting water and the small dam controlling the river's water level, are also part of the *noria's* successful construction. The aqueduct is a tall rectangular receptacle standing parallel to the wheel and designed to be as wide as possible in order to receive maximum water per rotation. Attached to this receptacle is the long duct set on an arcade that serves the adjacent areas, providing them with water for domestic and irrigation purposes. On average, a *na'ura* can raise 50 litres of water per second, and irrigate no less than 75 hectares.
1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.short_description: The city of Hama is famous for its waterwheels, or *norias*, which charmingly dot the meandering River Orontes, which passes through the city. The technique for building these waterwheels is an ancient one, but remarkably effective and still in use. The wheels are typically made of poplar wood, requiring regular maintenance, while their supportive structures, like aqueducts and dams, are made of stone. The dimensions of the total hydraulic construction are inter-related, depending on each other to collect the maximum amount of water efficiently and ensure its most effective distribution.
1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.method_for_datation: Some *nawa'ir* are dated by inscriptions but mostly by approximation based on archaeological evidence and historical sources. Recent excavations that have taken place under water are proving that most *nawa'ir* have ancient origins and have been continuously restructured throughout the ages.
1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.bibliography:
Burns, R., *Monuments of Syria: An Historical Guide*, 1999, pp.126–9.  
Delpech, A., et al, *Les norias de l'Oronte: analyse technologique d'un éléments du patrimoine syrien*, Damascus, 2005.
1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.author: Waal Hafian
keywords: Hydraulics; water supply; urban architecture; Orontes River

1b55ef6a-0fb1-56d2-9274-4f0775c2cee9.name: Austrian toy theatre set: 'The Caravan to Mecca. The Halt in the Desert' by Trentsentsky
1b55ef6a-0fb1-56d2-9274-4f0775c2cee9.short_description: With a desert landscape backdrop and cut-out figures on wooden stands, this toy theatre uses intricate detail and imagination to depict the stopping of a pilgrim caravan. With 45 cut out figures and with an original box, the set was made by Matthias Trentensky (1790–1868), a retired army officer and printer who became the Austrian Empire’s foremost maker of toy theatres. Miniature theatres based on popular plays were common in the 19th century particularly in Europe, although this theatre may have been produced as a result of the increasing fascination with the Arab world at the time. The artist is likely to be Theodor Jachimovicz who studied painting at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna and worked as a theatre stage painter for the State Opera House. Trentensky exported his toy theatres to England through the London company A&S Joseph Myers and Co. of 144 Leadenhall Street, importers of French, German, Swiss and Italian goods and toy merchants. It has been suggested that the theatres produced for London may be of better quality than those for the Austrian market. Other theatres produced for A&S Myers included those closely related to English themes, such as contemporary pantomimes. The collection also holds an uncut version of the theatre, a complete set of 24 plates with 168 illustrations.
1b55ef6a-0fb1-56d2-9274-4f0775c2cee9.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
1b55ef6a-0fb1-56d2-9274-4f0775c2cee9.author: Qaisra Khan
keywords: Camel; Children; Childhood; Geography; Hajj; Hijaz; Holy place; Ka'ba; Medina; Mosque; paper; Pilgrimage; Prayer; Prophet Muhammad; Qur'an; Religion; Theatre; Travel; Traveller; Mecca

1bd4ddad-a3bc-5a69-8b22-cef129e37f47.name: Figurine
1bd4ddad-a3bc-5a69-8b22-cef129e37f47.description: Animal figurines were a short-lived phenomenon of the late 12th to 13th centuries AD in Syria and Iran. The cow or bull figure was especially popular, but in Iran it was made to function as a vessel with a filling spout in the back and an open mouth through which the liquid poured, whereas in Syria the trend was for figurines with a purely decorative function. However, as the basic form of the cow would have been moulded – suggesting that multiple versions of the same figure were made – the function of these decorative figurines remains a mystery. The present example is rendered with perfect naturalism. It can be identified as a zebu cow and calf. The mother is shown standing while her calf suckles; the hanging dewlap, small hump, swept-back horns and large cloven hooves of the breed are accurately modelled. This breed is indigenous to Syria, and would have been what people saw in the fields of the Euphrates Valley.

1e36e46d-3a70-5c50-9e85-b70b2c3e4435.name: Lahri (grain silo).
1e36e46d-3a70-5c50-9e85-b70b2c3e4435.description:
During the reign of Sultan Mulay Isma'il, tribes often paid their taxes in kind, in particular with grain. The silos used to store the produce paid as taxes occupied a preferential position in the layout of royal towns and constituted an indispensable food reserve for supplying towns.  
Controlling these reserves was a strategic priority for the ruling body, especially during times of conflict and drought.  
For this purpose, Sultan Mulay Isma'il had a vast grain silo constructed, the Lahri, near to his palace. Its walls are built of pink adobe, a mix of clay earth, lime and stones, with occasional stone ashlars.  
The monument extends over an area measuring 182 m by 104 m. It rests on 305 arches and 23 south–east / north–west naves, giving an impression of depth and equilibrium.  
Composed of a series of relatively cramped rooms around a spacious central room (26.30 m by 10.70 m and 9 m to the ceiling), the building was used to store foodstuffs and the fodder needed for the 12,000 horses of the royal stud farm. A central avenue is still maintained all the way to the rear wall. The pillars supporting the semi-circular arches, 3 m in diameter, divide the room into 18 rows and 23 naves, originally covered with barrel vaults. This part of the monument is particularly impressive. A large space was reserved for the mules who brought the grain from different areas of the country.  
Its very thick walls maintained a constant temperature for the preservation of the foodstuffs. Moüette, who was a prisoner in Morocco for 11 years and who participated in the construction of Isma'il's *kasbah*, speaks of walls 30 spans, or 7 m, thick.  
The silo is now in partial ruin. A tower, which used to house cannons and other instruments of war to protect the royal palace and the *medina*, dominates the upper part.  
In the AH 12th / AD 18th century, the building was abandoned following the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, which affected the town of Meknès and destroyed part of this monument.  
Now restored, the silo is a highlight of the 'Alawid heritage of Meknès.
1e36e46d-3a70-5c50-9e85-b70b2c3e4435.short_description: Built in the AH 11th / AD 17th century during the reign of Sultan Mulay Isma'il on a site measuring 182 m by 104 m, these vast rectangular structures were in fact underground granaries whose vaults and ceilings have collapsed. Supported on a series of 22 arcades of 14 arches each, these silos adjoin the west walls of the House of the Norias, and dominate the Sahrij Swani. These granaries were used to store foodstuffs, in particular wheat, as a contingency for sieges and wars. They have been recently restored.
1e36e46d-3a70-5c50-9e85-b70b2c3e4435.method_for_datation: John Windus, who came to Meknès to arrange the purchase of captives on behalf of King George I, described it in 1720.

1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.name: Ewer (*ibrik*).
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.description: A ewer (*ibrik*) with a pear-shaped body, a handle and a spout decorated with plant motifs and inscription friezes. The shoulder of the ewer is filled with a frieze written in *naskhi* script. A second frieze, formed of plant motifs, appears directly below. Further inscriptions in *naskhi* script are found on the neck and spout. The floral motifs and inscriptions adorning the ewer are embellished with silver leaf, while the frame of the inscription on the shoulder is embellished with red-copper leaf. The inscriptions on the shoulder and spout wish glory, fame, success and long life to the owner of the vessel. This ewer is of great importance both as a dated example of Mesopotamian work and because its inscriptions provide the names of two Mosul craftsmen.
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.short_description: Mosul was an important centre of Islamic metalwork during the Zangid period. This centre had a great influence on the technique and style of Artuqid metalwork in Anatolia. The inscription states that it was made by a master called 'Iyas of Mosul. It has the characteristics of its period.
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.dimensions: Height (without lid) 39 cm; diameter (of base) 16.5 cm; maximum diameter 20 cm.
1f5849a0-4eae-5275-9603-dfe4acb6e862.method_for_datation: An inscription on the neck states that the ewer was made by 'Iyas, the assistant of master Abd al-Karim ibn al-Turabi of Mosul' in 627 / 1229.

21515d04-3a00-5d77-8767-38df44429375.name: Tall Abu Sarbut.
21515d04-3a00-5d77-8767-38df44429375.description:
Tall Abu Sarbut is located in the Central Jordan Valley about 70 km northwest of Amman, 1.5 km from Dayr Alla. It is a low hill that measures 250 m east to west and about 125 m from north to south. The highest point of the tall is at 252 m below sea level.  
Three seasons of archaeological investigations were conducted at the site between 1988–90 as a joint venture between the Department of Antiquities of Jordan, the University of Leiden and the Netherlands Institute for the Near East. The main objective of the project was to verify the nature and the extent of the site.  
Archaeological excavations uncovered a large Mamluk multi-roomed building with courtyards. In one of the courtyards a bread oven (*tabun*) was found. The walls were built of sun-dried mud bricks on stone foundations. The walls and the floors were plastered. Archaeological investigations demonstrated that the site was an important part of the sugar-production industry in the area; the sugar industry being a main source of revenue in the Jordan Valley during the Mamluk period. The nature of the archaeological finds discovered during the excavations showed that the site was not associated directly with the actual refinery of sugar but it was an important storage and distribution centre for the sugar that was produced in the area.
21515d04-3a00-5d77-8767-38df44429375.short_description: Tall Abu Sarbut is located in the Central Jordan Valley about 70 km northwest of Amman. It is a low hill that measures around 250 m x125 m, and its highest point is 252 m below sea level. It has structures built of sun-dried mud bricks on stone foundations. The site was an important part of the sugar-production industry in the area; the sugar industry being a main source of revenue in the Jordan Valley during the Mamluk period. Although not associated directly with the actual refinery of sugar, it was an important storage and distribution centre for the sugar that was produced in the area.
21515d04-3a00-5d77-8767-38df44429375.method_for_datation: The monument was dated by analysis of the material remains comprising mainly ceramics discovered during the course of archaeological investigations at the site, which dated the site to the 7th–9th / 14th–15th centuries.

21645a7b-fc42-55ef-a2ec-27424e1c67fc.name: Tile Plate
21645a7b-fc42-55ef-a2ec-27424e1c67fc.description: The surface is covered in white clay and slip decorated in cobalt blue, coral red and green with black contours under a transparent colourless glaze. The plate’s surface is decorated with symmetrically distributed branches of tulips and red carnations with blue spots rising vertically from a single stem. Two tulips and carnations in the centre of the composition are held in place by a bracket. The composition is embellished with tulip and carnation buds, small stylised flowers, with cobalt blue Chinese-style clouds interspersed throughout the design. The use of bud and clover motifs in the decoration of plates was common during this period. A narrow border of white half-rosette flowers with red centres is framed by cobalt blue inside the rim. A double tulip and open rose motif alternate on the back.

22d721a5-3840-5af9-8c84-912b213423e2.name: Citadel of Amman (Water Reservoir).
22d721a5-3840-5af9-8c84-912b213423e2.description: Within the Umayyad Citadel to the east of the palatial complex is a round water cistern, 6 m deep with a diameter that exceeds 17.5 m, and which could hold up to 1300 cu m of water. This cistern was the most important source of water at the Citadel. It was fed through inlet channels connected to a system for the collection of rainwater. These channels and the associated settling tank are partially preserved to the west of the cistern. Some earlier architectural elements including columns, shafts and capitals were incorporated into the wall of the cistern as building materials, such as the shaft of a stone column which was placed in the centre of the cistern and re-used as a depth gauge. The base and the walls were covered with a thick layer of hydraulic plaster which can still be seen. Stone steps along the western side lead down into the cistern. This access was necessary in order to clean the interior from the debris collected with the run-off water and to prepare the cistern for the rainy season. A deep well adjacent to the cistern from the north may be part of the water installations necessary to feed water to the bath complex located to the west of the citadel. This round cistern is closely related architecturally and stylistically to the local tradition of rectangular cisterns, despite the superficial similarity to the round Aghlabid cisterns found at Kairouan Tunisia
22d721a5-3840-5af9-8c84-912b213423e2.short_description: The water cistern on the Amman Citadel lies to the east of the Umayyad palatial complex. It is round, 6 m deep with a diameter of over 17.5 m, and could hold up to 1300 cu m of water. This cistern, fed by inlet channels connected to a rainwater collection system, was the most important source of water at the Citadel. Some earlier architectural elements were incorporated into the cistern wall, and a column shaft was re-used as a depth gauge. The interior was covered with a thick layer of hydraulic plaster. Stone steps along the western side led down into the cistern.
22d721a5-3840-5af9-8c84-912b213423e2.method_for_datation: By way of archaeological excavations within the palatial complex the cistern was dated to around 730 / the first half of the eighth century AD.

23d6b4ee-6380-5185-a38f-672a711e7d14.name:
Shaykh Safi al-Din asking his disciples to accept honey from the villagers but not meat  
From the manuscript of *Safvat al-Safa* (The Quintessence of Purity), the Hagiography of Shaykh Safi al-Din Ishaq Ardabili (1252/3–1334)
23d6b4ee-6380-5185-a38f-672a711e7d14.short_description: “Shaykh Safi al-Din asking his disciples to accept honey from the villagers but not meat” is one of fourteen paintings in the only known illustrated copy of *Safvat al-Safa* (The Quintessence of Purity), a tazkira and hagiography of Shaykh Safi al-Din Ishaq Ardabili (1252/3–1334). *Safvat al-Safa* gives detailed information about the life, sayings, virtues, and miracles of Shaykh Safi, the spiritual founder of the Safavid dynasty (1501–1736). *Safvat al-Safa* is a biography book with hagiographical accounts which falls under both genres. In Islamic literature, the term "tazkira" is used for biographical texts and "hagiography" is used for books on the lives of the mystics. *Safvat al-Safa* includes actual information on the life of Shaykh Safi al-Din Ishaq Ardabili as well as mystical and supernatural stories. It appears to have been the main source of the Safavid chroniclers for the early period of the dynasty, as there are numerous copies and translations. Safvat al-Safa has an introduction (*muqaddima*), twelve chapters (*bab*), and an epilogue (*khatima*). Each chapter has numerous sections (*fasl*) which include multiple short episodes (*hikayat*).
23d6b4ee-6380-5185-a38f-672a711e7d14.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; manuscript; painting; Safvat-al-Safa; The-Quintessence-of-Purity
materials: Opaque watercolour, ink, and gold on paper

2461a3b5-4ba8-5298-867c-456770c4b426.name: Bowl
2461a3b5-4ba8-5298-867c-456770c4b426.description: Bowls are among the most important copper artifacts in Omani hospitality. They are usually either wholly circular or circular with a channel and include various decorative designs. They may serve to either hold the cups in which Omani coffee is served, or as basins for guests to wash their hands.

255f45d9-17b4-565e-8c90-1983dbce43f3.name: *Majlis* Carpet
255f45d9-17b4-565e-8c90-1983dbce43f3.short_description:
This large-scale textile is termed the *majlis* (council) carpet. Handcrafted in Hamdan from wool and camel hair utilizing the Seneh knot, it represents the spatiality of the Gulf-Arab "sitting place". The *majlis* unites notions of privacy and hospitality appearing to be incompatible in one entity.  
  
While the carpet would have stretched from one corner of the *majlis* to the other with design elements such as the paisley, damascene rose, diamond-shapes and symmetry characteristic of Persian carpets, the discrete sections of the textile embody the different spatial components of the room. The outer segments reflect sitting positions of the head of the household, the family, friends and guests. The centrepiece would offer room to dance, perform music, play board games or display food and coffee. It would have stretched from one corner of the *majlis* to the other.  
  
Due to the cost of these large pieces of art, merchants began cutting apart the separable sections and selling fragments to decorate hallways and corridors. Only few of such majlis carpets may still be reassembled into their original composition.

26f69a41-3873-5f60-92a8-ec686e31453e.name: Lunch Box
26f69a41-3873-5f60-92a8-ec686e31453e.description: This brass box, inlaid with silver, was intended for holding food. It is rectangular with rounded ends and a coffered lid. The lid is secured by a central, frontal clasp terminating in a teardrop finial, flanked by two additional clasps on the sides and a curving handle secured by two rings on top. The body is divided into three horizontal zones. The central band bears an Arabic inscription written in bold thuluth script interrupted by four eight-petalled swirling rosettes, while the upper and lower bands are comparatively plain, containing only four rosettes and eight knotted arabesques. The inscription across the centre reads: “*umila birasm al-janab al-’ali al-maulavi al-imami al-muthaghiri al-mujahidi mawlana ‘izz al-dunya wa-al … al-din nasrallaha*”, (Made by order of his great Excellency, the lordly Imam, the defender of frontiers, the striver for the faith, our lord ‘Izz al-Dunya wa’l \[-Din\] … al-Din, may God grant him victory). Another box in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo bears a similar style of inscription, stating that it was made in Sana’a, Yemen. This attribution points to a similar place of production for the present box.

2778ce78-5836-53cd-89f8-bb048bc613b1.name: Bottle with stamped design
2778ce78-5836-53cd-89f8-bb048bc613b1.description:
The overall shape of the object consists of four distinct parts: neck, handle, and upper and lower hemispheres of the body. The decoration, of great complexity, consists of patterns frequently found on jewellery, which gives the impression of a goldsmith’s work transposed to clay. Included in this profusion are roundels framing a bird downed by a hawk or passing lion, twisted columns topped with discs in the shape of flowers, fish, lotus buds, palmettes, and palm trees, circular marks…  
It is a utilitarian but decorative piece intended for pouring water in apartments or reception rooms.

28485e93-6aee-597e-b6d4-519ba9eeb8e4.name: Caucasian Rug
28485e93-6aee-597e-b6d4-519ba9eeb8e4.short_description:
Although the Ummayad and Abbasid caliphates overthrew the Iranian empires in the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, the cultural influence of Persia remains. This Caucasian carpet displays a blend of influences from Islam and pre-Islamic Persia.  
  
Primary colours from natural dyes typically brighten carpets from the Shirvan region with blue likely representing water as a life's source. The symmetry in these textiles creates harmony with repeated shapes such as the *kubpa* (hexagonal medallion) with tooth-like edges and diamonds to protect from the evil eye.  
  
Bright colours and geometric figures adorn this rug with abstracted religious symbols. The *mehrab* (arched prayer niche) denotes the direction toward toward which Muslims pray, Mecca. The upper end of the carpet displays the date, 1281 Hegira (1864 AD). Two chequered rectangles resemble a chess board, which suggests a possible alternative use for this carpet for entertainment during travels.

2a96e20e-2325-5bea-be93-cd4c4d73eac0.name: Citadel of Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi.
2a96e20e-2325-5bea-be93-cd4c4d73eac0.description:
The Citadel of Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi, known also as Citadel of the Mountain (Qala'a al-Jabal), is one of the most important landmarks of Cairo and amongst the most imposing military citadels to be built in the Middle Ages. Having assumed power in Egypt Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi (Saladin) noted that despite its grandeur and vastness Cairo did not have a citadel to protect her like other great cities in the Levant such as Damascus and Aleppo. He therefore began to construct the citadel, ordering construction of its walls, semi-circular towers and its two gates: Bab al-Qarafa and Bab al-Mudarraj. Saladin's son, Al-Malik al-‘Adil (r. AH 596–615 / AD 1200–18) completed the building of the citadel and surrounded some of the towers with outer encasing towers, in order to increase their impregnability, these included three towers: Burg al-Imam, Burg al-Ramla and Burg al-Haddad. He also added two square towers: Burg al-Turfa and Burg al-Karkialan. These works were completed in AH 604 / AD 1207.  
In its present form the citadel is a great city, the borders of which are marked by massive walls and towers. It is divided into two parts: the northeastern section and the southwestern section. The northeastern section represents the citadel's military fortifications. It is confined inside an irregular rectangular area whose length from east to west measures 560 m and whose width from north to south is 317 m. The walls of this section are in proportion to each other due to the fact that they were built in, and are associated with, a single period.  
The southern side of the wall of the northeastern military section begins with Burg al-Muqattam, from the western side. This is a circular tower, dating back to the Ottoman period. Next is the Burg al-Suffa a quasi-rectangular tower, adjacent to which is the square tower, Burg al-Karkialan. This tower is followed by another, square tower, Burg al-Turfa. The southern side ends in the east with a circular tower, Burg al-Mubalat. The eastern side consists of four circular towers: Burg al-Muqawsar, Burg al-Imam, Burg al-Ramla and Burg al-Haddad. The northern side is composed of two great quasi-circular towers: one of which is Burg al-Sahraa, and the other does not have a name. On the western side of this section there is a gate, Bab al-Mudarraj, and the shared wall between the northern military section and the southern residential section.  
The walls of the citadel are 3 m thick and their height from within the citadel averages 10 m. The heights of the towers increase at times to over 20 m. A passageway leading to narrow, square rooms passes through the walls, the width of which measures about 90 cm. The towers contain rectangular chambers. There are two side-rooms in each tower in the form of two arms; the rooms have slits for shooting arrows. This section of the walls was built in a relatively short period of time that did not exceed seven years (AH 572–9 / AD 1176–83).  
The southwestern section of the citadel still preserves the features of a royal city resplendent with palaces and mosques. A successive number of rulers participated in building it, from the period of Saladin to the period of the Ottoman Pasha Muhammad Ali (r. AH 1220–64 / AD 1805–48). This section occupies an irregular surface area, which is slightly smaller than the area of the military, northeastern section. The greatest distance in it from north to south reaches 510 m, and from east to west 270 m. Al-Malik al-Kamil bin al-‘Adil (r. AH 615–35 / AD 1218–37) is considered to be the first to transfer the seat of government and administration to the citadel in AH 604 / AD 1208 during his occupation of the position of deputy (to his father) of the sultanate in Egypt. The Citadel of Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi continued to be the seat of government for close to seven centuries until Khedive Isma'il made the 'Abidin palace located outside the citadel the official seat of his rule in the year AH 1276 / AD 1874.  
The style used in the construction of the citadel walls and towers follows those used in the building of the walls of Fatimid Cairo in AH 480 / AD 1087, seen in features such as the attention paid to the alignment of stone, as well as the use of interlocking voussoirs seen in Bab al-Mudarraj, and the projecting balconies of Burg al-Haddad. However, new architectural elements also appear in the Citadel, such as the circular towers. There is a similarity between the architectural components of Citadel of Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi and those which are specific to two citadels in Jordan: the Citadel 'Ajlun (built AH 580 / AD 1184) and Citadel al-Kark which, incidentally, was restored by al-Malik al-‘Adil.
2a96e20e-2325-5bea-be93-cd4c4d73eac0.short_description: This citadel is one of the most important Islamic monuments in Cairo, standing proudly through the ages since its foundation by Salah al-Din (Saladin) on an outcrop of Muqattam Hill to the east of the city. A defensive fortress against the Crusaders, it served also as a residence for the rulers in times of unrest and continued as such until the time of Khedive Isma‘il in 1874 when he built ‘Abidin Palace to be his seat of rule. The citadel was divided within its walls into a military area and a residential area.
2a96e20e-2325-5bea-be93-cd4c4d73eac0.method_for_datation: This building was dated based on two epigraphic inscriptions bearing the name of the builder and the date of construction. The first inscription is on Bab al-Qarafa and bears the date, 576 / 1180; the second is on Bab al-Mudarraj and bears the date, 579 / 1184. Historical sources such as that by Maqrizi, *al-Khitat,* and *al-Nujum al-Zahira* by Taghri Bardi, confirm the validity of these dates. Further information with regard to dating can be found in Combe *et al*, detailed in the bibliography.

2bb20c6b-1cd4-5c87-a1f5-c0764436f8b3.name: *Taḏkerat al-Awliāʾ by Farid-al-Din ʿAṭṭār Neishabouri* (Social Gathering for Entertainment in Meadow)
2bb20c6b-1cd4-5c87-a1f5-c0764436f8b3.description: The *Taḏkerat al-Awliāʾ*, in which Farīd al-Dīn Attār (Hegira 618 / AD 1221) narrates stories of the saints, begins with the chapter devoted to Ja'far al-Sādiq and ends with Hallāj al-Mansūr. The work contains information about the lives of 72 individuals, including Imām al-ʿĀzam, Imam Shāfi'ī, Ahmad b. Ḥanbal, Weysel Karānī and Rābia al-Adawiyya, and their stories and sayings. Each person is allocated a chapter, and the word *zikr* (remembrance) is placed at the beginning of each chapter. The work is written in Persian in *taliq* calligraphy on paper. On pages 1b-2a an entertainment scene is depicted that covers the entire page, while on pages 2b-3a the first section is written in two facing medallions. The work contains 27 miniature scenes depicting various parables. The outer edges of the medallions are embellished with a profusion of *simurgh* birds (benevolent mythical creatures) and a variety of floral motifs crafted in the *ringar* technique. The chapter headings are illuminated in a style characteristic of the period.
2bb20c6b-1cd4-5c87-a1f5-c0764436f8b3.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
2bb20c6b-1cd4-5c87-a1f5-c0764436f8b3.obtention: Brought to the Museum on 13 April 1914  from the Sadreddin Konevi Tomb in Konya.

2c1e6a09-4e26-51fb-a7ae-7206e8f1288d.name: Tray (*sinija*)
2c1e6a09-4e26-51fb-a7ae-7206e8f1288d.description:
The term *sinija* (Tr. *sini*) relates to a large round brass or copper tray that functioned as a low table on which food was served.  
This artefact is a large, circular brass tray with stepped flat rim. The central medallion is decorated with incised geometric arabesque filled with intricate scroll ornamentation. It is further encircled by several narrow and broader bands decorated in the same manner of combining different geometric shapes with vine and scroll patterns.

keywords: tray; sinija; tableware; brass; Persia

2d3a9974-408a-5de5-bdff-8cfdae9e0b29.name: *Akbarnama*
2d3a9974-408a-5de5-bdff-8cfdae9e0b29.short_description: The Mughal emperors ruled India for more than three centuries. Akbar (r. 1556–1605), the third emperor, was the longest ruling and is considered the greatest of them all. His biography is known as the *Akbarnama* (‘Book of Akbar’) and is an official, imperial biography written by the emperor’s close friend and associate, Abu ’l-Fazl. Begun in 1598, it took almost ten years to complete the text. Two illustrated copies of the text were produced during Akbar’s lifetime, this being the later of the two. In the numerous illustrations that accompany the text, Akbar is portrayed as a powerful, dynamic and highly heroic figure, much as he seems to have been perceived by his contemporaries.
keywords: manuscript; illustration; figural decoration; miniature painting; elephant; Jesuit; religion; ceremony, royal; warfare; battle; court
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

2de63d8c-14d0-5261-834c-c9e9983b302a.name: *Al Hammath* (Sorrel), *Rumex Pictus*
2de63d8c-14d0-5261-834c-c9e9983b302a.description: The leaves of this plant were eaten with dried fish and white rice. People still collect and eat the leaves following the annual rainfall. The plant was also valued for its therapeutic qualities, specifically its use as a pain reliever.

2e402c4d-0004-5e48-84c2-e6f4b24d7d3e.name: Bowl with dark brown slip and white slip decoration
2e402c4d-0004-5e48-84c2-e6f4b24d7d3e.short_description: This earthenware bowl was covered in a dark brown slip before receiving an as yet unread, white floriated *kufic* inscription – possibly containing blessings. The secondary motifs evoking a textured background and rim, may suggest that the bowl was inspired by a metal prototype. Vessels like this have been associated with Nishapur and Afrasiyab.
keywords: Bowl; Kufic; Ceramic; calligraphy; inscription

2f89b9bc-9361-56b1-82d3-0071ee525367.description: *Al Ooma*, sardines were fried before being eaten, or more often dried and crushed into a fine powder and eaten with rice. They were also used as fertilizer and livestock fodder.
