2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.name: Small water-basin.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.description:
On the broad border of this wide basin there are depicted, between four round medallions, scenes of courtly pleasure hunts. Three riders are shown in every scene, undertaking various hunting practices. The hunters are fighting in tournament, armed with lances, swords, bows and arrows. One rider is accompanied by a hunting cheetah on a horse. These illustrations represent a view of an idealised life. Images of riders and hunters refer not only to the riding abilities of the princes, but also to the courage, strength and perseverance of the rulers. Depictions of hunters with falcons and leopards could be referring to the immense wealth of the rulers. Only rulers such as these could afford to keep and train such expensive hunting animals, only they could hold such lavish hunting parties. This princely lifestyle reached its height during the Mamluk period. The underside of the basin is decorated with plaited bands, and arabesques, vines and birds fill the spaces in between. The decoration is finished in gold and silver inlay. The precious metal decoration gives the brass receptacle a multicoloured appearance and rich tone.  
The coat of arms of Amir Sumul Abu’l-‘Izz, who belonged to the retinue of the ruling Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun, is set at the centre of each of the round medallions. It can be only guessed that Abu’l-‘Izz commissioned the basin on the basis of a fragment of inscription. Abu’l-‘Izz and his brother Salar, viceroy of Egypt, rebelled against the Sultan and were captured and imprisoned in 1310. At the bottom of the basin, two well-wishing inscriptions are addressed to the person who commissioned it, whose identity remains unclear. Sumul Abu’l-‘Izz’s name could have been inscribed here. If it had, the basin would have been dateable to between AH 693 and 710 / AD 1293 and 1310.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.short_description: The design of this brass water-basin with gold and silver inlays shows a frieze with riders hunting or at a tournament. They are separated by four medallions holding a coat of arms typical of the Mamluk nobility. The basin was commissioned for a Mamluk *amir*.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.method_for_datation: The coat of arms suggest that the basin belonged to the patron Sumul Abu’l-'Izz. He was in the service of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun from 693 to 710 (1293–1310).
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.method_for_provenance: The Mamluk coat of arms, which establishes the identity of the basin’s patron, points towards Egypt as the country of origin.
2fe554a9-e532-5b15-814f-963ca40c1b1c.obtention: As a donation from the Berlin collector Friedrich Sarre, who bought it in 1897.

30c59814-d0f8-5ae7-87c8-2350a319fd1f.name: Men meeting in a guesthouse
30c59814-d0f8-5ae7-87c8-2350a319fd1f.description:
The coffee fireplace is located on the narrow side of the guesthouse near the entrance door, and coffee pots of various sizes adorn its cornice. Guests are offered bitter coffee as soon as they enter the typically one-room building. The pot of coffee is ready and needs only to be heated.  
If necessary to support the guesthouse, villagers bring coffee beans or coffee powder from the nearest town. Bitter coffee is also served in private households on happy and sad occasions, such as religious feasts and funerals. The use of these guesthouses in rural northeast Syria corresponds to that of the urban room type *diwan* in Damascus, the *qa’a* in Aleppo, the *mudif* in southern Iraq, and the *mafraj* in Yemen.

30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.name: Base for a tray (*sinija*)
30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.description: The *Sinija* (Tr. *sini*) is a large, round tray made of copper or brass. It was used for serving food or as a floor dining table – a *sofra* (Tr. *sofra*). tTherefore it had an important place in the shared living culture of the Ottoman Balkans among urban populations of different confessional and ethnic backgrounds. The diameter of *sinijas* sometimes reached 1–2 meters or more. When used as a floor dining table, the *sinija* was placed on a wooden or iron base. Valued for their craftsmanship, locally produced or imported *sinijas* have also found a place in the interiors of the modern age as wall decor or top parts of decorative side tables placed on custom-made bases of different styles.
30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.dates: Hegira late 13th–early 14th century / AD late 19th–early 20th century
30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material, technique, and analogy with other similar examples
30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.author: Ana Samardžić
keywords: floor dining table; carving; Ottoman Balkans.

315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.name: Ram mould.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.description:
A ram-shaped mould made from two equal parts to form the body, and another small piece that forms the head. There are four hinged joints: one on its back, one on the top of its head and two at its feet. The horns of the ram are clearly visible behind the ears.  
The object seems to have functioned as a special kind of mould used for shaping bread or cake for children. Another mould in the shape of an elephant was found along with this one.  
The ram has particular significance for Muslims. It is mentioned several times in the Qur'an in for instance, *sura* 'Al Saffat' (chapter 37, verses 102–7), where the story of Abraham's sacrifice of his son Isaac is related and how ultimately Abraham sacrificed a ram in place of his son. Within the Muslim festival calendar is that of Eid Al-Adh'ha (Greater Bairam) when a ram is sacrificed, along with other animals such as a camel, a cow or a lamb.  
Rams are also a feature of the mosaic floors found in Jordanian Byzantine-period churches. The ram is also evident on the mosaic floor of the Umayyad palace, Qasr Hallabat. A number of Islamic-period metalwork pieces are made in the form of animals.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.short_description: A cast iron mould shaped in the form of a ram from the Umayyad palace of al-Fudayn. It was found along with another mould in the shape of an elephant and they were probably meant to produce bread or cakes for children. Metalwork representing animals is common in early Islamic art.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.dimensions: Height 17 cm, width: 16.5 cm, depth 6 cm.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.method_for_datation: The object was dated by its location in the archaeological strata and also in association with pottery located close to it which was characteristically Umayyad.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.method_for_provenance: The provenance is unknown, but the mould was probably produced in Syria.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.obtention: The mould was obtained as a result of an excavation which was carried out in al-Fudayn, a site located 70 km northeast of Amman, where an Umayyad palace and a mosque were discovered.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.bibliography: Humbert, J. B., "El-Fedei-Mafraq”, in *Contribution française à l'archéologie française jordanienne*, Amman, 1989, pp.125–31.
315346db-710f-5c89-a554-c7db806dc960.author: Aida Naghawy
keywords: Metal; mould; Ransom Story; Abraham

315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.name: *Reposadero* or vat-base
315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.description:
It has a cylindrical, hollow body with a straight base and a square-shaped rim, featuring a hole that would have served as a conduit for drainage. Both the base and the rim are slightly concave, the latter also has a whitish colour that could be interpreted as calcareous remains.  
  
The decoration is concentrated on the wall and consists of an epigraphic frieze between concave mouldings with marked edges. The central frieze is stamped with the inscription al-mulk with a six-pointed star positioned above the “m”.  
Functionally, the objects are known as *reposaderos* and served as supports for large water vats, which were both placed either in the courtyard or in domestic interiors. They preserved the water from impurities and kept it fresh, while also collecting any oozes liquid. By the spout of the *reposadero*, the water was transferred to basins or other vessels and could be used for washing hands or for human consumption. Furthermore, the stamped decoration, which repeats the word "*al-mulk*" or "the power", alludes to prophylactic practices of protection and praise of God.
315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.dates: Second half of Hegira 6th century / AD 12th century
315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.method_for_datation: Art-historical and archaeological studies have demonstrated the proliferation of different types of *reposaderos* in the domestic environments of al-Andalus from the end of the Hegira 6th / AD 12th and beginning of the Hegira 7th / AD 13th centurycenturies, following oriental models (Navarro 1995). This coincides with the generalisation of stamped decoration on ceramics for everyday use.

32d8b057-33a0-5b68-b4bf-587d420f1185.name: Ford Model-T popcorn car
32d8b057-33a0-5b68-b4bf-587d420f1185.description: This extraordinary truck popularised popcorn, an American movie snack. The Columbia Buddy Company converted one of three Ford Model-Ts into a popcorn vending machine on wheels. Besides fresh buttered popcorn made with the original popcorn equipment, this crimson red vehicle would sell ice-cold sodas and roasted peanuts. Special-purpose vehicles were not unknown, as model-Ts were also transformed into ambulances and fire trucks. The popcorn wagon presented a unique marketing and entertainment opportunity within a charming circus-like aesthetic.

33362f44-34f0-5545-a2a1-056208f5dff6.name: Sahrij Swani (Basin of the Norias).
33362f44-34f0-5545-a2a1-056208f5dff6.description:
According to the Meknès historian Ibn Zaydan, Mulay Isma'il had an ornamental lake, large enough to sail pleasure boats on, built inside the *kasbah*. In fact, the 'Alawid prince, a contemporary of Louis XIV, had this lake constructed to guarantee the supply of water, in times of siege or drought, to the palaces and mosques of the town, as well as to the public baths, homes, gardens and the orchards that surrounded the town and provided for its daily fruit and vegetable requirements.  
The masterpiece of the complex known as Hri Swani, the Basin of the Norias, Sahrij Swani, is an artificial lake notable for its size (148.75 m by 319 m with a depth of 3.20 m). Three tall crenellated walls that stood around the lake have today been reduced to an isolated section of rampart located on the southwest side towards the Bani Ahmad district and the remains of the base of an enclosure wall more than 2 m thick.  
The size of the lake is reminiscent of the lakes of the Middle Atlas mountains located to the south of the town. The lake was filled from two sources:  
\- Water from the ten wells dug near the Sahrij, below the silo, brought up using ten norias and ceramic channels. Water from the wells was used at times of trouble (war, etc.) and drought.  
\- Water from the Wadi Bufekrane which descends from the Middle Atlas mountains, crosses the southern part of Meknès and feeds the lake and part of the town of Meknès.  
Today the lake attracts tourists visiting the town and also its inhabitants, who come at weekends to cool down during the summer.
33362f44-34f0-5545-a2a1-056208f5dff6.short_description: Located beside the building containing the Meknès grain silos within the enclosure wall of the Royal Palace, the Sahrij Swani lake, or Basin of the Norias, or House of the Ten Norias, was created in the AH 12th / AD 18th century. A rectangular artificial reservoir, like the one at the Menara in Marrakesh, this hydraulic structure was intended to provide water for the buildings and monuments in Mawlay Isma'il's town in times of siege. It was supplied by the ten norias (waterwheels) of the neighbouring building and surrounded by three tall crenellated walls more than 2 m thick. This site has been restored very recently.
33362f44-34f0-5545-a2a1-056208f5dff6.method_for_datation: Ibn Zaydan provides the approximate date of 1107 / 1695 in *al-Ithaf*.

33362f44-34f0-5545-a2a1-056208f5dff6.author: Mohamed Mezzine

336e6afb-8f0e-5f3a-a491-c18e56f13628.name: *Hag Al Layla'* celebration
336e6afb-8f0e-5f3a-a491-c18e56f13628.description: *Hag Al Layla'* takes place in Sha’ban, the month before Ramadan. On this night, families hand out sweets and nuts – peanuts, almonds, *meez* and *nakhi* (chickpeas) – to the neighbourhood children. The children recite *dua’as* (verbal prayers) as they collect treats inside handmade cloth bags, however, should their neighbour refuse to hand out treats they may express anger toward that person. Traditionally, women give out the sweets, which are kept in a *geffah* (palm leaf basket), while sitting outside their front door. Each child would take care to visit every house in the neighbourhood.
336e6afb-8f0e-5f3a-a491-c18e56f13628.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: shaban; ramadan; hag al layla

33fb43d3-39d9-5067-a872-1b4b9314584b.name: Covered al-Buzuriyya Market
33fb43d3-39d9-5067-a872-1b4b9314584b.description: During the Mawlid (Feast of the Birth of Prophet Muhammad), people from all over Damascus rush to buy the first gift of this occasion, the *Mulabbas*, distinguishing the capital from other Syrian cities. This sweet, made of roasted almonds coated with sugar, is linked to the emotional history of the people of the capital because it is white, symbolising new birth, as in the birth of the Prophet. Many shops in the historic Buzuriyya market in Damascus are filled with sweets and chocolates in preparation for Mawlid al-Nabawi. According to one of its makers, the *Mulabbas* industry in Damascus dates back more than 150 years, and its main sales area is centred in the historic Buzuriyya Market.

33fcf5d8-adfd-5c10-84bb-8756c9079c6e.name: Coffee set
33fcf5d8-adfd-5c10-84bb-8756c9079c6e.description: Set contains tray and six porcelain inner cups with copper handles and saucers.

3440c04d-68d2-580e-aa99-011805aecccb.name: *Dallah* (Coffee pot), *Mezallah*; serving stage smallest pot
3440c04d-68d2-580e-aa99-011805aecccb.description: This copper *dallah* goes back to a type allegedly first used in 17th-century Baghdad, and by the 19th century, there were several production centres in the Arabian peninsula. Its design cleverly reflects its functional needs. The broad base ensures stability on the fire or in the sand, whilst the large spout prevents too much coffee sediment from reaching the cup. The lid is purposely weighted to avoid it opening during the pouring process. Throughout the Near and Middle East coffee lay at the heart of social rituals and hospitality, while providing sustenance during chats, debate and political discourse in the many coffee houses in the region. In this light, the quality of the coffee served was an important indicator of both the wealth of the host and status of the guest. In continental Europe, the fashion for coffee was at its height in the 17th and 18th centuries, with coffee houses the preferred meeting places for intellectuals and artists. In Britain, meanwhile, tea soon overtook coffee in popularity, even though certain religious organisations tried to promote coffee houses for the poor in order to steer them away from public houses that primarily sold alcohol.
3440c04d-68d2-580e-aa99-011805aecccb.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
3440c04d-68d2-580e-aa99-011805aecccb.dimensions: Length: 283mm, width: 250mm, base diameter: 80mm, opening diameter: 75mm
3440c04d-68d2-580e-aa99-011805aecccb.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: dallah; coffee pot

346fd021-610d-5725-a5ab-51fb974e49fc.name: Coffee preparer and his utensils
346fd021-610d-5725-a5ab-51fb974e49fc.description:
The coffee cook usually sits next to the fireplace. The embers might be in a portable fire bowl (*mawqid* or *manqal*), or in a chimney with a smoke outlet built into the guesthouse wall (*fkhayriyya, bakhura, nafila, tafiyya*).  
The making and serving of bitter coffee follows certain rules and traditions, among them that the coffee cook serves himself first and drinks in front of the guests. The explanation given for this tradition is that the *qahwaji* wants to control both the quality and temperature of the coffee.  
The order in which guests receive their coffee was traditionally fixed, but is not necessarily followed today. The highest-ranking or eldest man received his coffee first, followed by the men sitting to the right of this person to the end of the row, then beginning again with those persons to the left of the highest-ranking person to the last one, who was often seated near the door. During funeral services, and in Damascus today, the coffee will be served counterclockwise from right to left, regardless who sits where.
346fd021-610d-5725-a5ab-51fb974e49fc.bibliography: - Myriam Ababsa. “La madâfa à Raqqa: mutation d’un lieu de sociabilité tribale en attribut de notabilité citadine ”, Géographie et cultures, L’Harmattan, 2001, 16.
346fd021-610d-5725-a5ab-51fb974e49fc.author: Karin Pütt

34f380b0-4a42-5a73-b60e-c3be05e1e957.name: Bukhara Ewer
34f380b0-4a42-5a73-b60e-c3be05e1e957.short_description:
Fine engravings of Islamic motifs such as plaited bands, rows of ellipses and floral patterns such as rose and palm scrolls cover the pear-shaped body of this copper ewer originating from Bukhara (Uzbekistan), a hub of trade and culture located on the Silk Road. Additionally, the object is engraved with the inscription of the owner’s name - Ibrahim.  
  
Because food is eaten with the hands in Arab and Persian custom, hosts would frequently offer to pour water from this vessel into a guest’s hands in a washing ceremony. Until this day, people in the region may offer an opportunity to clean one’s hands in their home or majlis. Often, guests receive soap and a fresh towel as an act of politeness and hospitality.

34f94cfa-2246-5c81-93dc-34dc25afa481.name: al-Ghuta ash-Sharqiyya
34f94cfa-2246-5c81-93dc-34dc25afa481.description:
Stainless steel trolleys are used to transport the apricot paste to the drying area in the oasis, where it is spread onto the wooden boards. In this last operation, we find the traditional gestures: the workers coat the board with olive oil, and the boss, the most experienced, spreads the paste with a sure hand and using the old measure *kayl* (about 2.5 kg) of liquid paste.  
At daybreak, the apricot paste is left to dry on boards that are placed on the open ground. From the small workshop with rudimentary equipment to today’s industrial enterprise, this vast drying area in full sun remains the essential element of the *Qamr ad-Din* installation. The dough stays in the drying area for several days until it can be peeled off in long dark orange strips at the end of the day. Strips are folded and transported to the workshops, where the second phase of preparing the *Qamr ad-Din* takes place: the dough is cleaned, cut and packaged for the local market or for export.

3618877a-1f1a-5330-864f-53d4725fe233.name: *Mokhfia* conical dish
3618877a-1f1a-5330-864f-53d4725fe233.description: This *mokhfia*, a conical dish on a short pedestal, is polychrome earthenware, with a design known as “turtle”. The example is characteristic of Moroccan ceramics in its shape and decoration.

36adfe60-d1bb-5d20-835e-c6987c2d3ca0.name: Coffee group
36adfe60-d1bb-5d20-835e-c6987c2d3ca0.description: Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving *dallah* referred to as a *mezallah*, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the *mezallah* with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
36adfe60-d1bb-5d20-835e-c6987c2d3ca0.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: coffee; beans; coffee beans

370c5dcb-5b24-584f-9109-fe182b74b751.name: Long-necked amphora
370c5dcb-5b24-584f-9109-fe182b74b751.description:
This long-necked terracotta amphora from 19th-century Algeria is a prime example of impressive Kabyle pottery. These large terracotta amphorae are distinguished by their elongated necks, multilinear decorations, and distinctive horned handles.  
Even today, Kabyle women continue the tradition of coil-building and mould pattern techniques, decorating pottery with intricate geometric designs for household use.  
Skilled artisans create vessels of diverse sizes and shapes for storing water, milk, and oil, and for cooking and dining. The amphora’s decorative motifs, in black and brick red on a yellow slip, under a glaze, bear profound symbolic significance within Amazigh culture. These patterns, deeply ingrained in the Kabyle tradition, include a distinctive U-shaped design at the centre of the vessel that corresponds to the letter "ⵓ" in the Amazigh language, pronounced "oo" as in "moo". This symbolises either the moon, representing female fertility, or a horseshoe, symbolising fidelity. The firing process not only ensures the vessel’s durability, but also enhances the vibrant colours of the glazes, showcasing the exceptional skill and craftsmanship of Kabyle artisans. These artefacts speak to the cultural heritage and linguistic richness of the Amazigh people.

3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.name: Bowl.
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.description: A bowl on a high foot-ring, painted in lustre on a white clay slip. The interior is decorated with a bold design of a robed and hooded figure, traditionally thought to be a Coptic priest, carrying a lamp or censer. Beside him stands an object often thought to be a cypress tree, but sometimes interpreted as an *ankh* or ‘key of life’ cross, an ancient Egyptian hieroglyphic sign which the Copts adapted for Christian use. The priest’s robe, his lamp, and the tree are all decorated with thin white lines scratched through the lustre to create spirals and other motifs. On the outside of the bowl, the word ‘Sa‘d’’ is written twice in *kufic* script. Oddly, the word is written in reverse, i.e. beginning with the last letter. It is unclear whether the word is a blessing (‘good luck, good fortune’) or whether it is the name of a particular craftsman or workshop. It appears on a group of similar Fatimid ceramics over a number of decades during the reign of the Caliph al-Mustansir (AH 427–87 / AD 1035–94).
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.short_description: A footed bowl painted in lustre with a picture of a robed and hooded figure holding a lamp or censer. He is a Coptic Christian priest, and his presence on such a fine object suggests the importance of this community in Fatimid Egypt.
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.method_for_datation: This bowl belongs to a group of objects which all have the word ‘Sa‘d’ painted on them. These have been assigned to the reign of the Fatimid Caliph al-Mustansir based on comparisons with other media such as textiles.
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.method_for_provenance: Cairo was the Fatimid capital and thus the likeliest place that an object of such quality would have been made.
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.obtention: In 1910 the art collector Dikran Garabed Kelekian placed his collection of Islamic ceramics on loan to the V&A.  Fifteen of the finest pieces, including this bowl, were purchased by the Museum (with the assistance of the National Art Collections Fund) after Kelekian’s death.

388b0d1b-5233-57de-a649-d3f01bcaafa3.name: Lidded Jar
388b0d1b-5233-57de-a649-d3f01bcaafa3.description: This baluster-shaped pot is typical of imperial Mughal-style production. The decoration includes the traditional Kundan technique, where the stones are foil-backed and set into metal collets using high-carat gold foil, as opposed to being soldered. The technique dates back centuries in India but gained popularity during the Mughal period (AD 1526–1858), where today it remains the most popular method of setting stones. This lidded jar is decorated almost exclusively with green enamel in the champlevé technique, which etches the metal ground with fine lines before applying and fusing the enamel to the surface. Here, a series of fine lines can be seen through the translucent green enamel. The table-cut diamonds are arranged into six foliated panels set with floral sprays. The most unusual decorative feature is the green enamelled flower at the bottom of the base, detailed with petals ascending in size from the centre.
388b0d1b-5233-57de-a649-d3f01bcaafa3.author: Tara Desjardins

3b8b9f68-e0cc-5ffc-84c6-1dee91c19a09.name: Nejjarin Funduq.
3b8b9f68-e0cc-5ffc-84c6-1dee91c19a09.description:
Although they were constructed almost one century apart, the *funduq* (caravanserai) and *seqqaya* (fountain) of the Place Nejjarine (Carpenters' Square) constitute a single social and civic entity.  
Usually erected charitably and often as an annex to a mosque, this fountain is unusually connected to a hostel.  
The Nejjarin *funduq* occupies an almost regular rectangular space and faces northeast/southwest. It is accessed through a large opening extending onto a straight hallway. Two steps give access to the courtyard. This rectangular courtyard is surrounded on all four sides by galleries that in turn lead to bedrooms of different sizes.  
There are two upper floors above the ground floor. The façades of the courtyard are symmetrical.  
The building is noteworthy for its large portal (5 m high by 3 m wide) that dominates the square and the building. The composition of the portal is uniform and harmonious. Its decoration is based on a horseshoe arch resting on two full brick pillars set into the wall. This arch is surrounded by a second poly-lobed arch in sculpted plaster, whose spandrels are tiled with *zellij* (small tiles) bearing floral, and epigraphic decoration. Above the arch there is a band bearing an inscription and a succession of arcades in sculpted plaster or wood. The ensemble is crowned by consoles that support a large canopy in sculpted wood. They are marked by series of arches resting on pillars and wooden beams.  
The interior, similar to all *funduq*, was restored in 1998 and converted into a museum of woodwork.  
The Nejjarin fountain opposite the *funduq*, located near the centre of the square, is a rectangular pool which served as a drinking trough, in particular for the horses of the customers of the *funduq*. Its upper part and the back of the pointed horseshoe arcature that rises behind it are covered with ceramic marquetry. On either side of the arcature, two demi-columns support overhanging wooden lintels and cornices.
3b8b9f68-e0cc-5ffc-84c6-1dee91c19a09.short_description: Al-Nejjarin Funduq is a *caravanserai* built in the AH 12th /AD 18th century by Sultan Mulay Isma'ïl to house the large numbers of passing merchants in Fez. Built on a rectangular site, the *funduq* is noteworthy for its gateway, which dominates the square. The ground floor was used exclusively for stabling, with the guest rooms on the first floor. At the beginning of the 20th century, the *funduq* was used as a police station by the Protectorate. It was recently restored (1998) and turned into a museum of woodwork. It stands beside a beautiful 19th-century fountain.
3b8b9f68-e0cc-5ffc-84c6-1dee91c19a09.method_for_datation: There are no dates on the monument or the fountain, but classical texts such as Ibn Zaydan's *Ithaf* date the *funduq* to 1123.

3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.name: *Peškun*
3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.description:
Hexagonal *peškun* (Tr. *peşkun*) is made of carved walnut wood. It is divided into a bottom middle part with a hexagonal plate in the form of a shelf, making two stories for storing – an upper and a lower plate. Both plates are richly decorated with interlacing floral motifs. In the center of the upper plate, there is a motif of the six-pointed star, while beneath its edges a frieze of trefoil elements is formed. Each of the six vertical sides is divided by a plate into two zones with three openings in the shape of the oriental arch each.  
*Peškun* is the name of a traditional piece of Ottoman furniture in the shape of a table or stool. It was originally meant for sitting, although it had different purposes throughout history, especially as a decorative table in Balkan oriental interiors of the 19th and of the first half of the 20th century. Over time, the larger table (in the set of usually three pieces,) began to be used as a coffee table, while the smaller ones were used as stools. *Peškun* were ordinarily made of walnut wood, ornamented with incrusted floral and geometric motifs made of mother of pearl and bone.
3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.dates: Hegira late 13th–early 14th century / AD late 19th–early 20th century
3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material, technique, and analogy with other similar examples.
3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.author: Ana Samardžić
keywords: peškun; stool; side table; carving; Ottoman Balkans

3e0c77fe-e569-53cb-a6e6-0d26f3ac626b.name: Coffee pot
3e0c77fe-e569-53cb-a6e6-0d26f3ac626b.short_description:
This copper pot has been covered in a thin layer of silver and lavishly decorated. Its swelling shape shows the influence of the European Baroque style on the Ottoman decorative arts. Most metal coffee pots were made of cheaper materials such as tinned copper. In richer homes, coffee was served to honoured guests in pots like this one, made of precious metals (or imitations of them) and decorated in the latest taste.  
The Ottoman Baroque style developed from the 1740s as artists and designers began to apply non-figurative European motifs to Ottoman forms. It flourished until the 1820s, when new types of European ornament were introduced.
3e0c77fe-e569-53cb-a6e6-0d26f3ac626b.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
keywords: coffee; metalwork; Ottoman Baroque

3e51e99d-8ff0-545e-95fc-52a15be8b042.name: *A Coffee House in Tophane*
3e51e99d-8ff0-545e-95fc-52a15be8b042.short_description: A Thomas Allom composition which appears in the first volume of Robert Walsh’s book *Constantinople and Scenery of Seven Churches of Asia Minor* is *The Coffee-House*. This is an oil copy of the composition by Civanyan. Written by Robert Walsh, who served as the private priest of British ambassador Lord Strangford after 1820, the book was published in two volumes in London in 1838. It includes engravings and the book, which was later published in French, acted as an important visual resource on Istanbul and its engravings were used as models by numerous artists. In the corresponding text, Robert Walsh provides information on the interior organisation and decoration of the coffeehouse and relates various details ranging from making music and smoking pipes to the plays of the *meddah* (storytellers).
keywords: Thomas Allom; Jivanian; Orientalism; painting; İstanbul

3ed0bda5-ca9d-536f-b3ed-1c1519674199.name:
The rocky lotus: Sumulutun  
Folio from the manuscript of *Khawass al-Ashjar* (The Characteristics of Trees)
3ed0bda5-ca9d-536f-b3ed-1c1519674199.short_description:
Born around 40 AD in Anazarbus in Cilicia (today’s Turkey), Dioscorides exerted a great influence on scholarship and practice from the Middle Ages until the 16th century. His treatise *De Materia Medica* was first translated into Syriac, a language generally familiar to physicians in the Abbasid empire (750–1258).\[1\] The earliest Arabic translation directly translated from a Greek copy\[2\] was made by two scholars, Istafan ibn Basil and Hunayn ibn Ishaq, in the mid 9th century in Baghdad under the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil (r. 847–61).1 Ibn Ishaq was a physician, Arab scientist, and Nestorian Christian. Known as the “master of translators,” he was active in the Bayt al-Hikm (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad.  
According to sources, in 948, Byzantine Emperor Romanus I offered a Greek copy of *De Materia Medica* as a gift to the Umayyad caliph of Cordoba, ‘Abd al-Rahman III (912-961). There is no evidence to suggest a full Arabic translation of this copy was ever made in Cordoba.\[3\] In the intervening years, both the Greek text and accompanying illustrations continued to undergo revision as new copies were made.  
A famous Arabic copy made in the first quarter of the 13th century was widely recopied and distributed and is now dispersed throughout many private and public collections, including the Aga Khan Museum Collection. Known as the Khawass al-Ashjar, it describes the fabrication of medicines from some 500-600 plants; animals, like fish and shellfish; and minerals that serve as the basis for pharmacology in Near Eastern countries and beyond.
3ed0bda5-ca9d-536f-b3ed-1c1519674199.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

\[2\] Ibid.  
\[3\] Ibid., 9.  
  
Bloom, Jonathan, “The introduction of Paper to the Islamic Lands and the development of the illustrated Manuscripts,” *Muqarnas*, 17 (2000): 17–23. ISBN: 9789004116696.

3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.name: Ewer.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.description:
A ewer made of copper and inlaid with silver. Decorated with ornamentation and inscriptions in *naskhi* script; the text reads: 'The honourable Excellency, Tabtaq. Glory to his triumph'. Blazons decorate the surface of the ewer, bearing depictions of a goblet, thereby alluding to the position of cupbearer. Adorning the upper section of the ewer's body is a decorative band featuring a series of prominent roundels inside each of which is depicted a pair of confronting birds. The mouth is decorated with vegetal motifs and is equipped with a two-hinge cover and a strainer, which sits inside the mouth. The spout of the ewer has three decorative bands: the middle one carries propagandistic inscriptions in the *naskhi* script, while the other two are adorned with diamond-shaped units filled with vegetal motifs. The name on the ewer dates back to Amir Tabtaq, one of the elite officers of al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, who ruled from AH 689–93 / AD 1290–4. Tabtaq was Governor of the City of Qus in Upper Egypt during the third reign of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. A.H. 709–41 / AD 1309–40).  
The crafting of ewers was an industry that flourished in Iran; it then transferred to Iraq and from there to Egypt, during the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods. The different forms of ewers and the roles that they played were manifold; they were used to pour water for bathing, for hand-washing, or for *wudu* (obligatory ablutions before prayer). However, ornamental ewers were used to decorate the palaces and houses of *amirs* and sultans.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.short_description: The importance of this ewer stems from its fine decoration. It bears the name of Amir Tabtaq, a follower of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, and a cup blazon, the emblem of his post as cupbearer. Ewers came to Egypt and Iraq from Persia and took many shapes. They were used in palaces and houses for bathing, hand-washing and obligatory ablutions.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.dimensions: Height 40 cm, diameter (of base) 15 cm; diameter (of mouth) 10 cm.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.method_for_datation: The ewer is dated based on the name that it carries: Amir Tabtaq, who was one of the officers of al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, and the Governor of the City of Qus, during the third reign of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. A.H. 709–41 / AD 1309–40).
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.method_for_provenance: The ewer was crafted in Egypt, specifically for Amir Tabtaq, a fact verified by the inscription. Furthermore it was uncovered during an archaeological excavation in the Egyptian City of Qus. Likewise, the technique of inlay used is typical of the style that flourished in Egypt during the Mamluk period.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.obtention: This piece was uncovered during the course of archaeological excavations in the City of Qus in Egypt in 1966.

3f5acf05-17af-5634-925f-1feecdda3b69.name: Tray (*sinija*)
3f5acf05-17af-5634-925f-1feecdda3b69.description:
The term *sinija* (Tr. sini) refers to a large circular brass or copper tray, that functioned as a low table on which food and beverages were served.  
This large, circular plate is decorated with the court life theme. In the center of the composition is a large scene depicting the ruler on the throne, surrounded by courtiers, servants, musicians, and dancers, with small tables with jugs and cups. The central scene is encircled with small medallions with seated human figures in each of them. The background is filled with floral and vegetal patterns, as in the case of the next decorative band. In that band, there are twelve roundels with alternately combined court life scenes and inscriptions – verses from Omar Khayyam's Rubaiyat and Ghazaliyat of Hafiz. Next to the raised sides and lobbed rim is the last decorative frieze, with medallions with, again, seated human figures and animals.  
Inscriptions in medallions:

3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.name: Wellhead
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.description:
Wellhead in the shape of an external octagonal and internal semicircular prism, made of sifted reddish clay on which various decorative motifs have been stamped and complemented with green glaze. On a circular and smooth base, a prismatic shape rises, which is reinforced by the moldings that vertically decorate each of the walls, ending at the top with lobed modillions. Two decorative motifs alternate on its eight fronts. The first consists of a decoration of quadrilobed flowers included in a rhomboidal pattern, in the manner of the sebka network, all glazed in green and bordering its contours with manganese oxide. The second has a trilobed arch, whose central lobe is a sharp pointed horseshoe arch, and which houses a decoration with a mirror pseudoepigraphic motif ending in palmettes that end in a twisted stem. It ends, under the mouth of the border, with two borders: the lower one with a stamped seven-point star decoration, on which three bands with incised zig-zag lines and a central one with knife-corded thread, and the upper one contains a inscription in florid Kufic, transcribed by Sahwki Zayed (2015) as *at-tawfiq*, "The Providence", repeated five times on each side of the octagon. The presence of this inscription is confirmed in numerous Almohad works, and is common in the Merinid and Mudéjar works, but not in the Nasrid works. Its upper edge, thickened on the outside and rectangular in profile, is octagonal and smooth.  
  
Such wellheads can be understood within the broader development of water management systems in al-Andalus. Methods and objects were introduced and disseminated to optimise the water usage, an essential resource that significantly shaped everyday life. As part of these innovations, systems for water collection, distribution, and storage were devised. Among these, wells played a key role in accessing underground water, and wellheads such as this one were installed both in public spaces and in domestic courtyards.
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.initial_owner: Unknown / Daniel Aguilera Camacho (owner of the Córdoba house)
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.method_for_datation: The techniques of stamping and the *cuerda seca* technique (original and innovative technique, created in al-Andalus at the end of the 10th century that will continue to be used in later centuries), become widespread and reach their best expression in the AH 6th - 7th / AD 12th–13th centuries. Decorative motifs such as stars are frequent in pieces from the Almohad, Mudejar and Nasrid periods, throughout the AH 6th - 8th / 12th–14th centuries.
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.method_for_provenance: The stamping and the dry rope techniques (which were created in al-Andalus at the end of the 10th century and would continue to be used long afterwards) became widespread and reached their best expression in the Hegira 6th–7th / AD 12th–13th centuries. Decorative motifs such as stars are frequent in pieces from the Almohad, Mudéjar and Nasrid periods throughout the Hegira 6th–8th / AD 12th–14th centuries.

40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.name: Bowl with horseman.
40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.description:
The main decoration of the bowl consists of a large figure of a horseman, whose face clearly shows some Mongol features, on a background filled with plant shoots in relief.  
The decoration is characterised by a particularly delicate and elegant design painted in polychrome, with each colour requiring a separate firing.  
This piece belongs to a type known as *mina’i*’, in Persian ‘*haftrang*’(‘seven colours’). This technique effectively uses seven colours (red, blue, green, yellow, gold, white and black) applied on top of the glaze and occasionally, as in this case, with some details worked in relief and gilded.
40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.short_description: This piece belongs to a type of ceramic known as *mina’i*, recognisable through the use of seven colours in its decoration. In antiquity, the main centre of production for *mina’i* ceramics was Kashan in central northern Iran.
40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.method_for_provenance: *Mina’i* ceramics were mainly produced in Kashan (central northern Iran) and in all probability would have been made by the illuminators of the manuscripts produced at that time that were lost with the Mongol invasion of 1220. Consequently, they are an important historical document for the study of illuminations of that time.

40301340-cb49-5d31-8fc4-0266c8f1e953.name: *Medbasa* (Dibs/date-molasses Extraction Room)
40301340-cb49-5d31-8fc4-0266c8f1e953.description: Many markets in the UAE had medbasas, which were special rooms that contained grooves in the floor for collecting *dibs* (date molasses). Date palm leaf bags full of dates were piled on top of each other above the grooved floor. The combined weight of the bags pressed molasses out of the dates. The molasses drained between the grooves and into a pot where it could be collected and sold. Several *medabasa* rooms still exist in Sharjah and can be visited at Al Hisn (Fort) Museum and Souq Shinasiyya.

4045cd73-fd45-55dc-bfc3-29df4bf6d174.name: Lidded bowl (*sahan*)
4045cd73-fd45-55dc-bfc3-29df4bf6d174.description: A deep bowl on a rounded foot, with lid – *sahan* (Ar. *sân*) – was used for serving food. The bell-shaped lid is decorated with vegetal and geometric motives, with a small, circular, star-like handle on the top. The same type of leafy, vegetal pattern is engraved on the bowl.

41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.name: Pear-shaped bottle.
41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.description:
This piece is distinguished by its fine decoration painted in white, red and black with gold leafing on a blue background (*lajvard* in Persian, ‘lapis lazuli’) consisting of tiny stylised spiral motifs, large gold-leaf poly-lobed medallions and geometric decoration.  
Unlike *mina’i* ceramics, the decoration on lajvardina ceramics is mostly non-figurative and is characterised by the presence of floral, calligraphy and geometric motifs. This type of ceramic was used to produce elegant long-neck vases, polygon-sided recipients, cylindrical containers and diamond- or cross-shaped tiles.
41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.short_description: This bottle is recognisable as an example of the type known as ‘lajvardina’ by its white, red and black paint with gold leaf on a blue base. This latter gives the style its name, as *lajvard* mean lapis lazuli in Persian.
41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.method_for_datation: Lajvardina work has been dated using the famous treatise of the techniques of Islamic ceramicists written by Abûl Qâsim of Kashan in 1301. By that time, the *mina’i* ceramic technique was no longer in use, with Kashan ceramicists appearing to prefer the lajvardina technique. Production of these ceramics must therefore have started before 1301, as suggested by archeological finds at Takht-i Sulayman in northwest Persia from the excavations recently carried out in the Palace of Abaka-Khan (1265–81).

41ddc5d1-7460-5d12-80ee-4872e35c50e0.name: Incense Burner
41ddc5d1-7460-5d12-80ee-4872e35c50e0.short_description:
This bird-shaped incense burner would waft fragrance throughout homes, reception areas and mosques in Iran. Often hosts would sprinkle scented water over the censers for religious or ceremonial occasions.  
  
The province of Khurasan became known for intricate and distinct metalwork during the early Islamic Seljuq dynasty (12th - 13th centuries). Borrowing influences from Sassanid Persia and blending in new approaches to metalwork, the school of Khurasan produced candlesticks and incense burners in animal and bird shapes.  
  
While birds symbolize freedom, heaven and the power of soul over body in Islam, the feathered animal bestowed good fortune upon its owner in the Seljuq era. The censer displays words about nature in old *Saljuqi* calligraphy. Today the pigeon-appearing burner represents the unique class of zoomorphic metalwork with enduring influences on enchanted objects transformed into animals.

4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.name: Hexagonal dinner stand.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.description:
This piece assumes the shape of a hexagonal (six-sided) pedestal upon which dinner trays would be placed; it is therefore known as a dinner stand. Its top surface, which is also hexagonal in shape, has a central circular decoration comprising a radiating inscription in a plaited *kufic* script. The radiating form of the inscription increases its decorative impact as it appears to simulate the rays of the sun coming from a central medallion, in which the artist has inscribed the name of Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, for whom this table was probably made. Framing the surface of this piece, is an inscription in Mamluk *thuluth* script which includes the name of the sultan and a number of his titles, it reads: 'Glory to our lord the Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir al-'Alam, al-'Adil, al-Mujahid, al-Murabit, al-Muthaghir, al-Mu'ayyad, al-Mansur, the Sultan of Islam and the Muslims, the Destroyer of Apostates and Infidels, the Reviver of Justice to all, the Protector of the oppressed against the oppressors, the Protector of the Muslim community, the Protector of worldly and spiritual matters, ibn al-Sultan al-Malik al-Mansur Qalawun Al-Salihi'. And surrounding these inscriptions along the interior are a series of lobed semi-circles decorated with flying ducks that are distinguished by their vitality and movement.  
Each of the six sides of the pedestal's surfaces is comprised of four decorated panels arranged vertically one on top of the other. In the centre of one of these panels is a small door with two arched leafs which open to reveal an internal shelf. The panels are ornamented with openwork arabesque designs, composed of intertwining vegetal leaves and stems, lotus blossoms, and epigraphic inscriptions in *thuluth* script, on a background of openwork decorative motifs. The table has six short 'supports', posts that rest on the legs. A series of inscriptions are recorded on them, which indicate the name of the craftsman and his titles the English translation of which reads: 'Made by the poor slave hopeful of his God's forgiveness, known as the son of the teacher professor Muhammad, son Sunqur al Baghdadi al-Sanqari, in the year AH 728 \[1327\] in the days of our lord al-Malik al-Nasir, glory to his triumph'.  
Such objects, although used extensively as stands for food trays, were also used to carry the Qur'an or torches at night in mosques or palaces, as well as to carry drinks, vases and incense burners. It is possible that this pedestal, which belonged to al-Nasir Muhammad, had been used to carry these types of items in his private palace or in his *madrasa* which was built on the street of the coppersmiths *(Shari' Nahhāsin)* in Cairo. This supposition is made more likely in view of the fact that the object was recovered from the Bimaristan (hospital) of al-Mansur Qalawun, which is adjacent to the Madrasa of al-Nasir Muhammad.  
The dinner stand is one of the most valuable acquisitions in the collections of the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo for it demonstrates the prolific production of metalwork in the Mamluk period. The importance of this particular piece stems from its having been crafted specifically for Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, not to mention the fact that it contains the name of the craftsman who made it along with the date of manufacture. Its exceptional quality is magnified when its splendour and size are considered.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.short_description: This type of table, made from metal or wood, was extensively produced during the Mamluk period in Cairo. It was used to hold food or items that need to be elevated from the floor. This table is made of brass inlaid with silver on which the name and titles of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad and the maker's name were inscribed.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.initial_owner: Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who reigned three times: AH 693–4 / AD 1294–5; AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309; AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.method_for_datation: This piece can be dated based on the inscription it carries, which includes the name of the craftsman who made it and the date it was manufactured. This is in addition to the inscriptions on the piece which specifically name Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.method_for_provenance:
It is highly probable that the piece was crafted in Cairo, especially in view of the fact that it is decorated with epigraphic inscriptions in Mamluk *thuluth* script, a style prevalent in Mamluk pieces attributed to Egypt. Additionally, the design technique used in its manufacture and the decoration, closely resemble those used in a number of other objects known to have been made in Egypt, including a box (for a Qur'an manuscript) made of copper and inlaid with gold and silver, currently housed in the library of al-Azhar Mosque, which bears the name of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun and is dated 723 (1322). There is an almost identical box in the collections at the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin, known to have been taken from a mosque in Cairo; this is inscribed with the name of the same craftsman as the pedestal under discussion here: Muhammad ibn Sunqur al-Baghdadi. There is also a silver inlaid candlestick currently in the collections of the Islamic Art Museum in Cairo (reg. no. 15080) which bears the name of Sultan al-Nasir ibn Muhammad ibn Qalawun.  
Furthermore, in Cairo during the Mamluk period there was a *suq* dedicated to the manufacture and sale of inlaid metalwork. The author and historian al-Maqrizi refers to the market in his work *al-Khitat* (1853) as 'the *suq* of the inlay craftsmen' (Suq al-Koftiyin), which was located in a street that in present-day Cairo lies between al-Ghuriyya Street and al-Azhar Street. The market's documented presence further supports the supposition that this piece was crafted in Cairo.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.obtention: This piece was transferred from the Bimaristan of Sultan al-Mansur Qalawun to the Museum of Islamic Art. It was one of the first pieces to enter the collections at the time of the inauguration of the Museum in 1903.

43af2c13-f67f-56c2-8949-67eff891e370.name: Rosewater sprinkler
43af2c13-f67f-56c2-8949-67eff891e370.short_description:
This rosewater sprinkler belongs to a group of brassware that has sculpturally shaped motifs as its most distinctive decorative element.  
The most monumental pieces are a group of large candlesticks. But despite their size, they are surpassed by this masterfully executed bottle when it comes to decoration. Ten lions, and six birds were embossed in incredibly high relief and furthermore engraved and punched.
43af2c13-f67f-56c2-8949-67eff891e370.dates: Hegira 2nd half of the 6th century / AD 2nd half of the 12th century
keywords: Rosewater sprinker; Animal decoration; Ghurid; Metalwork
materials: Embossed, engraved, and punched brass, inlaid with copper and silver

43ffaf04-43ad-5080-a54a-5966af0905ea.name: Rosewater sprinkler
43ffaf04-43ad-5080-a54a-5966af0905ea.description: This *mirash* vessel is designed to hold and sprinkle rosewater onto the hands of guests as a sign of hospitality. These vessels come in a variety of shapes and decorations; the people of the Green Mountain in eastern Oman have traditionally pursued this craft for thousands of years, and their goods are known today for their quality and precision in manufacturing.
43ffaf04-43ad-5080-a54a-5966af0905ea.holder: The National Museum - Sultanate of Oman
43ffaf04-43ad-5080-a54a-5966af0905ea.author: Noora Al Balushi

48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.name: Large tray (*s’ni*).
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.description:
The decoration on this circular tray is arranged in concentric bands encircling a rosette with many petals. The first band is adorned with stylised leaves, followed by another band that is wider and engraved with alternating vegetal elements representing the cypress tree, as well as arabesque medallions. A signature in cursive lettering carries the name of the owner, 'sahibihi Al-Hadj Ibrahim (Zaytuna)' and, composed in Indian numerals, the date of the object's fabrication, 1156; which can be translated as: 'its owner al-Hadj Ibrahim (Zaytuna) 1156' (AD 1743). The last letter of the word *sahibihi*, which surrounds the whole of the inscription, ends in the form of a tulip, in imitation of the *tughra* (the signature of the Ottoman sultans). The third band features interweaving foliar ornaments enclosing small rosettes, and the last band features semi-circular arches adorned with flowers.  
In former times, the *s'ni* would be placed on a small painted wooden table as a means of serving the different daily meals. It is still used in Algeria.
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.short_description: Large circular dish decorated with concentric incised circles around a central rosette with several petals. The decoration in the gaps is mainly plant-based. A signature in cursive characters states the name of the owner and the date when the piece was made.
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.method_for_datation: According to the date on the object.
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.method_for_provenance: Algiers was the main manufacturing centre for this type of brassware.
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.bibliography:

Marçais, G., *Le musée Stéphane Gsell, musée des antiquités et d'art musulman d'Alger*, Algiers, 1950.
48232ccd-b83a-5ed3-a7ae-09f26487f289.author: Ali Benbella
keywords: Tray; copper; cypress; vegetal decoration; food; brass

4859f5a8-7af7-59f7-8271-982ef083627b.name: *Fellahs* (peasants) use a *shadouf* to draw water from the Nile from a well.
4859f5a8-7af7-59f7-8271-982ef083627b.short_description: Ernest Benecke (1817–1894), a French photographer of Anglo-German origins, was one of the first to be interested in the people rather than the monuments he saw during his travels in the Middle East. His pictures foreground daily life, as we can see from this photograph, which was taken in Egypt and shows a traditional mode of irrigation using the *shadouf*, a weighted appliance which allowed water to be poured from a well over a field.
keywords: Irrigation; Egypt

48bdc968-6993-58b8-bc33-10fac1289cbd.name: Showing how to roast the coffee beans
48bdc968-6993-58b8-bc33-10fac1289cbd.description:
After roasting and crushing the coffee beans, the equally complex cooking begins. The coarse coffee powder is boiled down in a large quantity of water.  
“In the meantime, the three *dells* (tinned copper pots with handle and lid) are put in readiness. The first and largest of these, containing either pure water or water with old coffee grounds, is put on the fire and heated until it boils. The swirling contents are then poured into the second container, which contains the ground coffee that has just been crushed; this second container is then placed on the fire (for about ten minutes), and carefully prevented from overflowing, until no more foam rises and the grounds remain completely boiled on the bottom. In the meantime, the landlord will have fetched some beans of *hêl* (cardamom.) and given them to be pounded in a mortar. The *hêl* is then thrown into the third *delleh* and the contents of the second are poured on top. This third pot is put on the fire again for a short time, but soon is put to one side so all the sediment settles finely on the bottom.” Formerly in some regions the coffee was strained through a piece of palm cloth inserted into the pot. But usually it is enough to let the coffee grounds settle, before the *qahwaji* pours the coffee into the serving pot (*masabb, delle*), from which the small cups can be filled with the three sips. Often the *masabb* is set on the edge of the embers to keep the coffee hot.
48bdc968-6993-58b8-bc33-10fac1289cbd.bibliography:
al-Hroub, I., Atlas of Palestine Rural Heritage, Bethlehem, 2015, 139.  
  
Blunt, A., “Bedoun Tribes of the Euphrates“, 1879 New York, 123.  
  
Euting, J., "Tagebuch einer Reise in Inner-Arabien" (First edition Leiden 1896), Hamburg, 1993, 84.  
  
Kalter, J., “Die Kultur der Nomaden”, Kalter, J., Pavaloi, M., Zerrnickel, M. (eds), “Syrien – Mosaik eines Kulturaumes”, Stuttgart, 1991, 130, photo 308.
48bdc968-6993-58b8-bc33-10fac1289cbd.author: Karin Pütt

49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.name: Dates group
49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.description:
As a sign of hospitality guests are given *fuala* (light refreshments). Coffee, dates, *betheetha* (a sweet made of dates and fired flour), *khabees* (a sweet made of saffron, ghee and fried flour), leavened bread, and *dibs* (date molasses) were served on a *saroud* (palm mat) and covered with a *mechabeh* (palm food cover) to protect the food from dirt and insects.  
When guest finished eating they were offered a *ghasool* (a bowl of water) or a *maghsal al yad* (pitcher and vessel) to wash their hands. At the end of a visit, guests were perfumed with a *merash* (perfume sprinkler) filled with rose water and other fragrances. Guest were also perfumed with '*oud* incense'.
49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab

49271df4-3589-5288-9f2d-848a3ad34181.name: Cup
49271df4-3589-5288-9f2d-848a3ad34181.description: Cup decorated with a series of lozenges with floral and leaf motifs. In the center a circular medallion dispays three fish and the number 25.
49271df4-3589-5288-9f2d-848a3ad34181.bibliography: Moratiou , M. (ed), *The Mando & Londos Oeconomides Collection of Coloured Glass*, Athens: Benaki Museum, 2013: cat. no. 17, p. 62.
49271df4-3589-5288-9f2d-848a3ad34181.author: Mina Moraitou

493fd5de-9ad8-584b-b87f-0c109a23012d.name: Tile Plate
493fd5de-9ad8-584b-b87f-0c109a23012d.description: The plate is coated with white clay and slip decorated with shades of grey and blue beneath a transparent colourless glaze. The plate’s scalloped, rimmed interior is adorned with a large medallion featuring flowers and leafy curling branches. The body is divided vertically into thirteen sections separated by grooves, each section decorated with a floral bouquet. The wide rim is encircled by a curving vine of alternating large and small flowers and leaves. The back of the plate is embellished with floral bouquets. The motifs are delineated in dark cobalt blue. Examples of this technique can be observed in the dull grey-blue flowers used in Chinese-influenced Iznik ceramics and pointed leaves seen on late 15th-century Ming porcelain. The production of plates in this style continued until the second half of the 16th century. In form and decoration these plates resemble Chinese porcelain of the Early Ming, Hsuan-te period (1426–1435).
493fd5de-9ad8-584b-b87f-0c109a23012d.dates: Hegira second quarter of the 10th century / AD first quarter of the 16th century

49b2df90-5908-57b9-bdfe-fdda5ade09fe.name: *Mehmaas* (Coffee roasting stirrer)
49b2df90-5908-57b9-bdfe-fdda5ade09fe.description:
*Mehmaas* (Coffee roaster) used to stir roasting coffee beans.  
Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *aljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving *dallah* referred to as a *mezallah*, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the *mezallah* with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
49b2df90-5908-57b9-bdfe-fdda5ade09fe.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
49b2df90-5908-57b9-bdfe-fdda5ade09fe.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: roaster; stirrer; coffee; coffee beans

4a2ff8cf-3035-5df6-b37d-f996ba871f8d.name: Illustrated manuscript of Sa'di's *Bustan*
4a2ff8cf-3035-5df6-b37d-f996ba871f8d.short_description: This illustrated manuscript of Sa‘di’s *Bustan* features a spurious colophon and four paintings, presumably all by the early twentieth-century artist Turabi Bek Khurasani. Turabi Bek was active during the first decades of the twentieth century – the final years of the Qajar dynasty. As confirmed by the paintings in this *Bustan*, some of which recall those in the renowned *Haft Awrang* of Jami (Mashhad, 1556–65) in the Freer Gallery of Art, he excelled in the Safavid revival style.
4a2ff8cf-3035-5df6-b37d-f996ba871f8d.type: Islamic, Indian & Southeast Asian works of art; manuscript
4a2ff8cf-3035-5df6-b37d-f996ba871f8d.holder: Shangri La, Doris Duke Foundation for Islamic Art
4a2ff8cf-3035-5df6-b37d-f996ba871f8d.dates: Hegira early 14th century / AD early 20th century (spurious colophon dated 779 AH / 1377 AD)
keywords: manuscript; Sa'di; Bustan; Turabi Bek Khurasani; Safawid revival; illustration; revivalism
materials: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper; gilded leather binding

4a7d2384-96d3-5574-ba51-84cb41cd1805.name: *Madkhan* (Incense burner)
4a7d2384-96d3-5574-ba51-84cb41cd1805.description: The burning of incense is part of the routine for welcoming a guest. A *Mmadkhan* (incense burner) is used to hold a smouldering piece of charcoal on which incense is placed. The heat causes incense to burn thus, releasing its scent. The *madkhan* is passed around from person to person to share and perfume their clothing.
4a7d2384-96d3-5574-ba51-84cb41cd1805.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
4a7d2384-96d3-5574-ba51-84cb41cd1805.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: incense; incense burner; ceramic

4b5af6a4-7de4-5e18-87de-8bf5e62763db.name: Dish
4b5af6a4-7de4-5e18-87de-8bf5e62763db.description: The Orientalism or Neo-Mudéjar style gave new light to old techniques such as ceramic with lustre decoration; the Manises workshops begun again to use lustre decorations and shapes from the Middle Age period.
4b5af6a4-7de4-5e18-87de-8bf5e62763db.author: Manuel Alonso
keywords: Neo-mudejar style; Applied Arts

4b991957-3850-5dff-ab19-d438bef7536d.name: Pre-Islamic ewer with female figures
4b991957-3850-5dff-ab19-d438bef7536d.short_description:
This silver-gilt ewer was made in Pre-Islamic times during the Sassanid dynasty. Four dancing female figures are depicted on the vessel’s pear-shaped body, each holding a ceremonial object. The women are framed by embossed arches and accompanied by birds. The neck of the vessel is decorated with a vine-leaf pattern.  
The iconography of dancing female figures is often associated with the maenads, attendants of the god Dionysus in Greek mythology. As the vessel is from the Sassanid dynasty, the link to Greek mythology is uncertain. It has been suggested that the motif of dancing figures originated in the Iranian cult of the goddess Anahita, where the ewer could have been used to serve wine during court celebrations or religious ceremonies. There is no evidence, however, to support this hypothesis.
4b991957-3850-5dff-ab19-d438bef7536d.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar objects e.g. the Sassanian ewer (67.10 a, b) in the collection of The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
4b991957-3850-5dff-ab19-d438bef7536d.bibliography:
Lebas, F., Lienert, U. and Rowinski, S., "Erwerbungen für die Asien-Sammlungen in den Jahren 1988 bis 1990,” *Jahrbuch des Museums für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg*, 9/10 (1990-1): 253-286.  
Luckhardt, U. and Heitmann, B., *Kunst für Hamburg von laut bis leise; 50 Jahre Stiftung für die Hamburger Kunstsammlungen*, Hamburg: Stiftung für die Hamburger Kunstsammlungen, 2006.
keywords: Metalwork; Sasanid

4bc307ac-f977-5e18-aec7-21b9827679aa.name: Cup with turned-out rim
4bc307ac-f977-5e18-aec7-21b9827679aa.description: Several examples of this type of tumbler with a wide rim are known and variously decorated. They belong to the production of Syrian and Egyptian workshops at the time of the Ayyubid sultans (1169-1260). This one bears an incomplete circular band with the calligraphic inscription in *naskhei*: “\[…\] glory to the sultan our master \[…\]”.
4bc307ac-f977-5e18-aec7-21b9827679aa.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute

4bccb3e9-a964-52ef-937f-7a6d6e11e5cf.name: *Interior of a house in Boussaada*
4bccb3e9-a964-52ef-937f-7a6d6e11e5cf.short_description: This painting, showing the interior of a traditional house in the Boussaada region, elicits a certain intimacy, recalling the muted atmosphere also evoked by Guillaumet's *Fileuse*. The nervous, moving brushstrokes and his use of melted or soldered lead are clear references to the style of the Dutch masters.
4bccb3e9-a964-52ef-937f-7a6d6e11e5cf.author: Dalila Orfali
keywords: Orientalism

4c1bace8-ab18-5e91-a949-35cf6a8187e1.name: Mevlevi Dining Table (*Somat*)
4c1bace8-ab18-5e91-a949-35cf6a8187e1.description: The term *somat* (feast table) was used to describe the table where Mevlevis ate. Spoons would be placed face down to indicate the dervishes’ gratitude and to prevent the contents from being seen. A pinch of salt was placed in front of everyone. When the food had been cooked, Kazancı Dede would bring the cauldron to the table and open its lid. After reciting a prayer, those present would invoke the name of Allah Hu.
4c1bace8-ab18-5e91-a949-35cf6a8187e1.bibliography: Bakırcı, Naci, *Konya Mevlana Müzesi*, Istanbul: BKG Yayinlari, 2010.

4c9c682b-e3ff-589b-807b-5e22f9819c18.name: Tankard
4c9c682b-e3ff-589b-807b-5e22f9819c18.description: A cylindrical tankard with one handle. The body is decorated with a series of white flowers with a blue centre and green leaves on a red ground. On the top and bottom there is a band in the form of a chain. The handle is decorated in blue and white.
4c9c682b-e3ff-589b-807b-5e22f9819c18.bibliography: Carswell, J., Gibson, M. (ed.), and Moraitou , M., *Iznik Ceramics at the Benaki Museum*, London: Gingko, and Athens: Benaki Museum, 2023: cat. no. 58, p. 112.
4c9c682b-e3ff-589b-807b-5e22f9819c18.author: Mina Moraitou

4d271fb9-86f6-54f6-8ff7-b1f5b8365eb6.name: Plate
4d271fb9-86f6-54f6-8ff7-b1f5b8365eb6.description: White clay and slip, decorated in yellow, green, blue, red and manganese purple tones under transparent glaze. The motifs are outlined in black. On the plate’s surface a female figure is seen from the front in a garden. She is wearing a yellow robe and blue and white striped shalwar. The shalwar, a garment of traditional Turkish origin, was made from the fabric called *selimiye*, which was widely worn in the Ottoman Empire during the second half of the 18th century. Figures depicted on Kütahya ceramics sometimes are presented in a schematic manner in traditional Ottoman attire. Female figures on these plates, which were mainly produced for export in the late 18th century, were sometimes referred to as concubines. In the years following the proclamation of the Republic, these plates, colloquially referred to as *kızlı tabak*, were included in the dowries of girls who were about to be married.
4d271fb9-86f6-54f6-8ff7-b1f5b8365eb6.dates: Hegira second half of the 12th century / AD Second half of the 18th century

4f35a232-fd44-5945-a2d3-5c34f4b1ae6a.name: Incense burner
4f35a232-fd44-5945-a2d3-5c34f4b1ae6a.description: Incense burners like this are usually made of clay mixed with water and kneaded until it forms a mixture that can then be shaped. The burner is then adorned with engravings, intricate drawings, and different colors. The incense burners are then fired in a kiln, after which they are ready for use. Note the handle; it makes the burner safe to carry from room to room. Incense occupies a central place in Omani life, as the passing of a fragrant burner at the end of a visit is customary in every region of the country.
4f35a232-fd44-5945-a2d3-5c34f4b1ae6a.holder: The National Museum - Sultanate of Oman
4f35a232-fd44-5945-a2d3-5c34f4b1ae6a.author: Noora Al Balushi

4ff662e6-ce17-5b02-96f0-77d7ed40404e.name: *Shahnameh by Firdowsi* (Sassanid Emperor Anushirvan Feasting)
4ff662e6-ce17-5b02-96f0-77d7ed40404e.description: The work begins with praise written in the centre of a multicoloured gilded illumination on a navy blue background on facing pages. All pages containing the eulogy and inscriptions on the pages with miniatures are illuminated in the style of Beynes Sudûr. All chapters in the *Shahnameh* begin with the illumination of the title page. The white text written above and below the miniatures and enclosed in an illuminated frame at the end of the *Shahnameh* states that the *Shahnameh*, which tells the history of Persia, was completed in seven years, that 12 of the most famous artists of the period worked on it, and that it was written by Mehmed al-Kâtib in Shiraz. The illumination of the work was by Mehmed bin Hüseyin of Shiraz in 1549. The book, one of the most distinguished works of the period, is notable for its intricate miniatures created in a superior technique characteristic of the Shah Tahmasb period. These miniatures were made by calligraphers and *musehhep* in Shiraz, for centuries a centre of the art of miniatures. Consequently, the decorative style of the Shiraz-Turkmen miniature school, evident in works created in Shiraz during the first half of the 16th century, is also noteworthy in this work. It is characterised by thin, elongated and elegant figures.
4ff662e6-ce17-5b02-96f0-77d7ed40404e.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
4ff662e6-ce17-5b02-96f0-77d7ed40404e.obtention: Brought to the museum in 1915 from the Pertevniyal Valide Sultan Library.
materials: Finished (*aharli*) paper, ink, gilding, leather binding

50900128-bb54-580c-9129-d9d24be9c5ef.name: Ten folios from the *Shahnamah* of Firdawsi made for Shah Tahmasp I
50900128-bb54-580c-9129-d9d24be9c5ef.short_description:
The ten folios come the *Shahnamah* made for the Safavid ruler, Shah Tahmasp I (r. 1524–1576). One of the finest illustrated Persian manuscript ever made, it has been referred to as the ‘Houghton’ *Shahnamah* after the collector who broke it up in New York in the 1970s. It is of large format, on fine gold-sprinkled paper, and with 258 illustrations. The format is independently conceived for each painting and must have involved constant consultation between scribes, painters and marginators. Folio 516, which in the Khalili Collection, is the only folio in the manuscript to bear a date.  
The manuscript was given by Shah Tahmasp to the Ottoman Sultan Selim II at the time of the latter’s accession in 1566. By 1903, the manuscript was in the possession of Edmond de Rothschild. It changed hands once again in the 1960s, when its then owner, Arthur Houghton Jr, began to disperse it. Today, some 140 of its paintings are in museums and collections throughout the world. The rest of the manuscript – the binding, the text block and 118 paintings – have been in the Contemporary Art Museum in Tehran since 1994.
50900128-bb54-580c-9129-d9d24be9c5ef.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art
50900128-bb54-580c-9129-d9d24be9c5ef.method_for_datation: Date and provenance are based on information within the paintings themselves, on historical records and on numerous detailed studies by a number of academics and authors.
50900128-bb54-580c-9129-d9d24be9c5ef.obtention:
Folio 119 only: ex-Edmond de Rothschild; Arthur Houghton Jr, Diane Woodner and Andrea Woodner; Christie’s, London, sale of 27 April 1993, lot 71.  
Remaining 9 folios: ex-Edmond de Rothschild, Arthur Houghton Jr and Khosrovani Collections.

525fce2f-a859-5439-8cdd-d1b640752ea5.name: *Ghotar* plate
525fce2f-a859-5439-8cdd-d1b640752ea5.description: In Morocco, the *ghotar* is a large dish for the presentation of food, such as *pastilla* (chicken cooked in pastry), or fruit.
525fce2f-a859-5439-8cdd-d1b640752ea5.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute

53cfa936-38e2-5b23-a6c4-d57b4297fc81.name: Peacock-shaped incense burner
53cfa936-38e2-5b23-a6c4-d57b4297fc81.description:
This peacock-shaped object, an incense burner (*mabkhara* or *majmar* in Arabic, *ud-suz* in Persian), is a stunning example of medieval Islamic artistry. It belongs to a common tradition of incense burners shaped like falcons, peacocks, and cockerels from Iraq and Iran, with examples dating back to the 9th century in the FBQ Museum collection. The artist ingeniously adapted anatomical elements to accommodate incense burning, concealing the incense chamber within the bird’s belly. The removable upper part facilitated the placement of coal and incense, while open metalwork allowed the release of scented smoke. The elongated tail served to disperse the fragrance. Crafted from bronze, this incense burner showcases exquisite inlay work with turquoise beads, adding to its aesthetic allure. The intricate details and figurative scenes were likely achieved through engraving and embossing.  
Despite its ornamental appearance, the incense burner is adorned with engraved animal-like imagery, figurative scenes, and turquoise bead embellishments. These beads, characteristic of Khorasan origin, enhance its decorative appeal, adding a touch of colour and vibrancy. The handle-less design and heat-sensitive turquoise beads suggest it might have been used as a pomander in ceremonies or palaces. In this role it would have held a mixture of ambergris and spices to produce an exotic fragrance. The unprofessional welding on the movable part suggests it might have become dysfunctional and been repurposed as a purely decorative item.

548a0da4-daad-5893-abb1-4453dabee1bc.name: Maulana Shams ad-Din Muhammad ‘Assar at-Tabrizi, *Mihr u Mushtari* (Romantic epic of the friendship of Prince Mihr with the youth Mushtari)
548a0da4-daad-5893-abb1-4453dabee1bc.short_description: Maulana Shams ad-Din Muhammad 'Assar at-Tabrizi (died 784 AH / 1382-83 AD) completed this romantic epic of the friendship of Prince Mihr and the youth Mushtari (*Mihr u Mushtari*) in 778 AH / 1377 AD. This manuscript was acquired for the Austrian National Library in 1677 in Constantinople by Peter Lambeck for 30 gold ducats and 15 kreuzer. It was copied in *nasta’liq* script by the scribe Hidayat-Allah in c. 977-88 AH / 1570-80 AD, possibly in Shiraz, Iran. According to the 16th-century Turkish historian Mustafa 'Ali, Hidayat-Allah came from Isfahan and was the pupil of the calligrapher Mu'izz ad-Din Muhammad Amin from Kashan. Four other manuscripts with miniatures – produced between 1564 and 1584 – are signed by him. Stylistically, the eight full-page paintings can be linked to the artistic output of the city of Shiraz, where the manuscript was likely created between 1570 and 1580. Its dating to the end of the 16th century becomes more certain through closer inspection of the compositions throughout; the stylization of landscape and architectural forms, the colour scheme, and sparse presence of the *taj-i haidari* (Safavid staff turban) that went out of fashion during this period.
548a0da4-daad-5893-abb1-4453dabee1bc.dimensions: 242 x 170 mm (165 x 97mm), ff. I, I*, 435 folios.
548a0da4-daad-5893-abb1-4453dabee1bc.method_for_provenance: On fol. 1a, there is a destroyed oriental owner's stamp. It was acquired in 1677 by Peter Lambeck in Constantinople for 30 gold ducats and 15 kreuzer. On fol. IIa: 'Ex Augustissima Bibliotheca Caesarea Vindobonensi N. 6'.
548a0da4-daad-5893-abb1-4453dabee1bc.obtention: Unknown but part of the Austrian National Library in the second half of the 17th century.

548a0da4-daad-5893-abb1-4453dabee1bc.scriber: Shams ad-Din b. Giyath ad-Din al-Hafiz al-Kirmani
548a0da4-daad-5893-abb1-4453dabee1bc.binding_desc: The dark brown leather binding has a flap, and on its front cover displays a central field with gold arabesque decoration of florals and cloud scrolls that are pressed from two matrices, incorporating the central medallion with two pendants. Flanking the shorter edges of the central block, circles and ovals form pseudo-title cartouches with inlays of gold leather filigree on red and blue paper and green silk backgrounds. All around, the frame mouldings are stamped in two shades of gold with rowed, elongated vine medallions. The back cover and the flap are decorated in the same manner. Doublures of lighter-coloured leather are overlaid with a medallion design of gold and brown arabesque filigree fillings against a pink, red, blue paper background, and green silk inlays. Their central panels are decorated with gold cloud band and floral vine ornamentation pressed with matrices. The binding was probably made in late 16th-century Shiraz, Iran.

keywords: Epic; mi'raj; painting; romance; Safavid
materials: Ink, opaque watercolour and gold on paper. Calligraphic *nasta'liq* script of 14 lines per page.
