556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.name: Ablutions basin.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.description:
This parallelepipedic tank marked with plain striations on the inside, the short sides and the corners, was beautifully adorned on the outside, and almost all of the decoration has survived on two sides. The design on the decorated face, whose inscription has been destroyed, is divided into two styles. The first one, rising from the base, consists of a large frieze of grooved foliage, dotted with buds and rosettes and wide-veined plain palms with calyxes, and double ones with acanthus leaves and buds. The second comprises a strip in relief with two lines of grooved intersecting knotwork, one curved and the other straight, bearing fleurons and veined palms. It is framed by an edge, set back, formed by vegetal knotwork accentuated with small stylised palm leaves in the shape of six-pointed stars.  
The short side is occupied by two identical animal scenes, sculpted on two vertical panels separated by an empty space. On each panel, there is an eagle spreading its tail, carrying two quadrupeds on its wings and two gazelles from its claws. Two winged ibex confronting each other on either side of a fleuron finish the scene in the lower part.  
Most of the ornamentation on the other two sides has been destroyed, leaving only the text in *kufic* characters sculpted in relief on the rim and the decoration of the framing ribbon on the large side, which consists of a frieze of aquatic birds and fish alternating on a plant background.  
The surviving elements of the inscription that crowned the entire rim of the tank include the last digit of the hegira date (300), and the name of the patron, 'Abd al-Malik, *hajib* (chamberlain) of Hisham II.  
The design and animal scenes of this beautiful example of Caliphate artwork are reminiscent of the tank at al-Mansur and would appear to be from the same Madinat al-Zahira marble workshop in Córdoba.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.short_description: This basin is the work of a marble workshop in Madinat al-Zahira, Córdoba, the princely city built by al-Mansur. It was brought to Marrakesh by 'Ali ibn Yusuf and placed in the ablutions room of the Great Mosque.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.dimensions: Height 70 cm, length 155 cm, width 82 cm, depth 50 cm, thickness of sides 10 cm, thickness of base 20 cm.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.method_for_datation:
1\. The inscription, partially destroyed, sculpted on the upper rim of the tank reads '(the year) three hundred, in the name of God! God's blessing. Victory and divine assistance to the Hajib \[followed with his honours\] Abu Marwan 'Abd al-Malik ibn Amir (…), this is part of what he commissioned (…)'.  
2\. We know that 'Abd al-Malik was appointed *hajib* of Hisham II between 381 and 398 / 991 and 1008) by his father al-Mansur.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.method_for_provenance: Although it was discovered in the Ibn Yusuf Madrasa in Marrakesh, which belongs to the Sa'did period (10th / 16th century), the name of the patron and the comparative study with the al-Mansur basin in the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid suggest that it was originally from Madinat al-Zahira in Córdoba.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.obtention: As state property from a historical monument.

559aa521-7185-5807-b191-e79fc16098c9.name: Tree of Life Carpet
559aa521-7185-5807-b191-e79fc16098c9.short_description:
Vegetal and animal motifs decorate this Iranian carpet with the central Tree of Life motif. Originating from Kerman in the Qajar dynasty, the pile is only cut once the knotting process is complete and the textile is taken off its loom.  
  
People of different faiths and geographic contexts have embraced the tree of life as a symbol of the essence and interconnectedness of all living things. As such, the motif becomes a thread binding people in their shared ideas of the evergreen tree from Bhutan to Germany, the Mayan Empire and the Iroquois People.  
  
Qajar depictions of the tree of life stem from pre-Islamic Zoroastrianism, considered to be the ancestor of all humans, animals and plants. In Islam, the life tree is called *sidra* or *tuba* and grows in paradise. The fruits known as *haoma* (also *homa*) feed those who enter heaven after death. The carpet displays fruits including grapes, pears, figs and pomegranate. The woven peacock, phoenix and eagle are protectors of the tree according to Persian mythology.  
  
A poem by Sufi poet Saadi frames the carpet within its border. The poetry mirrors the garden imagery, as one of Saadi's central themes and symbols of Persian cultural continuity.

564aae8a-774b-5338-a643-bbb087c1fa49.name: Tray (*sinija*)
564aae8a-774b-5338-a643-bbb087c1fa49.description:
A large, brass tray – *sinija* (Tr. *sini*) – of circular form, with raised sides, intended to be placed on a low wooden stand to serve as a table for food and beverages. The whole surface is decorated with intricate compositions of engraved ornaments and calligraphy. The small central medallion is filled with an ornament inspired by Rumi. Around it, there is a radial Arabic inscription with the year 1129 (Mamluk *thuluth* script) within a broader band, combined with flowers and leaves. The next frieze is filled with a complicated pattern made of interlaced palmettes and flowers.  
Inscription: ...كونوا أهل خير، تفضلوا، كلوا، واشربوا (Be good people, come \[please\], eat and drink...).
564aae8a-774b-5338-a643-bbb087c1fa49.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.

keywords: tray; sinija; tableware; brass; Ottoman Empire

567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.name: Collection of Mughal miniatures
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.short_description:
This album contains 70 miniature paintings realised using the courtly Mughal style, arranged on 66 folios. As the miniatures were composed by different artists they vary greatly in size and execution. It is assumed that these miniatures constituted a part of a large collection of miniatures that Maria Theresia had purchased to decorate the so-called "Millionenzimmer" (Millions Room), one of her private reception rooms in Schönbrunn Palace. Most likely, only part of the overall collection was used for the decoration resulting in the remaining miniatures then being gathered into two albums, Min. 44 and this one, Min 64. This thesis is supported by the contemporaneous renovations of the Millions Room, which we know for a fact that Maria Teresia undertook around the 1760's AD, and the arrival of the two albums into the collection of the Imperial Court Library in 1762 AD.  
The themes of the miniatures range from intricate courtly portraits and illustrations of Persian epics to classical scenes from Hindu-mythology.
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.dates: 10th to 11th century AH / 17th to 18th cenutry AD
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.method_for_datation: The date and origins of the miniatures were establish based on the artistic style of the paintings.
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.method_for_provenance: There are many Dutch marginalia throughout the album, mainly providing the titles of miniatures. It is likely that the miniatures in this album came to Amsterdam through the Dutch East India Company, from where they made their way to Vienna.
567ac179-c89c-5f43-a912-af9c71a221ec.obtention: A written record of the album appears in the card catalogue of the Imperial Court Library in the 19th century. Despite this, there is no information on how the miniatures and the album were obtained initially. It appears to have entered the collection at the same time as a similar album of Mughal miniatures (Min. 44), around 1762 AD.

57c9e92a-cab4-5c9c-a712-2d7757fdd1cc.name: Four ivory panels.
57c9e92a-cab4-5c9c-a712-2d7757fdd1cc.description:
The four panels made of carved and openworked pieces of ivory are outstanding examples of the repertoire of work commissioned by the court of the Fatimid period. They are among the most important works of art from this period.  
Two of these panels display a horizontal pattern, while the other two have been decorated linearly along the vertical axis. These latter vertical panels have been shortened slightly. Traces of red indicate that there was once a coloured frame or mount.  
Figures, carved to stand out in high relief, are depicted undertaking a variety of activities. Spiralling grapevines form a backdrop against which people are portrayed in action. Thick grapes hang off the plants. Huntsmen with falcons, helpers carrying small hoofed game, musicians (flute, oboe, lute, plucked stringed instruments), a reveller, pouring into his goblet from a jug, workers picking grapes, and falcons on the hunt – are all depicted in a lifelike and realistic fashion. The illustrations of animal fighting show a lion hunting down a bull, a falcon hunting a deer. A prince reclines on a bolster holding a goblet in his left hand. Everyone wears robes common to that era, made of fabrics decorated with a variety of designs. Even the headdresses are illustrative of the period rather than creations of fantasy.  
Some depictions refer to pre-Islamic art and reflect the continuing existence of older traditions. It was especially during the Fatimid period that the ban on pictures was circumvented in courtly circles and that representations of the human form were undertaken.  
From stylistic and thematic similarities, a good comparison can be drawn between the works on ivory and the woodwork and ceramics created during the Fatimid period, in which the finer technique seen in the ivory engraving demonstrates greater skill.  
What remains unexplained is their function. The panels could have been used to decorate or coat a wooden surface (such as a door or large trunk), or could have been used as part of a throne. The Arab historian al-Maqrîzî (AH 766–845 / AD 1364–1442) described a Fatimid throne made of ebony and ivory.
57c9e92a-cab4-5c9c-a712-2d7757fdd1cc.short_description: The function of these panels with themes from princely life is not known, but the carving of hunters with hawks, musicians and revellers against a background of vine scrolls demonstrates the artistic quality of Fatimid ivory carving at its best and thus may be a ruler’s commission for a palace.
57c9e92a-cab4-5c9c-a712-2d7757fdd1cc.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
57c9e92a-cab4-5c9c-a712-2d7757fdd1cc.initial_owner: Freiherr von Zu-Rhein Collection; F. v. Amerling Collection; A. Figdor Collection.
57c9e92a-cab4-5c9c-a712-2d7757fdd1cc.dimensions: Horizontal panels: length 36.5 cm, width 5.8 cm. Vertical panels: height 30.3 cm, width 5.8 cm. Depth of panels 1–1.5 cm.
57c9e92a-cab4-5c9c-a712-2d7757fdd1cc.method_for_datation: The fact that these panels have not been attributed to a particular building, and that stylistic comparisons to other works of ivory from southern Italy have demonstrated substantial differences, indicates that they might date from the Fatimid period, as they compare stylistically to other artworks from Egypt, above all to Fatimid woodwork.
57c9e92a-cab4-5c9c-a712-2d7757fdd1cc.method_for_provenance: As Fatimid woodwork from Egypt is the only art form that bears close stylistic comparison to these panels, so far it is thought that these most probably come from Egypt.
57c9e92a-cab4-5c9c-a712-2d7757fdd1cc.obtention: Bought from a private art gallery in 1936.

58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.name: Floor Spread (*sofra*) with Design of Tulips and Pomegranates
58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.short_description: A circular floor spread (*sofra*) with design of tulips and pomegranates. Around the outer edge is a narrow border of floral motifs. Within this comes a wide ring containing large tulips and artichoke or pomegranate motifs which have tulips within them set alternately. In the center is a double circle containing floral motifs like those in the border. The textile is mounted on a red velvet background. The design features red, blue, green, white, and yellow embroidered elements on a natural plain cloth background. There are slight repairs and many stains. The textile is pieced down the middle.
58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.dates: Hegira 11th century to early 12th century / AD 17th century
58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.method_for_provenance: This circular shaped *sofra* is filled with tulip motifs characteristic of Ottoman embroidery. Tulips were originally a wild flower growing in Central Asia, and by the late seventeenth century Ottoman artists had perfected representations of the tulip form.

588403a2-2a6d-58c2-a765-7c8f4bdf08f0.name: Lid (*sarpush*) for the plate (*dovra*)
588403a2-2a6d-58c2-a765-7c8f4bdf08f0.description:
The conical food cover (*sarpush*) was placed atop a round dish (*dovra*) to keep food warm while serving. It is usually made of copper and richly engraved with zoomorphic and floral motifs and inscriptions containing mainly name of the owner and/or master, year of production, *ayahs* from the Quran, as well as wishes for the owner's well-being. Such inscriptions were normally depicted inside cartouches. In 2015, the copper craftsmanship of Azerbaijani Lahij was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.  
  
On this item, the year Hegira 1280 (AD 1859–1860) and floral motifs are depicted. On the upper border there are two lines of Hafez and an inscription stating that the artifact's owner is Agha Bayram, son of the late Aghadadash. Additionally, another inscription reads as follows:  
"Remove the sarpush,  
So the beloved one could taste the food.  
Sarpush hugged the bowl.  
Immediately his heart forgot grief.  
He calmed down as his lips touched the dish and he ate food.  
He was born smart.  
May the conversations accompany the feast."
588403a2-2a6d-58c2-a765-7c8f4bdf08f0.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analyses with related material
588403a2-2a6d-58c2-a765-7c8f4bdf08f0.author: Rustam Afandiyev
keywords: Lidded plate; tableware; sarpush; dovra; copper; Azerbaijan

58b05d1c-5f36-5062-be5d-8dc0b6573bbf.name: Plate of polychrome ceramic from Fez
58b05d1c-5f36-5062-be5d-8dc0b6573bbf.description: This polychrome ceramic dish illustrates the refinement of Moroccan craftsmanship, especially that of Fez, a city famous for its pottery. In the centre, a six-pointed star outlined in yellow and blue immediately catches the eye. This motif is surrounded by rich floral and vegetal ornaments, arranged symmetrically, evoking the harmony and proliferation of nature. Stylised flowers, mainly blue and yellow, occupy spaces between the star’s branches, while green arabesques add dynamic and contrasting touches. The border of the plate is decorated with a multicoloured diamond pattern, alternating among blue, yellow and green, framed by a thin blue line. This detail gives a captivating finish to the whole, enhancing the composition’s effect.

59c2fb21-a451-5ddc-860d-380e07ae8190.short_description: The bowl has a broad centre painted in underglaze blue with a round tripartite blazon showing in the middle a stemmed cup. This is the emblem of the office of the Mamluk cupbearer or *saqi*. Blazons are not often met on underglaze painted ware but are most commonly represented on metalwork and earthenware ceramics of the sgraffiato type from the end of the 13th century on.

5d530e40-18f0-5e71-b689-999b1ed68ae4.name: Medical prescription.
5d530e40-18f0-5e71-b689-999b1ed68ae4.description:
A medical prescription written on paper using a simple *naskhi* script used in daily life. This prescription is attributed to Shams al-Din ibn al-'Afif, one of the most famous physicians practising during the reign of the Mamluk sultan, al-Ashraf Barsbay (r. AH 825–41 / AD 1422–37). The historian Ibn Iyas (d. AH 930 / AD 1524) mentions that al-'Afif was the most eminent doctor in Egypt, and that he was the head of Bimaristan (hospital) of Sultan Qalawun, in Egypt. In addition he was the personal physician to Sultan al-Ashraf Barsbay, and also responsible for granting doctors authorisation to practice. It is important to note here, that the afflicted who resided in Egyptian hospitals during the Mamluk period underwent both social and medical care, for they were clothed and paid until their treatment was finished. There were *Awqaf* (Endowments) made out to these hospitals, the proceeds of which defrayed the costs incurred by these institutions.  
The prescription itself is describing a treatment for the celiac disease. And although there are some grammatical errors in the writing of the description it is readable as follows:  
'*Praise be to the one God* ///  
*A* \[medicinal\] *powder known as “Sufuf al-Kifaya” \[complete in its treatment\] from the diwan of ///*  
*ibn al-'Afif, the head of the maristan of Egypt who said: Take /// a quarter cup of Qaraz \[a pod-like fruit of* Acacia Nilotica\], *the same \[measure\] of aniseed, the same \[measure\] of fennel,/// 2 ounces of Kirmani cumin, … an ounce of mahagony wood, /// an ounce of seed of clover dodder, an ounce of wormwood from al-Sham \[Syria\] and two ounces of almonds./// Roast the qaraz and fennel and grind and crush the remaining components. /// Put hem together and add 3 ounces of water of the sand \[al-ramli\] radish \[to the mixture\] /// and the same measure of the water of green fennel. The leaves /// of two bunches of sweet basil and the leaves of one bunch of mint, 3 ounces of the water of bearberry, /// then the leaves of a fresh chopped-up bunch of sweet myrtle /// and 3 ounces of celery water. /// Mix them together and add to the \[medicinal\] powder, then dry the mixture /// and continue this process until it has soaked up all the water. /// Then add a quarter of a ratl \[a measure, 449.28 g in Egypt today\] of white sugar /// and take it in the morning and evening. This is good /// for the celiac disease.'*  
The latest scientific studies in nutrition indicate that some foods might cause illnesses, which can lead to death. One of these ailments is celiac disease. Those who are afflicted with this disease are not able to absorb wheat protein as a result of a disorder in the function of the intestines. If the sufferer does eat wheat or one of its by-products he or she may develop chronic diarrhoea and weight loss, ending, finally, in death. Doctors during the Mamluk period knew about this illness, and this prescription describes a treatment which modern science arrived at only very recently. Worth contemplating is the variety of herbs and plants that appear on this prescription which have a number of positive effects in the treatment of stomach ailments.
5d530e40-18f0-5e71-b689-999b1ed68ae4.short_description: This medical prescription describes a cure for a stomach ailment. It is attributed to Ibn al-‘Afif, the most eminent doctor of the Mamluk period and head of the Bimaristan (hospital) of Sultan Qalawun, where patients were provided with free medicine, clothes and an allowance as well as medical care until their treatment was finished

5d530e40-18f0-5e71-b689-999b1ed68ae4.obtention: This document was uncovered during archaeological excavations that took place in 1931 in the city of Fustat.

Liquid that comes into contact with these formulas acquires their curative property. The centre is decorated with a representation of the *Ka'ba* on top and a six-pointed star on the reverse.

5e49717d-377e-51a8-a5cc-e5b4d8ad7979.name: Water jar
5e49717d-377e-51a8-a5cc-e5b4d8ad7979.description: This piece belongs to a set that came from a Turkish shipwreck in the Red Sea, in the Gulf of Aqaba, near Sharm al-Sheikh, during the second quarter of the 18th century. The precise origin of these ceramics is not known, but these water jars are similar to those still used in Egypt today. After the Ottoman conquest, Sultan Selim I deported Egyptian craftsmen from various trades to Istanbul. As a result, ceramics declined irremediably, and production was limited to utilitarian objects such as this one, whose designs are incomparable to those produced from the 9th to the 15th centuries.

5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.name: Pilgrim bottle.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.description:
A free-blown, globular-shaped glass vessel with enamel decoration. One of the wider sides and the lower half of both narrower sides are flattened. The colours of the enamel are wide-ranging: red, white, blue, pale-green, yellow, pink, mauve, and greyish black. Two applied handles sit on either side of the cylindrical neck. An eleven-pointed rosette within an eight-lobed flower containing vegetal scrolls decorates the flattened side. Decorating the curved side is a four-sided lobed motif, with a geometric shape filled-in with arabesques and surrounded by scrolls, terminating in human, animal, or bird heads. On the left of the curved side is a horseman in the act of killing an animal with a spear, he has a beard and a halo around his head and wears a conical hat with ribbons. Below this figure is a medallion with a female harp player, wearing a veil and a long tunic. On the other narrow side is a horseman under a tree killing a lion with a javelin; birds are flying overhead. He has a halo and wears a long coat and boots. In the circular medallion below him is a man sitting cross-legged, with a beaker in one hand, drinking. His tunic has decorative tiraz bands on the sleeves.  
The two horsemen recall those found in Christian iconography, whereas the figures in the medallions are typical of figures depicted in Islamic art. The mixture of motifs suggests the patron was either a Muslim who was familiar with Christian imagery or a Christian who appreciated the work of Muslim craftsmen. The shape of this vessel recalls leather flasks or unglazed ceramic pilgrim bottles, rather than other glass and metal objects. Although made of glass, this flask may have been carried on journeys or pilgrimages in a leather container. It was certainly a luxury object, perhaps made specifically as a gift.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.short_description: This enamelled glass pilgrim bottle is an interesting example of the crossover of Christian and Islamic cultures. Two of the figures decorating the vessel derive from Christian iconography of St George and the dragon, whereas the musician and drinker are found in Islamic art.
5e68b14d-8eb3-5454-8d3b-cd5efa2239df.dates: Hegira third quarter 7th century / AD third quarter 13th century.

5eb1c735-e657-5f39-8791-b8112b9f9ac5.name: Mamluk candlestick
5eb1c735-e657-5f39-8791-b8112b9f9ac5.description:
Crafted from copper alloy, this bell-shaped candlestick is a testament to the remarkable craftsmanship of the Mamluk period. Its design features intricate cursive inscription bands interrupted by roundels adorned with whirling rosettes, each meticulously engraved with the official titles of the owner. Notably, the inscription on the cylindrical base is upside down, adding a captivating detail to its design that invites further scholarly inquiry.  
One of the most intriguing aspects of this candlestick is the inscription on its neck, which suggests its ownership by a Mamluk sultan. However, the illegibility of the name presents a challenge to dating the object with certainty, leaving room for scholarly debate and analysis. Nevertheless, the presence of such prestigious ownership hints at the candlestick’s significance within the context of Mamluk court culture and patronage.  
Further examination reveals variations in copper composition between the base and the neck, and differences in script styles in the inscriptions. These subtle variations suggest the possibility that the candlestick was repurposed from a different object; perhaps originally one part served as a tray stand or another decorative item. This adaptive reuse highlights the resourcefulness and ingenuity of Mamluk artisans, who were adept at recycling materials to create new and innovative works of art.  
In addition to its artistic and historical significance, this candlestick offers valuable insights into the material culture and artistic practices of the Mamluk period through meticulous analysis of its craftsmanship, inscriptions and materials, with intricate details likely achieved through engraving and embossing.

611887bb-d44c-51a1-b6d3-d89221fb788c.name: Ewer
611887bb-d44c-51a1-b6d3-d89221fb788c.short_description:
The late 17th century witnessed the rise of Kütahya, the Ottoman second largest ceramic centre, situated in the south-eastern outskirts of Istanbul. Europeans, impressed by richness and refinement of its exotic patterns, called Kütahya "The Sevres of the East".  
This large egg-shaped ewer with strikingly thin walls belongs to rare samples of Kütahya ware. Painted with short rapid strokes of cobalt pigment on a snow white background it represents the best achievements of the second half of the 18th century.  
The original style of Kütahya décor genuinely combines different artistic traditions of East and West which were brought to the Ottoman culture due to trade activities of the Armenian community, settled in the town. Some researchers also suggest that the major part of the Kütahya ceramics was produced by Armenian potters.

611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.name: Aghlabid Reservoirs.
611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.description:
These two reservoirs were built using the same method. They are constructed of rubble and surfaced with a waterproof coating. The walls are consolidated by internal and external buttresses which alternate, thus providing maximum resistance against the water pressure. These buttresses are semi-cylindrical in shaped and topped with semi-spheres, combining aesthetics with technical performance.  
They are composed of three main sections:  
– The small reservoir measures 17 m in diameter and is reinforced by 17 internal and 26 external buttresses. Its holding capacity is 4,000 cubic metres. It is a filtering basin which receives the untreated water and rids it of most of the debris that it carries before decanting it into the large reservoir.  
– The large reservoir is circular in shape, measures 128 m in diameter and is 4.8 m deep. Its holding capacity is 57,000 cubic metres. No less than 182 buttresses were needed (118 external and 64 internal) to contain the pressure and guarantee the viability of the project, which was to store enough water for the needs of daily life in the town. A squat poly-foil pillar rises up from its centre. Formerly surmounted by a dome, it was used as a leisure pavilion.  
The water travels from here into two parallel dispensing water-tanks set perpendicular to the reservoirs. They are covered with barrel vaults held up by arch-beams that rest on pillars. Six openings at the top of the vaults allow the water to be drawn.
611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.short_description: These hydraulic structures are the most famous in the Muslim world. They were among 15 pools outside the city walls that provided water to Kairouan. The imposing majesty of these installations earned Kairouan the epithet ‘city of water tanks’ in the Middle Ages. There are two semi-cylindrical pools supplied by an ingenious system for draining rainwater and the water from a nearby depression filled by tributaries of the *wadi* Merguelli.
611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.method_for_datation: Historical sources: Ibn Khaldoun, *Histoire des Berberes*.

611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.history: The Aghlabid reservoirs, of which only two survive, were part of a group of about 15 reservoirs, located outside the city walls, which supplied the town with water. They are considered to be among the most important hydraulic works of the Muslim world. They provoked the admiration of travellers and led to the town being given the name 'city of the cisterns'. They were filled by draining rainwater as well as water from the tributaries of the *wadi* Merguelli, which flow in the surrounding lowlands. Its waters were harnessed by small dams and a conveyance canal which transported it to the small pool. In 350 (961), the Fatimid Caliph al-Mu'izz built an aqueduct that brought water from the Shreshira springs, located 40 km to the west of Kairouan.

61338d55-fb32-555c-a06d-c7ca35110c05.name: Les foggaras
61338d55-fb32-555c-a06d-c7ca35110c05.description:
An ingenious system of drawing and distributing water simultaneously in an extremely dry area, foggaras consist of a row of wells on a gentle and uninterrupted slope that allows surface water to flow to gardens.  
  
The well shafts are made by drilling a tunnel at the base of a mountainous area and following an aquifer, with the goal of bringing water to the surface for irrigation of agricultural land. The tunnels are horizontal and dug with extreme precision on a regular slope to allow the water to flow steadily.  
  
The tapped foggara water table is deeper than the water table under the dunes, but closer to the surface in the nearby plateau of Tadmaït (to the east), which makes it accessible by digging horizontally. The size of this network of wells is estimated at thousands of kilometres between the Gourara and the Touat; seven kilometres for just the Mghayer, the foggara of Timimoun. The punishing work of digging could not have been accomplished without the exploitation of many slaves. For this reason maintaining foggaras that collapse or become silted is problematic.  
  
The term foggara refers not only to this system of pumping from the water table, but also to the pooling of water to irrigate the palm groves. The oases of Gourara and Touat have comb-like structures (*kesria*) that direct the water flowing between the “teeth” (*kiel el-Ma*). The water is distributed according to the requirements of the private gardens, and routed through channels (*seguias*) that drain into ponds (*majens*) from which farmers draw water to the extent allowed. This system, specific to Saharan regions, is evidence of its early use, and of the people’s deep desire to live in harmony by sharing with each other the meagre resources of the Sahara in a strict but fair manner.

61c3680d-7e1f-5627-a43b-1ebb99008f0e.name: Folio with two miniatures from Persian translation of 'The Wonders of Creation and the Oddities of Existence' by Zakaria Qazwini
61c3680d-7e1f-5627-a43b-1ebb99008f0e.short_description: A folio from Persian translation of a popular cosmography treatise "The Wonders of Creation and the Oddities of Existence" by Zakaria bin Muhammad al-Qazwini. The book, written in AD 13th century, covers the fields of geography, astronomy, astrology and natural history, in a mixture of science and superstition. Both sides of the folio are embellished with miniatures featuring fruit-bearing trees.
61c3680d-7e1f-5627-a43b-1ebb99008f0e.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by V. Krachkovskaya (publication, 1926, origin), A. Ivanov (examination, 1966, date).
61c3680d-7e1f-5627-a43b-1ebb99008f0e.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927): the Khanenkos' collection.
61c3680d-7e1f-5627-a43b-1ebb99008f0e.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko in Paris, 1914, presumably from Fredrik Robert Martin's collection. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalised by Bolshevik regime in 1919.

63a0f023-76ca-5378-a69c-036e6ca9862e.name: *Divan-ı Hafız* by Şemşeddin Muhammed Hafız Şirazi
63a0f023-76ca-5378-a69c-036e6ca9862e.description: The miniature depicts a social gathering for entertainment. A servant offers a plate of pomegranates to the individual seated on the carpet in the centre, who is accompanied by a beautiful young boy clapping his hands and reciting a *ghazal* (love poem) to the accompaniment of musicians.

65786a69-ccf0-52e9-acec-40d5ded53000.name: Covered al-Buzuriyya Market
65786a69-ccf0-52e9-acec-40d5ded53000.description: Before the celebrations of Mawlid al-Nabawi (Feast of the Birth of the Prophet), shops in the historic Buzuriyya market in Damascus are filled with many types of sweets and chocolates. The most important sweet for Aid al-Mawlid is the *Mulabbas*, which consists of roasted almonds coated with a thin layer of sugar mixed with rose water. The shopkeepers arrange the various sweets inside the shops, while they place large bags of *Mulabbas* at the entrance to attract customers. The mosques organise the Mawlid celebrations, which take place between the Maghrib and Isha prayers in the evening, and a number of women like to host a Mawlid party in their homes. During the celebration of Mawlid, *Mulabbas* are distributed to all celebrants. Damascenes believe it is important to cook white food or serve white sweets on religious occasions, in order to greet the coming days with optimism symbolised by the colour white.
65786a69-ccf0-52e9-acec-40d5ded53000.bibliography:
al-Maliki, M. A., “On Celebrating the Birth of the Prophet”, Imam Ghazali Institute, 2016.  
  
Rabbat, N., “Ideal-type and Urban History: The Development of the Suq in Damascus” in Gharipour, Mohammad, ed. *The Bazaar in the Islamic City: Design, Culture, and History*. American University in Cairo Press, 2012.  
  
Zarcone, T., Mevlid Kandili. “La fête de la naissance du Prophète en Turquie”, Nathalie CLAYER et Erdal KAYNAR, “Penser, agir et vivre dans l'Empire ottoman et en Turquie”, Paris, Louvain, Walpole, MA, 2013: 308-320.
65786a69-ccf0-52e9-acec-40d5ded53000.author: Hiba Bizreh

65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.name: Covered Vessel with Relief Design of Arabic Inscription in *Kufic* Script
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.short_description:
A circular steatite vessel with a thin, flat lid with a vertical, eared wing handle that has a mushroom-shaped cut-out in the center. Around the exterior of the lid is a band of cross-hatching, and another band of the same width crossing the diameter of the lid. This band is also cross-hatched on one half, up to where it intersects with the handle, then becomes "transparent," filled only with the raised relief inscription beneath that covers the remaining surface of the lid.  
The vessel has straight sides with an upper and lower border of cross-hatching, enclosing a relief band of inscription. The stone is carved to form an Arabic inscription in relief, in an angular script style known as *Kufic*. The tops of the taller letters end in leaves and flowers, a popular calligraphic device in the 10th century. On opposing sides of the vessel are bar-like handles with deep gouges on their outer edges. The area where each handle attaches to the vessel is bordered by cross-hatching.
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.dates: Hegira Late 2nd to late 4th / AD 10th century
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.dimensions: Height with cover: 14.9cm; Diameter of cover: 21.9cm; Height of vessel without cover: 10.2cm; Diameter of mouth: 22.2cm; Width across handles: 24.8cm; Diameter of base: 22.2cm
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.method_for_datation: The stone is carved to form an Arabic inscription in relief, in an angular style known as *kufic*. The tops of the taller letters end in leaves and flowers, a popular calligraphic device in the 10th century.
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.method_for_provenance: Steatite vessels such as this one were used for cooking in the 9th–10th centuries in the northeastern Iranian city of Nishapur. Many small steatite objects have been excavated, but this is the largest complete vessel known.
keywords: Covered; Bowl; Stone; Mineral; Steatite; Nishapur; Khorasan; Iran; Asia; Persian

6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.name: Rosewater bottle.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.description:
The rosewater bottle has a pear-shaped body and a short round base. The tall, slender neck is shaped like a cypress tree and is fitted to the body with a knob, which has vegetal decoration and turns on a shaft.  
  
Pieces of polished turquoise are attached to the body, a technique called *firuzekari*. An openwork design with alternating bunches of tulips, roses and carnations, and cypress trees, has been created by carving out the metal background. There are *firuzekari* cypress trees on the sprinkler as well as palmettes in the same technique on the base. The entire surface is decorated with rubies and emeralds fitted into sockets. *Firuzekari* and gold were used decoratively on Qur'an covers in particular, during the last quarter of the AH 10th century / AD 16th century.  
  
Turquoise, a greenish-blue gemstone, is considered in Turkish popular culture to this day to be a talisman against the evil eye and is thought to prevent bad luck and accidents.  
  
In the Ottoman period such rosewater bottles, exquisitely crafted and decorated with precious stones, were used mostly by palace officials. Rosewater bottles were made of gold, silver, porcelain and glass; they had long necks, narrow mouths and large bodies. They were used for pouring or sprinkling rosewater over the hands of guests, including at religious gatherings such as *mevlid* (the celebration of the birthday of the Prophet). Normally a rosewater bottle would also have a tray and be used together with an incense-burner during such ceremonies.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.short_description: Rosewater was sprinkled on guests' hands during religious ceremonies and private meetings. Gold rosewater bottles were especially used by courtiers. According to Islamic tradition, rosewater carries the fragrance of 'rose', the symbol of Prophet Muhammad and its use adds to the meaning of the worship.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.dates: Hegira last quarter of the 10th century / AD 16th century.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.method_for_datation: Naturalistic motifs of tulips, roses, hyacinths, cypresses and pomegranates started to infuse the Ottoman decorative repertory in about the middle of the 10th / 16th century. As such motifs are found on our example as well as on similar works of art at the Topkapı Palace Treasury, this rosewater bottle is dated to the last quarter of the 10th / 16th century.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.method_for_provenance: The high-quality workmanship, as well as the existence of similar objects at the Topkapı Palace, suggests that this bottle was made in the Topkapı Palace workshops in Istanbul.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.obtention: It was brought to the museum on 10 January 1919 from the Tomb of Eyüp Sultan (Ayyub al-Ansar).
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.bibliography: *Anadolu Medeniyetleri III, Selçuklu–Osmanlı* (*Anatolian Civilizations III, Seljuqs–Ottomans*), Istanbul, 1983, p.181.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.author: Alev Özay
keywords: Firuzekari technique; rosewater bottle; hyacinths
materials: Gold, silver, various metals, porcelain and glass. Decorated with turquoise-work (firuzekari) and openwork.

66adc4ae-b72a-5645-9464-e6b42ed42fe6.name: Plate
66adc4ae-b72a-5645-9464-e6b42ed42fe6.description: Red clay with cream slip, decorated with purple-brown and mustard tones under a transparent colourless glaze. A traditional latticed decoration encircles the rim of the plate. The interior surface displays a particularly intriguing example of early Çanakkale ceramics. The centrepiece is a tow boat with waving pennant and regimental banners. In the 16th–18th centuries, depictions of the Ottoman navy can be found in various examples of ceramics, miniatures and wall paintings. These decorations are likely related to the city's seafront location and to Ottoman ships, of which the city's inhabitants were very proud. The unadorned lines of the oared and unmanned boats impart a naive quality to these plates, reflecting the diverse and creative enthusiasms of folk art.
66adc4ae-b72a-5645-9464-e6b42ed42fe6.dates: Hegira late 12th century / AD late 18th century

66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.name: *Divan-ı* Ali Şir Nevai (Social Gathering for Entertainment)
66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.description:
This copy of Ali Şîr Nevâî's *Divan*, a collection of poems written under his pseudonym, Fânî, is dated Hegira 943 / AD 1536–1537, and is signed by Mir Ali al-Bukhârî. It is written in Chagatai Turkish in *Nastaliq* calligraphy in two columns on papers of various colours with different patterns and *zerefşan* (gold leaf).  
On page 1a is a text written in a circular medallion with superscript text. This states that the work was prepared for Abdülazîz Khan, b. Ubeydullah Khan, one of the rulers of the Shaybânî Dynasty, an Islamic dynasty that ruled in Mâverâünnehir, Khârezm and Khorasan. At the top of the same page is the seal of Sultan Mahmud I's foundation, and below it is the seal of Derviş Mustafa Efendi, inspector of Evkaf. On the following facing pages is a scene of entertainment in the countryside. The title page is decorated with floral and geometric motifs. There are a total of eight miniatures in the work.  
The binding comprises two covers, the outer of which is leather over cardboard. It is decorated with Chinese clouds and various floral motifs on a gilt ground. The inner cover is made of brown leather, and the backgrounds of borders, corners, and edges of panels are navy blue. These sections with navy blue grounds are decorated with floral motifs obtained by the *kat’ı* (paper cutting) technique.
66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.obtention: The item was brought to the Museum from the Mahmud I Library on 13 April 1914.
materials: Finished (*aharli*) paper, ink, gilding, leather binding

670eba93-83b0-54bf-987d-360af123a3ea.name: Coffee cups
670eba93-83b0-54bf-987d-360af123a3ea.description: Coffee in Oman is traditionally served in small cups without any added sugar or milk. The host holds the cup between the fingers of their right hand and pours in coffee from a *dallah* held in their left. Coffee is typically served first to the most honored guests.
670eba93-83b0-54bf-987d-360af123a3ea.holder: The National Museum - Sultanate of Oman
670eba93-83b0-54bf-987d-360af123a3ea.author: Noora Al Balushi

67ae5352-aaad-57a1-9050-4df90cfc07e6.name: *Suz u gudaz* (‘Burning and Melting’)
67ae5352-aaad-57a1-9050-4df90cfc07e6.short_description: *Suz u gudaz* (‘Burning and Melting’) is a romance, an allegorical poem that tells of the soul’s yearning for God through the story of a Hindu woman who, following the custom known as *sati*, ended her life on her husband’s funeral pyre. The poet Muhammad Riza, known as Naw‘i (d.1619), was born in Khabushan in north-eastern Iran, but later travelled to India where he composed the poem for Prince Daniyal, son of the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605). The three paintings shown here depict the worship of fire, the young man telling his father of his beloved, and the two lovers seated in a garden with an attendant standing nearby.
67ae5352-aaad-57a1-9050-4df90cfc07e6.dates: Hegira mid 11th century / AD mid 17th century
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

68325b3d-407d-58cd-871d-f55852f7184e.name: Albarello
68325b3d-407d-58cd-871d-f55852f7184e.description: An albarello (plural: albarelli) is typically an earthenware jar originally designed for medicinal purposes and used to hold apothecaries' ointments and dry drugs. The origins of this type of pharmacy jar trace back to the Islamic world. Its craftsmanship and design influence spread to Europe through Muslim-European interaction. This particular albarello exemplifies 14th-century AD Valencian ware by Muslim potters. It has a cylindrical body, tall neck, and slanting shoulder on a short foot. It is decorated in blue and lustre glazes, with seven horizontal geometric bands that include many abstract motifs favoured for pharmacy jars, including two bands bearing *al-afiya*, a stylised inscription of the Arabic word for health and happiness. While the albarello was originally used for medicines, glazed jars like this one were used for storing and transporting items like wine, water, butter, honey and olives.
68325b3d-407d-58cd-871d-f55852f7184e.dates: Hegira second half of 8th century /AD second half of 14th century
68325b3d-407d-58cd-871d-f55852f7184e.author: Teslim Sanni
materials: Tin-glazed earthenware with lustre and cobalt blue decoration

69a91c1d-a3b0-5106-9135-ad44679f9576.name: Nilüfer Hatun Imaret.
69a91c1d-a3b0-5106-9135-ad44679f9576.description:
The monument was built in the style of a mosque with *tabhane* (guest-rooms) (also known as mosques with *zawiya*, or multifunctional mosques), many of which were built in Anatolia in the AH 8th–9th / AD 14th–15th centuries. It consists of a rectangular area with two rooms (the prayer hall and the central courtyard) flanked by a room on the north and south sides; there is also a portico for latecomers extending along the eastern side. The eastern façade is 40.50 m wide; the portico for latecomers 25.35 m wide. Inclusive of the portico for latecomers the building is 33.60 m in length.  
The portico for latecomers has five bays supported with four piers. Four columns join two pointed arches on each of the sides, and five pointed arches on the front. Contrary to custom, the portico for latecomers does not extend the length of the entrance façade. It has a dome over its central bay and vaults over the others. In the centre of the west wall is an entranceway to the central hall; above which is the building's foundation inscription on marble.  
The central hall is square and covered by a dome with a round lantern. The prayer hall to its west is divided in two by an arch. The eastern half has an eight-section dome, while the dome in the western half has been placed between cross- and star-vaults. The *mihrab* niche is in the south wall. The rectangular rooms to the north and south of the central hall have been transformed into squares using flat-top (Bursa-type) arches, and they are each covered with a dome supported on a transition zone of broken triangles. The east wall of each room has a hearth-niche.  
The building is covered with red roof tiles. Its walls are made of single rows of cut stone alternating with triple rows of brick. The upper parts of the walls feature four rows of brick dog-tooth eaves, while the domes have two rows of dog-tooth eaves.  
In the portico for latecomers the capitals of the columns are of marble, so also are the frame and lintel of the entrance door, the tympanum and the side piers. The walls have some decorative brick- and stonework. The piers with torus-mouldings on the entrance axis are noteworthy for their different decoration. Decorative plasterwork with friezes of palmette motifs in relief, embellish the dome in the centre of the portico for latecomers and the upper part of the walls of the entrance area.  
Several functions have been proposed for the Nilüfer Hatun Imaret. Some researchers claim that the building was a soup-kitchen, since the name *imaret* means an institution for distributing food to the poor. Others hold that the term *imaret* did not come to have this meaning until later and that, initially, the term was used for any building used for charitable deeds, and that in the AH 8th–9th / AD 14th–15th centuries buildings like this, of which many examples called *imaret* exist in Anatolia, were constructed to shelter itinerant dervishes.  
The building was badly damaged during the Turkish War of Independence (1919–1922) and was later used as a storage depot. After 1955 it was restored and opened as a museum. The museum displays ceramic finds from the excavations in Iznik as well as various antique and ethnographic objects recovered in archaeological excavations in and around Iznik.
69a91c1d-a3b0-5106-9135-ad44679f9576.short_description: Built of bricks, stones and marble this relatively plain monument is noteworthy for the variety of its superstructure, especially inside. It was built by Sultan Murad I in the name of his mother after her death. Daughter of the Byzantine *tekfur* of Harmankaya, Holofira married Orhan Gazi and converted to Islam, taking the name Nilüfer Hatun. She was renowned for her charitable work. The structure was built in the style of a mosque with *tabhane* (guesthouse), which housed the missionary dervishes who played a great role in the Islamisation of Anatolia during the AH 8th-9th / AD 14th-15th centuries.
69a91c1d-a3b0-5106-9135-ad44679f9576.method_for_datation: There is an inscription of three lines carved on a marble plaque above the entrance portal. The monument was built for Nilüfer Hatun, mother of Sultan Murad I and was completed on 30 Rabi' al-Awwal 789 / 8 April 1388.

6a082742-d8cb-5964-8ea7-e722c9a23660.name: Ceramic jar
6a082742-d8cb-5964-8ea7-e722c9a23660.description: A tall pottery jar with a flat base used for storage and short-distance transport, as indicated by its shape and four short handles. The handles are placed at the shoulder below a rimmed mouth. Under its yellow and pistachio-coloured glaze it is decorated with brown and green glazes in three horizontal registers. The band below the lip is delineated by a thin brown line at the top and a green stripe between two thin brown lines at the bottom, a motif that is repeated below the second and the third bands. It depicts a row of six-petalled flowers, outlined in brown, with a leaf on each side of the stem. The petals are decorated with a spot of green. In the second band, a brown-edged diamond pattern circles the body. The third band is decorated with a row of brown-edged leaves filled in with green. The pot is glazed inside in dark green. From historical documents (cookbooks or single recipes) we know some methods of traditional preservation; many of them remained in use in traditional communities in the 20th century, and even today. Meat or butter was preserved in relatively big pots, or salted in stoneware or earthenware jars. Curing with liquid and dry-curing were also used, the latter using salt mixed with other ingredients, such as spices, before smoking.
6a082742-d8cb-5964-8ea7-e722c9a23660.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum
6a082742-d8cb-5964-8ea7-e722c9a23660.owner: His Excellency Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani

6a082742-d8cb-5964-8ea7-e722c9a23660.method_for_provenance: Analysis of techniques, styles and motifs; analogies
6a082742-d8cb-5964-8ea7-e722c9a23660.author: Terézia Bardi

6a2ad1b6-4e61-5b64-aa4c-e23e31a8188c.name: *Sübhatü'l Ebrar* by Molla Camii
6a2ad1b6-4e61-5b64-aa4c-e23e31a8188c.description:
Molla Camii was a poet and scientist of the Naqshbandi order who was born and raised in Samarkand during the Timuri period (1414–1492). He was a highly renowned figure during his lifetime, and was frequently invited by the Ottoman sultans.  
In this miniature Prophet Abraham and a fire-worshipping priest are depicted. Prophet Abraham informs the pagan priest that he can invite him to his table only if the priest accepts Islam. The elderly priest, declaring that he would not alter his beliefs for a mere morsel of bread, rises from the table and departs. At this point, a voice from the heavens is heard saying it is unjust to compel an elderly man to leave the table hungry, regardless of his beliefs. Prophet Abraham then realises his error and invites the priest back to the table. The priest, after being invited a subsequent time, becomes a believer upon being told what had happened.  
In the miniature, Prophet Abraham's head is haloed and his face is veiled. He points to the food, indicating that the priest should join him.

6a3340c0-c680-5459-91d6-e838dcb5662c.name: Mortar (*havan*)
6a3340c0-c680-5459-91d6-e838dcb5662c.description: Mortars exist in varying sizes, some more easily suited to being handheld while others, such as this larger (and heavier) example, most likely was placed on a flat surface. This bronze mortar (*havan*) is octagonal – its edges considerably worn – around a cylindrical container with an everted rim and widening base. Moulded bull’s heads on two sides are fitted with looping ring-handles to facilitate transport of this heavy vessel. Its body is divided into three horizontal registers incised with a combination of running animals, calligraphic inscriptions and foliate scrolls. The middle panel features a series of single or triple beads in high relief, framed by polylobed arches – probably designed to hold the vessel more securely in place when grinding with a pestle. A band of eight panels of Kufic calligraphy alternating with foliate roundels runs around the top rim, forming a continuous blessing to an unknown patron. Two panels read: “*al yamoon wa … albta lmaa hbaa*” (continuous prosperity … eternal glory), with “*al-barakat*” (blessing) also legible. The upper band features the same decorative motif, yet the calligraphy is written in naskh script, with the word *al-izz* faintly visible. The lower band is engraved with running animals (a dog or feline) chasing its prey, a motif commonly seen across metalwork and lustre-painted ceramics from the period. The combination of both scripts (Kufic and naskh), appears less frequently, however, and suggests that this mortar is a transitionary one between the late Seljuk and Ilkhanid periods.
6a3340c0-c680-5459-91d6-e838dcb5662c.dates: Hegira late 6th, early 7th century / AD 12th, early 13th century
6a3340c0-c680-5459-91d6-e838dcb5662c.bibliography: Fraser, Marcus, *The Honar Collection of Islamic Art*, 2008.
6a3340c0-c680-5459-91d6-e838dcb5662c.author: Tara Desjardins
materials: Cast copper, tin, zinc and lead alloy

6a900d8a-d3e6-5851-b145-8c3ebfc27556.name: *Sabil* (Water Dispensary) and *Kuttab* (Qur’anic School) of ‘Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda.
6a900d8a-d3e6-5851-b145-8c3ebfc27556.description:
This monument has a special artistic importance, for it is a free-standing complex that consists of a *sabil* (water dispensary) and a *kuttab* (Qur'an school) both of which display many of the glories of Islamic art specific to the Ottoman period. The building represents the style of *sabil* that has three windows and which is a blend of the Mamluk and Ottoman styles.  
The *sabil* has three facades (south, north and west) that are identical and equal in length. Each façade contains a semi-circular arch, which is supported by two spiral marble pillars. In the middle of the arch is a large opening from which cups of water may be obtained for passers-by (windows for the procurement of water or *tasbil*).  
The opening seen here sits within a semi-circular arch supported by two marble spiral pillars. The *tasbil* are covered with copper grills in the form of intersecting tri-lobed arches; these allow drinking-cups to be passed through them. The spandrels of the arches are decorated with splendid geometric designs executed in fine polychrome marble. The walls of the outer façade contain interlocked stone courses in the form of whirling vegetal leaves. The façade of the *sabil* is crowned with nine tiers of *muqarnas*, which bear the floor of the first storey containing the *kuttab*. The entrance to the *sabil* is located on Tambakshiyya Street, to the left of the southern façade, and resembles the Mamluk portal. The entrance is composed of a recessed wall crowned with a tri-lobed arch and a semi-dome decorated with tiers of *muqarnas*. In the middle of the recessed wall is the door to the *sabil* the straight, top lintel of which is adorned with carved verses of poetry. Above the lintel there is a marble decorative unit comprising a central circle. It contains the foundation text surrounded by four tiny circles.  
The entrance to the *sabil* leads to a small vestibule, which contains three doors: the first is located to the right of the entrance and leads to the cistern chamber; the second is to the left of the entrance and leads to the room from which the water is distributed *hograt al-tasbil* (water dispensing room), and the third is at the rear of the vestibule leading to the stairs and up to the *kuttab*. The floor-plan of the water-dispensing room is rectangular (3.50 m x 4.50 m). Three windows are located within the recessed areas of the room's three walls, which overlook the street. The walls of the room are panelled with blue-glazed ceramic tiles and decorated with a multiplicity of vegetal decoration. The southern wall contains a panel of glazed tiles depicting a view of the Holy Ka'aba and the buildings surrounding it.  
The *kuttab*, or school room, has a rectangular floor-plan of the same dimensions as the *hograt al-tasbil*. The *kuttab* overlooks the street from three directions by means of three *mashrabiyya*, and it has seven marble pillars, which resemble the pillars on the façade. The pillars are topped by six stone pointed arches, crowned with an inclined wooden awning. A balcony projects from the *kuttab,* characterised by 14 exquisite slim wooden pillars which bear 15 arches supported by balustrades, made from beautiful turned wood. The balcony is roofed with a wooden awning that is lower than the first.
6a900d8a-d3e6-5851-b145-8c3ebfc27556.short_description: This building has special artistic importance as a freestanding establishment in the heart of al-Muizz Street. It consists of a *sabil* (water dispensary) with three façades and three windows covered with iron grills for distributing free drinking water to the local population, passers-by and travellers. The second floor is occupied by a *kuttab* (Qur'anic school for children) with a balcony overlooking three sides through *mashrabiyya* screens. The Mamluk and Ottoman styles blend harmoniously in the construction of this monument.
6a900d8a-d3e6-5851-b145-8c3ebfc27556.method_for_datation: The building was dated based on an inscription above the entrance that includes the name of the sponsor and the date of construction. Furthermore, a *waqf* deed is preserved in the archives of the Ministry of Awqaf or Endowments (file no. 941, dated 1158 \[1745\]), it also gives the name of the builder.

6b6b4b3d-5bf3-5fad-ab1e-65d67c460f9d.name: Dining room set with bench
6b6b4b3d-5bf3-5fad-ab1e-65d67c460f9d.description:
Displayed in the reception room of Yusuf Al-Sabai's former residence, now part of the FBQ Museum, is a striking dining set comprising a table, chairs, and a bench crafted in the Islamic arabesque style. Renowned for its intricate inlay craftsmanship, this set incorporates mother-of-pearl, ivory, and wood, utilising even the smallest wood chips and other available materials. This approach not only enhances aesthetic appeal but also minimises waste and encourages sustainable practices.  
The set features intricate geometric patterns and architectural elements such as arches and squinches influenced by the Coptic art of Egypt. This piece embodies the essence of Islamic decoration, characterised by unity and meticulous craftsmanship. Its rich ornamentation reflects the concept of *horror vacui* (fear of emptiness), and is evidence of the artist’s desire to fill any available space with intricate details.
6b6b4b3d-5bf3-5fad-ab1e-65d67c460f9d.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum

6bc80197-f494-512f-83bf-359f1180b074.name: Baking flatbread on a metal griddle in the Syrian Dead Cities
6bc80197-f494-512f-83bf-359f1180b074.description:
Flatbread is the staple food of the Syrian population to this day. It is mostly baked in state-licensed bakeries, where only thin flatbreads from superfine wheat flour are made. Rarely do women have to bake their own flatbread every day, as bakery flatbread is available in nearly all parts of the country. For special occasions and huge feasts the traditional flatbread is preferred. In a spirit of mutual help, often a neighbour’s wife bakes bread for the feast. In the photo, the wafer-thin flatbread is baked on a convex metal griddle (*saj*), which is heated on an open fireplace. This griddle bread (*khubz saj*) consists of wheat flour – preferably from coarse local wheat – and water and salt.  
The dough must be kneaded intensely to retain its stickiness and not tear. The wafer-thin flatbread consists of only one layer. In some regions – as visible in the photo – the dough is rolled with the help of a rolling pin, and in other regions it is beaten back and forth with the palms of the hands to obtain a large thin bread.  
The flatbread, when torn into pieces, serves as spoon and is eaten along with the food.
6bc80197-f494-512f-83bf-359f1180b074.bibliography: Pasqualone, A., “Traditional flat breads spread from the Fertile Crescent: Production process and history of baking systems”, Journal of Ethnic Foods, vol. 5, issue 1, March 2018, 15.
6bc80197-f494-512f-83bf-359f1180b074.author: Karin Pütt

6c5c8e73-e448-5d73-a3ad-4f85d6d02cff.name: Cup
6c5c8e73-e448-5d73-a3ad-4f85d6d02cff.description:
The production of raw glass in Cordoban workshops is documented at least since the 10th century. By using vegetable fluxes to replace natron, it was possible to implement local production and multiply its presence in luxury crockery.  
As glass crockery was understood as a sign of refinement, Abbasid caliphs such as Harun al-Rashid might have sponsored their industry in Baghdad. Similarly, it is thought that some of the great workshops found in the Iberian Peninsula may have been sponsored by rulers of al-Andalus, both in the Caliphate period and later.

6cac4f71-4c6d-5af5-91b7-33d7f396babe.name: *Iyar-i Danish* (‘Touchstone of Wisdom’)
6cac4f71-4c6d-5af5-91b7-33d7f396babe.short_description: The text of *Iyar-i danish* (‘Touchstone of Wisdom’) derives from the collection of Sanskrit animal fables known as Panchatantra and thought to have been compiled sometime before AD 500. Since then, several versions of the fables have appeared, in ancient Pahlavi, Persian and Arabic. The version known as *Iyar-i danish* was compiled at the Mughal court for the emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605). The fables are part of the genre of literature known as ‘mirrors for princes’, consisting of stories intended to instruct rulers in the art of statecraft. Each chapter of the text consists of a frame story dealing with a specific moral. The characters of the frame story then each tell their own stories of behaviour exemplifying the moral in question.
keywords: fables; stories; literature; manuscript; animal; Kalila wa dimna; lion; fox; miniature painting; illustration; education
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

6cd11199-5a66-5c15-872a-057190826a48.name: Rosewater sprinkler
6cd11199-5a66-5c15-872a-057190826a48.description: This *mirash* vessel is designed to hold and sprinkle rosewater onto the hands of guests as a sign of hospitality. These vessels come in a variety of shapes and decorations; the people of the Green Mountain in eastern Oman have traditionally pursued this craft for thousands of years, and their goods are known today for their quality and precision in manufacturing.

6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.name: Al-Hariri, *Maqamat* ('Assemblies')
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.short_description: The Arab poet Al-Hariri of Basra, or Abu Muhammad al-Qasim ibn Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Hariri (d. 516 AH / 1122 AD), wrote the *Maqamat al-Hariri* (‘Assemblies of Hariri), which is a collection of fifty stories written in the *Maqama* style of rhymed prose with intervals of poetry. Al-Hariri also extensively utilises Arabic idioms and proverbs. While this style of writing was developed a century earlier, Al-Hariri elevated this genre into a major literary form through this work. In his *Maqamat*, the anecdotes are told by the roguish wanderer and eloquent trickster Abu Zayd to the narrator, al-Harith b. Hammam al-Basri. This copy was written in calligraphic large Mamluk *naskh* script by Abu'l-Fada'il b. Abi Ishaq in 734 AH / 1334 AD. The quality of the manuscript, its courtly title page, and large format suggest that it was created in Cairo, then capital of the Mamluk Sultanate and Caliphate. The sultan who possibly commissioned the manuscript and who may be the one depicted on the dedicatory title page is An-Nasir Muhammad b. Qala'un, who was in power for the third time from 709 AH / 1309-10 AD to 741 AH / 1340-41 AD. The manuscript includes seventy paintings, which must have been completed by a group of artists or a workshop. It is likely that multiple pages are no longer extant. The images that are preserved reflect a Mamluk style of painting, including bright colours on a golden background, more monumentalised scenes, and a reduction to essential elements in expression and composition, especially when compared to the Persian-Seljuk style of Baghdad and Mosul book-painting. The figures’ facial features follow the Turkish-Mongolian ideal of beauty that emerged under the Seljuks in Persia. The essential principle of composition throughout the manuscript is the juxtaposition of individual figures with figural groups, whereby means of deliberate contrast or symmetry are employed. These compositions underline the textual structure of the stories. The manuscript probably entered the Austrian National Library between 1820 and 1840.
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.dimensions: 373 x 260 mm (c. 260 x 160mm), ff. II, II*, 195 folios.
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.method_for_provenance: On fol. 1a, a note in the margin with incomplete names.
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.obtention: Unknown but came into the Austrian National Library between 1820 and 1840.

6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.name: Bowl.
6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.description: A thrown, earthenware bowl with a wide and flaring shape that sits on a small, round pedestal base; it has been moulded by hand around the rim to produce a ring of indentations. The bowl has been coated with a slip of liquefied clay and decorated with a simple flowing design on the inside with black and blue underglaze. It is glazed overall with a thickly applied glaze that is a transparent, intense yellow.
6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.short_description: This North African bowl would have been used for serving a vegetable stew with meat and couscous, a wheat product. Thrown on a wheel, it has a lid that matches it in shape but has a slightly smaller diameter. Vessels like this are still made today.

711fba2c-8e7a-5558-8785-0e3951b191e0.name: Table
711fba2c-8e7a-5558-8785-0e3951b191e0.description:
In Arab households symbols of hospitality and the embrace of visitors were deeply ingrained in the cultural fabric, taking on multiple forms. Chairs and tables in spaces like reception halls often bore inscriptions extending warm greetings to guests, occasionally integrating profound aphorisms and verses of poetry. These inscriptions served as decorative elements and cultural expression, and reflected philosophical ideals central to the household’s ethos.  
The FBQ museum holds a remarkable 19th-century Syrian wooden table adorned with meticulously carved inscriptions in *thuluth* script featuring mystical verses attributed to Ibn al-Farid. These poetic excerpts, drawn from his renowned poetry “If my position in love with you", epitomise the fusion of artistic refinement and intellectual depth, enhancing the ambiance of hospitality within the domestic sphere. It says:  
أُمْنِيّة ظفِرَتْ روحي بها زَمَناً واليومَ أحسَبُها أضغاثَ أحلام  
ولو علِمْتُ بأَنّ الحُبّ آخِرُهُ هذا الحِمَامُ (الموت ) لَمَا خالَفتُ لُوّامي.  
A wish my soul held onto for a while,  
Today I deem it mere illusions that beguile.  
Had I known love’s end is but a final breath,  
I'd not have shunned the counsel, evading death.  
Ibn al-Farid (1181–1234) was an acclaimed Arab poet born in Cairo to parents originating from Hama, Syria. Revered as the greatest mystic poet among Arabs, his literary compositions are reputed to have been penned during states of spiritual inspiration.  
The table is crafted from wood with intricately-carved inscriptions inlaid with mother-of-pearl. The carving process involves meticulous engraving with overlapping work. This fusion of techniques reflects the cultural sophistication and skilled craftsmanship of 19th-century Syrian artisans.

71d208fd-0631-5cc6-ad2e-caf974f2e875.name: Coffee-making utensils
71d208fd-0631-5cc6-ad2e-caf974f2e875.description: Traditional preparation involves roasting the green coffee beans over a fire in a pan with a long handle (*mahmas*). A pusher (*yad al-mahmas*) is used to move the beans back and forth in the pan. Once roasted on all sides, the black coffee beans are poured onto the cooling tray (*mubarrad*, at left in the photo). In the large, typically wooden or metal mortar (*mahbash, hawun*) the cooled coffee beans are crushed by using a pestle (*nijr, mudgag*). The physical effort required to do this produces a loud, sonorous noise. It is said that some coffee cooks employed unique beating rhythms.
71d208fd-0631-5cc6-ad2e-caf974f2e875.bibliography: Euting, J., “Tagebuch einer Reise in Inner-Arabien” (First Edition Leiden 1896), Hamburg, 1993, 84.
71d208fd-0631-5cc6-ad2e-caf974f2e875.author: Karin Pütt

71e530f4-815b-573d-aae7-8e626e13cbde.name: Khassaki Sultan Complex
71e530f4-815b-573d-aae7-8e626e13cbde.description:
It took four years to complete the complex (959/1552–963/1556), making it the largest charitable institution in the whole city.  
The complex is vast and has two entrances. The northern one lies on Aqabat al-Takiyya, while the southern one lies on Aqabat al-Saraya. In the local language, *al-Takiyya* means “*the place where food is served free of charge*”. *Al-Saraya*, on the other hand, means the seat of the governor or the *wali* and is named after the Ottoman mayor’s residence prior to the British Mandate.  
The complex is attributed to Roxelane, the wife of the Ottoman Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent (926/1520–974/1566), known as Haseki Hürrem (the cheerful, good-humoured one). Ottoman sources refer to her as Khassaki Sultan, in other words the Sultan’s favourite and beloved. Khassaki Sultan endowed generous *waqf*s on her social and charitable project to guarantee the perpetuation of its activities. The revenues of 30 towns and villages in Palestine and other places went into its budget. She added to them a *waqf* of four more villages donated by Sultan Sulayman to support her *waqf* after her death. These villages were located in different regions in Gaza, Nablus, Jerusalem, Sidon and Tripoli.  
The complex consisted of four different sections, some of which have survived: A large *caravanserai* to accommodate travellers and traders. It consists of a large entrance that leads to a corridor with rooms on both sides. The corridor ends in an open courtyard, which is surrounded by more corridors that form the *caravanserai*s. These parts can be seen today from the southern entrance, though some of their functions have changed.  
A mosque for prayer, reciting the Qur’an and praying for the benefactor. It has many domes and arches. However, its exact location is unknown and it is presumed that part of it was demolished and that the current student refectory was built over it.  
A *ribat*55 rooms to house *sufis*, the poor and visitors. Like the mosque, its location is also unknown today. It seems that most of the rooms have been demolished and changed into other utilities, although it was probably east of the southern entrance where the printing shop currently stands.  
A large kitchen, a bakery, a mill, many storage rooms and a fountain to provide water to the residence have all survived and can be seen after entering the courtyard from the northern gate and turning east via some stairs. The kitchen continues to provide delicious soups every morning plus meat and rice during Ramadan and every Tuesday, even though the *ribat*’s *waqf* ceased long ago.  
This active institution was administered by a number of senior Ottoman employees. The Inspector was posted from Istanbul and was helped by approximately 50 members of staff, each having a detailed job description allocated to him in the *waqf*. Among the employees were a person who washed the cups, another who picked the rice, two chefs and their three assistants, a renovator, and a maintenance person who would look after the building. In addition to the running costs, the total annual wage bill was approximately 795.5 silver dirhams.

72293d68-7e1a-5946-bc56-664b0db6be36.name: *Kama’ Al Sahra* (Desert truffles)
72293d68-7e1a-5946-bc56-664b0db6be36.description: *Kama’ Al Sahra* (desert truffle, *Tirmania nivea*) are subterranean fungi rather than true truffles. They are a delicacy eaten on their own or prepared in traditional dishes. People collect the fungi soon after rainfall in spring. *Kama' Al Sahra* grows close to *Ragroog* (rock rose, *Hellanthemum lippil*) bushes, which is perhaps how people locate the hidden truffles.

7262d726-e0b4-585c-b021-af6abc741b84.name: Covered al-Buzuriyya Market
7262d726-e0b4-585c-b021-af6abc741b84.description: Apricot paste can be consumed in two ways. It can be eaten raw after cutting it into small pieces, or – especially during Ramadan – a syrup can be made from *Qamr ad-Din* after soaking it in water for several hours, straining, then cooling it. Sometimes orange blossom or rose water is added to the syrup. *Qamr ad-Din* is traditionally served thick and cold, and is thought to be particularly fortifying and a good energy source after a day of fasting. Some Damascenes add pine and ice cubes.
7262d726-e0b4-585c-b021-af6abc741b84.author: Hiba Bizreh

7269ff1c-7668-58a5-a38d-e8ec83dace0c.name: *Zafarnāmah by Sharaf al-Din ʿAli Yazdi* (Timur's Return to Samarkand and the Festive Celebrations in the Garden of Bagh-ı Behesht)
7269ff1c-7668-58a5-a38d-e8ec83dace0c.description: *Zafarnāmah* is a significant historical text from the 15th century that describes Timur's leadership and achievements. Written by Şerafeddin Ali Yezdî (Hegira 858 / AD 1454), the work was commissioned by Timur's grandson, Ibrahim Sultan. As a historical source, *Zafarnāmah* is invaluable for its comprehensive information about Timur's life. The book was compiled using notes taken by Timur's royal scribes and secretaries, indicating that its contents were meticulously selected. Its most significant source is the biography of Timur, *Zafarnāmah*, written by Nizāmeddīn-i Sāmī in 1404. The primary distinction between Şerafeddin's *Zafarnāmah* and Sāmī’s earlier *Zafarnāmah* lies in the novel information presented in Şerafeddin's later version, and the more elaborate embellishments, including miniatures, in Sāmī’s earlier one.  The later work was inscribed by Hamdullah ibn al-Sheikh Murshid al-Kātib in Hegira 891 / AD 1486–1487, and is written in Persian with black ink in *taliq* calligraphy on fine paper. The work contains ten miniature scenes of rich workmanship, most of which depict Timur. The miniatures generally portray battles, council meetings and festivities that took place during the Timurid period. The first page contains the foundation seal of Hacı Mehmed Aga, the trustee of Teke Sancağı (Antalya region). The following page displays an illumination comprising geometric and floral motifs on blue and gilt backgrounds. The titles of the chapters and some of the prayers are written in gilt, red and blue ink.
7269ff1c-7668-58a5-a38d-e8ec83dace0c.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
7269ff1c-7668-58a5-a38d-e8ec83dace0c.obtention: The object was brought to the Museum from Antalya Müsellim Mosque on 31 March 1916.
materials: Finished (*aharli*) paper, ink, gilding, leather binding

72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.name: *Surname-i Hümayun* (‘Book of the Imperial Circumcision Festival’).
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.description:
The *Surname-i Hümayun* ('Book of the Imperial Circumcision Festival') is a work dealing with the celebrations held for the circumcision festival of Prince Mehmed, son of Sultan Murad III, which lasted for 52 days and 52 nights in AH 990 / AD 1582. It documents, in both word and image, how during the festivities the craft guilds paraded their various products, how a variety of entertainments were organised, how banquets were held and food distributed to the public every day, how the sultan would scatter gold and silver among the people from time to time, how poor children were circumcised and given new clothes, how beggars were made happy, and how people who had been imprisoned for debt were granted their freedom by having their debts paid. For this reason the *Surname* is an important historical source providing for us a record of the AH 10th- / AD 16th-century Ottoman lifestyle; its economy, social life, culture, art and entertainment.  
  
The celebration was held in the Hippodrome, i.e. the 'Horse Square'. The Ibrahim Pasha Palace is depicted here, and the three-storey wooden spectators' gallery erected at one of its corners for the use of palace officials and representatives of foreign governments, is an indispensable element of the scenes in the *Surname*.  
  
One of these scenes represents the parade of the glassmakers' guild. Here the sultan, seated on the enclosed balcony of the audience hall in the Ibrahim Pasha Palace, watches the glassmakers' guild along with the assembled people and the guests sitting in the spectators' gallery. The glassmakers present the glass objects they have made, even showing the stages of glass production and the tools they use with the help of a furnace mounted on a wheeled wagon.  
  
Another painting in the *Surname* shows the procession of architects and engineers with a faithful replica of the Süleymaniye Mosque made of wood and ivory. This picture is noteworthy because it represents Ottoman art in all its splendour, celebrated in both the depiction of the architect Sinan, who was still alive in this period and probably participated in this parade, and, through his most monumental building: the Süleymaniye Mosque.  
  
The celebrations of the circumcision festival are transformed into a painted story through 250 double-page miniatures with compositions generally similar to the two seen here.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.short_description: *Surname* is a magnificent manuscript telling the story of the circumcision festival of Prince Mehmed, son of Sultan Murad III, held at the Hippodrome in front of the Ibrahim Pasha Palace in AH 990 / AD 1582. The setting, processions and events are depicted both in writing and in miniatures.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.type: Manuscript, paper, ink, watercolor, miniature painting
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.method_for_datation: Since some pages of the manuscript are missing, including the colophon, it has been ascertained from the Kepeci Ruus register in the archives (3 Safar 997/1583 no. 250, 37) that it was completed in 997 / 1588.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.method_for_provenance: It is known that this manuscript was prepared by the team of artists in the Topkapi Palace atelier, and that it was therefore produced in Istanbul.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.obtention: The *Surname* was made for Sultan Murad III in the Topkapi Palace atelier and is still in the palace library.

And, M., *Kırk Gün Kırk Gece*, Istanbul, 1959.  
Atasoy, N., *Surname-i Hümayun*, Istanbul, 1998.  
Atasoy, N., “Tarih Konulu Minyatürlerin Usta Nakkaşı Osman”, *Sanat Dünyamız*, 73 (1999), pp.213–21.  
İpşiroğlu, M.Ş. “Das Hochzeitbuch Murats III”, *Deutsch-Türkische Gesellschaft*, Bonn, 1960.
