72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.artist:
In the Surname, the writer Intizami describes the preparation of the work in a section entitled ‘Description of the painter and his qualities’, stating that it was prepared by Naqqash Osman (who, like himself, was from the town of Foça in Herzegovina) and his team, although he does not give the names of the members of the team. A document dated 997 (AD 1588) written by the court panegyrist Sayyid Loqman on the subject of raising the salaries of the team working on the Hünername and the Surname, though, does list the names of the team members. Although it is impossible to determine from this document who was working on the Hünername and who on the Surname (or on both), the document is important because it gives a general idea of which painters (naqqash in Turkish) and other artists might have been working on Naqqash Osman’s team. The names that appear in this document are:  
Calligraphers: Seyyid Kasım; Mustafa; Feramruz?; Ali; Abdurrahman.  
Bookbinders: Abdi Şaban; Mehmet Haydar; Kara Mehmed; Mehmed …; Recep Abdullah.  
Painters (naqqash): Osman; Lütfi; Ali; Mehmed Haydar; Velican; Mehmed Musavvir; Molla … ; İbrahim; \[another\] Osman; Ahmed Abdullah; Hüseyin Zergub; Mahmud Müzehib?; … Abdullah …  
Illuminators: Musa Ahmed; Yahya; Seydi; Abdi Zergub; Şaban; Hızır Gazi; Mehmed Abdullah; Mehmed Mustafa; Nasuh bin Abdullah; Perviz Abdullah; Abd … Yakub; Davud Abdullah; Yusuf Abdullah.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.author: Şebnem Tamcan
keywords: Miniature painting; calligraphy; glass; Süleymaniye Mosque; Ibrahim Pasha Palace; Sinan.
materials: Finished (aharlı) paper, ink, watercolour, gilding, leather (binding).

749834b9-5f86-513c-a750-311aca2067e7.name: Deer-Figured Water Container
749834b9-5f86-513c-a750-311aca2067e7.description: The ceramic, off-white paste and one-colour turquoise glazed figurine has a navy blue glazed relief decoration with lines and dots on the back. The deer on a rectangular base has a hole in the back and on the head, and the three antlers are curved and joined at the top.

74a9ac30-d924-5b63-8349-21d424570c93.name: Covered al-Buzuriyya Market
74a9ac30-d924-5b63-8349-21d424570c93.description: During the Prophet’s birthday, the historic Buzuriyya Market in Damascus is crowded with people buying the necessities for the occasion, such as sweets and chocolate. The celebration usually takes place in the evening after Maghrib prayers in many mosques. The Mawlid opens with a short recitation of the Holy Qur’an, then comes the “Mawlid Recitation”, which is a narration of the Prophet’s biography recited in a special style. After that, specialised chanting groups perform religious songs and praise of the Prophet, and the Mawlawiyya dance to their music. The ceremony concludes with the Isha prayer and the distribution of sweets.

78a0a931-9669-5643-bd59-4f57da550407.name: Relief
78a0a931-9669-5643-bd59-4f57da550407.description: Cereals and olive oil were the bases of the local diet, wealth and trade. Their production expanded in al-Andalus thanks to technical innovations such as hydraulic and irrigation systems. Their implementation facilitated the control of agricultural cycles and changed working methods. Farming expanded into arid lands, increasing and diversifying harvests. The diversity of cultivated grains –wheat, rye, etc.– made it possible to develop multiple recipes for bread, an essential food shared by the whole of society.
78a0a931-9669-5643-bd59-4f57da550407.method_for_datation: The piece came from archaeological excavations at Madinat al-Zahra.

78f02594-a873-58a6-aa68-7ebabf8da732.name: *Oud* (Incense)
78f02594-a873-58a6-aa68-7ebabf8da732.description: Incense is traditionally used — and particularly on special occasions — to perfume one’s clothing, hair and body, and scent the home to welcome and honour guests. Three popular types of incense in the UAE and the Gulf region are *liban* (frankincense) a resin from the *Boswellia* tree species; *Bukhoor*, a mixture of aromatic woods, spices and oils; and the rare and expensive *Oud*, made from shavings of agarwood (*Aquilaria* species) infected by a fungi (*Phialophora parasitica*). The infected wood produces a dense and fragrant protective resin, which releases a unique scent when heated.
78f02594-a873-58a6-aa68-7ebabf8da732.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
78f02594-a873-58a6-aa68-7ebabf8da732.dimensions: Varies and depends on the fragment of wood. Length: 40mm, width: 15mm
78f02594-a873-58a6-aa68-7ebabf8da732.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: Incense; Oud

78fd5c1b-903d-5e4d-a4fa-83c8d3da2f2e.name: Bowl with two dancing girls, a flowering tree and bands of script
78fd5c1b-903d-5e4d-a4fa-83c8d3da2f2e.short_description:
This bowl was made in the *mina’i* technique, which was developed by potters in Kashan and was very popular in the late 12th century. *Mina’i* ware is identified by the use of coloured pigments under the glaze. Like many vessels made during this period, the bowl is coloured with muted colours and gold overglaze and was fired several times.  
The Inside of the bowl is decorated with two figures dancing around a small flowering tree, their headdresses flying. The edge of the bowl is inscribed in *kufic* script, wishing the owner happiness. The colourful picture resembles miniature paintings of the era and it is reminiscent of the rural life and cultural ceremonies of the region, possibly referring to Norouz, the Iranian New Year ceremony.
78fd5c1b-903d-5e4d-a4fa-83c8d3da2f2e.dates: Hegira late 6th century-early 7th century / AD late 12th-early 13th century
78fd5c1b-903d-5e4d-a4fa-83c8d3da2f2e.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and by comparison with pieces from the Seljuq period.

79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.name: Wash basin and jug.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.description:
The jug and basin were used at court on dining tables for the washing of hands. Medieval Arabic sources include descriptions of this sort of utensil. The daughters of amirs, viziers, high-ranking noblemen, officials and merchants all had this hand-washing equipment as part of their trousseau. Judging by the iconographic motifs of its decoration, the Berlin jug and basin look as if they were made for a lawyer. The inscriptions include blessings of a general nature (well-being, wealth, health, knowledge and leniency) for the unknown owner. Its original magnificence is clearly visible, as it has been excellently preserved.  
Judging by its shape, with its flap lid and straight spout, the jug has been made as a sculpted three-dimensional form. Its body, shoulder and neck are decorated with three friezes featuring figurative motifs within medallions of different sizes. The medallions are filled with depictions of thrones and riders and images of planets. The base of the neck shows 11 arched fields with standing figures in the style of Christian representations. A unicorn is being hunted in the animal frieze on the jug’s shoulder. There are additional Arabic well-wishing inscriptions within the friezes or spread over the jug.  
In the bottom of the basin, six planets are drawn encircling the sun, and in a second frieze, the signs of the Zodiac are depicted in relationship to particular planets. As on the jug, the outer surface of the basin is decorated with six large medallions that depict a prince flanked by two bodyguards, scenes of hunting and revelry. They are linked together by an inscription wishing for strength and victory, knowledge and leniency, qualities belonging to Allah.  
The complexity of the design and the highest quality of craftsmanship substantiate the high status of the person who commissioned its making. The jug and the basin are even signed with the name of the craftsman, which demonstrates that the artist was also held in very high regard.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.short_description: The extremely fine design and workmanship of this basin and jug demonstrate the skill of the metal craftsmen working in Mosul around 1270. Commissioned by someone of high rank and depicting the planets and scenes of courtly life, the set may have been used for washing hands on special occasions.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.dates: Hegira second half of 7th century / AD second half of 13th century.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.dimensions: Jug: height 37 cm, diameter 20.6 cm; basin: height 17 cm, diameter 43 cm.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.method_for_datation: The artist, ‘Ali ibn ‘Abdallah al-‘Alawi, who signed both the jug and the basin, lived during the mid-7th / mid-13th century.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.method_for_provenance: The artist, who signed both the jug and the basin, includes in the inscription of his name an indication of his town of origin: al-Mawsili, ‘from Mosul’, signifying where he was born or where he worked. The signature and the motif of the figure with a crescent in front of its body suggest that it is very probable that this piece originates from Mosul.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.obtention: From a private art gallery in 1938.

7a68823e-191b-5fd3-bb5a-c45c2eb03deb.name: *Qolla* jar for provisions
7a68823e-191b-5fd3-bb5a-c45c2eb03deb.description: Directly inspired by the *khabiya*, a large jar for food preservation, this pot was used to store and preserve liquids such as oil or water, and various foods. The decoration includes a stylised branch motif with alternating leaves called *babbouch* (snail).

7a94e504-793e-5d4f-8a12-0fe92e32a0e7.name: Jug with depiction of animals
7a94e504-793e-5d4f-8a12-0fe92e32a0e7.short_description: The shape of this jug with handles ending in dragon heads comes from Timurid Iran. On the body of the jug and amidst Ottoman decoration hunting scenes are depicted with fantastic and real animals. On the neck paradisiac scenes: two naked figures under a tree, a bear holding a musical instrument and peaceful animals. This animal style originates in German Renaissance silver and was adapted into the repertory of the Balkan Christian workshops before passing into the Iznik ceramics.
7a94e504-793e-5d4f-8a12-0fe92e32a0e7.dates: Hegira 10th century / AD second half 16th century
keywords: Hunting; figurative decoration; animal decoration; Ottoman Balkans; garden; imaginary animal

7aacbb88-ad52-5968-8bde-ffaeaaf35c53.name: Tray (*sinija*)
7aacbb88-ad52-5968-8bde-ffaeaaf35c53.description: Copper tray – *sinija* (Tr. *sini*) – of circular form with raised omphalos in the middle, which is the center of the rosette with pointed petals and flower motifs within. The broad band that frames the central design is decorated with zoomorphic ornaments, composed of twisted vines and heads of different animals like leopards, lions, elephants, etc. Islamic brass or copper trays were used as serving trays for food and beverages, as well as decorative items in homes or public places.
7aacbb88-ad52-5968-8bde-ffaeaaf35c53.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.

7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.name: *Tabica* (small board).
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.description:
The splendid collar-beam framework of Teruel Cathedral, which has been erroneously described as a coffered ceiling, is one of the examples of Mudéjar carpentry most studied by art critics for several reasons, including its extraordinary iconographic and iconological complexity and its significance in the social context, and the interest generated by its style and dating, which has been helped by analysis of the wood. Among other items, the National Archaeological Museum holds two *tabicas* (small wooden boards) from the gables or planking, one of which shows a male figure and the other, the one examined here, a female figure.  
The woman is from the working class, a water bearer dressed in a long-sleeved, corded tunic or dress tied at the waist. The decorative horizontal lines give her a characteristic air. Her hair is short and her head appears to be uncovered, uncommon in figures on ceilings. She is carrying a two-handled jar. The flat colours are dominated by reds, whites and black outlines.  
It is possible to determine the *tabica*'s original position in the eighth section on the left, in the very place where a bomb fell during the war in 1936
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.short_description: This *tabica* (small wooden board) decorated the planks in the roof of Teruel Cathedral, showing the different classes of Mediaeval society. The figure is a water bearer dressed in contemporary costume: a long-sleeved dress tied around the waist.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.dimensions: Height 36 cm, width 23.8 cm, depth 1.7 cm.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.method_for_datation: From its style and from dendrochronological analysis of the wood.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.method_for_provenance: When giving this and three other pieces to the National Archaeological Museum, the donor, Pablo Gil y Gil, a professor at the University of Saragossa in 1869, reported that they came from the roof.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.provenance: Cathedral of Santa Maria de Mediavilla, Teruel, Spain.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.obtention: The piece was donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 19 August 1869.

7e379f31-6dae-5207-977d-3021cf599c7d.name: Coffee Cup Holder
7e379f31-6dae-5207-977d-3021cf599c7d.description: The base and body rim are segmented, and the inside of the segment is filled in with filigree. One hollow flower is attached to the inside of the slices on the body and to the borders where the segments meet.

7e9c43e1-9c01-5ae6-aa4e-69ea000166c4.name: *Shahnameh by Firdowsi* (Social Gathering for Entertainment)
7e9c43e1-9c01-5ae6-aa4e-69ea000166c4.description:
The text is written in verse and prose in six columns in black ink and *taliq* calligraphy on Harar paper. The outer edges of some pages are decorated with the *halkâr* technique, while the chapter titles are illuminated in a style typical of the period. Pages 1b and 2a are entirely covered with miniatures, with the scenes surrounded by illuminated edging. The book contains 32 miniature scenes, each depicting a story from the *Shahnameh* painted in the Timur-school style.  
The volume is bound in black leather over cardboard and is of a similar period. Four *salbek*s are at the corners, and in the centre of the white umbrella on the covers. The outer border panels are decorated with a variety of colours in the *kat’ı* technique.
7e9c43e1-9c01-5ae6-aa4e-69ea000166c4.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
7e9c43e1-9c01-5ae6-aa4e-69ea000166c4.obtention: The item was brought to the Museum from Hekimoğlu Ali Paşa Library on 1 March 1914.
materials: Finished (*aharli*) paper, ink, gilding, leather binding

8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.name: Bowl
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.short_description: Some *mina’i* ceramics enjoy a particularly close relationship to poetry. Many examples are inscribed with verses, and others are decorated with figures referring to well-known poetic themes and tales. Several of these colorful wares, including this bowl, appear to depict the act of poetic recitation itself: taking place at a *majlis* (an assembly of courtiers and literati for the purpose of poetic recital), it can be imagined that the performer here, seated at the left before a courtly audience, is delivering the verses inscribed along the exterior rim of the bowl, which begin: "If the beloved leaves me, what am I to do? If s/he does not see the wisdom of our union, what am I to do?"
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.method_for_datation: The bowl is dated Hegira Muharram 583 / AD March 1187. It is one of five *mina’i* bowls dated to the month of Muharram in its inscriptions. Among these, three have very similar scenes of a literary *majlis*. Two of them, the LACMA bowl and another in the British Museum (1945,1017.261) are dated Muharram 583, the third, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (64.178.1), dated 4th Muharram 582 / AD 27th March 1186, is signed by Abu Zayd. Both the Metropolitan Museum and LACMA bowls share the same curious figure at far left, a young man standing with his right leg bent and foot pointing downward; in the former, the figure is clearly holding his leg as though tired from standing. The LACMA bowl can be attributed to Abu Zayd, who not only created works in both *mina’i* and luster but was a talented poet. He is known to have included some of his own verses among the poetic inscriptions on his luxury ceramic wares.
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.method_for_provenance: The bowl is decorated in the *mina’i* technique. A modern designation from the Persian word for "enamel", *mina’i* is almost entirely restricted to Seljuq Iran. While *mina’i* wares once were variously attributed to several sites on the basis of archaeological finds, the evidence demonstrates at present that the central Iranian city of Kashan was the nucleus for the production of these objects as well as contemporary luster wares; in fact, both types of wares were made by some of the same potters, in the same workshops. The *mina’i* technique involves the application of as many as seven colors, resulting in a well-controlled, polychromatic decorative surface not possible in other contemporary pottery types. The method for producing the polychrome enamel pigments is described in a treatise on pottery making by Abu’l-Qasim of Kashan, completed in Hegira 700/1301 AD, by which time *mina’i* or haft rang (“seven colors”) wares, as they are known in the textual tradition, were no longer being produced.
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.obtention: Possibly acquired by Mr. and Mrs. Allan C. Balch (1864-1943, and 1863-1943, respectively) from MacDermid Parish-Watson, New York (d. 1948). Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Allan C. Balch, until 1945 (gifted to); LACMA, gift of Mr. and Mrs. Allan C. Balch.

81885d7a-1511-5ad9-862a-b08626bdae85.name: Pitcher (*dolcha*)
81885d7a-1511-5ad9-862a-b08626bdae85.description: The *dolcha* is used to serve various drinks such as *gulab* (rose water), *ovshara* (a syrup served cold), *iskanjabi* (a syrup made from honey and vinegar), which enhance the culinary culture of Azerbaijan. Rich, delicate floral patterns, *butas*, flowers, zoomorphic and geometric figures are depicted on the copper jugs of various shapes and capacities. Additionally, some inscriptions include the date of make and the names of the master, customer and owner are reflected: in this case, the date Hegira 1281 (AD 1864–1865) and the work order of merchant Abdul Ali are written on the lower right.
81885d7a-1511-5ad9-862a-b08626bdae85.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analyses with related material
81885d7a-1511-5ad9-862a-b08626bdae85.author: Rustam Afandiyev

8224937d-eb35-5a76-923e-7d2bb6181a08.name: Coffee-roasting spoon
8224937d-eb35-5a76-923e-7d2bb6181a08.description: In Oman, copper is a traditional material for making equipment related to the kitchen and dining room. Smiths still practice the trade along the coasts of al-Batinah and the interior; this spoon hails from the al-Dakhiliyah Governorate. Coffee-roasting spoons are one of the most important tools used in the preparation of Omani coffee in the *dallah* pot, where coffee beans are stirred until roasted and ready for grinding and boiling.
8224937d-eb35-5a76-923e-7d2bb6181a08.holder: The National Museum - Sultanate of Oman

823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.name: Ewer and basin set.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.description:
A set comprising two pieces: a ewer and a basin that was used for ritual ablution. The basin is large with a flaring rim. The ewer has a pear-shaped body, a curved handle and a lid. The flaring rim of the basin and the body, lid and lower part of the spout of the ewer are decorated with lozenges formed by small grooves. Vertical and horizontal grooves in the lozenges also form square motifs. On top of the lid are a flower-bud and leaf in keeping with the fashion of the time.  
  
The set is decorated in a gilding technique known as *Tombak* and engraved. In Turkish metalwork gilding, especially of pure copper artefacts, appears in the AH 12th / AD 18th century. Technically, this method of gilding involves spreading an amalgam of powdered gold and mercury on the surface of the object, which is then fired in a kiln. The mercury evaporates during the firing, while the gold powder adheres to the surface. Sometimes gold leaf is placed on a mercury-coated metal surface, and when the mercury evaporates during firing, the gold leaf is fixed to the object.  
  
The inscriptions on the ewer and the basin inform us that the objects were dedicated to the Tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, and they give the date of AH 1286 (AD 1870). Pertevniyal was the second *iqbal* (lit. 'fortunate one') of Sultan Mahmud II (r. AH 1223–55 / AD 1808–39). When she gave birth to Abdülaziz, she ascended to the highest female rank at court and when Abdülaziz ascended the throne in AH 1278 / AD 1861 she became the Valide Sultan (Mother of the Sultan, i.e. the Queen Mother). She had a complex built in her own name in the Aksaray Quarter of Istanbul. It comprised a mosque, a *maktab* (school), a *sabil* and a public fountain, and a tomb which was built for her in the courtyard of the mosque and in which she was buried when she died in AH 1300 / AD 1883. The Museum owns several objects taken from this tomb, some of which are in this exhibition.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.short_description: Gold has been the expression of economic power in all periods of history. *Tombak* is a technique that gives the look of gold to items and is used to decorate this ewer and basin set used by Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, mother of Sultan Abdülaziz, during religious ceremonies.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.initial_owner: Possibly Pertevniyal Valide Sultan (d. 1300 / 1883; queen mother from 1277–92 / AD 1861–76).
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.dimensions: Basin: height 12 cm, diameter 60 cm; ewer: height 30.5 cm.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.method_for_datation: Both the ewer and basin bear an inscription stating that they were dedicated to the Tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan and giving the date of 1286 (1870).
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.method_for_provenance: Both the ewer and basin were dedicated to the tomb of Sultan Abdülaziz's mother, Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, in Istanbul and, due to the fact that the *tombak* technique was used especially in Istanbul, it is highly likely that this set was produced there.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.obtention: The ewer and basin were transferred to the museum in 1926 from the Tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan in Istanbul, to which they were dedicated.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.bibliography: *Anadolu Medeniyetleri III, Selçuklu-Osmanlı (Anatolian Civilizations III, Seljuqs-Ottomans)*, Istanbul, 1983, p.305.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.author: Alev Özay
keywords: Tombak; ewer; basin; Pertevniyal Valide Sultan; Mahmud II; Abdülaziz.
materials: Gilded copper, known as the *tombak* technique.

84aca75b-106a-53be-b6ce-f390d4bbcb97.name: Pilgrim flask
84aca75b-106a-53be-b6ce-f390d4bbcb97.description: A round bodied pilgrim flask covered with intricate polychrome decoration and painted with floral motifs and circular medallions with checkered designs and red dots. In the centre, there is a stylised flower in yellow and dark blue.

85cf7a4a-6a0b-533a-a23e-b4e6fb959910.name: Offering bitter coffee in a guesthouse
85cf7a4a-6a0b-533a-a23e-b4e6fb959910.description:
The bitter, unsweetened coffee (*qahwa murra*) is drunk from a small, handleless porcelain cup (*finjan*), into which less than three sips are poured. The guest drinks the coffee immediately and is offered the opportunity to drink another cup. Out of politeness or taste, the guest accepts a second and possibly a third portion. To indicate that he does not want any more coffee, he waves the cup back and forth slightly between his thumb and index finger and adds the phrase *dayman*, meaning “May you always have the means to serve coffee!”  
There are various regional sayings about the three cups that are usually drunk. A Palestinian saying goes:  
“The first cup, take to the generous who would feed his tribe bread and butter in hard times;  
And the second cup, pass to the one who would sacrifice his soul to protect a refuge-seeker;  
And the third, take to the one who would come forward, undeterred by barking dogs.”  
The effect of the coffee on the body is immediate: the long boiling process causes the bitter substances contained in the *Coffea arabica* to be released in such a way that the stimulant is felt and the immediate thirst is quenched.  
Coffee was first introduced to the Muslim world by Sufis, who used it during their religious practises, as reported by the traveler Mustafa Ali, who visited Cairo in Hegira 1007/AD 1599.
85cf7a4a-6a0b-533a-a23e-b4e6fb959910.bibliography: Lange, K., "Heroic Faces, Disruptive Deeds. Remembering the Tribal Shaykh on the Syrian Euphrates", Dawn Chatty (ed.),
85cf7a4a-6a0b-533a-a23e-b4e6fb959910.author: Karin Pütt

86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.name: Public drinking fountain.
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.description:
This fountain was designed for the Mosque of Mustafa Lala Pasha. It resembles a bench and is made of fine marble decorated with calligraphic carving and geometric mosaics composed of coloured marble and mother-of-pearl. The upper section consists of a marble panel grandly engraved with two lines of Arabic inscriptions written in the busy and rhythmically over-lapping *diwani* script, a calligraphic type popular during the Ottoman era. A thin band of vegetal motifs divides the two lines of inscription. This central panel is flanked by a pair of curvilinear brackets that are also heavily ornamented with vegetal and calligraphic carvings.  
The inscription conveys that the fountain, referred to as a *rub*' (a unit of water measurement), was built and made available to the public in honour of Sultan Sulayman by the High Aristocrat Mustafa Pasha in AH 971 / AD 1564. The date seems to have been important as it is written numerically and alphabetically in three different locations within the inscription. This is the date upon which Mustafa Lala Pasha became the governor of Damascus and he would remain in this prominent position for the next five years. Of his *waqf* endowments to Damascus, he built a new mosque and a new *khan* with lavish water supplies. During the reign of Sultan Salim II (AH 973–81 / AD 1566–74) Mustafa Lala Pasha was assigned as the military commander to conquer Cyprus in AH 977 / AD 1570, one of the greatest victories of the Ottoman military.  
The inscription on this fountain translates as follows:  
“The one who built this public *rub'*, may God make it the most useful, during the era of the most God-fearing sultan, the Sultan Sulayman Khan son of the Sultan Salim Khan, may God the Most Exalted raise him to the throne of the sultanate, is the High Aristocrat Mustafa Pasha, may God include him in the intercession of his mediator, the heir of the Ottoman kingdoms of the Sultan Salim Khan, the most God-fearing, may God light up his realm with his brilliant light, the utterance of this text was dictated and inscribed in the year nine hundred and seventy-one, 971 \[1564\].”
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.short_description: An important marble fountain made in Damascus and dedicated to Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent by the powerful military aristocrat and governor of Damascus, Mustafa Lala Pasha.
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.initial_owner: The ruler of Damascus Mustafa Lala Pasha (r. AH 971–6 / AD 1563–9) in honour of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66).
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.method_for_datation: The inscription on the object includes the date of its completion in 971 (1564).
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.method_for_provenance: The fountain is dated by the documentary records at the Museum.
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.provenance: Mosque of Mustafa Lala Pasha, Damascus, Syria.
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.obtention: The Mosque of Lala Mustafa Pasha in Damascus was demolished between 1928 and 1930 so that the Suq al-Hal could be built. However, this piece along with a number of other archaeologically valuable objects, were relocated to the Museum for preservation. This piece was registered at the Museum in 1931.
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.bibliography: Abu al-Faraj al-Ush, M., *A Concise Guide to the National Museum of Damascus*, Damascus, 1969, p.183, p.244.

keywords: Marble; mosaics; public fountain; Damascus; Mustafa Lala Pasha; Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent; Selim II

869766dc-71ca-53a7-b67f-e1ed2b58d4ac.name: La Goulette
869766dc-71ca-53a7-b67f-e1ed2b58d4ac.short_description: The expansion of the city of Tunis necessitated the construction of a large modern port which would be accessible to large-tonnage ships. Thus, in the early years of the French protectorate, the port of Tunis, La Goulette, saw a sharp increase in traffic. As well as a fishing port, the primary function of La Goulette, it also became an industrial centre thanks to the construction of a power plant on the north side of the canal, which served the tramways and the electric railway going to the northern suburbs. Finally, on the eve of the war, La Goulette had also become a residential town, particularly popular in summer for its seaside resorts.
869766dc-71ca-53a7-b67f-e1ed2b58d4ac.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
869766dc-71ca-53a7-b67f-e1ed2b58d4ac.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
keywords: La Goulette port; Little Sicily

882edb61-7d84-519e-90cd-1e8568e3abc4.name: *Mokhfia* conical dish
882edb61-7d84-519e-90cd-1e8568e3abc4.description:
This conical plate, or *mokhfia*, is concave on a ring-shaped base. It has an arcade decoration called "turtle". In the centre of the dish a five-pointed star with green central point is inscribed in a double circle. Six blue dots are inside and five are outside of this star. From this central motif is a radiating design of five large green rounded forms, or scales, each with two dots on either side of a wide decorative stripe edged in yellow. The inside rim of the cup features a braided pattern enhanced with small blue strokes. This particular decoration and type of ceramic are characteristic of Moroccan work between the 17th and 19th centuries. They are widespread in Morocco and Spain. We note the Andalusian influence in certain motifs, such as the use of geometry.  
This piece cannot be attributed with certainty to a single production centre. However, Fes is the most important one of the period. The decoration with concentric arches called "turtle" is characteristic of these polychrome Moroccan ceramics. In the 19th century, the colours used were more assertive, the shapes heavier, and the designs less spontaneous than before.
882edb61-7d84-519e-90cd-1e8568e3abc4.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute
882edb61-7d84-519e-90cd-1e8568e3abc4.obtention: Purchased at auction on advice of Piasa, 2002.

893a0815-f9f4-52c7-8775-ffe7b752a7e5.name: al-Ghuta ash-Sharqiyya
893a0815-f9f4-52c7-8775-ffe7b752a7e5.description: The apricots are pressed using a press installed in the orchard or in the sheltered part of the facility. This press is equipped with two superimposed sieves, one with large holes to remove the stones and another with a much finer mesh to remove the fibres, leaving only the juice to pass through. The juice is collected in a large-capacity basin of more meticulous construction; the interior is tiled and surmounted by a fixed metal structure. The model of press dates from the 1970s. This operation takes place when the heat dies down at the end of the afternoon.

899ab17a-563d-52eb-b76f-6ab3b73e0e14.name: *Fanayeel* or *Fanyaal* (Coffee cups)
899ab17a-563d-52eb-b76f-6ab3b73e0e14.description:
*Fanayeel* (Coffee Ccups)  
Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving dallah referred to as a mezallah, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the mezallah with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
899ab17a-563d-52eb-b76f-6ab3b73e0e14.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
899ab17a-563d-52eb-b76f-6ab3b73e0e14.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: coffee cup; ceramic; coffee; cup

89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.name: Tray.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.description: A large brass tray with extensive silver inlay, much of it now missing. The layout is a study in circles: the central motif, a geometric pattern itself derived from intersecting circles, is linked to three circles which divide the surrounding inscription into equal parts. Within this arrangement there are further circles within circles. The whole composition serves as a framework for no less than seven inscriptions, whose verticals, arranged like spokes within wheels, provide a striking and satisfying visual contrast. The largest inscription reads, 'Glory to our master the Sultan, the wise, the diligent, the just, the warlike king – may his victory be glorified'! The same sentiments are reflected in all the inscriptions, right down to the tiny roundels which proclaim, 'Glory to our master, the Sultan'! A bold use of inscriptions, in which a laudatory text becomes the main part of the decoration, is a hallmark of Mamluk art. Although the identity of the patron is not clear (see below), a magnificent tray like this would have been a valued adornment of his court.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.short_description: A splendid brass tray extensively inlaid with silver to form geometric and calligraphic decoration. The bold inscriptions are particularly striking, although the identity of the sultan they praise is ambiguous. Such a tray would undoubtedly have been used at court gatherings.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.initial_owner: Possibly either of the Mamluk rulers Sultan Abu Bakr (r. AH 742 / AD 1341) or Sultan Muhammad (r. AH 762–4 / AD 1361–3).
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.method_for_datation: The style of the tray is that of the mid-8th / 14th century. The specific identity of the patron is ambiguous; the inscriptions make reference to 'al-Malik al-Mansur', a regnal name which was used by two Mamluk sultans in this period: Abu Bakr (r. 742 / 1341) and Muhammad (r. 762–4 /1361–3).
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.bibliography: Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East, London, 2004, p.97.
89f6478a-1ada-5ce1-adfa-ba98750e463f.author: Barry Wood
keywords: Inlay; geometric patterns; inscription; calligraphy
materials: Brass inlaid with silver and gold.

8a2ff55d-1f20-5c07-9cc0-adf4d8569dfe.name: Incense burner
8a2ff55d-1f20-5c07-9cc0-adf4d8569dfe.description: Incense burners like this are usually made of clay mixed with water and kneaded until a mixture is formed that can then be shaped. The burner is then adorned with engravings, intricate drawings, and different colors. The incense burners are then fired in a kiln, after which they are ready for use. Note the handle; it makes the burner safe to carry from room to room. Incense occupies a central place in Omani life, as the passing of a fragrant burner at the end of a visit is customary in every region of the country.
8a2ff55d-1f20-5c07-9cc0-adf4d8569dfe.author: Noora Al Balushi

8b04bc89-ef4a-56d1-a8a5-314527494983.name: Stag aquamanile
8b04bc89-ef4a-56d1-a8a5-314527494983.description:
This aquamanile in the shape of a standing stag illustrates that animal motifs were considered suitable for handwashing vessels in Fatimid Egypt in the 10th and 11th century. The object is characterized by a cup-shaped opening, through which it can be filled with water, and spouts located in the snout and nostrils. The front of the snout is closed, instead water flows out from openings located on either side of the mouth. The handle is shaped like a slender and highly stylized quadruped standing on the stag’s back; it leans its front legs against the neck, where the cup is positioned, and stretches its head upwards, as if trying to reach the water source. Notably, aside from several folds in its skin, the stag’s body is not ornamented. This makes it one of the few Fatimid aquamaniles, and indeed one of the few Islamic animal figures, with an unadorned body surface.  
  
The work is primarily compared with the only other known stag aquamanile, now located in Munich (Museum Five Continents, Inv.-Nr. 26-N-1). The motif of the drinking stag was transmitted into Islamic culture through the translations of the Physiologus, a didactic Christian text written in Greek by an unknown author in Alexandria during the 2nd century AD. It describes animals and fantastic creatures and provides accompanying moral commentary. Thus, both Christian and Islamic stag iconography refer back to the same source. In addition to stags and deer, there are other aquamanilia surviving today that originate from regions under the control of the Sasanian as well as the Umayyad, Abbasid, and Fatimid rule. These can be dated between the 6th/7th century and the early 13th century.  
  
The handle and the spout reveal the function of the object; it allowed for the pouring of two streams of water onto two outstretched hands, so they may be washed. Its material made it unsuitable for holding wine and its large size prevented its use as a drinking vessel. Aquamanilia were most likely used in a courtly context for lavish festivities and private events with wine, singing, riddles, games, and friendly competition between poets. This would also explain the iconography of the aquamanilia, which refers to courtly culture. The imagery of the falcon, for example, was usually intended as a representation of sovereign power and a sign of authority.

8b6cb8d7-5e2c-57b5-b1ee-487c8180ac0d.name: Khanqah of Baybars al-Gashanqir.
8b6cb8d7-5e2c-57b5-b1ee-487c8180ac0d.description:
The Khanqah of Baybars al-Gashanqir overlooks Jamaliyya Street, and is characterised by a large façade made of stone which is located on the western side of the building. The façade of the mausoleum, which is situated within the *khanqah* together with its enormous dome, occupies a large part of the building's façade. The entrance is located on the southern end of the facade and is composed of a recessed wall, crowned by an arch, with a semi-dome roof. The area below it is ornamented with corner *muqarnas* with pendentives. The entrance is panelled with marble, and carved with Qur'anic verses in black and white marble. Along the entire length of the building façade there is an engraved epigraphic inscription in *thuluth* script. The inscription consists of the decree to construct the building and grant it as an endowment for the *sufi*s, and also names the sponsor. Above the roof of the portal is a minaret that is composed of three stories, each of which is separated by *muqarnas* tiers. The minaret is crowned by a pinnacle in the form of a small lobed dome. It resembles the summits of Ayyubid minarets which assumed the form of a *mabkhara* (an incense burner) such as the minaret of the Madrasa of al-Salih Najm al-Din Ayyub, also in Cairo. The minaret also has the remains of ceramic tiling reminiscent of that used on the minaret of the Mosque of al-Nasir Muhammad in the Citadel of Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi, also known as Citadel of the Mountain (Qala'a al-Jabal).  
The *khanqah* consists of a rectangular, central open courtyard measuring 16.50 m x 20 m; there are two large *iwan*s on its east and west sides, the bigger of which is the *qibla iwan* measuring 10 m x 12 m. In the middle of the *qibla iwan* there is a stone *mihrab*, which is simple and devoid of ornamentation. This might be due to the fact that the building was a *sufi khanqah*. At the north and south sides of the courtyard are the cells or the living quarters designated for the *sufis*. The *waqf* deed for the *khanqah* indicates that the building comprised three stories which included 100 *sufi* cells for permanent residence. Today only 11 of these cells are extant. The floor of the mausoleum is decorated with black and white marble and the walls are adorned with fine marble revetment to a height of 3.6 m. The mausoleum contains the grave of the builder and a lofty *mihrab* panelled with fine marble. Many of the building's annexes, such as the bakery and the kitchen areas, have been destroyed.
8b6cb8d7-5e2c-57b5-b1ee-487c8180ac0d.short_description: The *khanqah* (a hostel built to accommodate Sufis) had 100 cells on three floors, and a kitchen that provided each Sufi (mystic) with meat, food, three loaves of bread and dessert daily. For its upkeep the Sultan used craftsmen from Damascus, Aleppo and lands in upper and lower Egypt. When Sultan Ruqn al-Din Baybars al-Gashanqir was dethroned, Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad arrested and killed him. He seized all the establishment's property and deleted the Sultan's name from the epigraphic band on its facade. The *khanqah* remained out of service for 20 years.
8b6cb8d7-5e2c-57b5-b1ee-487c8180ac0d.method_for_datation: The building was dated based on an inscription band in the entrance passageway, which includes the date that construction was completed. Furthermore, the *waqf* deed specific to the building mentions that the Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars ordered construction in 707 (1307) when he was a commander, and before he assumed power. The *waqf* document bears the number 6–22 and is preserved in the Office of National Archives in Cairo.

8b90eb6b-ced6-5988-a13e-7f83f166a462.name: Coffee Container
8b90eb6b-ced6-5988-a13e-7f83f166a462.description: It is made of Lüleci clay. The base is in the shape of a circle and has a rounded centre. There is a Mevlevi headdress on the cover. It is decorated with flowers and parallel lines.

8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.name: Cooking pot.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.description: Pot with vertical straight rim with flattened lip and external flange, circular mouth and cylindrical neck. The body is shaped like a truncated cone with sharp carination close to the base. It has two strap handles with a central ridge and convex base. There are horizontal incisions around the rim, neck and body and fire marks indicate that it was used in cooking. The object has been restored.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.short_description: Kitchen implement with an extremely simple form and very little decoration. This type of pot was found in an Almohad oven excavated in Mértola and appears almost exclusively in this region, which helps to identify it as a local product.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.dates: Early Hegira 7th century / early AD 13th century.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.dimensions: Height 21.5 cm, width 35 cm, diameter (of rim) 23.5 cm, diameter (of base) 19 cm.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.method_for_datation: It was dated to the Almohad period on the basis of stratigraphy, since it was found in the abandoned levels of one of the houses of the citadel vacated after the Christian conquest of Mértola in AH 635–6 / AD 1238.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.method_for_provenance: This type of pot has been found in an Almohad kiln excavated in Mértola and is almost exclusive to this region. This indicates that it was produced locally.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.name: Strainer.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.description:
The greyish earthenware fragment showing openwork at the centre was part of a jug with strainer. The slightly convex strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of the vessel and was intended to protect the stored liquid from pollution and insects. Its design is inscribed in a circle and shows a quadruped passing to the left. The motif is set against a filigree background of rhombs. The major outlines of the animal, usually called a gazelle, are incised into the material. The remaining surface of the body is left plain. A striated zigzag line between two circles surrounds the quadruped.  
Decorated strainers are known from excavations of sites dated to the AH 2nd–9th / AD 8th–15th century. Strainers of the Fatimid period, which was the high point of their development, show not only the most varied patterns, but also the most elaborated compositions and the finest execution. As well as gazelle-like quadrupeds, other zoomorphic motifs such as elephants, lions, hares, birds or fish are depicted on the strainers.  
The strainers are only small fragments of vessels, but they call attention to themselves. One reason might be the unexpected combination of simple earthenware, mostly undecorated on the outside, with costly designs inside the neck of the jugs. Another might be that the potters created a highly aesthetic form for a simple utilitarian object. The complex patterns of the openwork carried out within small areas reveal the skills of the craftsmen.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.short_description: Earthenware fragment which was integrated in a vessel as a strainer. The latticework displays a quadruped, possibly a gazelle, passing to the left. The strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of the earthenware vessel to protect the stored liquid from insects and pollution.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.method_for_datation: A strainer also showing a gazelle was excavated at al-Fustat and dated according to numismatic evidence of undisturbed loci to the 5th / 11th century.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.method_for_provenance: Similar strainers were excavated at al-Fustat and their place of manufacture ascribed to the city. According to F. R. Martin, this strainer comes from excavations at al-Fustat.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.obtention: Purchased from the collection of the Swedish art dealer and art historian F. R. Martin in 1921.

keywords: Earthenware; animal decoration; water; purity of water; zoomorphic imagery

8ef1e4eb-e7ca-506a-8117-7e5c9d0e9a18.name: Small Octagonal Pavilion Tent
8ef1e4eb-e7ca-506a-8117-7e5c9d0e9a18.short_description:
A tent comprising eight contiguous panels, each measuring 211cm x 135cm, and an octagonal canopy of eight triangular pieces. The plain-weave cotton exterior is embroidered with silk and metallic yarns, and the interior is lined with woven silk panels.  
The exterior of the tent is a plain-weave cotton, which is resistant to sunlight and less likely to be damaged by rain, while the interior is lined with more fragile and luxurious silk fabric. The form of this small pavilion tent inevitably recalls the shape of medieval Iranian octagonal tomb structures or gunbad, whose decorative brickwork frequently includes corner columns or "tent poles."  
One of the eight wall panels is designed to open as an entrance, and the central part of each wall panel is embellished by a fabric "grille" that clearly imitates Persian wooden or metal grille-work. The design provides plenty of shade and privacy coupled with maximum air circulation, and the door panel could be closed for additional privacy.
8ef1e4eb-e7ca-506a-8117-7e5c9d0e9a18.dates: Hegira Mid 12th to early 13th century / AD late 19th century
8ef1e4eb-e7ca-506a-8117-7e5c9d0e9a18.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.

90313d34-f14e-568c-b0bd-898e9a4aef37.name: Bowl
90313d34-f14e-568c-b0bd-898e9a4aef37.description: This bowl was made using the *mina'i* enamel technique. Patterns and figures are depicted in cobalt blue, brown, green, red and black on a white primed surface. The centre of the bowl depicts a round-faced, almond-eyed, human figure with arched brows holding a goblet while seated cross-legged on a throne. On each side of this figure is a person standing with folded arms.

90e3e9c4-c63a-5a36-8816-be80a1947fe7.name: Tray *majmayi*
90e3e9c4-c63a-5a36-8816-be80a1947fe7.description:
This large, round tray (*majmayi*) for serving pilaf appeared at large feasts, such as weddings, engagements and funerals. They are usually made of copper and richly engraved with floral motifs and inscriptions in Arabic, usually the name of the owner and/or master, year of production, *ayahs* from the Quran, as well as wishes for owner's well-being. Such inscriptions were normally depicted inside cartouches. In 2015, the copper craftsmanship of Azerbaijani Lahij was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. According to the calligraphic inscription on the item, it dates to 1869–1870. It has a wavy edge and an inscription of a couplet from Hafez’s poetry engraved in the cartouch:  
"Saqi, brighten our cups with the light of wine.  
Sing, Minstrel. The world is now as we wished it."
90e3e9c4-c63a-5a36-8816-be80a1947fe7.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analyses with related material
90e3e9c4-c63a-5a36-8816-be80a1947fe7.author: Rustam Afandiyev
keywords: tray; tableware; majmayi; copper; Karabakh; Azerbaijan

9107cee6-86c6-50d5-afa3-39c67845bd31.name: Cup stand (*zarf*)
9107cee6-86c6-50d5-afa3-39c67845bd31.description: These delicate silver pieces known as *zarf* are an important part of the coffee ritual in Turkey, as they work as a protection and stand for the hot cups. We can admire those pieces as a part of the scenography in the portrait of the marquise of the Cerralbo and his daughter in Turkish costume made by Abdullah Fréres.
9107cee6-86c6-50d5-afa3-39c67845bd31.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes
keywords: Silver; Commodities

92830f7a-b5c3-5e7e-9a7f-a0686de50300.name: *Peškun*
92830f7a-b5c3-5e7e-9a7f-a0686de50300.description:
This *Peškun* (Tr. *peşkun*) has a base of ten vertical sides that carry a protruding decagonal plate at the top. The sides are also divided horizontally into three zones, the highest of which has a central flower motif, the middle a honeycomb-like openwork ellipse, and the lowest an opening in the form of a pointed five-leafed arch, below which is a flower with leaves and a rounded three-leafed arch. On the upper panel, there is a star-shaped field with a flower in the center of it, while other floral motifs are in the spaces between the decagon and the arms of the star. All floral and geometric ornaments are made of mother-of-pearl and brass wire using the incrustation technique, while the edge of the decagonal top plate is ornamented with bone.  
*Peškun* is the name of a traditional piece of Ottoman furniture in the shape of a table or stool. It was originally meant for sitting, although it had different purposes throughout history, especially as a decorative table in Balkan oriental interiors of the 19th and of the first half of the 20th century. Over time, the larger table (in the set of usually three pieces) began to be used as a coffee table, while the smaller ones were used as stools. *Peškun* were ordinarily made of walnut wood, ornamented with incrusted floral and geometric motifs made of mother-of-pearl and bone.
92830f7a-b5c3-5e7e-9a7f-a0686de50300.dates: Hegira late 13th–early 14th century / AD late 19th century–early 20th century
92830f7a-b5c3-5e7e-9a7f-a0686de50300.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material, technique, and analogy with other similar examples.
92830f7a-b5c3-5e7e-9a7f-a0686de50300.author: Ana Samardžić
keywords: peškun; stool; side table; incrustation; Ottoman Balkans
materials: Walnut, mother of pearl, bone, brass; incrustation

92b5f36b-5cba-54c2-8f14-3426b9111ac4.name: Palais de la Rose
92b5f36b-5cba-54c2-8f14-3426b9111ac4.short_description: The Palais de la Rose is an example of "Moorish" architecture from Spain and North Africa with Italian influences. Its most notable features are the grand staircase, the great hall surrounded by a marble gallery, and the huge, luxurious courtrooms. It is richly decorated in a variety of styles, with Italian marble in rare colours and an elegant rococo style, as can be seen from the Neapolitan faience pottery, the vaulted ceilings, and the tympanums finely carved from stucco or naqsh hadida in one of the styles popular at the time, such as an eight-point star between two stylised cypress trees. Finally, palace-museum's four great rooms invite its visitors to learn about the history of the Tunisian army from antiquity to the War of Independence.
92b5f36b-5cba-54c2-8f14-3426b9111ac4.history: The Palais de la Rose was built in the late 18th century, within La Manouba's royal gardens. Although originally used as a recreational palace for the Husainid beys, it soon began to receive many famous guests or persons visiting Tunisia, such as Queen Caroline of Brunswick in 1816. During the reign of Ahmed Pacha Bey (1837–1855) the palace became a residence for foreign teachers at the École Militaire du Bardo, among whom was the famous hero of Italian independence, Giuseppe Garibaldi. From 1881, the beginning of the French protectorate in Tunisia, the palace became the occupying army's headquarters. Following independence, the palace was restored and thus regained its original splendour and the became home to the Musée Militaire National.
92b5f36b-5cba-54c2-8f14-3426b9111ac4.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
keywords: Architecture; art; painting; stucco; mosaic; marble; ceramics

93ee1091-8763-5b6d-885f-d833bd95f55d.name: Incantation bowl
93ee1091-8763-5b6d-885f-d833bd95f55d.description: The bowl is inscribed in Mandean script, in Aramaic Mandean dialect. The text spirals from the bottom of the bowl about fifteen times around. The beginning of the text is unreadable because of a crystal deposits and blackening. The name of the sponsor, the beneficiary of these incantations, which is typically stated at the beginning of the text, remains unknown here. The remaining lines consist essentially of a repetition of names of demons exorcised by linked formulas, including the female demon Lilith, her ancestors (“all her families and lineages”), and her offspring. The Aramaic communities of Mesopotamia are heirs to ancient beliefs dating back to the Akkadian and even Sumerian texts, according to which demons were of an inexhaustible variety. The Mandean, because of his dualistic faith, believes in evil spirits whose harmful actions he dreads. Magic is therefore an essential aspect of his religious life. This practice, consisting in burying the cups thus inscribed at the four corners of the house, was widely diffused among the various religious communities of Mesopotamia until the Muslim conquest and beyond.
93ee1091-8763-5b6d-885f-d833bd95f55d.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute
93ee1091-8763-5b6d-885f-d833bd95f55d.obtention: Purchased at Art Musulman gallery in 1984.

9759fb2e-169a-5a39-8d80-11289577854b.name: Al-Haswa Dagger (*khanjar*)
9759fb2e-169a-5a39-8d80-11289577854b.short_description:
Attributed to Imam Saif bin Sultan al-Yarubi I (*Qaid al-Ard’*)  
Collections of Sultan Qaboos bin Said bin Taimur  
  
Saif bin Sultan I was the fourth of the al-Ya’aruba dynasty Imams of Oman (ruled Hegira 1104–23 / AD 1692–1711). He made the ar-Rustaq Fort his residence, adding the *Burj al-Riah,* “the wind tower”.  
  
The Omani navy reached a great degree of development during the Imam’s reign, where his foreign policy was based on renewing the struggle against the Portuguese on the Persian, Indian and East African coasts. In Hegira 1110 / AD 1696, the Omani naval fleet attacked Mombasa, besieging the Portuguese who had taken refuge in Fort Jesus. The Siege of Fort Jesus (also known as the Battle of Mombasa), ended after 33 months when the remaining survivors surrendered. Soon after the Omanis took Pemba, Kilwa and Zanzibar, becoming the dominant power on the coast.  
  
At home, Imam Saif bin Sultan invested in agrarian reform, building new *aflaj* water management systems and maintaining old systems; expanding the plantation of crops such as wheat, barley and sugar cane; planting date palm and fruit trees; introducing new varieties of plants such as turmeric, saffron and coffee; and establishing beekeeping.  
  
Saif bin Sultan earned the title Qaid al-Ard’ meaning "the Earth's bond" or "the chain of the Earth" for the benefits he brought to the people of Oman.
9759fb2e-169a-5a39-8d80-11289577854b.dimensions: Dagger width: 17cm, dagger length: 33cm; Belt length: 133cm; Blade length: 31.5cm, blade width: 7.2cm
materials: Rhinoceros horn, steel, wood, leather and silver

9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.name: *Egyptian village scene*
9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.short_description: Egyptian men and women are seen here in a town or village on the Nile. In the shade of an overhanging tree a market stall displays its wares, including paper lanterns and bread. At the stall behind, sugar cane is for sale. In the background is a mosque with a white minaret, though not distinctive enough to establish the scene's locality. Pilleau had visited Egypt in the winter of 1842-43 with Lieutenant Colonel George Everest (after whom Mount Everest was named) and two other companions, on their way home from India. On his return to England he published a set of twelve coloured lithographs, Sketches in Egypt (1845), which, like the better-known publications of Wilkie, Roberts and Owen Jones in the same decade, fuelled popular interest in Egypt and the Holy Land.

99b86f8f-18fe-561f-b1d1-b10181beb328.name: Baking flatbread in a *tannur* in an Assyrian village in northeast Syria
99b86f8f-18fe-561f-b1d1-b10181beb328.description:
Inhabitants of the western mountain areas and parts of northeast Syria bake the thicker (1–2 cm) flatbread that is baked on the wall of a bulbous vertical clay oven (*tannur*). To achieve the required temperature of the oven wall the firewood must be burnt down to embers.  
These ovens consist of an interior part made from clay mixed with goat hair and chaff, which is fired to become the inner wall. If the *tannur* should be placed above the ground, it will be given a thick coating of at least 30 cm from pieces of sun-dried mud brick and mortar, with a worktop to the side. These huge ovens are often placed in the corner of the courtyard or sometimes outside the compound as a common oven. In Syria rarely is a *tannur* dug into the ground, like the one in the photo taken in an Assyrian village in the Upper Khabur valley.  
The *tannur* bread (*hubz tannur*) requires more time to prepare, as yeast is added, and the dough is kneaded intensively. Preferably local wheat is used.

9a80618f-fbfd-5d5e-b4ee-f9684139776e.name: Kirman carpet
9a80618f-fbfd-5d5e-b4ee-f9684139776e.description:
The name of Persia (modern Iran) is so intimately associated with oriental rugs that they are often referred to generically as “Persian”. The golden age of carpet weaving had been during the Safavid rule of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The dynasty collapsed in 1722/3 and the country remained in turmoil for decades. It is likely that with the fall of Safavids most urban based weaving diminished greatly or ceased. All that remained was local production on a much reduced scale. The revival of the Persian carpet trade dates from the 1860s and was mainly due to enterprising merchants of the north-western city of Tabriz.  
Kirman has long been one of the major carpet-producing areas of Persia. Development of the carpet industry is poorly documented in Kirman, although there is clear evidence that weaving occurred during the Safavid times. Some of the best wool in the country is grown around Kirman. Weaving was well-developed during much of the 19th century. The rugs of Kirman always display a brilliant variety of colours and the number of shades is enormous. The dyes are varied and imaginative. Insect dyes have traditionally been used for reds and indigo was used for blues, providing a variety of shades. Colours can range from ivory, blue magenta to more golden and saffron cast.  
Persian workshops in the towns of Kirman, Tabriz and Kashan were the main producers of pictorial carpets. They portray humans and/or animals and illustrate historical and mythological stories. Sometimes the composition makes one or more characters that show famous people or events from the past.  
This pictorial carpet was a gift to the Museum of Arts and Crafts from Kemal Nanić and his family. The figural compositions depict the scenes from the famous Persian tragic romance *Khusraw and Shirin* written by the poet and writer Nizami Ganjavi (1141–1209). The poem describes the romance of the Persian king Khusraw II Perviz (590–628) and his wife Shirin, an Armenian Christian. The novel includes Khusraw's courtship of Shirin, their marriage and her romance with the architect Farhad. After a series of heroic romantic episodes, Shirin agrees to marry Khusraw who later built her a palace called Qasr-e-Shirin (the remains are visible even today). For the construction of palace architect Farhad was hired. Shirin then fell in love with Farhad, but their romance ended tragically.  
The central field of the carpet is divided into four horizontal rows. Each row has a mirror image of a group of human figures. They illustrate scenes from the poem *Khusraw and Shirin*, including a famous scene when Khusraw glimpses Shirin bathing. The central field is framed with four equally wide borders. The inner border is the *laleh abbasi* (abbasi tulip) border. The other three borders are a variation of the floral meander border.

9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.name: Basin
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.description:
This basin was discovered in pieces at the end of the 19th century in the centre of Seville. Restoration work has reconstructed the bands of inscriptions, as well as the decoration on three of its sides.  
The front is decorated with three tri-lobed arches, framed by alfiz (frame) panels supported on columns. Each arch contains a plant sprouting leaves, palmettes, pinecones and intertwining stems. The space between the arch and the alfiz panel shows the same type of decoration, and the whole thing is framed by an inscribed strip.  
The right-hand side shows a space divided vertically into three parts. The central area is undecorated, probably to allow space for the water to come out, and the other two sides show similar scenes: eagles, seizing deer with their talons, bear two lions face to face on their outspread wings, while beneath them two griffins facing each other complete the scene. This iconography, of Sassanid origin, refers to power, abundance and eternity.  
Only the inscribed band is preserved from the third side, a strip with ducks and fishes, and, underneath it, the remains of a lion attacking a deer.  
We know from the inscription that this basin was commissioned for the royal palace of al-Zahira on the orders of al-Mansur, prime minister and favourite of Hisham II, who was still a child when he became Caliph in AH 366 / AD 976, following the death of his father al-Hakam II. The unstoppable rise to power of al-Mansur started shortly after the accession of Hisham II. With the intention of establishing a parallel dynasty to the legal Umayyad one, al-Mansur built a palatine city called Madinat al-Zahira. This new city, rival to Madinat al-Zahra, was in the eastern part of Córdoba, but limited material remains have survived to the present day. The city was burnt to the ground in AH 399 / AD 1009.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.short_description: Emulating the Umayyad caliphs who built Madinat al-Zahra, the hajib of Córdoba al-Mansur built the palatine city of Madinat al-Zahira, and he commissioned this ablutions basin for it, as stated on the inscription. Animal-shaped spouts would have emerged from the attached side pillars, of which only traces have survived.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.dimensions: Height 68 cm, width 150 cm, depth 77 cm.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.method_for_datation: The inscription in *kufic* lettering says: '…Almanzor Abi Amir Muhammad ben Abi Amir and glory to God. \[This was\] ordered to be made for the royal palace of al-Zahira and was finished with the help and assistance of God under the direction of the great Amiri Fata in the year seven seventy and three hundred'. Consequently, the basin has been dated to 377 / 988.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.method_for_provenance: There are two other basins attributable to the same period and place, one of which can be found in the Alhambra Museum, Grenada, and the other in Marrakesh (Morocco). This latter was made for ‘Abd al-Malik, son of Al-Mansur. The three pieces have similar decorations of eastern origin on one of their sides.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.provenance: The missing royal palace of Madinat al-Zahira (Córdoba), Spain.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.obtention: The basin arrived at the National Archaeological Museum in stages. The two most important parts, the front and part of one of the sides, were bought on 22 November 1882. Another fragment arrived in 1923. Finally, on 30 July 1930, the last piece arrived from the Provincial Archaeological Museum of Seville.

9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.name: Dhow collection
9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.short_description: The National Museum of Qatar holds, in its collection, a fleet comprising of 14 dhows. The growing collection includes a variety of traditional dhows, with several models dating to the early 20th century, as well as more recent replicas of traditional vessels. Originating from Oman, Bahrayn, India and Qatar, among other places traditional dhows represented include *jalbut* (small to medium sized), *shuw\`i* (medium sized, once used for fishing and coastal trade), *sanbuq* (largest type in the Arabian Gulf today) and *baglah* (traditional, deep-sea dhows once used for the long – haul transport of goods.)

9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.name: Jar with lid.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.description:
The spherical jar stands on a high foot and has a cylindrical rimless neck with a flat lid with a knob. The body is covered inside and outside with an opaque, pale turquoise-coloured tin glaze. In the lower part the glaze is not thick enough so that the reddish colouring of the body shines through the glaze. The abstract decoration of the jar is mainly composed of a series of vertical stripes alternating with dotted lines, called 'millipedes', around the neck and a scale pattern filled with stylised half-carnations on the spherical section of the jar. The foot-ring is undecorated. The colours used are a deep limonite yellow, two gradations of brown, a light one of iron oxide and a dark one of manganese, and cobalt-blue and copper green. The use of brown, yellow, blue and green as full, unmixed tones is the characteristic colour scheme of Moroccan polychrome faience. Faience is the type of decoration: after a first firing the potters put on the opaque tin glaze on the earthenware vessel; the mineral pigments used for the polychrome decoration were applied over the dried glaze; in a second firing glaze and pigments melted together.  
The small and large red dots irregularly spread over the whole outside surface of jar and lid are a striking feature. It is a paste with a base of red lead applied over the glaze by fingertip. After drying, the paste appears like red wax. However, this kind of decoration was not executed by the potters themselves. It was done by the faience traders, at first to cover the traces of the firing tripods on plates and later on all kinds of pottery vessels.  
Faience was an urban ceramic in Morocco whose most important centre of production was Fez. The objects made by the faience potters were mostly functional and for everyday use. This pot was possibly used for storing fat or yeast. Unlike other examples of this kind of stock pot, however, this one does not have the usual two handles.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.short_description: Jar on a high foot and with a flat lid with knob. The decoration is composed of vertical stripes alternating with dotted lines and stylised half-carnations. The colour scheme is characteristic of Moroccan polychrome faience. This pot might have been used for storing fat or yeast.

9faeadc1-e075-5681-bdc1-072dabd412c6.name: Miniature 'Wine-Server' ('Portrait of a Young Man')
9faeadc1-e075-5681-bdc1-072dabd412c6.short_description: According to the inscription in the lower left corner of the composition, the author of the painting is Reza Abbasi, the most prominent Iranian artist of the AD 17th century. The founder of the new style of painting and the head of the famous Isfahan school, Reza Abbasi has departed from the bright decorative colours of the classic Persian miniature and turned to a more restrained and unusual palette. He chose a thin and sensitive calligraphic line as his main means of expression. Wine-server (Persian: *saqi*) - a young man who served at banquets, pouring wine to guests. A flask in a form of a gourd in his right hand testifies to his role. The man is dressed in a malachite green robe. An orange silk scarf is untied and carelessly thrown over his shoulders. His full face, dreamy staring eyes, curls falling down on cheeks, small gentle hands and graceful posture, the smooth curves of which seem to echo the flexible lines of plants - all correspond to the traditional type of an effeminate youth-*saqi*.
9faeadc1-e075-5681-bdc1-072dabd412c6.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis and inscription reading by V. Krachkovskaya (publication, 1926, origin and date).

9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.name: Irrigation bucket
9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.description:
The cylindrical object features a straight mouth and pointed base, with retaining recesses located at the start of the mouth and base. The surface shows traces of hand modelling, leaving indentations on the body in the form of perimeter circumferences and on the base in parallel lines following the conical shape.  
  
Made of whitish porous, unglazed clay, it retains traces of *almagra* (reddish pigment) drips on both the exterior and interior. Functionally, such objects can be understood within the context of irrigation and hydraulic systems in al-Andalus. Their development enabled the introduction of new plant species, the expansion of arable land, and the diversification of the diet. These innovations changed working methods, the agricultural cycle, and the landscape.  
  
Waterwheels spread throughout the Iberian Peninsula. The waterwheel buckets, which were secured with ropes at the top and halfway down their cylindrical body, underwent technical improvements. These elements reflect a series of small but significant technical advances. The earliest ones, with an annular or pointed bottom, gradually were replaced by others with a perforated bottom that prevented their tilting and breakage in addition to the backward movement of the wheel.
9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.method_for_datation: Comparative study of typologies; references provided by previous owner.

9ffa2249-250d-57c6-aa02-12cdbaa08791.name: Covered al-Buzuriyya Market
9ffa2249-250d-57c6-aa02-12cdbaa08791.description: The historic Buzuriyya Market is located south of the Great Umayyad Mosque in Damascus. This photo shows the very crowded market during Mawlid an-Nabawi (Prophet Muhammad’s Birthday). The Buzuriyya Market dates back to the Ayyubid era (AD 12th century). In the 18th century, the Ottoman government and several khans developed it together. In 1893, the Ottoman governor of Damascus, Hussein Nazim Pasha, replaced the Buzuriyya Market’s wooden roof with a metal roof. During Mawlid the market is decorated with colourful flags, especially green ones, and banners bearing the name of the Prophet Muhammad. Shops are filled with sweets, especially *Mulabbas*, which is associated with Mawlid and distributed in mosques and homes to all.

a0252068-e151-5eac-8d48-3f1ff00fc162.name: Jug
a0252068-e151-5eac-8d48-3f1ff00fc162.description: This exquisite jug, a prime example of Ottoman silverware, stands at just under 10cm tall. Adorned with intricate interlacing floral reliefs against a finely stippled background, it features a bulbous body, cylindrical neck, and a dragon-headed handle. Reflecting Timurid influences of the 15th century AD, and crafted in the early 16th century, it bears the faint tughra (monogram) of Sultan Selim (ruled AD 1512–1520) inside the neck. Renowned centres in the Balkans produced similar high-quality metalwork during this period. The jug, likely used as a drinking vessel, was probably commissioned for an elite or royal member of the Ottoman court, as evidenced by its delicate floral designs and partial gilding.
a0252068-e151-5eac-8d48-3f1ff00fc162.dates: Hegira first half of 10th century / AD 16th century

a0806d9b-0bf1-52cf-8538-62ee4530485b.name: Bowl with floral arabesque
a0806d9b-0bf1-52cf-8538-62ee4530485b.short_description: This shallow bowl has a separate disc riveted to the centre. The ornamentation represents almost the entire repertory of mid-16th century Ottoman decoration. A split-leaf arabesque is engraved on the disc; the cavetto has interlaced quatrefoil medallions and cloud scrolls; on the outer walls the half medallions are engraved with saz and rosette design. Broken stems around the base recall the mannerism of the Sünnet Odası panels, the Rüstem Pasha tiles and ceramic dishes from circa 1545-50.
keywords: Arabesque; Saz design; Ottoman metalwork

a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.name: Alhambra vase.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.description:
This piece is one of the so-called 'Alhambra vases'. Formally, all of these are similar: a large egg-shaped body and a narrow, unglazed base from which two large, flat handles emerge, and an octagonal neck reinforced with vertical mouldings.  
The decoration of pale gold on a white base is arranged horizontally in broad bands of different widths that are separated from one another by other smooth, narrower bands. The central, and widest, band contains vegetal motifs and an inscription in *kufic* characters in white on a golden background, in which the word 'forgiveness' is repeated several times. Both above and below the central band there are other similar bands decorated with plant arabesques and gold circles, all joined by a thread. The decoration of the main body is completed by another two bands, one on the lower part with small arches and another nearer the neck with a *kufic* inscription, now almost completely disappeared.  
The neck, which has eight sides separated by mouldings, is decorated with stylised vegetal motifs. The handles, attached close to the body, are decorated with the hand of Fatima (*hamsa*) on each side.  
The Alhambra vases constitute the most important examples of Nasrid ceramic production. These pieces became extremely well known for their delicate decoration and large size, and were exported to other places. The best-preserved examples are to be found in Palermo (Regional Museum of Sicily), St Petersburg (Hermitage), Stockholm (National Museum of Fine Arts) and Madrid (Institute of Valencia de D. Juan and the National Archaeological Museum). Some are decorated exclusively in gold and others in gold and cobalt-blue, always on a tin-glaze background.  
Although its form derives from large storage vessels, its cumbersome size and the absence of any strengthening elements in the handles suggest a purely ornamental function.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.short_description: The so-called ‘Alhambra vases’ were luxury items because of the technical complexity of their manufacture and the beauty of their decoration and lustrework. The intended use is not known, but their renown led them to be exported to Sicily and Mamluk Egypt.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.method_for_datation: It is difficult to determine the date of manufacture of these vases. Nonetheless, all writers agree that, on the basis of the inscription, the oldest examples are those decorated solely with gold on white, which were produced from the last third of the 7th / 13th century and, in particular, during the 8th / 14th century.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.method_for_provenance: Although all of these pieces are known generically as the Alhambra vases, they were produced in Malaga and exported. From the 7th / 13th century, Arab writers begin to mention Malaga as a large centre for the production and export of ceramics with gold or metallic highlights.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.obtention: The piece was found by chance at the beginning of the 20th century during work to shore up vaults in the monastery of Santa María de la Defensión in Jerez de la Frontera (Cadiz). It was donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 29 July 1930.
