a0be739f-bf67-5116-9ebd-ce73ca66626f.name: Magharif (Spoon)
a0be739f-bf67-5116-9ebd-ce73ca66626f.short_description:
The date palm tree (Phoenix dactylifera), an enduring symbol of Oman, is identified with the early oasis Civilisation of Magan in the 3rd millennium BC and the taming of the desert. It is one of the few tree species specifically mentioned in the Holy Qur’an, and according to Islamic tradition Maryam (Mary) gave birth to 'Iesa (Jesus) in the shade of a palm.  
  
Highly simplified palm motifs such as those adorning this *magharif* (spoon), reminders of the teachings of the Holy Qur'an, appear as principle design elements often combined with geometric or floral elements to create circular or linear patterns as a repetitive motif.
keywords: Magharif; Spoon; Date Palm; Holy Qur'an; Floral

a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.name: Coin (*dirham*)
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.description:
This Umayyad coin, minted during the reign of al-Walid I (AH 86–96 / AD 705–15), bears an inscription in its centre that reads ‘*â ila illâ Allâh wahda-hu lâ sharîk la-hu*’ (‘There is no God but Allah, the One, there is none like unto him’) and the edge reads ‘*bismi-llâh duriba hadâ-l-dirhâm bi fî sanat ihda wa tis in*’ (‘In God’s name this *dirham* was minted in Sijistan in the year one and ninety \[91\]’).  
The front face bears two inscriptions, one in the centre and one on the edge. The central inscription reads ‘*Allâh ahad Allâh al-samad lam yalid wa lam yûlad wa lam yakun la-hu kufû’ an ahad*’ (‘God is one, God is eternal. He does not beget, nor is he begotten and there is none like unto him’) and the edge inscription reads ‘*Muhammad rasûl Allâh arsala-hu bi-l-hudâ wa al-haqq li-yuzhira-hu alâ al-dîn kulli-hi wa la-hu kariha al-mushrikûn*’ (‘Muhammad is the messenger of God. He has sent His messenger with the guidance and the true religion, and will make it dominate all religions, in spite of the idol worshipers’).
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.short_description: *Dirham* minted during the reign of al-Walid I. The basic coin in the Arab world until the arrival of the Mongols, the *dirham* takes its name from the Greek *drachma*. Coins usually weighed 2.97 grams.
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.method_for_datation: From the inscription on the edge of the obverse.
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.method_for_provenance: From the inscription on the edge of the obverse.
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.bibliography: Walker, J., *A Catalogue of the Arab-Byzantine and Post Reform Umayyad Coins*, London, 1956, p.159.
a0dd981d-e256-57f4-ba5c-7f37591cb8b5.dynasty: Umayyad; Caliph al-Walid I (r. AH 86–96 / AD 705–15)

a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.name: Aleppo Room.
a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.description:
A prosperous broker and a Christian citizen of the town of Aleppo commissioned the painted panels of the walls of the entrance room in his house at the beginning of the 17th century. The paintings within the Aleppo room thus make up the oldest collection from a Syrian dwelling house from the Ottoman period. The Christian patron engaged craftsmen from the best workshops of the time in his desire for the entrance room, into which his guests would first arrive, to be painted in a variety of themes. These themes were based on contemporary Islamic book illustration, consisting of floral and geometric compositions, rendered in the best traditional Ottoman style. Christian themes from the Old and New Testaments, and the depiction of Mary with Child, sit alongside courtly scenes like those portrayed in Persian book illustration. The selection of encircling Psalms, Arabic proverbs and Persian principles further add to the impression of a peaceful community of different religious beliefs living together.  
The central panels are found in the back part of the main niche, to the left and right of a wall cupboard. Courtly themes are repeated on the left-side panel, including a ruler sitting on a throne, a hunt and a hunting party with a prince holding a falcon. In contrast, Christian themes are portrayed on the right-side panel, and include the Last Supper, Salome’s dance in front of King Herod and the sacrifice of Isaac. Other panels around the room have individual depictions from either courtly or Christian subject matters, such as the love story of Leila and Majnun of Nizami (1141–1202) from the Haft Paykar, or the Virgin Mary and Child or Saint George. Real and imaginary animals are depicted alongside. It is the variety of the themes of these paintings that make these earliest surviving wall panels such a comprehensive collection, a variety that could perhaps only have arisen in the Syrian trading town Aleppo.  
The name Halab Shah ibn Isa, one of the craftsmen, appears on the cornice.  
  
Click [here](https://youtu.be/4toX47mtAIE) to **watch a video presentation** of this artefact.
a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.short_description: The painted wooden panels belong to the audience room in a house of a Christian merchant in Aleppo, Syria, which is the only surviving example of a painted and dated room from the 17th century. Its ornamental and figural repertoire includes Christian themes as well as Arabic verses.
a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.initial_owner: Isa ibn Butrus (Jesus, son of Peter).
a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.method_for_datation: Two dates are inscribed in different places in the Aleppo Room: 1009 (1600–01) and 1012 (1603).
a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.method_for_provenance: The Aleppo Room was obtained in 1912 by Friedrich Sarre in Aleppo. The deeds certify that the room was originally in House Wakil in Aleppo, where it was also photographed *in situ* prior to 1912.
a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.obtention: Acquired in Aleppo by Friedrich Sarre for the Museum of Islamic Art in 1912.

a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.name: Dish.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.description:
'Brazier' dish with a large, flat circular base and straight, shallow sides finished with a narrow brim. The piece is made of red clay and covered with a tin glaze. It is decorated with gold and cobalt-blue lustre on a creamy white background. The base of the dish, decorated with interlaced, small and stylized vegetal patterns, is divided into quadrants with alternating blue and golden motifs. The brim is decorated with the traditional ‘fish-like border’ pattern. Golden spirals fill and break up the white background throughout the piece.  
Technically, ceramics from the AH 8th and 9th / AD 14th and 15th century are no more than a continuation of the Almohad tradition. However, the incorporation of cobalt oxide into the glaze in the Nasrid era gave rise to a wide range of blues, and the application of copper sulphate, silver and red ochre to achieve metallic highlights resulted in some exceptional pieces. Centuries-old gilded Andalusian ceramics had their heyday during the Nasrid reign in Granada.  
The manufacture of this type of ceramic required three firings. The final firing, in a reduction kiln, was the most delicate as it required perfect control of the kiln and its temperature. The mix of metal sulphides had to adhere to the piece without the glaze from the previous firing melting again.  
The importance of the pottery workshops of the kingdom of Granada, and specifically of Malaga as the main centre of production, caused the expression *obra de maliqa* (made in Maliqa) to be used, with some variations, to refer to gilded ceramics regardless of where they were produced. This term was also used in the Christian world for pottery workshops of Nasrid origin that, from the late AH 8th / AD 14th century, began to move to various places on the east coast of Spain, of which Manises was the most important centre for highlighted ceramics produced in the Malaga style for Christian customers.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.short_description: This enormous dish represents a continuation of the technique and decorative style of Nasrid ceramicists in Mudéjar workshops to meet the needs of their Christian clientele, who wanted new shapes like this shallow dish with its flat base, straight sides and horizontal rim.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.dimensions: Height 4.5 cm, maximum diameter 41.5 cm, base diameter 34.8 cm.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.method_for_datation: The perfect development of the technique, the type of decoration and the style of the plant arabesques are characteristic of ceramics with golden highlights from the first third of the 9th / 15th century.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.method_for_provenance: The growing decadence of the Nasrid kingdom, along with the development of the maritime power of the kingdom of Aragon and its control over the trade routes of the Mediterranean resulted in Mudéjar centres, contemporaries of the Nasrid producers that used the same traditional procedures and decorative styles, springing up around the east coast. The intense colour of the cobalt and its shape are more characteristic of Valencian pieces, but only an analysis of the clays could determine the precise origin of the piece.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.provenance: Nasrid kingdom of Granada or Christian kingdom of Valencia, Spain.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum by the State on 6 June 1875.

a52ea6dc-cf4f-5836-a534-c806ce30745b.name: Tile Bowl
a52ea6dc-cf4f-5836-a534-c806ce30745b.description: The bowl’s surface is coated in white clay and slip and decorated in blue and white under a transparent colourless glaze. On the exterior a dark grey-blue ivy branch, reminiscent of a Chinese cloud, is adorned with large stylised flowers and shoots in cobalt blue. The contours are grey-blue. The exterior of the rim is encircled by a band of short angled lines, and the interior by a band of half rosettes. Inside the bowl is a medallion featuring a large stylised flower with six petals in the centre. This is a unique example of the influence of Chinese porcelain.
a52ea6dc-cf4f-5836-a534-c806ce30745b.dates: Hegira second quarter of the 10th century / AD second quarter of the 16th century

a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.name: Sufi assembly
a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.short_description: The miniature features a nocturnal landscape with a dervish surrounded by six male characters wearing costumes typical of the age of Shah Abbas I (1588-1629). The exquisite finesse of the drawing is enhanced by the subdued colour range, the gold highlights and the beautiful *nasta'liq* calligraphy of the Persian verses: ‘Don’t drink the wine-cup, for every drop is a king’s blood,/Don’t listen to the music, for every tune is just a tale of sorrow./The night has fallen; the drunken feast has neither lamp nor candle; /Join us, for the gathering of maids most fair is pleasant.’ (Translated into English from the Romanian version by Viorel Bageacu, 1987). The verses, as well as the image, are replete with Sufi symbolism.
a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.dates: Hegira early 11th century / AD early 17th century
a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.obtention: Donated by Prof. George Oprescu in 1960.

a5415d97-5be6-5b62-af8d-da90cb25b7f5.author: Mircea Dunca
keywords: Sufi
materials: Ink, wash and gold on paper

a5c93080-d37b-5926-ad79-2d9bb61932f2.name: *The Grand Bazaar*
a5c93080-d37b-5926-ad79-2d9bb61932f2.short_description: Amadeo Preziosi often presented genre scenes from Istanbul in his unique style. Specifically, he incorporated diverse scenes from the Bazaar in a number of his paintings. This venue, particular to Istanbul, has been of great interest to western artists, and in Edmondo De Amicis’s words “is not just a building but a town”. The Grand Bazaar, which housed shops for a wide range of commercial goods and catered to almost all of the needs of customers, offered an incredible visual richness and diversity to the western artist. A reflection of this opulence is also evident in Preziosi’s painting, which includes numerous details from daily life.
keywords: Amadeo Preziosi; Orientalism; painting; İstanbul

a5defb3f-7271-5a06-9b25-33267fdf495e.name: Vessel
a5defb3f-7271-5a06-9b25-33267fdf495e.description: The vessel is cream-coloured, with a ring base, convex body, long thin neck and scalloped rim. The figural, stylised geometric and floral decorations in a lustre technique cover the entire surface.
a5defb3f-7271-5a06-9b25-33267fdf495e.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts

a5f7ac5a-c7e3-5149-8a1c-17cd76006305.name: Two Chinese blue-and-white porcelain sealed ‘Zamzam’ water bottles
a5f7ac5a-c7e3-5149-8a1c-17cd76006305.short_description:
Prophet was known to drink from the well and use the water for significant purposes. The most famous *hadith* (Prophetic saying) regarding Zamzam states that the water is good for whatever purpose it is intended. Thus, over time, the water has been used for many purposes: in graves, to prevent harm, to cure and in ceremonies to obtain blessings.  
Similar examples to these bottles are in the Topkapi Palace in Istanbul and were used during ceremonies involving the mantle of the Prophet. During these ceremonies the mantle was dipped in Zamzam water and what dripped from the cloth was then collected in bottles similar to these. Other comparable types were simply sent from Mecca to Istanbul containing Zamzam water and closed with leather, string and sealed with wax.  
The well is believed to have been discovered by Hagar and Ismael, after being abandoned by Abraham in Mecca. It was later rediscovered by ‘Abd al-Muttalib, Prophet Muhammad’s grandfather, who is credited with having dug several wells, most importantly that of Zamzam. From then on the responsibility of giving water to pilgrims was to remain in the lineage of one of his sons.  
Water from the well of Zamzam was previously collected in buckets by a rope pulley mechanism and then transferred to earthenware vessels. Now the well is entirely managed subterraneously by electric pumps and the King Abdullah Zamzam Water Factory produces approximately 200,000 bottles of water a day.

a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.name: Süleymaniye waterway map.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.description:
The Süleymaniye waterway map is handmade on unfinished paper. The waterway was designed to supply water to the entire complex of the mosque, including its *imaret* (soup-kitchen), *maristan* (hospital), *maktab* (school) and public fountains. Fed by the Aypah (Kirazlı) and çınar springs, the highest-capacity branches of the Halkalı water supply system, this waterway supplied the Süleymaniye Complex as well as 80 other points in Istanbul. The map shows the waterway in detail from its source all the way to its end, including the places where it is joined by other waterways, the points where it enters the city through the walls, and especially the water-distribution centres and aqueducts.  
  
The map was prepared without a scale and has a schematic style. Therefore, many structures and neighbourhoods cannot be precisely placed. At the far end of the map there is the drawing of the Süleymaniye Complex.  
  
Such waterway maps tell the story of water from springs being conveyed via pipes, crossing valleys in aqueducts, its pressure adjusted at certain points, being sent off in various directions at distribution centres and reaching public fountains. These maps also provide information about the urban structure; how people lived, and the infrastructure and buildings in a given quarter. For example, the Roman Aqueduct of Valens (AD 375), known as Bozdoğan Aqueduct in Turkish is introduced as 'the big aqueduct in the Horse Market'. The names of the people and the structures receiving water from this aqueduct are also given. The water of the Halkalı network could be distributed to private estates only on the written permission of the sultan. For instance, we find the house of Süleyman the Magnificent's dentist, Moshe Hamon, (AH 899–962 / AD 1490–1554) listed as 'House of Hamudoğlu'.  
  
From the Süleymaniye Complex waterway map, we learn not only how the water was brought to the city but also about the quarters where the courtiers and dignitaries resided. Therefore, the waterway maps are important for describing the social topography of the city.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.short_description: Istanbul has always suffered from water shortage due to a lack of sufficient springs nearby and its demand was met by conveying water via aqueducts from afar. Waterway maps provide information about the routes from the springs to the city, monuments on the way and the social structure of the city.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.dates: Hegira second half of the 12th century / AD 18th century.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.method_for_datation: Although the map does not have a date it is clear from the names of people and structures therein that this is an 18th-century document. For example, it is known that water was supplied to Taygun Palace in 1161 / 1748, a building shown on this map; therefore, this map must have been prepared after 1161 / 1748.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.method_for_provenance: The map does not bear any date. However, that our copy is an 18th copy is clear from the names of people and structures given therein. For example, it is known that water was supplied to Taygun Palace in 1161 / 1748, a building shown on our map; therefore, this map must have been prepared after 1161 / 1748. Public services such as the water supply were under the supervision of the state and due to this fact the waterway would have been designed and constructed by the official architects of the Topkapı Palace.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.obtention: The map was transferred to the museum in 1923 from the Directorate of Supplies for Pious Foundations.

a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.name: *Divan-i Shahi* (Collection of Poems by Shahi)
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.short_description:
This manuscript is a *divan*, a collection of poems, by Amir Shahi Sabzavari. Amir Shahi Sabzavari, also called Shahi, was a poet and calligrapher at the court of Prince Baysunghur in Herat. Shahi died in 857 AH / 1453 AD.  
The manuscript contains 60 folios in total, of which five are illustrated. According to the colophon the scribe of this manuscript was Abd al-Wahid. Some of the folios are signed by their painter Abd al-Gani, who is also responsible for the astonishing lacquer binding.  
Judging by a portrait on the frontispiece that looks like Sultan Suleiman I. , the manuscript must have been finished during his reign between 926-936 AH /1520-30 AD. The manuscript was part of the collection of Polish orientalist Waclaw Rzewuski until his death in 1831 AD, when the manuscript was bought for the Imperial Court Library in Vienna.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.method_for_datation: Dorothea Duda recognizes portraits of Sultan Selim I. on the binding of the manuscript. She suggests that the manuscript might have been started during the reign of Sultan Selim I. but finished during the reign of Sultan Suleiman I., who succeeded his father in 1520. This is supported by the presence of an additional portrait of a man on the frontispice that looks like Sultan Suleiman I. The inclusion of both rulers therefore indicates a probable date of production somewhere between 926-936 AH /1520-30 AD.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.method_for_provenance: The provenance was established through documentation in the inventory book of the Imperial Court Library by Joseph Freiherr von Hammer-Purgstall.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.obtention: Following the death of  the explorer and orientalist Waclaw Seweryn Rzewuski in 1831 AD, the manuscript was bought directly from his collection for the Imperial Court Library in the same year.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.bibliography:
Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften I. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 4, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1983: 185-187.  
Duda, Dorothea, "Islamische Lackeinbände - ihre künstlerische Entwicklung und ihr Verhältnis zum Buch als Gesamtkunstwerk", *Journal of Turkish Studies* , 26 : I (2002), 163-203.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.artist: 'Abd al-Gani painted the binding as well as folios 1b-2a and fol. 18a.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.binding_desc:
The richly decorated lacquer binding on this manuscript is an artwork in itself. Executed in the Shirazi style, this binding has courtly scenes painted on its front and back cover. The doublures of the manuscript are decorated with a medallion surrounded by floral ornaments, painted in two kinds of gold on a black background.  
The front cover depicts a group of men set in an outdoor scene. The men in the upper half of the painting are wearing Ottoman turbans, while some men on the lower half are wearing head gear that look like a mixture of the hats the *Janissaries* wore and those the *silahdars* wore. As the *Janissaries* were part of the elite infantry of the Ottoman army and *silahdars* were close aides of the Ottoman sultans it can be assumed that the binding was in fact manufactured within the realms of the Ottoman Empire.  
Additionally, Duda notes that the man in the middle of the front cover and the man sitting on a throne on the back cover have similarities with formal portraits of Sultan Selim I. She consequently advocates that at least the binding must have been commissioned during the reign of Selim I.
a87439ea-aee1-50f5-a0b5-501d95e7044f.author: Leonie Fernsebner
keywords: Divan; Shahi
materials: Blue, green and gold ink on thin, white paper. Calligraphic *Nasta'liq* script of 11 lines per page. 2 decorative pages, 5 miniature paintings.

a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.short_description: During the nineteenth century, European centres of glass production, particularly those in France and Bohemia, created Islamic-style works of art to be exported to countries like Egypt, Syria, Iran, and India. This bottle – one in a set of three – was certainly produced for an Iranian recipient, for it features portraits of the Qajar shah Nasr al-Din (r. 1848–96). Purchased in 1959.

aab30960-8950-5111-bdd0-0a590079ba20.name: Spontaneous feast for a *shaykh* at Tall Tishrin in northeast Syria
aab30960-8950-5111-bdd0-0a590079ba20.description: Unexpected important guests are also lavishly served, such as the tribal *shaykh* in the photo; his visit is considered an honour for the host family. Although the women, assisted by the elder children, immediately start to prepare, it might take at least two hours until the feast is ready. The family might own the chicken to be slaughtered, or its meat can be bought from a nearby butcher. In the meantime, the host chats with the guests, drinking tea or coffee with them. When the meal is ready, the bigger boys will carry in the food, taking meticulous care to place the big plate in the middle and the small bowls in such a way that everyone will help themselves, and therefore is on an equal level. Only then does the host invite the guests to eat.

ab2b67d7-838e-59c7-9a3d-24e8458ff5d8.name: Tankard
ab2b67d7-838e-59c7-9a3d-24e8458ff5d8.description: Iznik pottery, originating from the town of Iznik in western Anatolia, emerged during the reign of Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II (AD 1451–1481). Initially influenced by blue and white Chinese Ming porcelains, Iznik ceramics evolved to incorporate vibrant hues. This cylindrical tankard, adorned with intricate carnations and tulips in blue, green and red, likely hails from the mid- to late 16th century, a pinnacle era for Iznik pottery. The distinctive red pigment, introduced circa 1570, possibly originated from iron-rich Armenian clay. Notably, cross-hatched black lines on the tankard suggest it was crafted based on a leather prototype.

ad8d142b-0f91-580b-88d2-b78b4b99e310.name: Sherbet *gabi* and *pialas* set
ad8d142b-0f91-580b-88d2-b78b4b99e310.description:
A set consisting of the vessel, a large tray and a number of *pialas* (a type of local bowl for drinking). The liquid (usually sherbet) from the vessel was poured into the *pialas* by a ladle and served to guests during feasts. The surface of the whole set is generally richly decorated with images of people, inscriptions in Arabic, and more. This particular set is decorated with human images and inscriptions that read as follows:  
"Husayn, the apple of Ahmad's eye,  
Memory of Heydar!  
Again, what is this rebellion that has covered the people of the whole world  
Again, what is this song of mourning, what is grief, what is lament?  
What a great resurrection this is again,  
On the day of resurrection, your trumpet will rise from the earth to the majestic throne.  
That’s why this sad morning has come,  
The people of the world turned upside down  
As if the Sun has risen from the west, so that the excitement would cover all parts of the world.  
There is so much sorrow in the palace of Jerusalem,  
People in Jerusalem are very sad.  
It is the mourning of remarkable person, the most honourable of the children of Adam.  
Husayn fluttered in blood in the soil in Karbala. Husayn is the light of the Land, West and the East, the Sun and the Sky. He grew up in the arms of the Prophet Muhammad.  
He (his soul) cries of the thirsty now from Karbala, reaching the highest Star.  
While the eye of the wind cries at him  
Blood began to flow on the porch of Karbala.  
People didn't see *gulab* \[rose water\] but tears.  
On that day, the people of Kufa didn't even give him water.  
They had deep respect for the Karbala guest.  
They all drank and turned to the beast, and to the devil.  
In Karbala, Suleyman's water was drained.  
The enemy neighbours shamelessly  
Went towards the tent of the Sultan of Karbala.  
Fate became a *Sahand* \[obstacle, mountain\] to zeal.  
Out of fear of the enemy, a cry rose in the holy place.

ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.name: Cauldron.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.description:
A cauldron (a huge cooking pot) from the Complex of Khassaki Sultan, also known as a charitable institution or *takiyya* (asylum) for the needy. The building, completed in AH 964 / AD 1557, is located in Jerusalem. As a patroness of charitable institutions, Khassaki Sultan undertook the construction of this complex, and endowed it with a *waqf*. This establishment is considered to be one of the largest social institutions to survive from Ottoman Jerusalem. In its day, it offered meals, daily, to the poor of the city, students, scholars and others who were among those who were entitled to food in accordance with the requirements of the *waqf*. The number of people who benefited from this institution on a daily basis exceeded 1000, thus requiring the availability of large spaces to prepare huge quantities of food in enormous cooking utensils. Despite the changing administrative and political circumstances in Palestine during the past few centuries, this institution still occupies a minor social role today.  
The Islamic Museum acquired three cauldrons from the complex of Khassaki Sultan. The cauldron exhibited here was produced using tin-plated copper, constructed by means of coiled copper which forms part of the body of the cauldron. The coil is then fixed together with solid copper nails, as hammering was not used on these large pots as it was with smaller cooking vessels. The cavity of the cauldron has been fixed to the base by a series of nails that surround the junction of the base with the body. The vessel has four large carrying handles. The body is supported by a group of copper stays that sometimes form extensions to the handles and are fastened to the cauldron with nails, or that are simply located between two of the handles. It seems that the cauldron was coiled only in the middle of its cavity, for its hollow has been tin-plated and secured with copper nails in the same manner as was used to fix the base. The cauldron contains an inscription that appears to have been added at a later period, it reads: “The *waqf* of the late mother of the sultan who had built edifices in Jerusalem under the charge of Hajji Khalil Aga … designated formerly 1235 \[AD 1819\]”. There is another date next to this that reads, “1161 \[AD 1748\]”.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.short_description: This is a large cooking utensil made of copper that was used to prepare meals in the Khassaki Sultan charitable institution established in Jerusalem by the wife of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent. The great size of this cauldron reflects the amount of food that was prepared on a daily basis.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.initial_owner: Khassaki Sultan (also known as Haseki Hürrem Sultan or Roxelana; d. AH 965 / AD 1558), wife of Sultan Sulayman, the Magnificent (r. AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66).
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.method_for_datation: The piece has been dated in accordance with the date of construction of the Complex of Khassaki Sultan, since it was probably made to be used there.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.method_for_provenance: The cauldron does not contain any distinguishing marks that enable us to narrow down the place of its manufacture. However, the manufacture of vessels such as this was, and still is, undertaken in Palestine and Syria so it is possible that this piece was made in one of these two places.
ada2243f-108b-5eed-b2bf-2399e60e1491.obtention: The piece was transferred from the Complex of Khassaki Sultan to the Islamic Museum in 1928.

ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.name: Blossoming almond trees.
ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.description:
One of Portugal's most well-known legends tells of how it was that almond trees came to be part of the landscape of the southern region of the country. An Arab prince, married to a Christian from the north, noticed that his wife lived in a permanent state of melancholy, and so one day he asked her for the reason for this enduring mood. She told him that she missed the snow, frequent in the north of the Peninsula, but which rarely fell in the more southerly regions. The prince then ordered the planting of almond trees, whose blossoming at the end of the winter would create the illusion of fields covered with snow.  
This romantic and highly lyrical legend does nevertheless contain some basis of truth and demonstrates deep links with the Portuguese land.  
Al-Mu'tamid, a poet and lord of the Abbadid dynasty (AH 461–84 / AD 1069–91), one day set a challenge to Ibn Amar, as they were travelling along the Guadalquivir: 'The breeze turns the river / into a coat of mail'. The response came from Itimad, a slave woman of Romaik: 'A better coat of mail cannot be found / since the river freezes it'. Impressed by the slave's beauty and by her poetic inspiration, al-Mu'tamid took her as his wife and made her queen. The family and geographical origins of Itimad were confined to helping construct the legend. Although the story told relates to the region of Seville, al-Mu'tamid was born in Beja and was a lord of Silves, having later governed a large part of the south of the Iberian Peninsula.  
Deposed from power, al-Mu'tamid ended up living in exile in Morocco, where he died on 30 Dhu'l-Hijja 487 / 10 January 1095. Itimad lies at his side in a mausoleum in Agmat.
ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.short_description: Towards the end of the winter, the landscape of the Algarve is marked by blossoming almond trees. Legend has it that they were planted by an Arab prince in homage to his beloved, who came from the north, in order to create the illusion of snow, which is rare in the south. The legend is based on the romance between the Abbadid prince Al-Mu‘tamid and the slave girl Itimad. Impressed by her beauty and poetic inspiration, Al-Mu‘tamid married her and made her queen. Itimad’s geographical and family background helped to create the legend.
ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.dates: From the earliest Muslim presence in the region.
ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.author: Isabel Cristina Ferreira Fernandes
keywords: almond trees; Southern Portugal; landscape; legend; traditions; al-Mu'tamid

ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.name: *Suq al-Hamidiyya, Damascus*
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.short_description: The Suq al-Hamidiyya, built in 1886 and 1894, is by far the biggest and most famous suq in Damascus. This bazaar street also links the two most important historic buildings, the Umayyad Mosque and the Citadel. It was built along its western section by incorporating earlier structures, whereas the eastern part of the street was a completely new construction cutting through the existing buildings. The commercial thoroughfare is 450 metres long and 8.70 to 9.90 metres wide, its enormous size and the high standard of its execution accentuate new design principles. So in various respects, this suq is a very interesting example of structural change in a traditional commercial centre.
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.author: Stefan Weber

aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.name: Bowl with stand
aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.short_description: This bowl with a bulging rim sits on a stand. The decoration is made of two layers of concentric patterns around a central circle, filled with winged motifs. These green and brown patterns are painted on a yellow background. Although this kind of bowl is usually used to serve couscous, in the town Nabeul, and particularly for the occasion of Islamic New Year, each child is presented with a *methred* bowl, filled with golden couscous, dried fruit, dates, a hard-boiled egg and sweets. This all surrounds a statuette made of sugar, moulded and coloured to resemble an animal (such as a rooster or a gazelle) or a figure, like a doll or cavalier.
aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.holder: Musée de la Céramique Sidi Kacem Jelizi
aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
keywords: Floral motifs; winged motifs; cermaics from Nabeul

aee0d03f-b711-5643-8552-3ef51656eff4.name: *Jarrita* vase with two handles
aee0d03f-b711-5643-8552-3ef51656eff4.description: This drinking vase has a pear-shaped body and two rounded handles that join a short neck that widens toward the top; it rests on a low base. The decoration, painted in dark blue and a beautiful shade of bronze-gold on the ivory opaque glaze, is placed symmetrically on both sides of the handles. A frieze of pseudo-epigraphy whose drawing seems to recall the word *al-'afiya* (good health)... is drawn in blue on the neck over a glossy background of a wormlike pattern. On the body, eight-lobed medallions in bronze-gold have a blue pseudo-epigraphic pattern in the centre. On each side of the handles is a scalloped almond composition. Directly below each handle is another pseudo-epigraphic motif against a glossy background. A series of horizontal lines rings the lower part of the body. The lustre decoration with metallic reflections is a process peculiar to the arts of Islam. The technique is seen as early as the eighth century on fragments of Egyptian glasses; it was later applied to ceramics, beginning in the ninth century in Mesopotamia under the reign of the Abbasids. It is a decoration painted on a glazed piece that has undergone a first firing. The lustre consists of a mixture of copper and silver oxides to which are added sulphur and red ochre, and a binder to permit a brushed application. A second firing in an oxygen-poor atmosphere results in the incorporation of the oxide particles, now reduced to a metallic state in the softened glaze. Quite characteristic effects are produced when the pieces are observed in light. The secrets of this complex and sometimes unpredictable technique were jealously guarded in pottery workshops. Nevertheless, the process spread to both the East and the Muslim West, and in Spain its development was encouraged by the Nasrid rulers, especially in Malaga. Since the Reconquest, the craze for Hispano-Moorish ceramics (*loza dorada*), continues, since production is exported to Muslim countries and Christian Europe. Cobalt blue and brown lustre, combined in bold compositions, as here, give a characteristic identity to a process that is still used, for example in Manises (in Valencia).

aee0d03f-b711-5643-8552-3ef51656eff4.dates: Hegira last quarter of 8th century or beginning 9th century / AD end of 14th or beginning of 15th century
aee0d03f-b711-5643-8552-3ef51656eff4.dimensions: Height: 16.2cm, Diameter: 13.4cm, Length: 18cm, Base diameter: 9.8cm, Opening diameter: 9.5cm

b01b60d5-e457-5cea-b280-e145d44183d1.name: *Haal* (Cardamom)
b01b60d5-e457-5cea-b280-e145d44183d1.description:
*Haal* (Cardamom) used to flavour the coffee.  
Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving dallah referred to as a mezallah, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the mezallah with their left hand and distribute the fanayeel (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.*
b01b60d5-e457-5cea-b280-e145d44183d1.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
b01b60d5-e457-5cea-b280-e145d44183d1.dimensions: Varies and depends on the piece. Length: 15mm, width: 5mm
b01b60d5-e457-5cea-b280-e145d44183d1.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: cardamom; coffee

b01b920c-bd76-5e6a-b3c9-4e331c550bdd.name: Karagöz and Hacivat Shadow Play
b01b920c-bd76-5e6a-b3c9-4e331c550bdd.short_description: Shadow play consists of solid figures being shown and moved behind a semi-transparent screen. The characters of Hacivat and Karagöz plays reflect the multi-ethnic makeup of the Ottoman Empire. They are represented with a high level of detail through their figures, attitudes, dances, etc. Shadow play received its basic character in the 17th century and developed further in the following centuries, eventually becoming one of the most popular traditional forms of entertainment among Turks. It was performed by a single artist that is called a *hayali* (imaginary person) or *hayalbaz*. One of the main characteristics of shadow play is that the *hayali* changes his voice and manner of speaking depending on the character he was animating.

b1c9d73d-7178-5324-9b0c-d946356b48ab.name: Plate
b1c9d73d-7178-5324-9b0c-d946356b48ab.description: Red clay, cream slip, decorated in purple-brown and mustard tones under a transparent colourless glaze.  It is one of the few surviving examples of a plate used on a daily basis. In a naive manner the giraffe is depicted tied to two trees. The rim is decorated with an intermittent lattice pattern. The model for the giraffe was sent as a gift to Sultan Mahmut II in 1823 by the governor of Egypt, Kavalalı Mehmet Ali Pasha. It was kept on a ship anchored in Çanakkale harbour that was being resupplied on its way to Istanbul. Upon seeing the giraffe in the harbour, ceramic masters were inspired to produce a new motif in their workshops by reproducing the giraffe on plates.
b1c9d73d-7178-5324-9b0c-d946356b48ab.dates: Hegira 1st half of 13th century / AD early 19th century

b1fe1635-a0ea-5d86-871f-4148f5ba34cc.name: Plate
b1fe1635-a0ea-5d86-871f-4148f5ba34cc.short_description:
The genuine enthusiasm that Chinese blue-and-white porcelain aroused in Iran since AD 14th century led to various attempts of Persian potters to unravel the main Chinese secret and to devise ways to simulate the unparalleled effects of porcelain.  
Along with plates and bottles that more or less closely imitated Chinese porcelain in the motifs and style, an authentic Iranian style of cobalt-blue décor developed in the 17th–18th century. This plate depicting tigers and birds in dense thickets of forest or garden, freely arranged in a decentralized composition, was possibly made in Kerman of the early 18th century.

b2a64729-0616-53e6-bc8d-4d7583ceac8c.name: Plate
b2a64729-0616-53e6-bc8d-4d7583ceac8c.short_description: Sultan Abdülhamid II founded in 1891 the *Yıldız Çini Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu* (Yıldız Royal Tile Factory) in the garden of Yıldız Palace in order to revive Turkish tile art and give it a new direction and momentum. Vases, hanging wall plates and many sorts of daily-use wares were produced in the factory, including writing and dinner table utensils, card plates, lidded bowls, pans, *aşure* (a kind of dessert) trays, sugar bowls, tea and coffee cups. This plate features a dark green background on which there is a *tuğra* (monogram) made of gilding and a border around the edge.
keywords: yıldız ceramic; Turkish decorative arts

b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.name: Raqqa lustre bowl.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.description:
The thin wall of the bowl is decorated symmetrically on the inside with a quatrefoil motif that covers its entire surface. A stylised trefoil leaf is painted within each of the four petals. Corkscrew tendrils, each with a bifid leaf, occupy the spaces between the outer contours of the petals. The outer edge is emphasised with a lustre stripe.  
A collection of about 100 pieces of pottery, to which this piece belongs, was found at Tell Minis in Syria. At first it was thought that such pieces were imported into Syria from Egypt, but the discovery at Tell Minis confirmed that they were made in Syria. Meanwhile, the findings gained from excavating in the urban area of Raqqa have confirmed that a large number of these ceramics were produced in Raqqa. Some of these feature inscriptions. The decoration is very reminiscent of Fatimid ceramics, modified by the introduction of lustre painting and the use of quartz fritware. It can be assumed that, following the end of the Fatimid dynasty (AH 564 / AD 1169), Egyptian manufacturers of ceramics moved to Syria, where they introduced the new techniques. The existence of identical ceramic pieces strongly suggests that pattern drawings were used in the workshops.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.short_description: Small thin-walled bowls with figurative or vegetal patterns in a reddish colour are typical of Syrian lustre-ware pottery of the Ayyubid period. The design of this bowl with four petals in ovals and arabesque leaves in the spandrels is very clear and perfectly fits the round shape of the bowl.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.dates: Hegira late 6th–early 7th century / AD late 12th–early 13th century.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.method_for_datation: The excavations in Raqqa confirm that lustre ceramics glazed with reddish-brown lustre were made in Syria during the Ayyubid period. The technique was brought over by potters from Egypt following the downfall of the Fatimids.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.method_for_provenance: Findings made in Tell Minis and in Raqqa have led to the conclusion that this type of ceramic originated in Syria.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.obtention: From a private gallery in London, 1992.

b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.name: Public fountains.
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.description:
Al-Djazaïr and its *fahs* (rural surroundings) possessed a large number of fountains. Their number, for the walled town, varied from seven according to Haëdo in the AH 10th / AD 16th century, to 125 according to the knight of Arvieux in 1674–5, and to 'seventy-three as recorded in 1840' (S. Missoum, *Alger à l'époque ottomane* – see Bibliography). A large number of these fountains were built during the AH 12th / AD 18th century by *deys*.  
Benefactors were responsible for the creation of these fountains. Attached to each one, on a plaque of marble or shale, in Arabic or Ottoman Turkish, is an inscription extolling the merits of the benefactor. Under the auspices of a *khudjat al-'uyun* – a sort of 'fountains secretary' – an administrative body was responsible for managing the *habus* (estate donations) that were collected on behalf of these fountains.  
One of these fountains, known as the fountain 'de la Calle aux Vins', has ended up on an exterior wall of the present National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Art. Built by the *dey* Husayn in AH 1235 / AD 1820 outside Bab al-Djazira (Gate of the Island', also referred to as Gate of the Holy War) and below the battery of al-Andalus, it was moved for the first time in 1867 to 'underneath the stairway of the present bastion of the Gate of France' (undated report on the proposition of making an endowment to the state; but the agreement on the endowment is dated 13 May 1905). Then it was moved a second time to the Park of Liberty (formerly Gallant Park), to be placed against the wall of the Department of Antiquities, where, in correspondence dated 27 May 1968, it is the subject of an account of the maintenance work carried out by the chief architect of historic monuments.
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.short_description: The town of Al-Djazaïr had a number of public fountains, most of which were built during the AH 12th / AD 18th century by the Ottoman *deys*. These fountains bore, on a marble or slate plaque, the names of the benefactors who commissioned them and were managed by an body under the aegis of the 'fountains secretary'. In AH 1235 / AD 1820, *dey* Husayn had a fountain built outside Bab al-Djazira, the gateway that bears an inscription in his honour.
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.method_for_datation: Through an inscription in Arabic and Osmanli: 'Everything lives through water. The governor of Algiers along with his sultan, who is Husayn Pasha, incessantly strives, with virtuous intentions, to accomplish good deeds. His bounty attempts above all to bring running water in sufficient quantities to all places. It is he who commissioned the building of this fountain. He gives life to him that is thirsty and deprived, in this place that lacks water. Drink fresh water thanks to the generosity of Husayn and his love. Year 1235 [1820].'
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.bibliography:
Belhamissi M., *Alger par les eaux XVIe–XIXe*, Algiers, 2004.  
Missoum, S., *Alger à l'époque ottomane*, Aix-en-Provence; Algiers, 2003.  
National Archaeological and Historic Monuments Agency, Archives, notably the report on endowments to the state, undated.
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.author: Ali Lafer
keywords: Fountain; water

b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.name: Spice box.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.description: A circular spice box made from brass that is incised and inlayed with silver. The container is original but the lid is a replacement, a fact verified by the decoration on the lid being distinctly different to that on the container. The lid is decorated with concentric bands surrounding a roundel in the centre. The roundel contains an arabesque quatrefoil with secondary leaf motifs surrounded by a band of leafy scrolling. The pattern is interrupted by three roundels with motifs of eight-pointed stars, created from trefoils and leaf motifs, and issuing from a central lozenge motif. A broader band occupies the main part of the lid; it contains 12 complex interconnected knot motifs that are separated from each other by vertically disposed, twisted-rope designs. The composition issues from pseudo-*kufic* elements above and below. The outermost band repeats the decorative scheme of the border around the central roundel, but on this occasion it is interrupted by six roundels rather than three. The container displays a guilloche around the upper body. Below, separated from the guilloche by a ridge, the main part of the body has four large roundels with scrolling borders, filled with alternating arabesque scrolls and a coat of arms. The areas in between the roundels are filled alternately with a three-knot design, issuing from pseudo-*kufic* elements top and bottom, or a geometric interlace pattern, rising from a pseudo-*kufic* base and terminating in trilobal motifs. The lower body is enhanced by a band of leafy scrolling, interrupted by four roundels with quatrefoils.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.short_description: During the AH late 8th–9th / AD late 14th–15th centuries Mamluk metalworkers developed a range of wares specifically for the European market and decorated to European taste, a fact borne out by the appearance of European coats of arms and blazons on many examples. This box conveyed expensive spices to the West.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.method_for_datation: Containers such as this one were made specifically for the European market during the late 8th– 9th/ late 14th–15th centuries, a fact borne out by the appearance of European coats of arms and blazons on other examples of the period.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.method_for_provenance: Pieces like this are known to have been made in the Mamluk realm, probably Damascus, during the Mamluk period.
b4d34b89-c6b2-5e46-8e41-4f74dec4c93d.obtention: Purchased from W. Wareham, London, in 1870.

keywords: Veneto-Saracenic; arabesque; pseudo inscriptions

b4e72974-c00c-5720-9454-206dc84e1405.name: Pashmina Niche Rug
b4e72974-c00c-5720-9454-206dc84e1405.description:
The new carpet style in the time of Mughal ruler Shah Jahan (1628-1647) was the flower style, featuring the naturalistic depiction of flowering plants. The refined elegance of the decorations, the use of expensive silk and pashmina and the high knot count are characteristic of the luxury carpets of this period. The silk warp was frequently dyed in bands. The flower style lived on in the works of the post-Shah Jahan workshops.  
  
In the field, the ivory-coloured *mihrab* (prayer niche) with lobed arch is adorned on both sides by a crimson half cypress growing from a finely delineated column base. From the apex of the *mihrab* hangs a trapezoidal lamp; in the centre below, a three-branched floral bush grows from the bottom of the *mihrab*. Faint glimmers of the colourful bands (ivory, yellow, crimson, blue and green) can be seen in the plain ivory surface. The crimson spandrel is adorned on both sides with symmetrical floral patterns – vines, leaves and poppy blossoms. As is typical of flower style rugs, the major border of the rug contains lotus flowers against a dark blue ground and is enclosed in ivory field minor borders.
b4e72974-c00c-5720-9454-206dc84e1405.provenance: Kashmir or Lahore, North India or Pakistan
b4e72974-c00c-5720-9454-206dc84e1405.obtention: Purchased from Adolf Roger, an art dealer of Budapest, 1895

b5a220ba-715c-5b3c-87dd-4d32b38cbcb1.description: *Kwar*; a low, circular wooden brazier that stands on four legs. The *kwar* is filled with sand to protect it from the hot charcoal that is used to roast coffee beans, prepare bread, heat milk, or to add the smell of incense or *oud* to the room.

b5eeb317-b1a2-5710-8891-111d70b464e6.name: Ewer for Zamzam water
b5eeb317-b1a2-5710-8891-111d70b464e6.description: Pear-shaped ewer with strap handle and serpentine spout. Brass lid and stopper for the spout are both screw-threaded, which allows them to be securely sealed in place. The body and neck engraved with floral pattern, with applied palmette bosses to each side with trefoil suspension loops (one is missing).

b6518af0-5029-5a94-8521-524613b875bb.name: Citadel of Aleppo.
b6518af0-5029-5a94-8521-524613b875bb.description:
The Citadel of Aleppo is a masterpiece of medieval Islamic fortress architecture. Its massive ovoid shape and extensive defences enclose an area of approximately seven hectares. The natural hill upon which the Citadel was built has long been used as a stronghold (including evidence of a Hittite temple from the first millennium BC). During the Hamdanid reign of Aleppo under Sayf al-Dawla in the AH 4th / AD 10th century, early constructions of a citadel took place. The Citadel's strategic importance was reactivated by the time the Crusades began.  
When Nur al-Din ruled Aleppo in the early AH 6th / AD 12th century, he rebuilt its fragmented interior and fortified the remnants of the earlier fortress. His expansion included the construction of Maqam Ibrahim, an important shrine with legendary associations to the Prophet Abraham. However, the majority of the citadel's surviving features date to the period of Saladin's son, al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi, who ruled between AH 582–613 / AD 1186–1216. He ordered the deeper, 22-m moat, the magnificent bridge, the glacis of smooth impregnable stone, the enlarged towers (or *burgs*), and the outstanding gateway designed to ambush any enemy who managed to approach. Unlike Damascus, Aleppo was more exposed to Frankish attacks from nearby Edessa and the western coastlands. There was also the threat of the powerful and stealthy "Assassins", followers of the esoteric Isma'ili sect of Shi'i Islam.  
Al-Zahir rebuilt many of the civil and religious constructs initiated by Nur al-Din, including the Citadel's beautifully proportioned Great Mosque and the administrative Dar al-'Adl (House of Justice) facing the Citadel. Some scholars speculate the existence of a tunnel between the two.  
Most importantly, al-Zahir Ghazi constructed the royal palace complex and baths within the Citadel walls. This represents a new development in the history of Islamic architecture. Palatial residences were not usually constructed behind military fortresses but due to high- level security during this period, a new model emerged. The palace was renovated by al-Aziz Muhammad in AH 627 / AD 1230, but most of it was destroyed by the Mongols.  
Altogether, Al-Malik al-Zahir's project radically changed both the scale and scope of the Citadel and its surrounding area, making it the impressive sight it is today. Decorative elements appear particularly around the gates. Two well-known examples are the Lion Gate and the Serpent Gate, each decorated in high-relief figurative stone carving. Lions had long been used as signs of power and royalty; here symbolising throne guardians. The serpents and dragons on the other hand curl backwards to bite themselves; they mark the limits of a protected and controlled area.  
Parts of the Citadel, especially the entrance block and bridge, underwent renovation during the Mamluk period, some time in the AH 7th / AD 14th century. Stylistically this is evidenced by the more flamboyant decorative features.
b6518af0-5029-5a94-8521-524613b875bb.short_description: This masterpiece of medieval fortification is the hallmark of Aleppo since the AH 6th / AD 12th century. Its entrance block alone is an impressive work. Linking the citadel to the city by a stately ramp, it also includes two massively constructed towers which conceal a U-shaped corridor that would force an attacking army to change direction six times, while exposing them to projectiles and burning liquid from gaps in the vaults above. Most of the citadel's construction, both military as well as the palatial and religious buildings within, date to the Ayyubid al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi (d. 613 / 1216).
b6518af0-5029-5a94-8521-524613b875bb.method_for_datation: Various inscriptions and historical records have preserved an accurate account of the various stages of the Citadel's construction and evolution.

b666eda8-3aa4-5e7c-a57e-1511705d233d.name: Brass *Badiye* Bowl
b666eda8-3aa4-5e7c-a57e-1511705d233d.description:
This is a broad-bodied, wide-mouthed bowl shaped by the hammering technique and decorated all over with inlaid gold and silver leaf. The rim is bordered with lotus, flowers and leaves. This type of ornamentation can also be seen in the book decorations of the Qaitbay Period. Immediately below this border are round medallions and rectangular cartouches with inscriptions adorned with knotted weave motifs. The lower part of the body is encircled by scalloped niches with floral decorations and a pattern of intertwined Ys and Ts (truncated meander). The composition adorning the bottom of the bowl, decorated with geometric interlaces formed by the arms of a multi-pointed star on a background of curved branches and *rumili* (stylised designs), is one of the most beautiful examples of its period. In Mamluk art similar compositions were used with the same skill in woodcarving, bookbinding and stonemasonry.  
  
The composition, carving of the surface and placement of silver and gold leaf are typical of the Mosul school. Some of the craftsmen of Mosul origin, fleeing the Mongol invasion, migrated to other regions and worked under the Artuqids, the Ayubids of Syria and Egypt, and later the Mamluks. The Kaygbay bowl was probably made by a Mosul craftsman.  
  
The inscriptions read: "Our glorious Sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf, the victorious Kaidbay, may his victory be blessed".
b666eda8-3aa4-5e7c-a57e-1511705d233d.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts

b71ad5bf-0537-5bae-a28c-3289c9d237b7.name: Beylerbeyi Palace.
b71ad5bf-0537-5bae-a28c-3289c9d237b7.description:
Beylerbeyi Palace is a seaside residence in the Beylerbeyi district (formerly known as İstavroz Bahçeleri or 'Cross Gardens') on the Anatolian side of the Bosphorus Strait. The various parts of the palace complex have been put together independently, regardless of symmetry. The main structure, the palace building, is a two-storey brick construction rising on a high basement. It occupies a rectangular area oriented north to south and measures approximately 65 m x 40 m. The southern section is designed as state apartments (*mabeyn*), the northern section as the family's living quarters (*harem*). The main building has a symmetrical and axial layout; in contrast to the Western influence apparent from the outside, its plan resembles that of a traditional Turkish house, arranged around a central courtyard with *iwan*s. The wall which runs along the quay, enlivened with repeating triple pilasters, includes two gates opening onto the water and two small seaside pavilions, one for men and the other for women. These splendid gates, called waterside or sea gates, were used to secure the entrance to the palace from the water. The sea gates, one of which was designed to belong to the men's quarters and the other to the women's, show Eastern influence; their design is interesting, enlivening as they do the two ends of the straight line created by the shore-side wall.  
The other buildings in the complex, dispersed throughout the complex within walled gardens and connected to one another by stairs and ramps, are the Marble Pavilion, the Yellow Pavilion and the private stables. The Deer House, Bird House, Lion House, the Pavilion of the Pashas and Music Pavilion are no longer standing.  
The façades of the Beylerbeyi Palace, like the organisation of the inner spaces, take eclectic forms. It is clear that Sultan Abdülaziz was inspired by his new palace and interested in its decoration. The façades include arches and windows in the Greek and Roman styles, a balanced Classical scheme is achieved also by the use of round arches and limited architectural forms; the plastic effect of Baroque designs is also apparent. In contrast to the evident Western influence seen in the external decoration, the interior spaces are heavy with traditional Ottoman and Eastern motifs. Many rooms and salons feature paintings of seascapes as well as military motifs like swords and flags. Since no provision was made for a heating system in the palace, it is inferred that the whole complex was designed as a summer palace.  
The first Beylerbeyi Palace was wooden and built for Sultan Mahmud II (r. AH 1223–55 / AD 1808–39 by the architect Krikor Amira Balyan. The present Beylerbeyi Palace was designed and built under the auspices of the architects Sarkis Balyan and Agop Balyan, and on the orders of Sultan Abdülaziz between 1276 and 1281 / 1861 and 1865, after the original palace was abandoned following a fire during the reign of Sultan Abdülmecid (r. AH 1255–77 / AD 1839–61). Over the years the Beylerbeyi Palace hosted many foreign guests; its last resident under the Ottoman Empire was Sultan Abdülhamid II (r. AH 1293–1327 / AD 1876–1909), who was dethroned. During the Republic period (after 1923) some sections of the palace were used to host state guests; these were opened to visitors in 1985 and renovated for various artistic activities. The Beylerbeyi Palace serves today as a palace museum linked to the National Palaces.
b71ad5bf-0537-5bae-a28c-3289c9d237b7.short_description: One of the most magnificent Ottoman coastal palaces, Beylerbeyi Palace is located on the Asian coast of the Bosphorus. It was commissioned by Sultan Abdülaziz and consists of the main palace structure and its auxiliaries. Its façade and interior decorations blend various Western influences with Eastern motifs. This summer residence is remarkable for its rich decoration and its two sea-pavilions on the water are the most striking and typical examples of Orientalism in Istanbul. It was opened to the public as a museum in 1984.
b71ad5bf-0537-5bae-a28c-3289c9d237b7.method_for_datation: Archival documents, inscriptions found on the monument, newspapers of the period, travel journals and the works of historians of the time are all useful in dating the monument. In addition, stylistic details of the palace complex provide important clues as to the period in which it was constructed.

b86322b9-31bb-52dc-86d7-821809e043fd.name: Pottery bowl
b86322b9-31bb-52dc-86d7-821809e043fd.description: A glazed small pottery bowl decorated under a blue, light green, and brown radial design under a greyish glaze. The rhythm of the five colours evokes the five pillars of Islam, elevating the object from an ordinary houseware to a spiritual level. The radials point to a blueish spot in the middle of the bowl. The rim is lined with the same blue as one of the radials inside the bowl. We see the radial underglaze or lustre design in some beautiful AH 6th / AD 12th-century Kashan Iranian pottery bowls.

b95967f4-71c0-5313-9654-d9eb492b2fb1.name: Candlestick (*Mash ‘al*)
b95967f4-71c0-5313-9654-d9eb492b2fb1.description:
This Safavid cylindrical candlestick is crafted from brass and adorned with intricate decorations. It features a blend of floral and geometric motifs alongside bands of *nasta’liq* script inscriptions. These are verses from Persian mystical poetry, particularly those by the renowned 14th-century poet Hafez Shirazi, including the famous line:  
الا یا ایها الساقی ادر کأسا و ناولها

ba61949f-4fe6-55e5-a72f-065204514600.name: Long-necked bottle
ba61949f-4fe6-55e5-a72f-065204514600.description: This monochrome bottle with a long neck has a facetted design, imitating metal bottles. This type of object appears in painted miniatures in which the cupbearer pours wine from an identical bottle. Prohibited by the Qur’an, wine nevertheless could have medicinal and digestive virtues, according to Al-Râzî: “the usefulness of wine for the preservation of health, and the improvement of digestion, is certain if it is given its rightful place, and if its quantity, quality, and timing are in accordance with the rules of the art".

bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.name: Fragment of a pottery bowl.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.description:
The Raqqa region contains a group of Abbasid palaces that have been labelled with the letters A, B, C and D. This ceramic fragment was found during archaeological excavations carried out in Palace A. The fragment is part of a delicate bowl that was made in a mould and decorated around its girth with Arabic *kufic* script that reads: “from the work of Ibrahim al-Nasrani that has been made in Hira for the Amir Sulayman, son of the Commander of the Faithful." The Commander of the Faithful, or Caliph, in question is the Abbasid Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (r. AH 136–58 / AD 754–75). The text indicates that this piece was made in Hira by Ibrahim al-Nasrani and transported to Raqqa. The name of the craftsperson (al-Nasrani, i.e. the Christian) indicates that he was probably a master craftsman in the Christian ceramic-producing quarter of al-Hira.  
The base of the bowl was stamped with geometric and stylised vegetal motifs including palm trees.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.short_description: Although this bowl is delicate and fragmented, its moulded band of early *kufic* inscription has mostly survived. It includes the name of the craftsman, Ibrahim al-Nasrani, evidently a Christian, the place of production in Hira and the dedication to Sulayman, '\[son\] of the commander of the faithful'.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.initial_owner: Prince Sulayman (son of the Abbasid Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (r. AH 136–58 / AD 754–75).
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.method_for_datation: The inscription on the fragment associates it with the rule of the Abbasid Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (136–58 / 754–75).
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.method_for_provenance: The text inscribed on the vessel fragment specifies Hira, in Mesopotamia (Iraq) as the place of production.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.provenance: Produced in Hira in southern Mesopotamia (Iraq).
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.obtention: The fragment was found during an archaeological excavation carried out in 1948 in Palace A by the Syrian General Directorate of Antiquities under the direction of archaeologist Nasib Salibi.

bd8ff36e-5588-5aad-949e-bfd038a77ce8.description:
The piece has a round, wide mouth, single handle, round, wide body and thin ring bottom.  
The exterior is decorated with yellow gilding and dark red, white and blue encaustic floral decoration on a white ground. The inner surface is white. The handle and base are brass and were added later. There is a flying bird figure on the upper part of the handle.  
The saucer is made of silver and has a rounded form and wavy rim. The entire circumferenceis decorated with vine leaves and grape clusters in relief. The centre is curved upwards and stamped

bdeda37e-0f4a-5fd6-ad87-d9dacdb11131.name: ‘Imara al-‘Amira (Flourishing Edifice).
bdeda37e-0f4a-5fd6-ad87-d9dacdb11131.description:
The 'Imara al-'Amira contains four architectural components: a large kitchen, with its subsidiary additions which includes two ovens, a bakery and a fountain; a large *caravanserai* and a mosque as well as a *ribat*, composed of 55 rooms, for Sufis and the poor. This large building has two entrances, the northern entrance on Aqabat Takiyya Street and the southern entrance on Aqabat al-Saraya Street. The northern entrance has a transition zone, known as a *derka*, which leads into an open courtyard. In the northern section of the complex are the remains of an adjoining entrance and the kitchen, storage areas and a fountain, in addition to a two-storey building. The southern entrance leads into a corridor with walls that are rich in decorative stonework, which finally leads into the open courtyard surrounded by arcades that form the *caravanserai* (*khan*) of the 'Imara al-'Amira. To the east of the *caravanserai* with itsopen courtyard, there is a building that was constructed in the AH 13th / AD 19th century, known as Adaliyya. Perhaps it was built on the site of the *ribat* that vanished over the course of time. The Adaliyya building faces a hall of which little remains but for four cross vaults it may, however, have been part of the mosque of the 'Imara al-'Amira. To the east of the hall there is a dome-covered shrine that is believed to be the final resting place of Sa'ad al-Din al-Rasafi, author of the work, *al-Manhal al-Safi wa al-Mashrab al-Wafi \[The Pure Spring and the Inundated Fountain\]*.  
The multiplicity of elements that make up the complex indicate that it served several purposes: as a place for religious worship; for charitable purposes, as may be noted by the kitchen which was and still is used for the preparation of food for the poor and the needy and for trade and economic purposes, represented by the *caravanserai* that accommodated merchants and consummated mercantile trading.
bdeda37e-0f4a-5fd6-ad87-d9dacdb11131.short_description: This grandiose social complex was also known as 'Khassaki Sultan' after its patron, the wife of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent. The complex was built as a result of incorporating a number of buildings and other additions. It includes a large kitchen, two ovens, two bakeries, a *sabil* (public fountain), a large *khan* (inn), a mosque and a Sufi ribat. It has two entrances and a number of open plazas. The complex provided food daily to the needy as well as to visitors, regardless of their identity or religion, as did the *zawiya* and the *arbita* (Sufi hospice and teaching establishment). Over 1000 meals were offered daily.
bdeda37e-0f4a-5fd6-ad87-d9dacdb11131.method_for_datation: The building is dated by *waqf* documents associated with it, among which is record number 270 in the Shari'a Court of Jerusalem (Folio No. 18–49). This document is further supported by the archives of the Palestinian Museum (Rockefeller Museum). Through these documents it is possible to deduce that the construction of the 'Imara al-'Amira began in 959 / 1552 and was completed in around 964/ 1557.

be60fc30-4879-59b7-9f1b-3a7a358298d0.name: Jug and basin set (*aftafa-layan*)
be60fc30-4879-59b7-9f1b-3a7a358298d0.description:
The *aftafa-layan* is a jug and basin set with a separating lid used for washing, usually made of copper and richly decorated. It was widely distributed in the Near and Middle East and used during large feasts. The lid was used as an esthetic cover for the basin. It is decorated with inscriptions and floral elements. One or two lines from Hafez’s ghazal poem were written on the upper border of *aftafa*. The edge borders of the *layan* are decorated with inscriptions. The inscription in the cartouches on the border read as follows:  
"It's time to enjoy the flowers and life.  
Sagi! Give the water of life.  
In the meadow, wine and jam \[bowl\] are pleasant.  
Along with crimson tulips.  
Wasted youth is a pity, it can't be considered a life."
be60fc30-4879-59b7-9f1b-3a7a358298d0.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analyses with related material.

bf8c236d-a3f0-57db-aaff-72a234666a2c.name: Portrait of Sultan Selim II
bf8c236d-a3f0-57db-aaff-72a234666a2c.short_description: This large album portrait of Sultan Selim II (reigned 1566–74) reveals much about his reign. It was Selim’s father, Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (reigned 1520–66), who solidified the geographical borders of the Ottoman Empire and refined the central administration of his government, allowing his son and successor to pursue more sedentary pleasures such as literature, art and wine-drinking. Nicknamed “Selim the Sot” for his affection for wine, the sultan was nonetheless a great bibliophile and patron of architecture, music and the arts of the book. The painter, poet and naval commander Haydar Reis depicted Selim II as larger than life; the robust sultan in his luxurious fur-lined and brocaded gold garment dwarfs both the page boy and the interior in which he sits in a cross-legged position on a carpet. This composition was one of a number of conventions for Ottoman royal portraiture developed in the 1570s and is similar to portraits in Loqman’s *Kiyafetu’l Insaniye fi Semailu’l-Osmaniye*, a study to record the physiognomy of the Ottoman sultans.
bf8c236d-a3f0-57db-aaff-72a234666a2c.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; painting; portrait; sultan; ruler

c0f8bfaf-f9ca-5ac0-84ba-67ebfcaf39e4.name: Tablecloth (*dastarkhan*)
c0f8bfaf-f9ca-5ac0-84ba-67ebfcaf39e4.description:
A *dastarkhan* is a thin white *palas* (a kind of traditional, flat-woven carpet popular in Azerbaijan) that functioned as a tablecloth for Azerbaijanis and other Turkic peoples. The central field of Azerbaijani *dastarkhans* was rectangular, usually plain, and the borders spotted vivid decoration in contrast with the *dastarkhans* produced in Central Asia that boast elaborate designs. A *dastarkhan* denoted a sacred meaning, as its ornaments protected the food and the breadwinner and brought abundance to the family.  
In the central field of this artifact, there are inscriptions in the old epigraphic alphabet, stylized images of birds (symbolizing protection), butas (symbolizing different abilities bestowed on a person) and branches (symbolizing blessings). Images of arrows on the *dastarkhan's* border symbolize honour, prosperity and blessings.

c11ef512-f9e7-5a23-bafe-934bc32549ba.name: Hearth of Ateşbaz-ı Veli (*Makam-ı Ateşbaz-ı Veli*)
c11ef512-f9e7-5a23-bafe-934bc32549ba.description:
Ateşbaz was a Mevlevi *dede* (elder) who lived during the lifetime of Mevlana. It is said that one day an elder was preparing a meal in the kitchen when he discovered that he had exhausted his supply of fuel. He informed Kazancı Dede of the situation. Upon receiving the reply, "If there is no wood, you should have put your foot," he did not hesitate, and placed his foot into the fire, cooking the food in its flame. This earned him the name Ateşbaz, or "playing with fire”. A sign reading *Ya Hazret-i Ateşbaz-ı Veli* (O His Holiness Ateşbaz-ı Veli) used to be hung over the hearth in Mevlevi kitchens.  
According to sources associated with the Mevlevi Order, Sultan Veled, the son of Mevlana, engaged in a period of asceticism lasting forty days. This involved seclusion and reduced food, sleep and speech. Once the forty days of asceticism had been completed, Ateşbaz would prepare a meal. The first mausoleum for a cook was constructed for Ateşbaz in Meram, Konya.
c11ef512-f9e7-5a23-bafe-934bc32549ba.bibliography: Bakırcı, Naci, *Konya Mevlana Müzesi*, Istanbul: BKG Yayinlari, 2010.

c13e07a9-25e9-500c-a2eb-4f7568251a1e.name: Qajar Carpet -Hunting Scene
c13e07a9-25e9-500c-a2eb-4f7568251a1e.short_description: The pictorial carpets of Qajar Iran illustrate royals and famous people in various scenarios. This Persian Kashan wool rug displays a hunting scene with a portrait of a king or a nobleman sitting on a chair embellished with crowns, drinking and holding a copper ewer in his other hand, and a wide variety of animals and plants. The phoenix above the nobleman, a popular creature in Persian mythology, represents immortality. Hunting dogs symbolize honour and glory, while the gazelle symbolizes innocence. The imagery of water is significant, denoting purity and the source of life, and in which the fish embody undying love. The cypress tree signifies Persian perseverance and pride.

c166cd2d-8939-540b-a898-6cea4e8dc0ae.name: Brocaded velvet
c166cd2d-8939-540b-a898-6cea4e8dc0ae.short_description: Figurative design flowered in Safavid textiles in the AH 10th century / AD mid-16th century. These figures often share the same features as book paintings from the period. This velvet is unique due to the large size of its figures, unknown on other velvets of the AH 10th century / AD 16th century, and the richness of surface textures. Uncut loops of metal-wrapped silk thread have been added in some areas to the traditional silk pile, contrasting with the glittering metal thread background.

c1dc368c-d1ca-53c8-a0da-a63bd4ed9f6b.name: *Jobbana* covered pot
c1dc368c-d1ca-53c8-a0da-a63bd4ed9f6b.description: The word *jobbana* comes from the Arabic word *jben*, which refers to cheese. This lidded jar was originally used in Morocco to curdle milk, but was used also to preserve butter or serve *harira*, a soup with which the Ramadan fast is broken in the evening. The delicacy of the decoration of this pot is characteristic of the workshops of the city of Safi, a city on the west coast, whose name is inscribed under the base. The tone of blue reflects the use of a handmade nickel-based pigment. Ceramic production development in Safi would result from the arrival of potters from Fes who appreciated the quality of clay in banks near the city.

c2c6489a-b997-5d3e-a98c-d31891a7ba03.name: Large *khabiya* jar
c2c6489a-b997-5d3e-a98c-d31891a7ba03.description: This large jar, *khabiya*, is intended for the storage of grain, semolina, oil, or water. Its motifs are typical of Tunisian craftsmanship, whose main production centre was in the pottery district (Qallaline) of Tunis. These motifs, the *taouq* (rim decoration), the strip of vertical hatching, and the band of ovoid kernels (*qloub*) are linked by similar designs. The composition is arranged in parallel bands, with the repeated use of yellow, green and brown.

c2e80ac9-c3fb-51a3-8cd2-d3cc5c1a3b20.name: Tray stand
c2e80ac9-c3fb-51a3-8cd2-d3cc5c1a3b20.description:
This Mamluk bronze tray stand exemplifies the iconic shape, size and ornamentation characteristic of Mamluk metalwork, with a notable influence from China in the shape of the tray. Originally serving as a portable support for a food tray, it would have been accompanied by multiple table stands.  
Adorned with intricate *thuluth* inscriptions, geometric and floral motifs, and interrupted by cartouches, this stand is a testament to the exquisite craftsmanship of the Mamluk artisans. Distinctive Arabic inscriptions grace the upper and lower parts and the exposed section of the lower rim. Epigraphic analysis reveals that these inscriptions identity of the owner – a high-ranking official (Amir) in the Mamluk court hierarchy who belonged to the second-highest rank. The display of titles underscores the owner’s esteemed position and societal status. One of the inscriptions, “*Al-maqarr al-‘ali al-mawlawi al-amiri al-kabiri al-‘alimi al-‘adili al-ghazi al-mujahidi al-maliki al-nasiri*”, suggests that the owner is a follower of Al Sultan Al-Nasir. While many Mamluk sultans held the title Al-Nasir, it is unclear which one is referred to here. However, the decoration style indicates that it likely belongs to the period of Al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun (1258–1341). Crafted from bronze, this tray stand displays intricate detail achieved through engraving and embossing. The *thuluth* inscriptions, geometric and floral motifs, and cartouches are meticulously executed, reflecting the skill and artistry of Mamluk metalworkers in Egypt during the 14th century.
