c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.name: Mosque lamp.
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.description: An enamelled glass and gilt mosque lamp with a wide funnel-shaped neck and a rounded rim. The lamp has a squat body, steeply sloping shoulder and a flattened base, and a tall pedestal foot with a pronounced pontil mark on the underside. Six trailed suspension loops are placed around the body at regular intervals. The lamp is decorated comprehensively with enamel decoration executed in red, blue and light-green, embellished with gilding. Around the neck is a wide band of *thuluth* script executed in blue enamel, surrounded by a floral border. An excerpt from the Qur’an (*Sura* 2; verse 256), the inscription is interrupted by decorative roundels rendered in gold, red and green, each of which contain a little cup in the centre. The lower neck and upper body are decorated with floral bands interrupted by roundels with individual floral motifs. On the main body, another inscription in *thuluth* script gives the titles of the official who commissioned the lamp: Zain al-Din Mubarak who, according to the blazon above, was cupbearer to the sultan, al-Malik al-Salih, who is also named in the inscription. There were two rulers with the same titulature, both of whom were the sons of Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun: the first, al-Malik al-Salih Isma’il (r. AH 742–5 / AD 1342–5); the second, al-Malik al-Salih Salih (r. AH 751–4 / AD 1351–4).
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.short_description: Glass mosque lamps with enamelled decoration were commissioned in large numbers by the Mamluk elite in Egypt and Syria. Decorated with Qur’anic inscriptions and the titles of the patron, they were destined for the numerous mosques and *madrasas* endowed by the Mamluks throughout Cairo and the empire.
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.method_for_datation: The appearance of the name of al-Malik al-Salih on this mosque lamp assigns the piece to the reign of either al-Malik al-Salih Isma’il (r. 742–5 / 1342–5) or to al-Malik al-Salih Salih (r. 751–4 / 1351–4).
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.method_for_provenance: Mosque lamps of this type were made in large numbers in both Egypt and Syria during the 8th / 14th century.
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.obtention: Purchased by NMS from the Major W. J. Myers Collection in 1900.

c343e522-683c-5e4b-8f73-edba72f1ed53.name: Aş Evi (Bektashi Kitchen)
c343e522-683c-5e4b-8f73-edba72f1ed53.description:
The most significant part of the Hacı Bektaş Velî Dervish lodge is the Aş Evi (kitchen), which is accessed via a large door with two wings. After traversing two corridors, one reaches the location of the main Aş Evi. On the right side of the first corridor is the grave of the father of the Ash House, which is marked by an inscription dated 1560 on the door of the second corridor. To the right of this corridor is a window that opens to the room of the Father of the House, while to the left is the Pantry Room, where meat is cooled.  
The main hall of the house is entered through an arched doorway and is divided into two parts by a large arch based on the north and south walls. In the centre of the hall is the stone where meat was chopped and fat was drained. On the south, north and east walls there are six large and small hearths where food was cooked.

c466c19a-6e61-556b-a637-4712a73de575.name: Three fragments of woven fabric decorated with female figures carrying rose water bottles
c466c19a-6e61-556b-a637-4712a73de575.description: These silk weavings once framed a large blanket with an embroidered middle section and have been remounted to the original fabric sheet. Depicted on the background, which used to be gold, are young women in elegantly curved stance holding rosewater bottles in their arms. Curved blossoming plants emerging from a rise in the ground are visible in the spaces between the figures. The décor is arranged in offset horizontal rows: the direction of the women’s gaze switches in each row and the colouring of the garments is repeated after every fourth row. Miniature paintings were often used as templates for silk weaves during this era. An especially delightful detail is the circlet-shaped feathered headdress with a long scarf that falls behind the back and is elegantly ruffled. This type of headdress was common until c. 1620 and is defining for the time in which this silk weaving was created.

c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.name: Dish.
c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.description:
A dish with the shield belonging to the Tondi family of Siena, Italy, in the centre surrounded by radiating chains of 'bryony' flowers (those with blue petals and lustre-painted centres) alternating with chains of blue 'parsley'-shaped leafs (those that are made up of ragged trefoil shapes), and both interwoven with lustre-coloured spindly 'fern' leaves. This style of dish belongs to a distinctive range that was much sought after in Spain and in other parts of Europe where it was exported in large quantities. This explains the presence of the Italian family's shield, for this type of lustre-ware was extremely popular in Italy.  
  
Manises was one of the main pottery-making towns in Valencia, and played a leading role in the manufacture of lustre-wares for export to Europe, principally to France and Italy. Manises's pottery left for export from the Valencian port of Grao where many Manises potters owned pottery warehouses and shops. These potters were a mixture of Christians and Moors (Muslims), the latter of which were not permitted to take their skills to work outside the town, testifying to the value of their special skills to the economy of Manises. By the mid-16th century (AH 956), Manises had a major monopoly on the production of lustre-wares in Valencia.
c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.short_description: The old name for this type of Mudéjar-style Spanish lustre ceramics is ‘Hispano-Moresque’, a term indicating that the potters who made it were a mixture of Christians and Moors (Muslims), the latter of which were restricted to practising their much-praised skill outside the town of Manises in Valencia.
c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis and identification of the shield belonging to the Tondi family of Siena, Italy.

c4af05d4-9269-5543-8456-f8734f0e243b.name: Conical cup
c4af05d4-9269-5543-8456-f8734f0e243b.description:
Stoneware, celadons, and porcelain from China fascinated the Arab, Iranian, and Turkish worlds. The chronicles of the reigns of the Abbasid caliphs bear witness to this, as do the collections of the Ottoman sultans.  
In the absence of kaolin, and to replace porcelain, ceramists opt for a new clay mixture, obtained from pulverised quartz pebbles, white clay, and frit (pulverised mixture of quartz pebbles and soda from vegetable ash). These are the available materials. The mixture is soft; this piece mimics the translucency of porcelain. This technique was not known in the West until the 18th century, evidence of the technical progress made by Eastern ceramists.

c4fe88f8-b165-52e3-b23f-fce061f8c81f.name: A Prince Meeting a Muslim Holy Man
c4fe88f8-b165-52e3-b23f-fce061f8c81f.description:
The young man in princely attire seated in the presence of a mullah, a Muslim holy man, is thought to be one of the sons of Emperor Jahangir (1569–1627, reign 1605–1627). The facial features of the prince conform to portraits of Sultan Khurram (1592–1666) who became the emperor Shah Jahan (reign 1627–1658).  
The young prince appears to be around 18 years of age. Khurram had an early interest in art and even commissioned court paintings at the age of 14. This miniature may be seen as an illustration of the prince's interest in Islam. Unlike his forefathers, Shah Jahan was a practicing Sunni Muslim. He is best remembered for building the Taj Mahal, the stunning white marble memorial to his beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal.  
  
The painting is unsigned, making the identity of the artist unclear, but a tentative attribution can be made on stylistic grounds to the gifted court painter Manôhar (active c.1580–1620) and his atelier. The artist worked at court for at least forty years during the successive reigns of Akbar (1542–1605), Jahangir, and Shah Jahan.

c5b5daa1-000f-54c3-95f9-2872725c902d.name: Tile Bowl
c5b5daa1-000f-54c3-95f9-2872725c902d.description:
The bowl has a round and flaring rim. Its round body narrows towards the ring base. It is decorated with dark blue, green, red and yellow gilding on a white glazed ground. On the external part of the bowl, there are Surahs of al-Falaq and al-Ikhlas in medallions.  
Produced in China for the Ottoman market.

c7f58b8f-d101-5a99-a3cc-dcb898bbfeeb.name: An Algerian woman grinds her meal in an old wooden mill
c7f58b8f-d101-5a99-a3cc-dcb898bbfeeb.short_description: Many Western photographers took great interest in women's daily lives, or in daily rural tasks. In this photograph from 1920 an Algerian woman is pictured as she grinds wheat with a wooden pestle and mortar.

c8452185-b564-5d73-9086-7f2303088f36.name: Coffee Pot
c8452185-b564-5d73-9086-7f2303088f36.description: A coffee pot decorated with an image of a mosque and an Istanbul scene. Decorated in *savat*, or niello, an engraving technique using a black sulphide alloy.

c87b0cb3-05b6-5a2d-aa6c-454893216166.name: *Sema* Practice in *Matbah-ı Şerif* (whirling practice in the kitchen)
c87b0cb3-05b6-5a2d-aa6c-454893216166.description:
The *Matbah-ı Şerif* (kitchen) was constructed at the same time as the dervish cells by Murad III in 1584. Some sections of the building have two floors. The building's present form dates from repairs made in 1867. The kitchen's upper section, separated by a marble wall, can be accessed via marble steps. The space is characterised by two barrel-vaulted domes and is illuminated by eight wooden windows. The portals, decorated with plant motifs, harmonise with the simplicity of the surrounding environment.  
The floor is covered with wood, as *Sema* (whirling) practice was done in this section. The nail visible in the corner of the marble wall on the right side of the room has been identified as a *Sema* training nail (note the nail in the centre of a practice board in photo).

c9b1b21a-3afb-57cb-86e1-8e151adf4e75.name:
Haftvad and the Worm  
Folio from the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
c9b1b21a-3afb-57cb-86e1-8e151adf4e75.short_description: The vast historical scope, imaginative power, and national importance of the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), an epic poem completed by Firdausi in 1010, have inspired countless works of art in all media. This folio AKM164 (folio 521 verso) from the *Shahnameh* produced for Safavid ruler Shah Tahmasp (r. 1524–76) centres around Haftvad, a modest man with seven sons and one daughter whose fate is entwined with the rise of the Sasanian dynasty (224–651).

c9e2a362-f0a6-5922-bdbb-3b8f58f34d64.name: *Mechabeh (food cover)*
c9e2a362-f0a6-5922-bdbb-3b8f58f34d64.description:
*Mechabeh* (palm food cover) used to protect food from dirt and insects.  
The cover is formed by braiding nine to 11 palm leaves together to form a flat strip. The strips are sewn together to form a cone shaped cover.

ca7280db-3428-5b5d-8d37-2c4fe8ed2c6b.name: Ewer
ca7280db-3428-5b5d-8d37-2c4fe8ed2c6b.short_description:
For centuries, romantic myths have surrounded the ewer. The name Ashkdan translates to “tear-container”, alluding to use of the vessel. According to Persian folklore, women would bottle-up tears shed for their husbands during long separations. Upon their return, husbands could measure their love. Shia mourning rituals also emphasized tear-preservation in commemoration of martyrs that were believed to have curable powers.  
This ewer with a striking swan-neck and tear-shaped opening depicts humans, birds, and scrolls of ellipses typical for the Safavid dynasty (16th – 18th century). Although the tear-legends have endured over time, scents rather than tears might flow within the vials. Persians to this day pour perfume or rose water from vessels with long necks onto hands and clothing.

ca7afc73-93f0-57b7-bf5b-affec7602629.name: al-Ghuta ash-Sharqiyya
ca7afc73-93f0-57b7-bf5b-affec7602629.description: Sugar, or glucose today, can be added and mixed with the juice in the basin. The introduction of glucose into the dough is another innovation that transforms the final product. Traditionally, only a small amount of sugar was added to the dough. Beginning in the 1960s and 1970s, glucose syrup was gradually introduced. In addition to treating the fruit with sulphur, mixing glucose into the dough meant that the product could be preserved more safely and for longer. What's more, the resulting paste was softer and more attractive. The glucose syrup is poured into the basin from which the pressed juice flows. Manufacturers have gradually increased the percentage of this inexpensive ingredient to the detriment of the quality of the dough.

ca84a358-0e08-5345-bc08-43570cf84e04.name: *Women grinding corn in Sinai*
ca84a358-0e08-5345-bc08-43570cf84e04.short_description: Many of the most popular subjects of stereographs were of topographical views or of scenes unfamiliar to the western audience for whom they were generally produced. This group of Islamic women from Egypt's Sinai Peninsula is shown grinding corn. Their faces are hidden by veils. The veil turns away the gaze while at the same time attracting it. The secrecy of the veil prompted fascination for what was often seen as the mysterious and exotic world of the East or the 'Orient' to 19th-century western viewers. In contrast, the men in the background confront the camera.

cbadcbe0-3272-59a1-a3b3-967703ee5993.name: Alms Vessel
cbadcbe0-3272-59a1-a3b3-967703ee5993.short_description:
Known as the Prophet’s *mudd* vessel, this bronze pot would collect and measure the alms given as charity by the people of Medina in Saudi Arabia. The cylindrical jar features the *basmala* or Muslim invocation and Qur’anic verses in *thuluth* and *naskh* script.  
  
Commissioned by the Naqib al-Ashraf, Mohamed Jamal Allah, the pot represents a replica of the original *mudd* vessel employed by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) to gather and distribute charity money. Inhabitants of Saudi Arabia would quantify money using the Abbasid Islamic economic measure called *mudd*.  
  
With *zakat* (charity) as one of the pillars of Islam, wealthy Muslims are obligated to donate alms. Muslims base the amount of *zakat* on a surplus of wealth, rather than one’s income, while a minimum amount prevents the application of this tax. This minimum amount called *nisab* akin to the modern-day minimum wage determines who should give and receive charity. *Zakat* meaning "purity" or "purification" enacts a reciprocal gift-giving exchange, where the recipient and charity-giver accept blessings from God.

cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.name: Lustre bowl.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.description: The inner surface of the bowl is decorated with two patterns: symmetrical arabesques and bands of intertwining *kufic* calligraphy. Both motifs are framed within eight separate boxes, and the two patterns alternate with each other. Both are painted in golden brown lustre over a white glaze. The surrounding space is covered in dots or small entwining scrolls. The outer surface is decorated with hastily painted flutings and a braided band, over a light blue glaze. The bowl is one of the most important examples of Nasrid ceramics given its display of painstaking paintwork and the fact that the place where it was made is noted on its ring-base.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.short_description: The technique of lustre-ware pottery was introduced to al-Andalus from Egypt and outstanding quality was soon attained. This bowl with a design of geometrical and vegetal panels has an inscription on the foot stating that it was made in the Spanish city of Malaga.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.dates: Hegira mid-8th century / AD mid-14th century.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.method_for_datation: The production of lustre-ware in Andalusia began in the 6th / 12th century. In 750 / 1350, the Arab chronicler Ibn Battuta noted the production of ceramics in his writings on Malaga. This bowl is the only intact item by which the source may be verified. Overall the decoration also corresponds to other branches of the arts and crafts of that period, an example being the decorative patterns used in textiles.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.method_for_provenance: There is an inscription in cursive Arabic script on the bowl’s base stating that it was made in Malaqa (Málaga). Thus the bowl acts as an important marker for the identification and dating of the entire collection of Spanish lustre-ware from the same period.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.obtention: A gift donated by Friedrich Sarre. The bowl was bought in 1901 in Italy by W. v. Bode and was given to Sarre as a gift, which he later donated to the museum.

cd089341-0bb9-55f0-b578-8f53eb67a553.name: *Woman with a Cat*
cd089341-0bb9-55f0-b578-8f53eb67a553.short_description: During the rule of the Zand and Qajar dynasties in Iran (1750–1925), artists created paintings that combined both Persian and Western sensibilities. From Europe came the tradition of large-scale oil painting, while the subject matter of youthful beauty, patterned textiles, and court life was quintessentially Persian. Many of these works were arched at the top because they were originally intended for display in arched niches of buildings.

ce05bc9c-4579-5b05-b81e-5aae5c270b67.name: Pottery jar
ce05bc9c-4579-5b05-b81e-5aae5c270b67.description: Although blue and white porcelains were described as vulgar by Chao Zaho (Chao Mingzhong) in his 1388 book about art and antiquities (the first book for connoisseurs) entitled *Gego yaolun* (The Essential Criteria of Antiques), these porcelains became more beloved and fashionable from their earliest appearance in Chinese and European markets. The first use of these two colours: blue (evoking the infinity of sea and sky) and white can be traced back to the Near and Middle East. They had a large impact on Chinese ceramics. Blue is also said to be effective against bad intentions. The pigments used for underglaze blue in Persia were lapis lazuli (*lajavard*) and cobalt, which was cheaper. The inside of the bowl is decorated with dynamic, loose floral motifs applied with sparse brushstrokes under the greyish-white glaze of the bowl on a small base. The rim is lined with blue.

d06f4d6a-a257-5324-a2d7-ce12318aa95d.name: Dish.
d06f4d6a-a257-5324-a2d7-ce12318aa95d.description: The deep pottery dish has a flat foliated rim and is decorated in underglaze cobalt-blue, bright turquoise, green, relief opaque red and black for the outlines. The centre of the dish shows a symmetrical design of two curving red dotted tulips and two smaller red flowers on stalks clasped together with a pointed, scalloped medallion between them. Small roses and other flowers springing from a leafy tuft fill the area underneath. The shape of the dish, with a foliated rim, and the stylised pattern of waves breaking on rocks on the rim are of Chinese origin. The latter developed into a popular Iznik design with a tendency to stylisation during the AH 10th / AD 16th century. The rocks and waves, originally painted in different colours, are both blue on this dish, a characteristic feature of later Iznik ware. The pointed, scalloped medallion developed in the courtly ateliers, used to decorate textiles or tiles, occurred on pottery from the AH 980s / AD 1580s. Vessels from the second half of the AH 10th / AD 16th century are mostly not imperial commissions, even if they show designs of the courtly ateliers. The potters, producing for the local market, created their own compositions by combining single elements of various styles and sources. On the back the dish is painted with four blue coloured tulips alternating with four rosettes on a white background. The transparent glaze on the back is slightly yellow coloured.
d06f4d6a-a257-5324-a2d7-ce12318aa95d.short_description: Polychrome underglaze painted dish with a foliated rim. In the centre is a symmetrical design of flowers and a medallion. The single elements, originally designed in the courtly workshops, were combined in a pattern by the potters themselves. The wave and rock motif on the rim is of Chinese origin.

d06f4d6a-a257-5324-a2d7-ce12318aa95d.method_for_provenance: The floral decoration and the shape are both specific to Iznik ceramics.

d1fc6e82-6e79-5203-89e4-cd774dcda7fd.name: Pertevniyal Valide Sultan Mosque Complex.
d1fc6e82-6e79-5203-89e4-cd774dcda7fd.description:
The complex, which comprises several buildings around a central mosque (*külliye*), was commissioned by Pertevniyal Valide Sultan and consists of a mosque, a tomb, a *sabil*, a public fountain, a clock-room where timepieces for calculating prayer times accurately on a daily basis were kept, a library, and a theological school (*madrasa*). The mosque is a single-domed, square prayer hall, following the traditional plan. In front of its strongly vertical mass is an additional two-storey building that comprises the portico for latecomers, men's and women's areas, the sultan's loge and various rooms. Attached to this additional building, separate from the main body of the mosque, are two minarets, each with a single balcony. The square prayer hall measures 10 m x 10 m and is extended with arches on four sides. The mosque's east, west and south façades are all emphasised with turrets and the outward projections of their central sections are each crowned with a triangular pediment. Each section has two rows of three windows. The dome, separated from the walls and brought inward, is supported on a high, 12-sided drum.  
The Pertevniyal Valide Sultan Mosque is noteworthy for the density and variety of its decoration. The projecting central sections of the façades and the windows on the drum of the dome are executed in the Gothic style. The design of triple blind niches above the windows, for instance, borrow elements from Ottoman decorative art, while their location recalls examples from North African and Andalusian architecture. The blind niches, as well as the decorative compositions of arabesques and palmettes on the façades, are, like the *muqarnas*, elements borrowed from Classical Ottoman art. The corner turrets, each of which terminates in a lobed onion-dome reminiscent of Indian architecture, are decorated with niches containing *muqarnas,* again borrowed from Classical Ottoman architecture, as well as the simple blind niches and various geometric motifs.  
The interior space, like the façades, is densely decorated. Ottoman motifs are used in painted decoration (*kalemişi*) in which blue dominates. A cornice with *muqarnas* surrounds the upper section of the lower row of windows. On the surfaces of the walls, as on the façades, classical Ottoman elements are found including blind niches, *muqarnas*, arch motifs, arabesques, and Chinese-inspired floral ornament. The marble *mihrab* and *minbar* are plain.  
The building, which reflects the stylistic characteristics and innovations of the period of its construction, was built in an eclectic style with a strongly Oriental inclination.  
The simultaneous use in the Pertevniyal Valide Sultan Mosque of different elements from several styles and disciplines, such as Gothic, Ottoman, and Indian architecture and decorative arts, illustrates the influence of this eclectic viewpoint, which was widespread throughout Europe in this period.  
The *madrasa* built by order of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan burned down in AH 1328 / AD 1911, while the tomb, *sabil* and clock room were removed during the renovation of Aksaray Square and surroundings in 1956–9. Following various works to the roads in the area the mosque remained below the level of the street, while parts of the tomb were taken to the graveyard (*hazire*) adjoining the tomb of Sultan Selim III. Later, the tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan was rebuilt in the complex courtyard using original parts of her tomb that had been dismantled, taken to the *hazire,* brought back to the courtyard and remounted. Her body was removed first to the Topkapı Palace, then to the tomb of Sultan Mahmud II, and then returned to her own tomb, where it remains today.
d1fc6e82-6e79-5203-89e4-cd774dcda7fd.short_description: The complex was built by Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, wife of Sultan Mahmud II and mother of Sultan Abdülaziz, who was known for her charitable works. It comprises a mosque, a mausoleum, a *sabil* (water dispensary), a fountain, a clock-room and a school. The mosque reflects the characteristics of its period. The square prayer hall covered with a dome is extended with a wide arch to four sides. Mainly Oriental in style, the mosque is lavishly decorated. It was built with an eclectic taste bringing together elements from Gothic, Ottoman, Islamic and Indian arts.
d1fc6e82-6e79-5203-89e4-cd774dcda7fd.method_for_datation: According to the inscription above the gate to the courtyard, construction was completed in 1288 / 1871. Some documents indicate that the foundations were laid in ceremonies in Sha'ban 1285 / November 1869 and that construction took three years.

d23ab450-22c3-5cba-b10f-0719d1398789.name: Mirror box
d23ab450-22c3-5cba-b10f-0719d1398789.short_description:
The mirror box is signed with the characteristic formula "*kamtarin muḥammad baqir*" (the most humble Muhammad Baqir) and dated Hegira 1174 (AD 1760/61). Muhammad Baqir is one of the most famous Persian artists in the 18th century. He was the pupil of Muhammad ʿAli Ashraf (active Hegira 1134-1190 / AD 1722-1777) and worked in the 1750s on the borders of the so-called St. Petersburg album. Without doubt, this mirror box is one of his early independent lacquer works.  
  
Muhammad Baqir's oeuvre comprises border paintings for albums, single-leaf drawings and lacquer works. A striking feature of his art is his fascination in works by such renowned late Safavid artists as Muhammad Zaman (active Hegira ca, 1072-1105 / AD ca. 1662-1694) and ʿAliquli Jabadar (active Hegira 1059-1086 / AD 1649-1675) whose work he either copied or used as inspiration for his own creations. This is also the case with the three figurative panels of this mirror box. Thus, the half-naked bathing woman with a red towel sitting on a small rock can be compared to Muhammad Zaman's illustration of the bathing Shirin in a *Khamsa* from 1674/75.
d23ab450-22c3-5cba-b10f-0719d1398789.method_for_datation: The artist signed and dated his work.

d364400e-08ec-5cf3-9810-eaa259a97ddd.name: Pitcher
d364400e-08ec-5cf3-9810-eaa259a97ddd.description: This ceramic pitcher has a handle, a straight cylindrical neck and a ring base. It is dark blue and turquoise under a transparent glaze. There is an inscription border around the rim. The neck is decorated with vertical lines, and the shoulder has dark blue motifs on a turquoise ground. The body is covered with a geometric design of hexagons.

d364400e-08ec-5cf3-9810-eaa259a97ddd.dates: AH end of 5th–end 7th century/ AD 12th–13th centuries

d3c49832-be80-5864-92b1-0536f5ce79f7.name: *Tawa* (Roasting pan)
d3c49832-be80-5864-92b1-0536f5ce79f7.description:
*Tawa* (roasting pan) used to roast coffee beans.  
Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving dallah referred to as a mezallah, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the *mezallah* with their left hand and distribute the fanayeel (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
d3c49832-be80-5864-92b1-0536f5ce79f7.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
d3c49832-be80-5864-92b1-0536f5ce79f7.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: roasting pan; pan; coffee; coffee beans

d5d23f2f-61a6-5999-8a66-d5d4b3d9da12.name: *Saroud (palm mat)*
d5d23f2f-61a6-5999-8a66-d5d4b3d9da12.description:
*Saroud* (palm mat)  
The mat is formed by braiding nine to 11 palm leaves together to form a flat strip. The strips are sewn together to form a circular flat mat.
d5d23f2f-61a6-5999-8a66-d5d4b3d9da12.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab

d6aabbc5-689a-572b-bc5c-97c69c34d4f6.name: Mina'I bowl
d6aabbc5-689a-572b-bc5c-97c69c34d4f6.short_description: A typically round bowl sitting on a short circular foot. The interior is decorated with pairs of seated figures dressed in brightly coloured clothes separated by small pointed cypress trees with a man on horseback in the centre. Below the rim on the inside is a calligraphic band whilst on the exterior is a red and blue decoration.
d6aabbc5-689a-572b-bc5c-97c69c34d4f6.dates: Late 6th-early 7th century AH / Late 12th-early 13th century AD

d8e1d81f-2112-5652-987b-f417b3f15ad1.name: Scalloped ewer
d8e1d81f-2112-5652-987b-f417b3f15ad1.description:
This pitcher with gadrooned (scalloped) body is used to rinse the hands and face of a guest who has arrived at a host’s residence. The shape of the object is well known in Türkiye and India; it was also reproduced in ceramics.  
The mark of the owner is visible in two places: under the spout, in an almond cartouche, and again in a hexagon whose sides are extended by a three-lobed floret.

d9cffa1d-0e9d-59ee-a8f9-0f2a12a3c7dd.name: Dish serving for dried fruits or nuts
d9cffa1d-0e9d-59ee-a8f9-0f2a12a3c7dd.short_description: Sultan Abdülhamid II founded in 1891 the *Yıldız Çini Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu* (Yıldız Royal Tile Factory) in the garden of Yıldız Palace in order to revive Turkish tile art and give it a new direction and momentum. Vases, hanging wall plates and many sorts of daily-use wares were produced in the factory, including writing and dinner table utensils, card plates, lidded bowls, pans, *aşure* (a kind of dessert) trays, sugar bowls, tea and coffee cups. Many native and foreign artists have worked in the tile factory of Yıldız. One of them, Halid Naci received training in tile painting in Sevres, France after his education at the *Sanayi-i Nefise Mektebi* (School of Fine Arts) and he was assigned to be head painter of the tile factories after his return.
keywords: yıldız ceramic; Turkish decorative arts

da76c25e-e703-5257-a4cf-5bf924f5d270.name: Ewer and dish
da76c25e-e703-5257-a4cf-5bf924f5d270.short_description: Veneto Saracenic refers to a large group of 15th and 16th century metal ware, primarily in European collections. It is attributed to Muslims artists working in Venice. Such ware is domestic in nature and includes bowls, spherical incense burner and candlesticks. They are made of bronze or brass and are usually inlaid with geometric or arabesque motifs in silver, with occasional traces of gold and frequent additions of a black compound.

dba5d352-7562-5547-8859-795834833d9c.name: Wikala (*caravanserai*) of al-Ghuri.
dba5d352-7562-5547-8859-795834833d9c.description:
There are a number of *wikala*s or *caravanserai*s in Cairo that date back to the Mamluk and Ottoman periods. *Wikala*s were international centres of commerce between countries and regions, and this fact necessitated the presence of sleeping accommodation for merchants and their clients from all over the world who might stay in Cairo for a period of time. The Wikala of al-Ghuri is distinguished from others of its kind in Cairo by the fact that most of its architectural constituents are preserved. Today this *wikala* is considered to be an on-site museum for the art of *mashrabiyya*, as it boasts 29 of the finest examples of these turned-wood lattice window-screens, which form a basic component, beside stone, in the architectural design of the building. The *wikala*, in fact, offers a rare example of Mamluk *mashrabiyya* within the context of the building for which they were made.  
The principal façade of the building is on the north overlooking the street, and contains nine *mashrabiyya*s. The entrance, crowned by a tri-lobed arch, leads to a straight passageway which opens directly onto the rectangular open courtyard of the *wikala*, in the midst of which is a marble fountain. This arrangement was aimed at attracting customers, as much as it was to facilitate the easy transportation of goods to and from the storage areas of the *caravanserai*.  
There are four stories that overlook the courtyard of the *caravanserai*. Each of the two lower floors hold more than 20 rooms covered with stone vaulted ceilings; these were used as storage areas for the traders who resided at the *caravanserai*. These rooms overlook the courtyard by way of colonnades, characterised by pointed arches supported by stone piers. The upper two stories were designed as residential units, each consisting of two floors. In between the two floors there is a hidden level containing the kitchens and storage areas. The facades of these units overlook the courtyard by means of a splendid group of *mashrabiyya* that project from the walls and which are supported by wooden brackets. In the lower part of the *mashrabiyya* are two rows of windows, furnished with wooden screens that have movable covers (or flaps) opening upwards, thus allowing those who are within the rooms to see the courtyard without anyone seeing them in the upper stories. By this means, the design of the *caravanserai* accomplished friendly contact and closer intimacy between its residents from different countries and regions, while also ensuring their privacy, as each apartment was separated both vertically and horizontally from the next.  
The Ministry of Culture has recently transformed the building into a centre for the conservation of traditional handicrafts, especially the art of wood-turning and stucco coloured glass. The centre also houses the ateliers of modern artists, whose presence together with the other craftsmen, assists in the efforts of continuity and preservation at the site, and of the artistic and cultural welding between the traditional and modern.
dba5d352-7562-5547-8859-795834833d9c.short_description: This *wikala* is an intact example of the caravanserais that spread through Cairo in the Mamluk period, when trade with the outside world reached its peak. It comprises residential quarters for travellers and merchants, storerooms and an open courtyard, where transactions took place. Its most outstanding feature is a wonderful group of windows covered with turned wood *mashrabiyya* (screens) overlooking the courtyard and the façade.
dba5d352-7562-5547-8859-795834833d9c.method_for_datation: Dating of the building is supported by historical sources such as *Kitab al-Nujum al-Zahira*, by Ibn Taghri Bardi. A study of its architectural constituents and decoration such as the *mashrabiyya* also helped in dating it.

dbe5d877-10e6-5723-8ea6-cd192909e5b0.name: Tile panel in the form of a fireplace surround
dbe5d877-10e6-5723-8ea6-cd192909e5b0.short_description: Islamic art may often operate on two visual levels: surface impressions and detailed study. A quick peruser may find pleasure from a work of art's bold colors and designs, but those who take the time to look more closely will be amply rewarded. In this tile, shaped to surround a small fireplace, dancing and acrobatic female entertainers, kings in repose who drink wine from small glasses, quietly seated aged advisors, thoughtful soldiers, and busy musicians fill the composition.

dc123c01-a94a-53ca-b79e-5fb7aeb83571.name: Vat
dc123c01-a94a-53ca-b79e-5fb7aeb83571.description:
Globular vat with a conical base, a flaring neck, a flanged rim and winged handles. The paste is whitish and unglazed. Its decoration consists of a stamped, alternating series of lozenges and eulogetic epigraphy arranged in perimeter friezes.  
  
A common feature of Andalusian homes, these large earthenware vats were strategically placed in the courtyards or in interior rooms to preserve goods such as oil, cereals, or water, as well as to store domestic objects. In this case, the porous nature of the unglazed clay suggests that this example functioned specifically as a water vat, as it would have filtered and cooled the water, keeping it clean and fresh.  
  
Beyond their practical function, some vats had also an aesthetic value, as can be seen in the stamped decoration or glazing. Decorations included epigraphic motifs invoked to protect the vats' contents. The production and use of these vats continued after the Castilian conquest.

dc123c01-a94a-53ca-b79e-5fb7aeb83571.method_for_datation: Archaeological and art-historical studies have established certain formal features that allow us to date the piece to the 7th–8th century Hegira / 13th–14th century AD. The globular body and stamped decoration are particularly present in the Almohad world, evolving towards more stylised forms, with more pronounced winged handles.

ddfbe2bf-75cf-508a-af85-5d9ab86020a7.name: Enamelled flask
ddfbe2bf-75cf-508a-af85-5d9ab86020a7.short_description:
The finely decorated flask has a tall neck decorated with a fleur-de-lis band with enamel highlights, a plaited guilloche band and a row of male standing figures wearing church vestments. Two of the figures hold open books, perhaps missals. The body bears a band of seated figures, drinkers and musicians. Between the figures are beakers, a wine flask or footed dishes. On the shoulders of the flask rosettes alternate with large birds, evidently pelicans – in medieval Western Europe a symbol of Christ and the institution of the Eucharist.  
The robbed figures and the pelicans may suggest that the flask was ordered for a European, perhaps a pilgrim, as a memento of a visit to the Holy Land or as a gift to a Christian church or monastery.  
The flask is a superb specimen of the skills of Ayyubid glassworkers. The application of enamel to the glass indicates that this flask was made at an early stage in the development of enamelling, which would be consistent with an Ayyubid date.

ded7dbe8-bac2-5eb8-a10a-58b0b930b749.name: Bektashi Dining Table
ded7dbe8-bac2-5eb8-a10a-58b0b930b749.description:
The inscription indicates that the Aş Evi section, the most significant of the twelve houses in Bektashism, was constructed in 1560 by relatives of Malkoç Bali Bey, the Governor of Silistre, in his honor.  
The Aş Evi section, which is an independent building where the meals of the lodge are prepared, contains a room that is used by the Aş Evi Babası as a daily sitting room. In this room, he watches the kitchen work and decides on the meals to be prepared that day. It contains karakazan and halife boilers and kitchen utensils.  
The meals prepared in the Aş Evi were made available to the employees of the Dervish lodge and guests, as well as to the poor and the needy.

df34e2f3-4b74-586f-9068-15107f458dd8.name: Lidded bowl (*sahan*)
df34e2f3-4b74-586f-9068-15107f458dd8.description: Small rounded lidded bowl – *sahan* (Ar. *sân*) – with lobed rim, for keeping and serving food. The lid is bell-shaped, with a small brass lifting handle on the top. The bowl is decorated with an abstract geometric pattern, while lid's decorations are in the forms of flower petals with leafy branches within.
df34e2f3-4b74-586f-9068-15107f458dd8.dates: Hegira late 13th century / AD late 19th century
df34e2f3-4b74-586f-9068-15107f458dd8.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.

df4709cd-ab73-5f8f-9d79-ecac52cd3487.name: Damascus Room
df4709cd-ab73-5f8f-9d79-ecac52cd3487.short_description: The Damascus Room is a residential winter reception chamber (*qa‘a*) typical of the late Ottoman period. Among the earliest extant, nearly complete interiors of its kind, the room’s large scale and refined decoration suggest that it was part of the house of an affluent family. Poetry inscribed on the walls indicates that the patron was Muslim and possibly a member of the religious elite who claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad. Because wealthy homeowners periodically refurbished reception rooms in accordance with shifting trends, Damascene houses and their interiors rarely date to a single building phase. Although an inscription dates most of the woodwork to 1707, alterations were made to the room in subsequent years.

df86393e-c508-5ae4-9acc-14d37c1a879f.name: Coin (*dinar*).
df86393e-c508-5ae4-9acc-14d37c1a879f.description:
A gold coin worth a *dinar*. Inscriptions in *kufic* script appear on the obverse and on the reverse. The centre, obverse, holds a five-line inscription that reads: 'To God / Muhammad / Prophet / of God / Sanctioned by God'. The margin, obverse, bears a circular inscription that reads: 'Muhammad, the Prophet of God. It is he who has sent his messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to prevail it over all religion even though it is hated by the pagans'. On the reverse, the coin bears at its centre four lines of inscription that reads: 'There is no God except / the One God / Who has no Partners / Authorised by God'. On the outer margin, reverse, there is a circular Qur'anic inscription (Chapter 30, 'Romans', verses 4 and 5): 'With Allah is the Decision in the Past and in the Future. On that day will the Believers rejoice with the help of God'. Along the interior margin, reverse, a circular inscription states: 'In the name of God this coin was struck in Egypt the year 268 AH' (AD 881).  
When Ahmad ibn Tulun ruled as Governor of Egypt (r. AH 254–70 / AD 868–84), he aimed toward the unity of the Islamic provinces, and in AH 266 / AD 880 was able to establish a large Islamic State. Due to the fact that numismatics was the most important insignia of authority and dominion, he undertook the enterprise of minting coinage in his name in order to affirm his power over the State. The Abbasid coinage, which was struck in the name of the Abbasid caliphs, was in circulation in Egypt at the time of the establishment of the Tulunid state. This type of coinage continued in use in the period of Ibn Tulun where Arabic inscriptions and the name of the contemporary Abbasid caliph appeared on the reverse of the coin. In view of the fact that Ibn Tulun did not contest the legitimacy of the Abbasid caliphate, the name of Ahmad ibn Tulun was included under the name of the Abbasid caliph.  
Ibn Tulun was instrumental in purifying gold and raising the standard measure of the Ahmadi *dinar* to the point where it was accepted as the basis of transactions to the exclusion of all other currencies. Likewise, the Ahmadi *dinar* continued to be the model that other currencies followed. No alterations occurred subsequently in later caliphates to its standard measure or its inscriptions except for the substitution of the names of the contemporary Abbasid caliph and Tulunid ruler.
df86393e-c508-5ae4-9acc-14d37c1a879f.short_description: Coin minting as a sign of power and sovereignty was practised under the Muslim caliphs and sultans, who put their names on the coins. This piece bears the name of the Abbasid caliph and under it we find the name of Ahmad ibn Tulun, the ruler of Egypt.

df86393e-c508-5ae4-9acc-14d37c1a879f.method_for_provenance: Egypt has been narrowed down as the city where the coin was minted in view of the fact that Egypt is named as the place where the coin was struck.

e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.name: Bowl.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.description:
A large conical bowl with an upturned rim that is made of tin-glazed earthenware and decorated with lustre. The exterior of the bowl is ornamented with abstract tree-like motifs, while the interior features a spectacular image of a large sailing ship that is complete with multiple masts and riggings, fore and aft decks, flags, and a rudder. Below the ship, four large fish swim back and forth; around it, tightly wound curlicues and other abstract motifs fill the surface of the bowl. The ship’s sail bears a motif which has been interpreted as the arms of Portugal, possibly indicating that the bowl was commissioned by a wealthy Portuguese merchant. This, plus the fact that the most important centre of Spanish lustre production in the 9th / 15th century was Christian Valencia, initially led scholars to believe that this bowl was Valencian ware. However, scientific tests in 1983 showed the presence of mineral deposits in the bowl which come not from Valencia, but from Málaga. This city, one of the most important port cities of the medieval western Mediterranean, had been the premiere centre of lustre production in Spain until it was eclipsed by Valencia in the early 9th / 15th century; production there appears to have ceased a few decades later. This bowl, then, is spectacular proof that the potteries of Málaga continued to create first-class lustre ceramics right up until the end.  
  
The fish beneath the ship, as well as the tree-like motifs on the exterior of the bowl, are strikingly similar to Fatimid work of centuries before, and remind us that the lustre industry in Islamic Spain was born precisely when Fatimid workers brought the technique from Egypt.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.short_description: A large bowl with lustre-painted decoration that includes a representation of a ship at sea. The ship’s sail bears a coat of arms which has been interpreted as that of Portugal; thus this bowl may have been commissioned by a wealthy Portuguese merchant.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.dates: Second quarter of the hegira 9th / AD 15th century.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.method_for_datation: Stylistic grounds; the large tree-like motifs on the exterior of the bowl, in particular, are characteristically Nasrid.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.method_for_provenance: In 1983 scholars established that the bowl was produced in Málaga, once the centre of lustre production in Spain until it was eclipsed by Valencia in the early 9th / 15th century (see description above).

e0b9788f-2138-5261-bd75-1329e810829d.name: *Sabil* (Water Dispensary) and *Kuttab* (Qur’anic School) of Sultan Qaytbay.
e0b9788f-2138-5261-bd75-1329e810829d.description:
The *sabil* (a water dispensary) is constructed out of stone and is distinguished by the opulence of its southern and western facade. The elevated and narrow entrance located on the southern face, is crowned with a tri-lobed arch and decorated with stone and polychrome-marble designs. It is similar to the entrance of Ashrafiyya Madrasa in Jerusalem. To the left of the entrance, just above the grill, there is a large, square decorative panel in polychrome marble and stone. The panel is divided into nine sections and arranged in three rows, consisting of carved vegetal and geometric designs. These decorations are not common in Mamluk buildings and are reminiscent of those seen in illuminated manuscripts. This design brings to mind one on the cover of the manuscript by al-Busairi entitled, *al-Kawakib al-Duriya fi Madh khayr al-Bariya \[The Shining Stars in Praise of the Most Blessed of Creation\]*, popularly known by the name of 'al-Burda'. This manuscript, which is preserved in Dublin, Ireland, suggests that decorative designs were transferred with no restriction from one art form or medium to the other. It also indicates that the decorative designs were drawn on paper first of all as a template, and then adapted to various mediums, whether metal, stone, marble or wood.  
The *sabil* is made up of three stories. The first level is deep below ground and constitutes the water cistern built out of solid rock. A marble lid covered the mouth of the cistern which was then filled annually after being cleaned and purified. The second level is located at ground level, and consists of a room overlooking the street by way of an iron grill through which water was handed out to passers by, while allowing sufficient ventilation to air-cool the water. The water-dispensing room contains a marble panel, over which the water flows to be gathered in a trough below the window, thus the water is further air-cooled. The third level of the fountain-house consists of the *kuttab*, added in the Ottoman period, which taught orphaned children to memorise the Qur'an.  
This building is considered one of the most prominent of Sultan Qaytbay's monuments in Cairo. In addition to its façade, which contains beautifully lavish decoration, this is the first example of a free-standing *sabil-kuttab* in Egypt. Sultan Qaytbay built another *sabil* in Jerusalem which is topped by a dome. In Cairo, *sabil*s became increasingly popular and were prolific during the Ottoman period. Today, there are approximately 100 *sabil*s in the City of Cairo.
e0b9788f-2138-5261-bd75-1329e810829d.short_description: *Sabils* are spread all over Cairo to provide free drinking water for inhabitants, passers-by and travellers. Such buildings were charitable institutions that sultans, amirs and the wealthy vied to build. They were commonly situated in the corner of a mosque or an architectural complex. This *sabil* built by Qaytbay is considered to be the first freestanding construction of this type. Above the *sabil* is a *kuttab* to teach orphans the rudiments of Islam, the Arabic language and memorising the Qur'an.
e0b9788f-2138-5261-bd75-1329e810829d.method_for_datation: The building was dated based on an inscription flanking the entrance, which bears the name of the patron, Sultan al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaytbay, and his titles as well as the date of construction.

e0dd9b89-fd8e-5b2e-a57e-fda48b2a6792.name: *Peškun*
e0dd9b89-fd8e-5b2e-a57e-fda48b2a6792.description: Оctagonal *peškun* (Tr. *peşkun*) decorated with floral and geometric motifs, each side having a blossom branch ornament that rests on a pointed draped arch at the bottom spreading to the top of a side. A heart-shaped branch has a flower at the top, while its bottom makes a central part of an opening in the shape of braces. The leaves surround the branch and are placed in a horizontal rectangular field at the top of the side as well. Eight sides carry an octagonal plate at the top with a central flower and floral motifs that surround it. The inner octagonal of the plate’s edge is decorated with leaves. All ornaments are made of mother-of-pearl and brass wire using the incrustation technique, while the edge of the octagonal top plate is ornamented with bone. Peškun is the name of a traditional piece of Ottoman furniture in the shape of a table or stool, originally meant for sitting, although it had different purposes throughout history, especially as a decorative table in Balkan oriental interiors of the 19th and of the first half of the 20th century. Over time, the larger table in the set (of usually three pieces) began to be used as a coffee table, while the smaller ones were used as stools. The *Peškun* was ordinarily made of walnut wood, ornamented with incrusted floral and geometric motifs made of mother of pearl and bone.
e0dd9b89-fd8e-5b2e-a57e-fda48b2a6792.dates: Hegira late 13th–early 14th century / AD late 19th century–early 20th century
e0dd9b89-fd8e-5b2e-a57e-fda48b2a6792.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material, technique, and analogy with other similar examples.
e0dd9b89-fd8e-5b2e-a57e-fda48b2a6792.author: Ana Samardžić
keywords: peškun; stool; side table; incrustation; Ottoman Balkans

e249d142-ee34-5f84-8b9c-0144ff7e19d8.name: *Shahnameh by Firdowsi* (Social Gathering for Entertainment)
e249d142-ee34-5f84-8b9c-0144ff7e19d8.description:
The Persian text was composed in verse and prose, divided into four columns, and written in black ink and *taliq* calligraphy on pale paper. The work comprises a total of 202 miniature scenes, which collectively represent the pinnacle of miniature art. The vast majority of these miniatures depict scenes from the *Shahnameh*, making this a work of great importance.  
The circular medallion on the *Zahriye* (titular inscription) page of the work is decorated with a profusion of richly coloured floral, leaf and branch motifs, and Chinese clouds. The medallion is inscribed at its centre in black ink script on a gilt background. The inscription states that it was prepared for Sultan Ali Mirza, (ruled 1478–1505) of the Karkiya Dynasty, one of the most important dynasties of the Timurid Period.  
The binding is leather affixed to cardboard, typical of this period. The exterior covers are crafted from black leather embellished with a variety of animal figures, including birds, sheep, foxes, gazelles, deer, and floral motifs. The inner covers are burgundy leather featuring intricate floral and animal motifs on a green, blue, and gilt background.

e249d142-ee34-5f84-8b9c-0144ff7e19d8.obtention: The item was brought to the Museum from the Hâlet Efendi Library on 28 May 1917.

e27cfedb-4426-5918-bebf-2002418ec65c.name: Storage vessels and two-part cooking pot
e27cfedb-4426-5918-bebf-2002418ec65c.short_description:
The contrast between the public and private, male and female spheres offer the Berber women "free space" which allows them to express their own view of life. In the seclusion of the home they make the space of everyday life viable, and visibly materialise a particular life design, in that they symbolically reproduce their bodies: in the hand-built up pottery, repeating the image of "body as vessel." In a world controlled by men, the women have developed a cultural model which is based on their corporeal experience.  
In art, the French philosopher Gilles Deleuze maintained, it is never to do with the reproduction of forms, but with the capturing of powers. Therefore, no art is ever just figurative: "Art is the language of emotions (…). Art has no opinion." The women produced their pottery exclusively for personal use. Limits were only placed on their completely free artistic development by the social norms which applied in their environment and which govern the relationships between people.

e388c5d6-a7bc-53e2-8fe9-b004758a5838.name: Bowl with *tuğra* of Bayezid II
e388c5d6-a7bc-53e2-8fe9-b004758a5838.short_description: This hemispherical bowl has a facetted honeycomb cavetto and a rivet in the centre showing where a disc was once attached. The underside is engraved with elongated split leaves found on late 15th century illuminations and Iznik ware. One of the cells is stamped with the *tuğra* of Bayezid II, the earliest known monogram of a sultan which serves as a control stamp guaranteeing the purity of the silver.

e39d2fbb-2774-52a9-868e-e26f46c215f7.name: *Preparing Medicine from Honey*, folio from a dispersed manuscript of an Arabic translation of the *Materia Medica* of Dioscorides
e39d2fbb-2774-52a9-868e-e26f46c215f7.short_description: This scene from a translation of *De Materia Medica* by Dioscorides is typical of the Baghdad School of illustration, which employed bold colors and symmetrical compositions to depict urban life. The use of an architectural structure to divide the painting into six sections is typical of the period, as is the fact that the oatmeal-coloured paper remains visible. This folio, which comes from volume 5, chapter 9 of the work, depicts a pharmacist preparing a honey‑based medicine in a cauldron while an assistant upstairs distributes it into jars.

e3f36ab1-bb2a-5793-ac55-177827b3e390.name: Plate
e3f36ab1-bb2a-5793-ac55-177827b3e390.description:
This enamelled bronze plate in the FBQ Museum shows the Cuerda Seca (dry cord) technique, a method of enamelling that emerged during the Seljuk period in Persia.  
Renowned for its beauty and utility, enamelling serves both aesthetic and practical purposes, offering protection against corrosion while providing stunning decorative elements.  
While both Cuerda Seca and the Persian Minakari technique are used in enamelling, they differ in their execution. In Minakari, the coloured enamel powders are applied directly onto the metal surface, resulting in smooth and continuous colour blending. In contrast, Cuerda Seca uses a greasy material to create boundaries between different enamel colours to prevent them from blending during firing, producing sharp motifs with clearly defined edges in various hues. Both techniques yield vibrant and decorative surfaces, showcasing the artistry and craftsmanship of enamelling traditions in the Islamic world.

e58c69db-bd74-5185-a678-96228b8d0ba3.name: Water seller's jar
e58c69db-bd74-5185-a678-96228b8d0ba3.short_description: The egg-shaped jar has a narrow neck the top of which is covered by a dome-shaped lid. There is a curved handle on each side of the neck base and a long, straight spout. The lower part of the jar is made of unglazed and undecorated earthenware, a common material for water vessels that enables water evaporation thus keeping the water inside cool. The upper part is made of copper alloy, engraved with decorative bands of intertwined floral motifs; knot work patterns; stylised four-legged animals amongst a vegetal design; and two calligraphic bands. The jar sits in a knotted rope net with handle for carriage on the water seller’s back.
e58c69db-bd74-5185-a678-96228b8d0ba3.author: Hazelle Page
keywords: Water jar; Water seller; Everyday life; Egypt

e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.name: Ewer.
e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.description: A ewer carved from a single piece of rock-crystal. It has a pear-shaped body, beaked rim, and slightly splayed foot; a handle, which originally had a vertical thumb-piece at its apex, joins the rim to the lower part of the body. The body of the ewer is decorated on either side with identical scenes of a bird of prey attacking a four-legged animal with horns (a gazelle?). These vignettes are framed by large, leafy arabesque motifs. The whole design is contained within a delicate raised band which goes around the neck and down the body of the ewer on either side of the handle. This band acts as a frame and gives the design the feel of a textile wrapped around the ewer’s body. All of the details are drilled and cut with great skill, including the texturing in the form of lines and dots covering the bird and animal and the leaves of the arabesque patterns. Objects like this ewer were among the thousands of precious items looted from the Fatimid treasury during the unrest of 450 AH / AD 1060. A number of these made their way to Europe, where they were used as reliquaries in church treasuries.
e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.short_description: A pear-shaped ewer carved from a single block of the clear, colourless quartz known as rock-crystal. It is one of a number of luxury wares carved from rock-crystal for the Fatimid court in Cairo. Many such objects made their way into European church treasuries, where they were used as reliquaries.
e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.method_for_datation: There is a clear relationship between this ewer and a group of others in European collections, one of which has an inscription naming the Fatimid Caliph al-‘Aziz (r. AH 365–86 / AD 975–96). The decoration on the V&A ewer, including the arabesque pattern, is more complex and mature than is that on the others, suggesting a later date. Finally, Fatimid rock-crystal production was severely disrupted when violent social upheavals began in AH 452 / AD 1061.
e69c15fd-110a-59c2-9a6e-7ae708a7ea8e.method_for_provenance: Cairo was the Fatimid capital and thus the likeliest place that an object of such quality would have been made.

e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.name: Dish.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.description: Ceramics with metallic highlights were exceptionally successful in the late Middle Ages, and were sought after by the finest European courts. The coats of arms of royalty and nobility, in particular Italians such as the Tedaldi or Nasi families, are commonly depicted. These ceramics, so colourful and elegant, are reminiscent of Gothic painting. The manufacturing and decorating processes were complex, as the pieces required several firings to obtain the different colours. This dish was turned on a potter's wheel. Its surface is covered with a white or cream tin glaze. The sides are concave and the brim slightly inclined. The topside is decorated in gold and deep blue. The central, golden coat of arms, inscribed in a toothed blue border, shows an eagle with outstretched wings. It is possible that it belonged to the Despujols family, and it is repeated in other pieces. The coat of arms is surrounded by a thin strip of fringes and spirals and tiny fern leaves. Near the edge, there is a wide band with large gilt pinecones in reserve, alternating with large deep-blue flowers. The remaining spaces are filled with arabesque leaves. On the underside there is another eagle in the same position as the first, covering the entire area, and fern leaves in the empty spaces. The heraldic coats of arms, as well as telling us about the tastes of high society, are useful for determining when the pieces were manufactured, as they include data on family history.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.short_description: Dish decorated in a manner typical of AH 9th-/ AD 15th-century Mudéjar ceramics, with Nasrid-style motifs such as the gold and blue motifs on the front combined with the coat-of-arms of the family that commissioned the piece. In this case, an eagle appears on both sides of the dish.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.dimensions: Height 9 cm, diameter 45 cm, diameter of base 14.5 cm.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.method_for_datation: From its style and from comparison with other similar dishes. In this case, the coat of arms that decorates it serves as a historical reference.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.method_for_provenance: From its formal and stylistic characteristics, from the archaeological digs that have been carried out and from the extensive documentation that is available.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum from Vicente Juan y Amat on 27 June 1872.

e74099f6-1c27-5325-b008-aca137d56990.name: *Saka Postu* (small alcove where a new apprentice observed elders)
e74099f6-1c27-5325-b008-aca137d56990.description: Upon entering the printing house through the large wooden door, one passes through the vaulted corridor and reaches the barrel-vaulted chamber. In the left-hand corner there is a raised platform covered by a hide over a carpet. Here *Nevniyaz* (a newly accepted apprentice) would sit and observe for a period of three days, at the conclusion of which he would decide whether to stay or leave.

e9446de8-0118-5c68-aa90-cc7965c9040a.name: Nilometer.
e9446de8-0118-5c68-aa90-cc7965c9040a.description:
The Nilometer (Kiosk of the Nile; known in Arabic as *al-Miqyas*) is considered among the enduring architectural foundations tied to the Egyptian culture and way of life. It is in fact unique in the Islamic world. Its importance goes back to a time when measuring the rise of the waters of the Nile was closely related to the levying of taxes on agricultural lands. Taxes were levied only when the waters of the Nile had risen to a certain designated level, which would irrigate the land during flood season.  
The Nilometer itself is the equivalent of a well whose walls are built from skilfully hewn stone blocks. The thickness of the walls increases the greater the depth. The well consists of three levels: the lowest level is a circular base, while the middle level is a square whose sides measure more than the diameter of the level below. The highest level is also square in shape, and bigger than the middle level. It is due to this design that the walls can bear the horizontal pressure of the earth that increases the greater the depth.  
The waters of the Nile would flow into the well by means of three tunnels, which discharged their waters into the well by means of three 'mouths' on the eastern side that are in the form of subterranean entrances in the wall. These openings are oriented towards pointed arches supported by compact decorated columns with globular bases. These arches are considered to be not only the oldest known examples in Islamic Egypt, but precede the European Gothic type by three centuries. We may also view similar examples on the arches of the Ibn Tulun Mosque in Cairo (AH 265 / AD 879).  
A staircase curves around the inside walls of the well and extends all the way to the bottom. Adorning the upper reaches of the well on two sides, the northern and the eastern internal walls, are inscriptions in *kufic* script, which represent the oldest (dated) Arabic inscription in Egypt ever recorded. In the centre of the well stands the principal component of the monument, an octagonal marble pillar whose length extends to 16 cubits (10.50 m). It is engraved with measurements in cubits *(kirat*) and inches *(zira')*, which demarcate the water inundation levels.  
Ahmad ibn Tulun (r. AH 254–70 / AD 868–84) carried out restoration of al-Miqyas in AH 259 / AD 873 and replaced the two bands of ancient inscriptions with more contemporary ones on the south and west sides. He placed his name within the new inscription, but kept the original date of construction untouched. Throughout the ages the building has been subject to many restorations and renovations (Fatimid, Mamluk and Ottoman). It was renovated in the modern age in 1925 when the Mamluk dome crowning the outside of the building was replaced by a conical-shaped roof covered by lead panels.
e9446de8-0118-5c68-aa90-cc7965c9040a.short_description: Set on Roda island in the Nile, the Nilometer is a unique structure in Islamic architecture. It gained its importance from being the means for calculating tax levies on agricultural lands according to the size of the Nile flood every year. Its design and the building materials used in its construction helped it to resist corrosion by water for over one thousand years.
e9446de8-0118-5c68-aa90-cc7965c9040a.method_for_datation: Historians concur that al-Miqyas was built in the year 247 / 861 by order of the Abbassid Caliph al-Mutawakkil, although some scholars trace its foundation back to the Caliph al–Ma'mun (r. 169–217 / 786–833). However, the historian Ibn Khalkan (d. 681 / 1282) mentions that the name of the al-Mutawakkil and the year the Nilometer was constructed (247 / 861) was engraved within an inscription on the walls of the well, and that this inscription dated to the foundation of the monument. This inscription has now been lost and may have been removed when Ibn Tulun carried out his restoration of the building in the year 259 / 873.

ea3d8d8e-c04b-5794-9b49-13d8075523c6.name: Spouted bowl (*sahlah bu mirzab*)
ea3d8d8e-c04b-5794-9b49-13d8075523c6.description: Bowls are among the most important copper artifacts in Omani hospitality. They are usually either wholly circular or circular with a channel and include various decorative designs. They may serve to either hold the cups in which Omani coffee is served, or as basins for guests to wash their hands.

eb9313ce-3a64-5d73-bea2-13a7a7012be8.name: Magic cup
eb9313ce-3a64-5d73-bea2-13a7a7012be8.description:
The bowl is lined with inscriptions inside and out – verses from the Koran, the most beautiful names of God, religious and talismanic expressions – alternating with magic squares. On the outer perimeter, images of the zodiac and planets engraved inside medallions were scrupulously obscured at a later date with floral motifs, no doubt in order to avoid the association of the Koranic text with representations of living creatures.  
Consuming drinks or food in such cups, thus closely connecting religion, medicine, and astrology, permitted one to resist the effects of poisons, fevers, and other physical ailments. *The Thousand and One Nights* invoked a divinatory purpose too.

ecf2b49c-b70f-51b8-8c61-216edf4189e1.name: Plate
ecf2b49c-b70f-51b8-8c61-216edf4189e1.short_description:
This elegant plate was crafted in Guangzhou (formerly Canton) in AH 1309 / AD 1891-1892, exemplifying the refined artistry of Chinese export porcelain during the late Qing Dynasty. The intricate design showcases scenes of daily life, featuring pagoda-style architecture and traditional Chinese elements, capturing the cultural essence of the period.  
  
A particularly intriguing feature of this piece is its inscription. Written in Arabic-Persian script, it bears the phrase هو الباقي (He \[Allah\] is the Everlasting), emphasising divine permanence. Additionally, the inscription includes the word فرمايش (ordered), indicating that the plate was specially commissioned for Mohamed Sadiq Khan, who is most likely Sarwar al-Malak, a renowned musician from the courts of Shah Naser al-Din and Shah Muzaffar al-Din. This suggests that the plate may have been part of the Persian royal court’s cultural or artistic exchanges.  
  
At the lower part of the plate, we can also notice the marking "ص 92". While its exact meaning remains uncertain, it may indicate the production year (1892) or serve as a workshop code or inventory mark.  
  
This plate stands as a remarkable testament to the artistic and cultural exchanges between China and the Persian-speaking world, seamlessly blending Chinese craftsmanship with Persian artistic and literary influences.

ed2b34d8-0b3b-5e62-9f3b-c352b83a9b49.name: Tile Cup
ed2b34d8-0b3b-5e62-9f3b-c352b83a9b49.description: The drinking vessel is composed of a white clay and slip with polychrome decoration beneath a transparent colourless glaze. The composition features a series of tulips and stylised carnation branches of varying sizes rising vertically from separate roots on a white ground. The red, green and blue motifs are outlined in black. Beginning in the second half of the 16th century, it appears that the emerald green glaze, which was used extensively, would run during the firing process. It is posited that the quality of ceramics began to decline in tandem with the deterioration of the economy. Examples from the 16th century demonstrate that the naturalistic floral motifs, which were widely employed in Classical Ottoman style, were still being used during this period.
ed2b34d8-0b3b-5e62-9f3b-c352b83a9b49.dates: Hegira late 10th century / AD late 16th century

edd94d46-2a69-592f-80d7-0c535b109eff.name: Coffee
edd94d46-2a69-592f-80d7-0c535b109eff.description: Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving *dallah* referred to as a *mezallah*, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the *mezallah* with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
edd94d46-2a69-592f-80d7-0c535b109eff.dimensions: Varies and depends on the coffee bean. Length: 10mm, width: 7mm
edd94d46-2a69-592f-80d7-0c535b109eff.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: coffee; beans; coffee beans

ee84f4a0-84fc-5ae3-9c0f-88b366037681.name: Qasr al-Azm.
ee84f4a0-84fc-5ae3-9c0f-88b366037681.description:
Qasr al-Azm, the largest and oldest completely preserved private residence in Damascus, covers a space of about 5,500 sq m. It is a typical example of Damascene domestic architecture, with its simple outer appearance and its splendid interior furnishings. The division of the apartments according to official space and private space is also typical of Muslim domestic architecture in general, a feature not seen in their Christian or Jewish counterparts.  
From the entrance with a guard's room to its left, a long, winding cross-vaulted corridor leads into the *madafa* (“chamber of the coffee-server”), before entering the official apartments (*salamlik*). The *Salamlik* is arranged around a small courtyard with an *iwan* on the south wall, flanked by two reception rooms. There are also guest rooms and a small kitchen for catering. From this area there is access to the most splendid area of the building, the *haramlik,* where the family functioned and the women and children stayed. The rooms in this area are arranged around a spacious courtyard measuring 56 m x 24 m, with two fountains and a garden at the centre. The chambers on the north side of the courtyard served as living rooms in the winter. They are provided with a portico (*riwaq*) supported by antique-basalt columns brought in from Dar'a and Bosra. Opposite the *riwaq* there is the magnificent tripartite reception hall (*qa'a*) with splendid stone-paste decoration, and small gardens to the north and east sides. At the southeast side the *iwan* faces the large rectangular fountain. The bathhouse or *hamam*, an unusual feature in private houses, is adjoined. There is also a kitchen section, similarly arranged around a courtyard, and remises for the vehicles and horses.  
The use of high-quality materials for the palace interior can be seen by the basalt from Hauran, limestone from Mezze, Zabadani and Aleppo, and marble that was probably imported from Italy. Elaborately painted wooden panels decorated the walls and ceilings of the reception rooms. In 1830 the building was renovated and furnished with *trompe l'oeil* paintings according to the fashion of the time.  
The construction of As'ad Pasha al-Azm's residence required two years and over 800 workmen for completion. The 18th-century chronicler, al-Budairi, reports the consequent scarcity of workmen and construction materials at the time, and that the city's water supply was interrupted in order to be divert it to the palace.  
Excavations in the 1920s revealed the probability that the palace was built on a site of former importance, such as the residence of the Mamluk Governor Tankiz (AH 712–29 / AD 1312–27). The spiritual and socio-political prestige of the location comes from its proximity to the Umayyad Mosque. With new Ottoman *caravanserai*s constructed to the south, the political and commercial power of the Azm family is further attested as As'ad Pasha built the largest and most splendid *caravanserai* in the city in AH 1171 / AD 1757, still known as Khan As'ad Pasha.
ee84f4a0-84fc-5ae3-9c0f-88b366037681.short_description: This is the largest completely preserved private house in Damascus. It occupies more than 5,500 sq m. In typical Damascene domestic architectural style, the outer appearance is simple but the interior is splendid. It includes an official or formal 'male' space and a private or familial 'female' space, each provided with a courtyard of flower gardens, fountains and reception rooms decorated with *ablaq* masonry, stone paste patterns and painted wooden panels. This palace, prestigiously located in the religious and commercial heart of the city, was the residence of the Damascene Governor Asad Pasha al-Azm.
ee84f4a0-84fc-5ae3-9c0f-88b366037681.method_for_datation: The 18th-century Damascene chronicler, Ahmad Budairi al-Hallaq reports for the year 1163 (1750) that construction work on the palace commences.

ef6f3f6c-f567-5300-9a2c-887d4b9a516c.name: Anonymous, *Ruznamce-i shemsiyye ve qamariyye* ('Small calendar of solar and lunar years')
ef6f3f6c-f567-5300-9a2c-887d4b9a516c.short_description: The anonymous Arabic treatise titled *Ruznamce-i shemsiyye ve qamariyye* (‘Small Calendar of Solar and Lunar Years’) was compiled for the years 905 AH / 1499 to 1000 AH / 1592. It was possibly written in the 16th-17th centuries in Ottoman Syria. The Latin marginalia *Deo Trino et Uno honor Lausq infinita* on fol. 8a were probably written by a later Christian owner, while the owner’s stamp on fol. 8b is by Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall, from whom the manuscript was purchased by the Austrian National Library in 1842. The extant European half-leather binding corresponds to a possibly Viennese production date in the 19th-century. The calendar itself is composed in a format similar to Ottoman prayer calendar scrolls and their tabular arrangement. Particularly fascinating, however, is the fact that small paintings are pasted in the margins of the manuscript, which is atypical for this manuscript format. These paintings include both zodiac images as well as monthly allegories. The zodiac miniatures are stylistically relatable to Timurid Shiraz of the early 15th century when patrons had great interest in astrology and the natural sciences. It can be hypothesised that these paintings were cut out from an older calendar or astrological treatise and reused in a new context. They are visually integrated into the page layout, as the border is drawn around the images. The monthly allegories, in contrast, are pasted over these borders and hence must have been added later. They display themes from a Christian context mixed with Islamic artistic conventions, the scenes reminiscent of Islamic metalwork. As such, it is possible that the calendar was later owned by a Christian who pasted this second group of illustrations onto the pages.
ef6f3f6c-f567-5300-9a2c-887d4b9a516c.method_for_provenance: On fol. 8a, an owner's stamp by Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall dated to 1223 AH / 1808 AD is visible.
ef6f3f6c-f567-5300-9a2c-887d4b9a516c.obtention: Acquired  in 1842 from Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall.

f02545d3-2c1e-56ed-999c-fd59a3ff72c3.name: *Shahnama*
f02545d3-2c1e-56ed-999c-fd59a3ff72c3.short_description: This is a fragmentary copy of the *Shahnama* (‘Book of Kings’), the verse epic that tells the story of the pre-Islamic kings and heroes of Iran. The manuscript was probably produced for the Iranian ruler Shah Abbas the Great, sometime after his accession in 1587, and contains sixteen paintings, two of which were added later, in about 1676. The paintings are amongst the finest examples of Persian painting ever produced, each one finely rendered and filled with abundant detail.
