f02afe0c-f6ec-51aa-8c81-d0230b93ff9f.name: Animal-head ewer
f02afe0c-f6ec-51aa-8c81-d0230b93ff9f.description:
The Kashan turquoise ceramic animal-head ewer is a stunning example of Persian ceramics from the 12th century. This vessel showcases a vibrant turquoise blue glaze with a top in the likeness of a horned animal head, complete with a spout resembling a long open beak. It stands on a short foot, with a globular body transitioning into a slender neck. A partly curved handle, like a rope, extends from the head to the body. At the top, two curved horns and an upward-pointing finial enhance its overall elegance.  
The exquisite craftsmanship of this ewer highlights the skill and creativity of Persian artisans. This ewer originated in Kashan, renowned for its pottery tradition. The turquoise glaze adds to its allure and symbolises prosperity and protection. The animal motif holds various symbolic meanings, representing virtues and beliefs deeply ingrained in Persian customs and rituals. Used in ceremonial contexts, such as feasts or religious rituals, the ewer reflects ancient Persian traditions and cultural practices.  
Highly prized by collectors and enthusiasts alike, this Persian Kashan turquoise ceramic animal-head ewer serves as a timeless reminder of the beauty and sophistication of Persian craftsmanship. Its rich cultural heritage and artistic significance make it a cherished artefact, showcasing the legacy of Persian artisans.  
The ewer is crafted using traditional ceramic techniques prevalent in Kashan during the 12th century. Skilled artisans shaped the vessel by hand. The firing process ensured the durability of the vessel while bringing out the brilliance of the turquoise glaze, resulting in a masterpiece of Persian ceramics.

f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.name: Plate.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.description:
Chinese earthenware ceramics with a dichromatic decorative scheme of white and blue were very popular and widely admired in the Islamic world. Their export to the eastern Mediterranean began as early as the AH 2nd / AD 8th century. This type of vessel with its bright whiteness and extensive blue decoration was the most popular export ware during the Chinese reigns of the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties. They exported profusely, both by land and sea, especially during the AH 8th / AD 14th century.  
Artisans in the Islamic world imitated these Chinese ceramics because of its popularity and because they were not always readily available. Thus imitative Chinese ceramics were themselves a valuable commodity.  
This plate is decorated with a bouquet of flowers that incorporates gracefully sweeping stems bound with a ribbon. A decorative band of stylised vegetal motifs surround the bouquet, and a band of stylised geometric motifs articulates the rim of the plate. The decoration is executed in various shades of blue on a white base.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.short_description: This ceramic dish was found in the Citadel of Hama and it clearly indicates the intercultural influence of exported Chinese blue-and-white porcelain on Syrian and Egyptian Mamluk pottery.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.method_for_datation: The Danish excavations revealed objects that have been dated to the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods, primarily from the 7th–8th / 13th–14th centuries. However, since this piece is influenced by Chinese ceramics, especially in the use of blue and white, and since such ceramics were exported to the Islamic world beginning in the 8th / 14th century, it is believed that the object belongs to this later period.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.method_for_provenance: This object was found in Hama, known as a production centre for this kind of ware. However, the underglaze painted wares found in Syria (Hama and Damascus) and Egypt (Fustat and Alexandria) are essentially identical, so it is difficult to assign a definitive provenance.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.obtention: The plate was found during archaeological excavations that took place in the Citadel of Hama between 1931 and 1938 by a Danish expedition under the direction of Harold Ing Holt. The piece was registered in the Museum in 1934.

f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.name: Members of Court of Sultan Selim II Mounted as an Album Leaf
f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.short_description: From the late sixteenth century until the formation of the Republic of Turkey in 1922, the Ottoman sultans maintained a strong tradition of imperial portraiture. Influenced by European oil painting and Persian miniatures, Ottoman portraits provide important information about court ceremonies, changing fashions, and members of the court. The right side of a double-page composition, this painting was created as a pendant to a portrait of Selim II (r. Hegira 974-982/1566-1574) on the left, now in the collection of the Aga Khan Museum, Toronto. The musicians, servants, and courtiers, who are identified by their inscriptions, face left, toward the sultan, in a show of deference to their ruler. Taken together the pair of paintings depict a *majlis* scene reflecting the pleasure-oriented atmosphere of Selim’s court. It is possible that the figure of the court jester at far right is a self-portrait of the artist.
f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.method_for_datation: Less formal than official Ottoman royal depictions, this painting (and its pendant) was likely made prior to Selim’s ascension to the throne in 1566 and was probably produced during his time as a prince governing Kütahya. Several of the figures depicted with captions can be further identified as boon companions of Selim II, one of whom, Turak Çelabi, died in 1561-62, suggesting a terminus ante quem for the work.
f03b716a-a1e0-58f0-b452-2c2a089e34f2.method_for_provenance: It is signed “Nigari, slave of Sultan Selim Khan.” Nigari was the pseudonym used by the famed Turkish navigator Haydar Reis, who was also well-known as a portrait painting under Sultan Suleyman and his son and successor Selim II.

f13296ae-615e-5b30-99df-9e194b691b4f.name: Coffee Mortar and Pestle
f13296ae-615e-5b30-99df-9e194b691b4f.description: A carved wooden mortar and stone pestle for pounding coffee beans. Coffee drinkers consider coffee ground by hand to be the most desirable kind.

f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.name: Large dish.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.description: A large dish with a surface edge that bends outward to a rim embellished by a consecutive series of triangles that resemble the jagged teeth of a saw. The interior of the dish is painted with a portrayal of a seated woman playing a stringed instrument that looks like a guitar. She wears a long garment with a V-shaped collar and wide sleeves, which is decorated with thick stripes and cross shapes. She wears a choker-type necklace, the V-shape of which sits inside the neck of her garment. The designs on her garment, in which the folds around the legs are embellished with decorations, are distinctive to Fatimid apparel. The musician's face is portrayed in profile. A toque, which resembles a turban, crowns her head and two locks of her hair appear from under the headdress on either side of her face along with a small tuft of hair behind her neck. The background around the figure is embellished with irregular surfaces demarcated by thin strokes filled with circles, dots and painted branches from which cone-shaped leaves grow. On the left-hand side of the woman is a delicately designed ewer surrounded by stylised vegetal-leaf designs; from the mouth of the ewer two flowering branches emerge. Below the rim of the dish underneath the painted serrated edge are a series of thick lines.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.short_description: Economic prosperity in the Fatimid period led to the flourishing of the lustre-ware ceramic industry. Such lustre-ware vessels, where the metallic lustre resembles gold, incorporate a variety of decorations including splendid scenes of Fatimid daily and social life.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.method_for_datation: The dish was dated based on the study of its painted female musician, and specifically the design and decoration of the clothing she wears. The figure reflects the distinguishing traits that mark the portrayal of people in Fatimid art, including circular moon-shaped faces and almond-shaped eyes. The turban seen on the heads of men, and the toques on the heads of women, are also indicative of the period. In addition, the decorations that are present on the dish are borrowed from the vegetal and non-vegetal decorative motifs seen most commonly on wood, ivory and metal objects of the Fatimid period. This date is further supported by a comparison between this dish and other similar examples that bear the signatures of potters who are associated with the period.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.method_for_provenance: The place of manufacture was narrowed down to Egypt in view of the fact that ceramic production and metallic lustre-ware products were renowned in Fatimid Egypt. This industry grew and flourished in Fustat where archaeological excavations have uncovered a large number of ceramic pieces similar to this dish.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.obtention: The dish was bought in 1944 from a dealer of antiquities, Fuqyan Jaan.

f2c92da1-bd97-52aa-b11f-4ac0d34fc18e.name: Khan al-Khalili.
f2c92da1-bd97-52aa-b11f-4ac0d34fc18e.description:
Khan al-Khalili is a world-renowned market and tourist landmark to which most visitors flock in order to buy products and gifts of the East. It also contains the largest gold and silver market in Egypt. In AH 786 / AD 1384, during the reign of al-Malik al-Zahir Barquq who ruled twice (AH 784–91 / AD 1382–9 and 792–801 / AD 1389–98), Amir Jaharqas al-Khalili set up an inn (*khan*) on the site of the Za'afran tomb. In AH 917 / AD 1511 Sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri destroyed Khan al-Khalili and constructed *rubu'* (small hotels) in its place, as well as warehouses and shops, which are known today by the name of Wikalat al-Kotn (Cotton Caravanserai). There were three principal entrances to the *khan* but little remains of these today except for one gate: Bab al-Ghuri, also known as Bab al-Badistan (*Badistan* being Turkish for cotton or linen), which is located at the west end of the road leading from al-Husayni Shrine to the interior of Khan al-Khalili.  
Bab Al-Badistan resembles the portals leading into Mamluk mosques and *madrasa*s, especially those that were erected during the period of Sultan al-Ghuri, a good example of which is the entrance to the Mosque of al-Ghuri (built AH 909 / AD 1504). This entrance consists of an arch that contains beautiful geometric decoration carved into the stone. The spandrel of the arch is decorated with geometric designs of white and black marble, in the middle of which is the blazon of the sponsor. The entrance of the portal is surmounted by an epigraphic inscription that includes the name of the sponsor and his titles. A tri-lobed arch decorated with *muqarnas*, which contains beautiful vegetal motifs, crowns the portal. There are three *mashrabiyya* screens in the windows, mid-way between the arched opening of the gate and the tri-lobed arch.  
The *khan* region was neglected during the Ottoman period, but began to flourish again in the period of Muhammad Ali Pasha (r. 1220–64 / AD 1805–48).  
It is known that many late 19th- and early 20th-century personalities of the Egyptian Revival (*nahda*) were amongst those who frequented the coffee houses in the region of Khan al-Khalili, when they were still students. The prominent Egyptian political leader, Sa'ad Zaghloul (1860–1927), expressed how areas such as that around Khan al-Khalili endeared themselves to him during his student days at al-Azhar. Many other prominent personalities of literature, arts and music also frequented the coffee houses in the region of Khan al-Khalili to discuss and exchange ideas and works in an atmosphere that emanated the essence of Egyptian, indeed world, history.
f2c92da1-bd97-52aa-b11f-4ac0d34fc18e.short_description: A world-famous name in the heart of Fatimid Cairo, this is one of the oldest markets in Egypt. It is a tourist attraction and a meeting place to buy souvenirs and antiques. This historical area, with its narrow streets, alleys and old buildings, allows the visitor to enjoy the feel and smell the aroma of history, while watching craftsmen at work on their traditional products.
f2c92da1-bd97-52aa-b11f-4ac0d34fc18e.method_for_datation: The monument was dated with the help of historical sources such as *Bada'i al-Zuhur* by Ibn Iyas; the presence of both the name and titles of the sponsor is seen on the blazon at the entrance.

f31ff28f-d559-5abc-880d-148f4aa71f67.name: Table (*khwan*) with scenes of princely leisure and inscribed with Persian poetry
f31ff28f-d559-5abc-880d-148f4aa71f67.short_description: This low, rectangular wood table on four legs is extensively ornamented with lacquerwork on the table top. Around the interior rim are painted and gilded floral arabesques surrounding inscriptions in cartouches. On the surface of this table, young men and women repose, feast, and hunt in abundant landscapes, and their style of depiction echoes manuscript illustrations of canonical Persian poetry.

f4b200cf-1a1b-5c49-9a62-cb9310e74f00.name: Coffee-house
f4b200cf-1a1b-5c49-9a62-cb9310e74f00.short_description: Traditionally, social life in the Islamic world revolved around the tea-house or coffee-house, where men would gather to drink tea and coffee, eat sweet pastries or savoury food, and to smoke flavoured tobacco in water pipes (*narghile* or *qalian*). There they would play board games, listen to music and poetry recitations or discuss current events. This scene of a Turkish coffee-house would originally have been part of an album of images.
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; border decoration
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

f54ccda0-cd2f-59b9-b97e-ba28a8e6ef05.name: Pedestal bowl or tazza
f54ccda0-cd2f-59b9-b97e-ba28a8e6ef05.description: A deep bowl, decorated in blue and white, with a sloping rim and supported on a pedestal base. The rim has been embellished with a pattern of rocks and waves, whilst the cavetto is decorated with floral sprays with a medallion surrounded by palmettes at the very centre. The base is also decorated with floral sprays.

f5534c7f-4ba5-5e47-aca4-efc34893cbc5.name: Textile.
f5534c7f-4ba5-5e47-aca4-efc34893cbc5.description: The fabric is decorated in the centre with a large motif of a vase of flowers inside a pointed frame that rests on two small columns, at the base of which there are two cypress trees. The lower part of the fabric depicts a gated entrance crowned with a crescent moon beneath an epigraphic motif in Arabic characters. On either side there are large cypress trees beside star motifs. The entire piece is framed with plant volutes with lance-shaped leaves and four- and five-petal flowers. The decoration consists of gold- and silver-plated wire embroidery.
f5534c7f-4ba5-5e47-aca4-efc34893cbc5.short_description: This fabric is of Turkish origin produced in the late Ottoman era and is characterised by naturalistic floral motifs, in which the influence of Western decorative trends can be clearly seen.
f5534c7f-4ba5-5e47-aca4-efc34893cbc5.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
f5534c7f-4ba5-5e47-aca4-efc34893cbc5.method_for_provenance: This fabric was produced in late-Ottoman Turkey in the 13th / late 19th century and is characterised by the use of naturalistic floral motifs that clearly show a strong influence of more Western decorative elements.

f68354eb-cd48-5520-b352-24d135f08193.name: Covered Box with Design of Figural, Vegetal, and Geometric Motifs
f68354eb-cd48-5520-b352-24d135f08193.short_description:
A twelve-sided brass box with silver and gold inlay has a cover with a central hemispherical dome on the top. The cover is relief decorated with interlocking geometric and vegetal patterning, separated by plain bands of meander. The main register of the dome has circles containing kneeling figures. The dome is surrounded by a stepped, scalloped area, surrounded again by a broader scalloped step, points of the scallops corresponding in location. This broader step has the same incised decoration. The cover tapers in slightly around a plain bottom lip and joins to the box at a thin band of stylized guilloche.  
The box has the same type of background relief decoration, registers separated by bands of meander. The roundels contain seated, cross-legged figures. The box rests on a convex bottom.  
There is some wear and abrasion over the entire surface of the box. The very top of the dome has a notable hole; some of the metal has been folded back over the top \[this was the point of attachment for a handle and a ring that appears in older photographs of the object, but has since been removed\]. Also, one area on the side of the cover seems to have a small metal "plug" type of repair.

f71b30b4-5cfa-55d7-a2fa-6790d5d186d8.name: Tray (*sinija*)
f71b30b4-5cfa-55d7-a2fa-6790d5d186d8.description:
The term *sinija* comes from the Turkish word *sini*, which describes a large round brass or copper tray that functioned as a low table on which food was served. These plates were typically decorated with ornaments arranged inside concentric belts, around the central roundel.  
In this case, inside the central roundel is the stylized, leaf-like motif. In the widest, central belt, the same motif is alternately composed of cypresses and ibrik motifs. The rim is flattened, and decorated with geometric patterns.
f71b30b4-5cfa-55d7-a2fa-6790d5d186d8.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material

f795fd67-bd2c-50a0-87cd-f4f308542324.name: Earth and celestial globe, the so-called 'St. Gallen Globe'
f795fd67-bd2c-50a0-87cd-f4f308542324.description: For many years, the so-called St. Gallen Globe, one of the prized objects of Swiss cultural history, was a source of contention. The globe featuring Mercator maps of the earth and the celestial sphere was created by Tilemann Stella in northern Germany towards the end of the sixteenth century, as a document discovered in 2016 reveals. Although they were not suitable for navigation, globes were extremely popular in the early modern period. What makes the St. Gallen Globe so special is its combination of world and celestial globes. Entitled as a gift, which, however, was later satisfied, the globe was incorporated in the library of the Abbey of St Gallen where it was kept until 1712. During the Second War of Villmergen the globe was robbed and carted off to Zürich where it was displayed in the Wasserkirche (Water Church). St Gallen demanded the return of the globe, but to no avail. When the Swiss National Museum was established in 1898, the globe passed into the hands of the Swiss Confederation; it has been on display in the museum ever since. The dispute over the treasure, which went down in Swiss history as the cultural heritage conflict between Zürich and St Gallen, was only resolved in 2006 when the St Gallen Abbey library received a true copy of the contested globe.
f795fd67-bd2c-50a0-87cd-f4f308542324.method_for_datation: In 2016 a document was found which revealed the globe’s origin.
f795fd67-bd2c-50a0-87cd-f4f308542324.obtention: The globe was donated 1595 to the Stiftsbibliothek St. Gallen and robbed 1712 by Zürich troops during the second Villmerger-wars. Since then it is in the property of the Stadtbibliothek Zürich, now called Zentralbibliothek. When the Landesmuseum opened its doors in 1898 it was given into possession of the Landesmuseum as part of the “Morgengabe”.
keywords: scientific Instruments; terrestrial and cellestial globe; St. Gallen Globus

f7b54067-2ca1-5b6d-bcf0-c61b4f118231.name: Bayezid II Complex (*külliye*).
f7b54067-2ca1-5b6d-bcf0-c61b4f118231.description:
The Bayezid II Complex is of the *külliye* type comprising a large collection of buildings of which the mosque is central. Located on the north shore of the Tunca River, it occupies an area of some 22,000 sq m and is surrounded by walls. It consists of a mosque, two guest-houses (*tabhane*s) adjoining the mosque, a *madrasa*, a hospital (*darüşşifa*), a soup-kitchen (*imaret*), food-storage areas, and (outside the courtyard walls) a double bathhouse (*hammam*) and a bridge. The double bathhouse at the west of the complex no longer survives. The bridge over the Tunca River, built to connect the *külliye* to the city, has large spans of pointed arches.  
The *madrasa* and *darüşşifa* are on the western side of the central courtyard, which is accessed through a gate in the north wall of the outer courtyard. The *imaret* is on the eastern side, while the mosque is on the south side. On the east side of the courtyard gate is the fountain of Sinan Ağa.  
The single-domed, cubic mosque is adjoined by *tabhane*s on its east and west sides. Each of these guest-houses has a four-*iwan* plan and contains nine bays. The rectangular courtyard, north of the prayer hall, is accessed through three gates in its north, east and west walls. The courtyard is surrounded on all four sides by domed porticoes and has a marble fountain in the centre. The seven-bay portico for latecomers extends along the façade of the mosque and its central dome, decorated with *muqarnas*, is higher than the others. The building's two minarets rise from the outer corners of the *tabhane*s. Each has one balcony, both are almost 38 m high, and have grooved bodies, 3.25 m in diameter. The dome covering the square prayer hall is approximately 20.55 m in diameter and rises on pendentives.  
The *mihrab*, *minbar* and sultan's loge are all made of marble. The geometric decoration on the *minbar* and the gallery are noteworthy. The wooden door wings, cupboards and window shutters are richly decorated. In addition to geometric and floral decoration, the ornament includes various inscriptions.  
The single-storied *madrasa* occupies a rectangular area and has an open courtyard with porticoes on all four sides; the fountain in the centre of the courtyard is in a ruined state. The entrance is in the middle of the east side. The north, south and west wings contain a total of 18 students' cells behind the porticoes. Both the portico bays and the students' cells are domed. The classroom is a square space of approximately 7.36 m x 7.37 m located in the centre of the west side. It is covered with a large dome, and the mezzanine built onto its east wall, which looks like a balcony, is the library.  
The *darüşşifa* to the west of the mosque is made up of a main building and two courtyards. The main building is hexagonal and consists of a central domed space with six *iwan*s opening onto it, and rooms between the *iwan*s. Both the *iwan*s and the rooms are each covered with a single dome. The south *iwan* is deeper than the others and extends to the outside.  
The *imaret* to the east of the mosque comprises a kitchen, oven, dining hall, pantry, storage space, and stables. It was built in two clusters of structures.  
Today the *darüşşifa* and the *madrasa* have been appropriated by Trakya University and are open to visitors as a Museum of Health and a Fine Arts Museum.
f7b54067-2ca1-5b6d-bcf0-c61b4f118231.short_description: One of the monumental Ottoman complexes, it was built on the bank of the River Tunca. Covering an area of 22,000 square m the complex comprises a mosque with two *tabhane*s (guesthouse) adjoining it, a *madrasa*, a hospital, an *imaret* (soup-kitchen), storerooms within the walls, a double-bathhouse outside which has not survived, and a bridge over the river. Its foundations were laid with a ceremony attended by the sultan himself. It is known that musical therapy was applied at its hospital and its *madrasa* is said to have served for medical training.
f7b54067-2ca1-5b6d-bcf0-c61b4f118231.method_for_datation: Historical documents tell us that Sultan Bayezid II himself participated in the ceremonies to mark the foundation of this complex in Rabi' al-Akhir 889 / May 1484. The mosque, according to the inscription by Sheikh Hamdullah over the main portal, was completed in AH 893 / AD 1488. It is thought that the other buildings of the complex were also finished on the same date. The fountain lying east of the gate to the outer courtyard was ordered built in AH 1080 / AD 1670 by Sinan Ağa.

f982124c-5947-5618-a36f-528cc79bcd18.name: Sugar Bowl
f982124c-5947-5618-a36f-528cc79bcd18.description: Made of white porcelain. There are two handles on the side starting from the rim and going down to the bottom. The surface is decorated with floral and leaf motifs painted in yellow gilt. The handles are also painted in yellow gilt. The cover is decorated with embossed flowers, roses and leaves painted in yellow, blue, green, pink and red.

fa4916ad-b0f5-5f83-898a-6d97cf9229fd.name: Vase with zoomorphic design
fa4916ad-b0f5-5f83-898a-6d97cf9229fd.description: This vase with zoomorphic decoration perpetuates the shape of ritual libation vases of Zoroastrianism, a religion originating in Iran in the first millennium BC. The pouring spout is topped by a bull’s head whose snout is hollow. Its decoration, in relief, is divided into separate concentric registers whose motifs are geometric and floral.

fb0a9d2b-8b7a-5bd9-808e-71eac145b020.name: Wedding banquet with German guests
fb0a9d2b-8b7a-5bd9-808e-71eac145b020.description:
During big events like weddings or funerals, several plates (*siniyyat sufra*) must be placed in a long row, where about six people on each side can eat from one big plate. Following old traditions, mutton meat is placed on a mountain of rice or on many layers of wafer-thin flatbread. A very rich, well-seasoned meat broth is poured over all.  
When the guest has finished eating, he/she will say *dayman*, meaning “May you always have the means to eat like this!” and stand up to give another person the opportunity to take his/her place to eat. A member of the family will bring water, soap and a towel to wash the guest’s hands after eating.  
The big feast takes place on the last day of the wedding celebrations, usually after three days of dancing to the sounds of musicians in the courtyard of the groom’s family or in a village plaza.  
Feasts often are set up according to gender, depending on whether guests are family members, more distant relatives or acquaintances. Women who belong to a mixed-gender group are asked whether they prefer to eat with the men or with the women of the house. In the photo, a German tour group was invited to a wedding party in a village.

ffe08b8f-98ad-5e02-a0ff-ceaa5ae4d13f.name: Collection of Persian poetry
ffe08b8f-98ad-5e02-a0ff-ceaa5ae4d13f.short_description: The collection of Persian poetry is a work of Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sayyid. The manuscript in *nasta\`liq* script contains two miniatures attributed to Aqa-malik and representing a princess in a garden.
keywords: Manuscript; nasta`liq; Safawid

ffff8d3d-ab9b-5733-9ca0-900b6b34002e.name: *Ghotar* concave dish
ffff8d3d-ab9b-5733-9ca0-900b6b34002e.description:
The radiant design is organised around the seal of Solomon, or eight-pointed star, that adorns the centre of the dish. The contour of the star is painted blue, and a flower with eight green petals is inside it. The star is on a white background with small yellow patterns outlined in black. Oval patterns extend from the points of the star. Decorated concentric bands complete the ornamentation of the piece.  
The decoration and form are characteristic of Moroccan ceramics between the 17th and 19th centuries. They are widespread in Morocco and Spain, and even in France. An Andalusian influence can be seen in certain features, such as the use of geometry. The piece reflects the polychrome earthenware made in Fes, but also in Safi, a production centre. In the 19th century, colours were more assertive, shapes heavier, and decorations less spontaneous than before. This piece is of high technical and aesthetic quality.
ffff8d3d-ab9b-5733-9ca0-900b6b34002e.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute
